title: Guantánamo Bay 2.0? The rise of legal violence inside US detention centers
description:
Many held in Guantánamo Bay have claimed that members of the United States military physically and mentally assaulted them during their detention.
Detainees’ testimonies of violent punishments by ICE agents are all too reminiscent of the experiences of Guantánamo Bay prisoners.
Guantánamo Bay was established in 2002 to detain individuals believed to be linked with the perpetrators of the September 11 attacks.
Ending legal violence Like many who were imprisoned in Guantánamo Bay, most of the migrants in detention today have not been convicted of any crime.
If these steps are not taken, the use of legal violence and the policies of impunity that underpin them will only grow.
text:
The United States government has a long history of dehumanizing foreigners both inside and outside its borders. The treatment of prisoners in Guantánamo Bay and of migrants currently detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) provide just two recent examples of the extensive use of criminalizing language to justify targeting these groups. The George W. Bush administration routinely labeled those incarcerated in Guantánamo Bay as “terrorists” and associated them with the September 11 attacks, often without direct evidence. Today, the Donald J. Trump administration labels migrants as “animals,” “criminals,” and “rapists.” This type of dehumanizing language suggests that detainees do not deserve legal rights, and it leads to the broad erosion of the civil protections that shield people—whether or not they are US citizens—from arrest without charge and trial or harsh and unusual punishment.

The state’s curtailment of due process and other civil rights in these cases has led to a rise in legal violence: harm inflicted by a government body while enforcing state policy. Many held in Guantánamo Bay have claimed that members of the United States military physically and mentally assaulted them during their detention. Similar abuse is still taking place today against migrants in ICE detention centers. Detainees’ testimonies of violent punishments by ICE agents are all too reminiscent of the experiences of Guantánamo Bay prisoners.

The US government and military have not taken the lessons of the War on Terror to heart, and the United States is still using violence against people it detains. There has been very little pressure from legislators or the courts to dissuade the government from using legal violence—a direct failure of the very systems that allowed this kind of violence to become legal in the first place.

Mass incarceration and violence toward migrants

Since Trump took office as president of the United States for the second time, his administration has pushed ICE to detain anyone deemed to be residing in the country illegally. This has led to the mass incarceration of Latinos and other migrants all over the nation. According to The Guardian, a total of 68,400 individuals were held in detention as of December 2025. The majority of detainees have no previous criminal record. A recent Human Rights Watch report documented dozens of executive orders rolling back migrants’ right to due process, guaranteed by the Fifth Amendment, and limiting their ability to seek legal redress while detained.

These new executive orders have systematically allowed the state to punish those detained prior to legal due process or the filing of charges. The result is legal violence inflicted against migrants detained in defiance of their constitutional rights. For example, officers are now legally allowed to interrogate suspected illegal migrants using violence and make arrests without warrants.

The Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS) has done very little to limit the powers granted to ICE. In fact, some recent SCOTUS rulings have expanded ICE’s powers. In September 2025, SCOTUS eliminated restrictions on ICE’s use of racial profiling when making arrests. In the case of Noem v. Vasquez-Perdomo SCOTUS ruled that ICE could conduct raids in public places opening the door to using race, ethnicity, and language to determine their targets. This is unambiguously racial profiling and encourages violence toward especially Latinos regardless of their immigration status.

Several reports documenting migrant accounts of violence committed by detention officers and ICE have been released since Trump’s executive orders and SCOTUS’s legal decisions on immigration enforcement. One of many migrants who spoke with the ACLU reported that detention officers had beaten him, breaking his tooth and damaging his ear to the point that he began to lose hearing. This violence was carried out in one of the largest detention centers in the country, located at the Fort Bliss military base in Texas.

One man in a Florida detention center, speaking to Human Rights Watch, recalled officers turning up the air conditioning to intentionally freezing levels in the cells. Several people in the same location are also being denied life-saving medications needed to treat chronic illnesses.

Are detention centers the new Guantánamo Bay?

Guantánamo Bay was established in 2002 to detain individuals believed to be linked with the perpetrators of the September 11 attacks. The Center for Constitutional Rights has outlined the violent experiences of prisoners detained at Guantánamo Bay, which included practices like those used today in ICE detention centers.

The Bush administration authorized the use of violent practices in Guantánamo Bay by declaring that those imprisoned there were “unlawful enemy combatants” and thus ineligible for the protections of the Geneva Conventions. By eliminating application of the Geneva Conventions, the Bush administration removed a major barrier imposed by international law to prevent the torture of prisoners. More recently, the Trump administration has similarly rejected the Geneva Conventions by cutting funding for the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) and condemning their operations.

The Center for Constitutional Rights has shared the experience of Abu Zubaydah, who was subjected to waterboarding, sleep deprivation, stress positions, and confinement inside a coffin-sized box. Ahmed al-Darbi similarly reported that officers played painfully loud music for several hours and chilled his cell to extremely cold temperatures until he confessed to the crime he was accused of. The government framed these practices as interrogation, but it’s clear that they constitute torture.

Many of the prisoners in Guantánamo Bay were never formally charged with any crime. Instead, they were imprisoned indefinitely and subjected to intense and violent interrogation tactics in hopes of eliciting confessions. These abusive practices were justified by a Military Order that allowed prisoners suspected of terrorism to be held outside US jurisdiction. This was an intentional move to limit the court’s reach and provide for increased use of force against those held in Guantánamo Bay and impunity for the officers who carried it out.

Ending legal violence

Like many who were imprisoned in Guantánamo Bay, most of the migrants in detention today have not been convicted of any crime. Legal violence does not change; only its target does.

To prevent the continuation of legal violence, we must challenge the system. The executive and military orders that allowed violence and mistreatment of prisoners in Guantánamo Bay laid the foundation for the laws currently supporting ICE’s violent and indiscriminate campaign of immigration enforcement. The United States Constitution already prohibits abuse inside penitentiaries and detention centers. Cruel and unusual punishments are strictly prohibited.

The courts must consistently apply the protections provided by the United States Constitution, and they must disempower ICE. This includes protecting due process rights for migrants, firing officers who act with racial bias, eliminating officers’ rights to interrogate detainees using violence, and investigating each facility where abuse has been reported. If these steps are not taken, the use of legal violence and the policies of impunity that underpin them will only grow.

name: Human Rights
title: Trump 'Disappeared' Them in 2025. I Found Them, Locked Up and Famished
description:
I found five of them this month, held prisoner in a house in Juba, South Sudan.
The deportees told me that they had not been beaten and that they appreciated that South Sudan has limited resources.
The United States, having sent the men here, should pay for the deportees’ costs, he suggested.
Three of the men say they have children in the United States who are American citizens.
The men spend their days working out and listening to a radio, their only connection to the outside world.
text:
Since taking office last year, the Trump administration has deported more than 500 immigrants to African countries with which they have no connection, often by bribing or coercing weak governments to take them.

Then the detainees mostly disappear.

I found five of them this month, held prisoner in a house in Juba, South Sudan. They were nearly starving, can’t regularly communicate with their families or anyone else and don’t have any path to get to their home countries or, in the case of some of them, to ever see their American citizen children again.

“I don’t know if I can tell you without being killed, but it’s horrible here”, said Enrique Arias Hierro, 48, a Cuban with a criminal record who until his deportation had lived in the United States since the age of 2. My interview with him was monitored by South Sudanese guards and a diplomat, but Arias Hierro pressed ahead with his complaints, saying, “I’ll take the consequences”.

“Sometimes there’s no food for two or three days”, he added. “Sometimes there’s no water for a month. Once for two and a half months, we had no drinking water”, and survived with nonpotable water.

The Supreme Court last year allowed deportations to South Sudan, over the dissents of liberal justices. However, the court has scheduled fast-track hearings for December on whether such deportations to third countries violate the Constitution and international protections against torture.

I hope the justices will take note of what has happened to those sent to South Sudan.

The five I met include two from Cuba, two from Myanmar and one who appears to suffer from mental health problems and could not tell me where he was from or anything about himself.

These deportees are held together in what the South Sudanese government calls a “safe house” behind a high wall and a locked gate, with multiple guards constantly present. The home itself is spacious, not at all like a prison, but they are not allowed to leave, have phones or contact anyone, and the deportees complained that electricity and toilets often don’t work. The biggest problem, they said, is a lack of food and water, leading one man to lose 30 pounds and another 50 pounds.

One of the men, José Manuel Rodríguez-Quiñones, from Cuba, said that he had once asked for clean water and as punishment was locked in his room.

“I was locked down for three days”, he said. “I didn’t eat for three days”. The others confirmed that.

Most of the time, each man is given three liters of water — less than a gallon — every two days, for drinking, bathing and toilet flushing, they said. (The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine recommend that men drink three liters each day.)

One reason these deportees would be hard to send elsewhere is that at least four of the five have criminal records, including for attempted murder and armed robbery. (They completed their sentences in the United States before being deported, South Sudan says.) The Trump administration referred to them as “sickos” and “barbaric, violent criminal illegal aliens”.

Asked for a comment, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security told me that the deportees “were so heinous even their own countries would not take them back”, and added, “We will not allow barbaric criminal illegal aliens to terrorize American citizens”.

There’s nothing wrong with deporting undocumented immigrants who commit crimes. That happens all the time, under Democrats as well as Republicans, and it is a problem when they can’t be deported to their home countries. But foisting them on impoverished African countries where they are not treated humanely seems to me a moral and practical failure.

For its part, the South Sudanese government told me in a statement that the deportees are “provided with food, clean water, sanitation, clothing and other essential provisions”.

“The government of South Sudan covers the cost of their accommodation, provisions, administration and medical care from its own national resources”, the statement said. “The United States government made no financial provision toward these expenses”.

The deportees told me that they had not been beaten and that they appreciated that South Sudan has limited resources. They acknowledged that one of them had received dental care while others had received medical treatment for malaria. But they desperately wanted more food and water and some path out.

Why were deportees originally from Cuba and Myanmar sent to South Sudan, a poverty-stricken, unstable country that has periodically teetered on the edge of civil war? The State Department website warns, “Do not travel to South Sudan for any reason”.

Remote, troubled countries appear to have been the attraction. “The point is to scare people”, an unnamed U.S. official said of third-country deportations, according to a report by Democrats on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

The idea appears to be to deter new immigration and to encourage undocumented residents to go home rather than risk being “disappeared” into a place like South Sudan. When the Homeland Security Department celebrated a Supreme Court ruling in September resuming third-country deportations, it included a link to instructions to self-deport.

Some immigrants have been sent to stable African countries, like Ghana, but others to the Central African Republic or the Democratic Republic of Congo, which, like South Sudan, are in tumult. These deportations are expensive, with the transfer of eight immigrants to South Sudan, via Djibouti, costing more than $700,000, according to Democrats on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

While the Trump administration canceled AIDS programs that had been saving the lives of children with medicines costing less than 12 cents a day, it effectively paid African countries $32 million to accept people it wanted to deport, by the calculation of Democrats on that same committee.

South Sudan initially resisted taking certain deportees from the United States, but Secretary of State Marco Rubio responded by issuing a blanket ban on visas for all South Sudanese. So South Sudan, extremely fragile and vulnerable to American pressure, promptly caved.

Some countries received large payouts from the United States for taking third-country deportees — in at least one case, more than $1 million per deportee — but South Sudan hasn’t clearly received any benefit at all, except that America is once more granting visas to its citizens.

It’s understandable that South Sudan isn’t eager to spend money on deportees when it can’t afford food and water for its own people. A child under the age of 5 dies about every 15 minutes on average in South Sudan, overwhelmingly from preventable causes.

One South Sudanese diplomat present during my meeting with the deportees, embarrassed by the complaints about the lack of food and water, noted that much of the country lacks both. The United States, having sent the men here, should pay for the deportees’ costs, he suggested.

It’s not entirely clear why South Sudan doesn’t release the deportees or let them communicate regularly with their families and lawyers. (It says it does, but the lawyers dispute that.) My guess is that after the scare about all visas being canceled, it is afraid of doing anything that might offend President Trump.

So these deportees languish.

For my visit, I was picked up by a government car with its license plate covered (prompting brief alarm among U.N. officials that I had been kidnapped). I was not allowed to bring a camera or other recording device and was physically searched on arrival to ensure that I had nothing but my notebook and a pen.

South Sudan issued the deportees new clothes ahead of my visit, and gave them a good meal and ample water, they said. Electric lights were fixed, and incense was lit to dampen odors. The deportees said they appreciated all that, but what they most want is some indication that their imprisonment will eventually end.

“Trying to wait is hard”, said Kyaw Mya, one of the deportees from Myanmar. “I want to get out of here. I want to be free”.

South Sudan was able to send three other deportees to their home countries — Mexico, Laos and Vietnam. But Cuba has refused to accept Arias Hierro, who said he has lived in the United States since 1980, or Rodríguez-Quiñones, who said he moved to America in 1995. Both said they would go back to Cuba if it would accept them.

The two deportees from Myanmar, who said they had been in the United States for 10 years and 20 years, belong to the Karen minority that the Myanmar government is fighting in a civil war. They seem as uninterested in going to Myanmar as its government is in accepting them. They said they would like to be sent to refugee camps in Thailand — but for now they have no prospect of getting there.

Three of the men say they have children in the United States who are American citizens. The men spend their days working out and listening to a radio, their only connection to the outside world.

Human Rights Watch, in an excellent report on third-country deportations, describes the practice as “a U.S. policy that violates international human rights law and is designed to instrumentalize human suffering as a deterrent to migration”.

When I was about to leave, I asked if the deportees had any last messages they wanted to convey.

“Have the U.S. pay for food and water and basic things humans should have”, Arias Hierro said.

Kyaw Mya said: “I don’t have hope. I need hope”.

And Rodríguez-Quiñones asked me to tell his family: “I love you. I don’t know when I’ll get out of here. But I love you”.

title: Immigration officers make arrests at Seattle airport in 'distressing' scene, delaying flight
description:
SEATTLE -- Masked immigration officers detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, causing what the airline called a "distressing" scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight.
Online flight data showed that Alaska flight 1306, which had been scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m., was delayed.
Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.
"We are concerned by this morning's law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306," the airline said.
"We need a system of immigration enforcement and border security that is effective, ethical and humane.
text:
SEATTLE -- Masked immigration officers detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, causing what the airline called a "distressing" scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight.

Video of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as a woman screams that her daughter is being taken and she has a work permit.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who "overstayed his visa in violation of our nation's laws."

During the confrontation, another passenger "hurled hot coffee on the officers," the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

Online flight data showed that Alaska flight 1306, which had been scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m., was delayed.

Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

"We are concerned by this morning's law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306," the airline said. "We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests."

It added that the airline is committed to "treating every guest with dignity and respect."

The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The video showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases look on.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns "directly with the appropriate authorities."

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would "engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred."

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE's tactics were "deeply un-American" and called for the agency's abolition.

"The video is horrific and it is chilling," Ferguson said at an afternoon news conference with labor leaders and local elected officials. "We need a system of immigration enforcement and border security that is effective, ethical and humane. And ICE is not it. It is beyond reform."

Ferguson also said he was looking into how ICE agents accessed the jet bridge and he believes they violated a state law he signed in March limiting facial coverings on law enforcement officers.

April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, representing over 600,000 workers, said union members were aboard the flight. She said the action disrupted travel during one of the busiest times and only days after flights were grounded nationwide due to a communications problem. "Airport workers are already managing extraordinary stress, passengers are already anxious and instead of restoring calm and confidence, federal agents introduced more fear and more chaos," she said.

text:
Washington state officials condemned Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Saturday after plainclothes officers in masks detained two people who were boarding a flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport.

Part of the incident was caught on video by onlookers. The video appears to show at least one person being detained by the officers on the bridge into the airplane. The officers are seen holding people down on the ground and pushing away bystanders. A woman is heard saying that she and the other person have work permits.

The Port of Seattle said the incident happened as travelers boarded an Alaskan Airlines flight from Seattle to Los Angeles.

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that ICE conducted "a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza" who the agency alleged "overstayed his visa."

The agency added that during the arrest other travelers allegedly "began to obstruct and assault our law enforcement officers."

"One passenger hurled hot coffee on the officers," the DHS spokesperson alleged. "Other passengers began obstructing federal officers."

Federal auditors raise concerns about billions ICE is spending to expand immigration detention

That woman who allegedly threw the coffee was detained and identified as Sofia Hernandez Mejia. In the statement, DHS said she is also a Mexican national "and visa overstay."

"She will be charged with assaulting a federal officer," DHS said in a statement.

DHS did not say where the two people were taken after they were detained.

Washington Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson said in a news conference later in the day that officials were still working to understand what happened but said the video of the incident was "horrific and chilling."

"Masked agents who do not identify themselves dragged screaming individuals off a jetway as they are trying to do something ordinary in our country, boarding an airplane," he said.

The Port of Seattle echoed the governor's sentiment, saying in a statement it was "outraged" over the incident. "Immigration enforcement actions at SEA are conducted without the Port's participation or knowledge," the statement said.

"The Port has continually asked, and local federal immigration authorities have previously agreed to protocols at SEA, and we are in conversation with DHS on whether any of these protocols were breached," the Port of Seattle said.

"This incident was not only distressing for the affected family but the passengers around them, and Port officials continue to engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred," the agency added.

Rep. Adam Smith, a Democrat, said in an X statement that the incident was "absolutely unacceptable."

"ICE's conduct across our country is putting people in harm's way, undermining public trust, and stoking fear in our communities," Smith said in his statement.

Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson also slammed ICE over the incident in a X statement, calling the tactics used in the video "unacceptable and un-American."

"I am outraged by videos of masked ICE agents causing chaos and dragging a woman off the jetway at Sea-Tac airport," she said.

ICE agents accused of throwing pregnant US citizen to ground, pepper-spraying her

Alaskan Airlines said in a statement it did "not direct or coordinate immigration enforcement activity, and we remain committed to protecting the privacy and safety of our guests and employees wherever possible."

"In this instance, Alaska Airlines was not provided advance notice of the enforcement action, and we are working to understand the circumstances surrounding what occurred, including whether the proper protocols were followed," the airline added.

Alaska Airlines said it would be working with the governor and Port of Seattle "to ensure the collaborative standards and practices that have kept our air system safe and secure for decades are respected moving forward."

ABC News' Alyssa Pone contributed to this report.

But in a situation like this—one that, by the deliberate action of ICE agents, dissolves into chaos—it’s impossible to make sense of what’s going on.

text:
At around 7 a.m. this morning, masked ICE agents arrested two people boarding an Alaska Airlines flight scheduled to depart from Sea-Tac International Airport to Los Angeles at 8:10 a.m. The videos of the arrest are painful to watch. A woman screams, begs, implores that she has a work permit in the US. But in a situation like this—one that, by the deliberate action of ICE agents, dissolves into chaos—it’s impossible to make sense of what’s going on.

According to reports, the confusion that erupted between ICE agents and travelers resulted in the arrest of the person of interest and a second person accused of throwing coffee at an officer. The details of the arrest are still coming in, but videos of it have gone viral and ignited national attention and local outrage. The fact that we have these horrifying videos is a testament to quick-thinking passengers who knew what to do if you see ICE. May the evidence these bystanders created be used well.

We will have more information about all of this in the coming days. But know that this is exactly the kind of thing the overwhelming majority of Americans voted against on November 3, this senseless and socially traumatizing cruelty. Our leaders can say all the words they want, but our votes now demand accountability from all quarters. We need action. Enough is enough.

A protest at the airport has been organized by Seattle Indivisible. It’s scheduled for 7 p.m.

text:
The Port of Seattle and Alaska Airlines are reviewing an immigration enforcement arrest involving two passengers as they boarded an Alaska Airlines flight from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport to Los Angeles Saturday morning.

The arrest caused a scuffle between passengers and masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents in the jet bridge area during boarding for Flight 1306, the airline said.

Several bystanders recorded video of the arrest, quickly uploading and sharing it to social media.

In a statement Saturday evening, posted hours after the videos went viral, ICE explained, "ICE officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an illegal alien from Mexico who overstayed his visa in violation of our nation’s laws. During the arrest other travelers began to obstruct and assault our law enforcement officers—a federal crime and a felony. One passenger hurled hot coffee on the officers. Other passengers began obstructing federal officers. The individual who threw the hot coffee was identified as Sofia Hernandez Mejia, an illegal alien from Mexico and visa overstay. She was subsequently arrested as well. She will be charged with assaulting a federal officer."

ICE added, "Assaulting and obstructing law enforcement is a crime and a felony. Secretary Mullin has been clear: anyone who assaults or obstructs law enforcement will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the fullest extent of the law. Our brave law enforcement is facing more than a 1,600% increase in assaults, 3,300% increase in vehicular attacks, and an 8,000% increase in death threats against them. This violence must end."

WATCH BELOW: Gov. Bob Ferguson and community leaders speak on the violent ICE detainment incident at SeaTac Airport

ALSO SEE | Trump admin touts record number of deportations as public grows weary about approach

Videos circulating on social media showed officers dragging someone away on the jetway as a woman screamed that a family member was being taken and that they had a work permit.

Online flight data showed that Alaska flight 1306, which had been scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m., was delayed.

The arresting officers wore masks, unmarked jackets, and khaki pants. The video showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases looked on.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past.

ALSO SEE | New law prohibits face coverings for law enforcement in Washington state

The Port said it was “outraged” by the incident and that immigration enforcement actions at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport are conducted without the Port’s participation or knowledge.

Port officials are speaking with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to determine whether previously agreed-upon protocols were breached.

The incident was distressing for the affected family and nearby passengers, the Port said. It added that officials are working with federal authorities to learn more.

Alaska Airlines said it was not previously aware of the law enforcement activity and is reviewing the details.

The airline said the safety and well-being of its guests and employees remain its top priority.

The incident occurred just days before airport officials are expecting roughly 875,000 travelers to fly in and out of Seattle between Nov. 25-30, a 1% increase from Thanksgiving 2025.

Ferguson provided the following statement on the incident: "ICE is completely and totally out of control. Like many Americans, I’m outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities. Today’s actions at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport are just the latest example of ICE’s deeply un-American tactics. I’ll have more to say this afternoon."

Rep. Pramila Jayapal's statement: "This morning, masked ICE agents terrorized our community, dragging at least one woman on the ground and arresting her as she was in line to board her flight. This behavior is totally unacceptable. Violent arrests are the hallmark of fascist states, not a democracy. Soon, Democrats will take back control of Congress and we will continue the critical work to rein in these out of control agents and hold them accountable. My heart goes out to those directly affected, and the passengers and airline workers whom ICE traumatized today."

In addition, Rep. Adam Smith also provided a statement: "This morning, masked ICE agents detained at least one passenger waiting to board an Alaska Airlines flight at Sea-Tac Airport. The masked agents forcibly dragged the individual off the jet bridge, taking them into custody. Let me be clear: this is absolutely unacceptable. ICE’s conduct across our country is putting people in harm’s way, undermining public trust, and stoking fear in our communities. I am incredibly concerned about the conduct of immigration enforcement and believe that ICE is operating as a paramilitary force that is a profound threat to our community. There is no question that this agency needs to be reined in before causing more chaos and fear."

Congresswoman Suzan DelBene (WA-01) released the following statement: “Time and time again we’ve seen ICE cause terror and violence in our communities. I’m outraged by today’s incident at the Sea-Tac Airport, where masked agents dragged a passenger off the jetway and forcibly detained them. It’s clear that ICE is out of control, creating unnecessary fear and instability in communities at home and across the country. The American people do not want their tax dollars to fund these appalling incidents. I am deeply troubled by the reckless conduct of immigration enforcement agents. There has to be oversight and accountability. Congress must act to rein in this lawless agency."

Michele Storms, ACLU of Washington Executive Director, offered this reaction: "The ACLU of Washington strongly condemns Immigration and Customs Enforcement's arrest of at least one passenger inside a crowded jetway at Sea-Tac airport. The Trump administration’s practice of conducting immigration enforcement with masked and unidentifiable agents has resulted in civil rights violations at an unprecedented scale. Their cruelty turns everyday locations like schools, bus stops, grocery stores, and airports into sites of fear and chaos, and complicates holding agents accountable for abuses. ICE violence is intentional and will not stop unless Congress or the courts hold this rogue agency to account."

Port of Seattle full statement:

We are outraged about this morning’s incident involving ICE and two passengers as travelers boarded AS 1306 to Los Angeles. Immigration enforcement actions at SEA are conducted without the Port’s participation or knowledge. The Port has continually asked, and local federal immigration authorities have previously agreed to protocols at SEA, and we are in conversation with DHS on whether any of these protocols were breached. However, the Port remains committed to the safety of all of our travelers and staff and airline team. This incident was not only distressing for the affected family but the passengers around them, and Port officials continue to engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred.

Alaska Airlines full statement:

We are concerned by this morning’s law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306. We recognize how distressing this incident has been for employees and guests. Alaska Airlines is required to comply with applicable laws and regulations when interacting with law enforcement officials. We do not direct or coordinate immigration enforcement activity, and we remain committed to protecting the privacy and safety of our guests and employees wherever possible. In this instance, Alaska Airlines was not provided advance notice of the enforcement action, and we are working to understand the circumstances surrounding what occurred, including whether the proper protocols were followed. We will work with the Port of Seattle and government authorities to ensure the collaborative standards and practices that have kept our air system safe and secure for decades are respected moving forward.

The Associated Press contributed to the reporting in this article.

text:
US President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown is affecting Indians. According to a report by American Community Media, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested 6,111 Indians between January 2025 and August 2026.

This is the record of Indians arrested in the US. Meanwhile, 5,235 were held in deportation centres and 2,349 were deported.

The organisation Stop AAPI Hate said the ICE agency had stepped up raids ahead of the midterm elections in November. However, no new figures on the arrests have emerged yet. The organisation claimed that Indians recorded the highest numbers of arrests, detentions and deportations in the Asia-Pacific group. ICE took action against people of Hispanic and Black origin in the southern states.

She had a green card, but was still held in custody for a week

Babli (name changed), a 60-year-old Indian-origin restaurant operator in California, was detained. She had been called to the immigration office for the biometrics process related to her green card application. Babli has been living in the United States since 1994. Her green card has also been approved. Her family alleges that she was harassed because she was Indian and was released from custody after a week.

ICE has arrested more than 850 Indians in California. According to AAPI, the most action was taken in Fresno, Bakersfield, Stockton and San Bernardino in the Democratic state of California.

Number of Indians deported from the US in 2025 highest in 16 years

According to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) official, both the number of arrests and deportations of illegal immigrants have increased. The number of illegal immigrants deported by the end of this year is set to reach a record high. More than 3,000 Indians deported last year, 2025, had all entered the US illegally.

ICE issued removal orders to 801 Indians in June alone. However, a removal order does not result in immediate deportation. It can be challenged in court, or the person concerned can leave the United States voluntarily. The number of Indians deported in 2025 was the highest in 16 years.

According to the Human Rights First organisation, Indians are being deported on Oman Air. They are being flown to New Delhi on a 20-hour flight from Harling, Texas. Deportation flights are being used this year. Last year, the United States deported people on Hercules military aircraft.

Action taken even for crossing traffic lights or social media posts

Professionals who entered the US on valid visas are being deported after being accused of various violations. There have also been cases of students being deported for running a red light in an American city.

Some students were deported after being held guilty of criticising the Trump administration on social media platforms such as X, Instagram and Facebook. In Texas, an H-1B visa holder lost his job, even though he had the right to remain in the US for 60 days and look for a new job.

Meanwhile, ICE conducted a raid while he was working part-time at a restaurant. The visa holder was arrested. ICE held him guilty of a visa violation and deported him to India.

3,567 Indians were deported from the US in 2025

In 2025, the US deported 3,567 Indian citizens. India's Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) provided this information in June 2026. The ministry said that 1,076 Indians had been deported by June 2026.

On 5 February 2025, the US sent 104 Indians to Amritsar for the first time on a military aircraft. Many of them were handcuffed and shackled at the feet. The incident sparked controversy across the country after photographs emerged. There was also an uproar in Parliament.

"Today is the latest example of the violence that ICE has inflicted on our communities as it works to further Donald Trump's cruel immigration agenda," Bob Ferguson said at an emergency news conference following the incident on Alaska Airlines Flight 1306, which was bound for Los Angeles.

Declaring the agency's culture "bankrupt" and "beyond reform," Ferguson argued that the US requires "effective, ethical, and humane" border enforcement. "The chaos and violence of ICE must come to an end."

Earlier Saturday, writing on US social media platform X, Ferguson condemned masked agents who do not identify themselves for "dragging people off jetways" and engaging in "deeply un-American tactics."

A passenger’s video shared with The Seattle Times showed multiple agents dressed in black and face masks detaining one person boarding the aircraft, while a woman struggling on the floor near a spilled cup of coffee shouted: "We have a work permit!"

- Officials demand investigations, oversight

Port of Seattle Commissioner Hamdi Mohamed, joined by Commissioner Sam Cho, called the arrest "unconscionable" and contrary to Washington's Keep Washington Working Act, which limits cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

While acknowledging that the Port of Seattle Commission, which operates the airport, lacks authority over federal agencies, Mohamed said: "Let me be crystal clear: a badge does not make you above the law." She vowed criminal investigations if laws were broken and urged Congress to exercise oversight.

Federal lawmakers echoed the demands on X. US Sen. Patty Murray condemned the "disturbing video" of agents forcing a woman to the ground and vowed accountability. Rep. Pramila Jayapal called violent arrests "the hallmark of fascist states, not a democracy." Rep. Adam Smith said ICE operates as a "paramilitary force" that erodes public trust.

A representative for the Defend Migrants Alliance, a coalition of grassroots groups, unions and faith communities, identified the detainees as Sophia, a former leader of Western Washington University's Latina Student Union, and Ricardo, demanding their immediate release.

The Department of Homeland Security and ICE had not publicly commented on the arrest, disclosed the detainees' charges or immigration status, or confirmed whether agents followed airport notification protocols.

text:
Eva Yi Xie, 24, a third-year Ph.D. student in neuroscience, was taken into custody by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) as she boarded a flight at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia. She remained in custody on Friday, The Washington Post reported, citing university officials.

Her research group at Princeton, the Brody Lab, said on X that Xie had just presented a poster at the Society for Neuroscience's annual meeting. She sent colleagues a call for help on the workplace messaging app Slack before they lost contact with her, the lab said, adding that she was being held in Chantilly, Virginia.

"She's a brilliant neuroscientist, mentor, and friend," the lab wrote. "She should be home."

Her adviser, professor Carlos Brody, called the detention "wildly unfair" in a statement to The Daily Princetonian. "Detaining her, with the intent of deporting her, makes no sense whatsoever," he said.

Xie came to the U.S. legally from China in 2016 as a minor and later applied for asylum with her family, according to her lawyer, Kerry Doyle. The claim is still pending, with an immigration court hearing set for January 2028.

Doyle told the Post that Xie holds valid work authorization and has no criminal record.

Her lawyers have filed a habeas corpus petition in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, arguing that ICE detained her without a warrant, the student newspaper reported.

Late Friday, Judge Anthony Trenga ordered ICE not to move Xie out of the district without a further court order and to respond to the petition by 5 p.m. on Wednesday.

Rodney Priestley, dean of Princeton's Graduate School, told graduate students in an email late Thursday that the university would stay in close contact with Xie's family, her legal team and her colleagues, The Guardian reported. "We hope she is able to soon resume her studies at Princeton," he wrote.

The university has arranged legal counsel for Xie, spokesperson Michael Hotchkiss said.

Xie attended the Bronx High School of Science in New York and graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 2024 with degrees in computer science and mathematics, starting her doctorate at Princeton the same year. Her research uses computational and experimental neuroscience to study how the brain makes decisions.

Immigration lawyers say ICE has stepped up arrests at airports this year. Kelly Rojas, co-director of the Detained Adult Program at the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, told the Post that at least five people, including Xie, had been detained by immigration officials at Washington-area airports in recent weeks.

On July 28, a public health researcher at Johns Hopkins University was arrested at Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport as she boarded a flight to Florida, CBS News reported. The Department of Homeland Security said she had overstayed a visa that expired in 2024.

text:
A federal judge ruled that Oscar Belgal, the man who was shot in the Bronx last month by federal immigration officers, will remain in custody as the Trump administration pursues his deportation case.

District Judge Hector Gonzalez of New York's Eastern District said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement had the legal basis to arrest Belgal, whom ICE agents were trying to capture in October when police say federal agents fired seven rounds at Belgal’s SUV, wounding him in the neck.

Gonzalez found that ICE had an independent, credible basis for its arrest warrant, including biometric confirmation of Belgal's identity, prior criminal history, and federal records indicating he lacked legal immigration status, according to the order issued Friday.

Legal Aid lawyers argued that ICE did not properly evaluate whether Belgal should be detained before taking him into custody.

Judge Gonzalez disagreed, citing his prior arrest on a first-degree robbery charge and a conviction for fourth-degree grand larceny, among other things. While ICE officials were late to file proper documents formally initiating immigration removal proceedings for Belgal, Gonzalez ruled the tardiness did not lead to prejudice or legal harm.

Belgal, a citizen of the Dominican Republic, has said that he didn’t know that the men who ambushed and shot him were ICE agents until he later woke up in the hospital. According to an NYPD account, Belgal accelerated his SUV forward as plainclothes federal officers approached him with their guns drawn. His 5-year-old son was nearby when ICE agents opened fire, according to his attorneys and police accounts.

Lawyers had argued that the agents’ use of deadly force violated Belgal’s constitutional rights and agency policies, but the judge said the habeas petition filed by Belgal only covers whether someone’s custody is unlawful or not; it doesn’t extend to alleged police misconduct during an arrest.

Gonzalez did write, however, that Belgal could pursue an excessive-force claim through a separate legal action.

The Legal Aid Society said it was “deeply disappointed” in the ruling in an unsigned statement.

Belgal is currently detained in the Metropolitan Detention Center in Sunset Park, Brooklyn.

text:
McALLEN, Texas (KRGV) — A federal judge in McAllen dismissed a Donna family’s lawsuit over a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement raid at their home.

In an order signed Nov. 9, U.S. District Judge Randy Crane granted the federal government’s motion to dismiss the case, saying the family lacked standing to pursue the lawsuit.

The lawsuit was filed Feb. 18 in federal court and accused ICE officers of entering the family’s home on Jan. 9 using an administrative warrant, which is not signed by judges.

As previously reported, a video obtained by Channel 5 News shows ICE agents jumping a fence into the family's yard that same day at around 7 a.m.

Video captures Donna family's detainment by alleged federal agents

According to the lawsuit, Humberto Garcia claims he saw trucks outside the home he shares with his three sisters, Andrea, Anna, and a minor identified as L.G., as well as their parents.

The parents are noncitizens but were in the process of obtaining lawful permanent resident status, according to the lawsuit.

Humberto was about to leave for work when he saw ICE agents jump the fence surrounding his home.

The lawsuit said ICE agents pointed their guns at Humberto and attacked him without speaking or identifying themselves. Officers knocked Humberto to the ground, scratched his face, and "several agents had their feet on his back."

The lawsuit claims an officer kicked Andrea's feet, causing her to fall. ICE officers began yelling at her and asking for her father. At this point Andrea asked to see a warrant, but ICE officers did not produce or show one.

ICE officers then accosted Anna, who was bruised from being tightly gripped by agents, according to the lawsuit.

L.G. was asleep inside the home when the raid happened. The lawsuit said she is disabled and suffers from a medical condition that "makes her bones break easily."

L.G. was awakened by officers banging on the windows of the home, according to the lawsuit. Officers then pointed guns at L.G. and "forced her to kneel and raise her hands."

The lawsuit said ICE agents gave the family two minutes to come outside, or they would break down the door. The mother complied and ICE agents entered the home without the family's consent to retrieve the father. The mother was later deported to Mexico.

The government moved to dismiss the case on Sept. 3, arguing the family could not sue on behalf of noncitizens, lacked standing because the claimed injury was too speculative, and had failed to state a claim.

Crane, a Bush-appointed judge, did not rule on whether the ICE agents had permission to enter the property, but agreed with the federal government and said the court did not need to decide the claim-by-claim constitutional arguments because the standing issue controlled the case.

In the filing, Crane wrote that the family had not shown a real and immediate threat of future injury and that past exposure to allegedly illegal conduct was not enough, by itself, to support injunctive relief.

Crane cited Supreme Court precedent in finding the family was seeking forward-looking relief without showing the threat of future harm was certainly impending.

The case was dismissed without prejudice.

text:
Masked immigration officers arrested two passengers on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, federal officials said, causing what Alaska Airlines called a "distressing" scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight.

Videos of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as a woman screamed that her daughter was being taken and she has a work permit.

Online flight data showed that Alaska Airlines Flight 1306, which had been scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m., was delayed.

Alaska Airlines said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

"We are concerned by this morning's law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306," the airline said. "We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests."

It added that the airline is committed to "treating every guest with dignity and respect."

In a statement provided to CBS News Saturday evening, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, the parent agency of ICE, said that ICE officers "conducted a targeted enforcement operation" on a Mexican national identified as Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza who had "overstayed his visa."

During the arrest, a second passenger "hurled hot coffee" at the officers, the DHS spokesperson said in the statement. That second passenger, identified by DHS as Sofia Hernandez Mejia, is a Mexican national who had also been determined to have overstayed her visa, the spokesperson said.

Mejia was also subsequently arrested and will face federal charges of assaulting a federal officer, DHS said.

Democratic Rep. Adam Smith of Washington said in an earlier statement that "masked ICE agents detained at least one passenger waiting to board an Alaska Airlines flight at Sea-Tac Airport. The masked agents forcibly dragged the individual off the jet bridge, taking them into custody."

The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants. Videos showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases looked on.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past. ICE sources told CBS News in July that the uptick in arrests stems from increased collaboration between ICE and the Transportation Security Administration.

On Thursday, a Princeton University student and Chinese national was detained by ICE at Ronald Reagan National Airport in Washington, D.C., after attending a neuroscience conference, the school and her colleagues said.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns "directly with the appropriate authorities."

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would "engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred."

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, called the incident "just the latest example of ICE's deeply un-American tactics."

"ICE is completely and totally out of control," Ferguson said in a statement. "Like many Americans, I'm outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities."

Democratic Rep. Pramila Jayapal of Washington said in a social media post that she was "disturbed by the reports of this detention at Sea-Tac," adding that her office was "working to gather more information on the situation."

DHS numbers obtained by CBS News last week found that ICE arrested 491,000 people in FY 2026, a record, including nearly 475,000 administrative arrests, also a record. Administrative arrests are those in which alleged undocumented immigrants are arrested for civil violations rather than criminal charges.

In a "60 Minutes" interview earlier this month following the heavy losses suffered by Republicans in the midterm elections, President Trump appeared to acknowledge that his administration's immigration crackdown may have contributed to his party's poor showing.

"For getting people out, I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out," Mr. Trump told "60 Minutes." "But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally. Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out. And there's a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes."

Of his deportation policies, the president said: "I think it was too tough. A lot of people would say that it's great, but a lot of people think it's too tough."

description: President Donald Trump has ordered federal contractors to notify the White House of any congressional requests for information on their work and to coordinate their responses with the administration —
text:

(CNN) — President Donald Trump has ordered federal contractors to notify the White House of any congressional requests for information on their work and to coordinate their responses with the administration — a move that Democrats say is unlawful as they prepare to launch investigations into his administration next year.

Commuters cross Pennsylvania Avenue near the US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, March 12, 2025. The number of continuing claims, a proxy for the number of people receiving benefits, filed by federal workers for the week ended Feb. 22 was 8,215, up from 7,412 the week prior.

An executive order signed by the president Friday said contractors must “abide by any instructions received from the White House and contracting agency related to the withholding of communications that the White House or the agency has determined are protected by executive privilege.”

“If the executive branch cannot be assured that those communications will remain confidential, agencies and the White House will be chilled from sharing sensitive information with contractors, which will stymie the operation of critical Government programs,” the executive order argues.

The order warns contractors that their agreements with the federal government could be terminated if they fail to comply with its directives.

It also accuses certain congressional leaders of “harassing private companies that contract with the federal government” for information and reminds them that their probes must have a “valid legislative purpose.”

Maryland Rep. Jamie Raskin, who is poised to chair the House Judiciary Committee when Democrats take control in January, called the executive order “unprecedented and blatantly unlawful.”

“Federal contractors are paid with taxpayer dollars, not Trump’s personal billions,” Raskin said in a statement Saturday. “Public contractors have both a duty and a right to speak truthfully when Congress calls, and Congress has a duty to investigate and stamp out all the waste, fraud, kickbacks, shakedowns and corruption choking the government and driving up costs. After two years of MAGA Republicans in Congress colluding with Trump Inc., accountability and the Rule of Law are coming.”

Democrats have mused about investigations into the work Trump has ordered across Washington, DC, including the construction of the White House ballroom, the repairs to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and the planned renovations of the Kennedy Center.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who will chair a key Senate investigative panel, earlier this month sent letters to a slew of companies asking them to cooperate with a planned inquiry into the ballroom. The Connecticut senator previously requested from the construction firm carrying out the project information about the ballroom’s anticipated cost and how it came to chosen as the builder.

Democrats have also said they will seek to address the influx of contracts the Department of Homeland Security has granted in Trump’s second term.

“Once we have control, then there’s a lot more we can do on guardrails,” Rep. Rep. Henry Cuellar, the ranking member on the House Appropriations Homeland Security subcommittee, has told CNN, referring to bringing the funds under his committee’s oversight.

While still in the minority in Congress, Democrats have sought to investigate the department’s controversial purchasing of planes and contracts to aid Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportation operations, as well as contracts for the construction of additional border wall in Big Bend National Park .

U.S. President Donald Trump watches as the last piece of steel is hoisted for construction of the White House ballroom during an event on November 04, 2026 in Washington, DC. President Trump signed the beam and took questions from reporters.

DHS also came under scrutiny last year after ProPublica reported that a firm run by the husband of the agency’s chief spokesperson, Tricia McLaughlin, was subcontracted to produce an advertising campaign for the department in a $200 million deal. McLaughlin told ProPublica at the time that DHS had no visibility into which subcontractors were selected and that she recused herself because of the conflict of interest.

Friday’s directive marks the latest guidance put out by the White House in anticipation of Democrats’ investigations. White House counsel Will Scharf last week penned a memo stating that executive agencies and departments within the Trump administration must obtain approval from the White House before any personnel agree to testify before Congress.

More broadly, the White House has taken a combative approach to the planned oversight of the administration. Scharf last week wrote Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, saying that the administration “ will not be extorted and will not be cowed by unlawful process motivated by animus, pettiness, hatred, or any other unlawful motive to intimidate, penalize or interfere with the lawful functioning of government.”

In a separate letter to Democratic committee leaders, Scharf stated that Trump administration officials do not have to comply with demands to preserve or turn over records because of those Democrats’ current status in the congressional minority.

Garcia condemned the president’s order on Saturday.

“Today’s executive order is the latest in the Trump Administration’s blatant attack on Congress’ constitutional right to conduct oversight,” Garcia said in a post on social media. “What is the White House trying to hide? Donald Trump wants to stop us from exposing the rampant waste, fraud, and corruption by his Administration, but we’re just getting started.”

Meanwhile, a top Congressional Democrat on Friday warned that lawmakers will withhold government funding for systems developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX if the Trump administration and tech billionaire refuse to disclose who is responsible for ordering the slowdown of Ukraine’s military-grade Starlink satellite service — the subject of another potential investigation next year.

This story was updated with new details.

CNN’s Priscilla Alvarez, Audrey Ash, Annie Grayer, Katelyn Polantz, Zachary Cohen and Tierney Sneed contributed to this report.

text:
President Donald Trump has issued a new executive order directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with the administration about congressional inquiries and to withhold communications the White House considers privileged.

The order, issued late Friday, says companies must coordinate with the White House and U.S. agencies on "appropriate responses" to any such requests. It warns that contracts could be terminated and future work with the federal government suspended if contractors and subcontractors fail to comply.

The directive is the Republican administration’s latest effort to push back against what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats.

Trump’s counsel, Will Scharf, told federal agencies on Monday that before agreeing to appear before Congress they must seek approval from his office and the White House’s Office of Legislative Affairs. Scharf also suggested in a recent letter to Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, that some congressional investigations may amount to "blatant criminality."

Responding to the latest executive order, Garcia said Saturday it was part of the administration’s "blatant attack on Congress’ constitutional right to conduct oversight."

Rep. Jamie Raskin, who is leading Democratic investigations from the House Judiciary Committee, criticized the order as "totally unprecedented and blatantly unlawful." Raskin said public contractors have a "duty and a right to speak truthfully when Congress calls."

In a fact sheet, the White House wrote that the new requirements will protect "executive privileges from congressional overreach." The White House added that some congressional leaders have tried to intrude on executive branch privileges by "harassing private companies that contract with the federal government."

Executive privilege allows the president to keep information from the courts, Congress and the public to protect the confidentiality of White House deliberations, but the protection is not absolute. Presidents of both parties have long used executive privilege to resist congressional inquiries, though such claims can lead to lengthy legal fights over whether the privilege applies.

The latest executive order applies to all contractors and subcontractors, encompassing tens of thousands of businesses.

Editor's note: The Associated Press contributed to this report.

text:
U.S. Senator John Hickenlooper, D-Colorado, is prepared to oppose the Trump administration's policies in a Senate controlled by Democrats.

Hickenlooper won his reelection November 3 against Republican Mark Baisley. Hickenlooper had 60% of the vote, compared to Baisley’s 35%. And Hickenlooper, who was in a minority last term with the GOP controlling the Senate, will be part of the 56-seat Democratic majority when the new term starts at noon January 3.

Local voters backed Republican challenger Mark Baisley heavily, with Kiowa County giving Baisley 85 percent of its vote in the November 2026 Senate race while the statewide seat went to Hickenlooper.

In the U.S. House, Colorado Democrats unseated two Republican incumbents and one Democratic incumbent as the Democratic Party took control of the House from Republicans for the next term. Democrat Melat Kiros defeated U.S. Representative Diana DeGette, a Democrat, in the primary, then beat Republican candidate Christy Peterson in the general election in the 1st Congressional District. Democrat Manny Rutinel in the 8th Congressional District won by an overwhelming majority, defeating one-term U.S. Representative Gabe Evans, R-Fort Lupton. And in Colorado's 4th Congressional District, retired Navy Admiral Eileen Laubacher, a Democrat, won in a narrow margin against the U.S. Representative Lauren Boebert, R-Windsor.

Hickenlooper first entered the political sphere in 2003 when he became the mayor of Denver. He served in that capacity until 2011 and was elected governor in 2012. He has remained a U.S. senator representing Colorado since 2020.

Hickenlooper’s team did not respond to The Center Square’s request for comment.

Since President Donald Trump’s first term beginning in 2016 and his second term beginning in 2024, Hickenlooper has expressed his stark opposition to Trump and his administration’s policies. Most recently, he dubbed Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act – a 331-page law aimed at expanding tax cuts, reforming Medicaid, and increasing funding for immigration and border enforcement – the “big bad beautiful betrayal.”

He has frequently blamed the president for the rising costs of gas, groceries and living, arguing it is a result of Trump’s intervention into Iran. He also said at a pre-election debate in October that he regretted the confirmation of every single cabinet member for the Trump administration.

Hickenlooper has been outspoken against the conflict with Iran and the administration’s attempt to withhold and unevenly distribute federal funds to “blue states” as compared to “red states.”

Another Democrat, U.S. Representative-elect Kiros too has been a staunch critic of the administration’s conflict with Iran, federal budget cuts to Medicaid and the president’s stance on social issues relating to LGBTQ care and the treatment of illegal immigrants.

Kiros won against Republican candidate Peterson with 78% of the vote, compared to Peterson’s 14%. Kiros will represent the Denver area, which is home to nearly 750,000 people.

Kiros’ team did not respond to The Center Square’s request for comment.

In a post-election media interview, Kiros said her win represents a shift from maintaining the “status quo,” claiming people are “fed up with this administration, and they’re also not going to tolerate Democrats trying to go back to business as usual.”

Kiros has labeled herself a Democratic socialist but ran as the Democratic Party nominee, though she has been critical of the party for what she says is its disregard for Democrats' longtime commitment to the working class.

She further told the media that her first priority once she enters Congress would be to pass “Medicare for all” legislation.

“We have the plan to get it done,” she said. “And it's now that we have to end this cycle of over 100,000 Americans dying every single year because they don’t have access to healthcare.”

Kiros also indicated that she takes the concerns surrounding government transparency and accountability from her constituents seriously.

“The only way we earn back that trust is by delivering material changes. That’s why I fought or ran a campaign on Medicare for All, on housing first, on universal childcare and elder care, and making sure that we’re holding our government elected officials accountable, to make sure that we are not allowing corruption to continue to be the corrosive force in our politics that it is today,” she told the media.

U.S. Representative-elect Rutinel, the Democrat elected to the flipped seat for Colorado’s 8th Congressional District, ran against Republican incumbent Evans and won with 56% of the vote. Like other Democrats, Rutinel has criticized the Trump administration on numerous issues, but particularly on immigration as the issue hits close to home for him.

Rutinel is a first-generation immigrant born in Los Angeles and grew up with a single mother who was an immigrant from the Dominican Republic. He served as an economist for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and later as a first responder when Hurricane Maria hit Puerto Rico.

He currently represents Colorado’s 32nd district in the state House of Representatives, which serves Adams County. He will represent the 8th Congressional District, which encompasses northern Denver suburbs in Weld and Larimer counties.

The Democrat wrote on his campaign website that he plans to “stop Trump’s immigration cruelty.” He said this includes preventing taxpayer dollars from funding the government to build “immigration prison camps” like Alligator Alcatraz, an immigration facility in northern Florida.

Rutinel told The Center Square that he “support[s] restoring healthcare funding, reversing Trump’s corrupt and chaotic tariff policies, and bringing an end to the unplanned forever war in Iran that’s putting American lives and risk and raising gas and diesel prices here at home.”

He said he plans to lower healthcare costs by expanding Medicaid’s power to negotiate lower prices on prescription drugs. Rutinel also indicated he supports abortion and that “politicians have no place in a private medical decision.”

Regarding his plans to bolster the Colorado and national economy, he wrote that he would increase vocational certificates, which would increase funding for programs to help high school students pursue careers outside of the traditional four-year college path.

Rutinel won in an upset victory against Evans, who initially called for a recount of the votes. Evans has since declared his bid for the state’s 4th Congressional District for 2028.

“For the folks who voted for Gabe Evans, I want you to know: You are my neighbor, too," Rutinel said during The Center Square interview. "I'll be your congressman and work for you as much as anyone.”

Laubacher, the retired admiral and Democrat, defeated U.S. Representative Boebert, the Republican incumbent, by a narrow margin of 1%. Boebert conceded the race on November 13.

Laubacher did not respond to The Center Square’s request for an interview

The congresswoman-elect, who was previously registered as a Republican, switched to independent and then registered as a Democrat in March 2025, has been critical of some of the more progressive members of Democratic Party. She's been particularly critical of proposals such as Medicare of all and complete dissolution of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Her website states that she wants to make life more affordable for Coloradans. To her, this would come about by reforming healthcare, especially in rural areas within the state. She has promised to fight to end Trump’s tariffs, enact tax cuts for the middle class, and make data centers pay for the cost of energy and infrastructure they would require.

Laubacher has also pledged her commitment toward making life for rural Coloradans better by supporting ranchers and farmers by passing a long-term Farm Bill, which has yet to pass in the U.S. Senate. It passed in April in the U.S. House.

Other priorities of Laubacher would be to secure the border and prevent “uncontrolled illegal immigration and removing dangerous criminals who are here illegally.” She said she plans to do this through bipartisan legislation that will further reform the immigration system.
