text:
Democratic Washington Governor Bob Ferguson called U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) "completely and totally out of control" after video circulated on social media Saturday showing federal agents detaining two passengers on a jet bridge at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport.

The detentions occurred as passengers were boarding Alaska Airlines Flight 1306 to Los Angeles, according to the airline. Footage shared online showed federal agents restraining a woman and escorting another individual from the boarding area. The woman in the video says: "They're taking my dad ... We don't have papers, we have a work permit.

The Department of Homeland Security told Newsweek that they arrested Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, "an illegal alien from Mexico who overstayed his visa in violation of our nation’s laws."

"During the arrest other travelers began to obstruct and assault our law enforcement officers—a federal crime and a felony. One passenger hurled hot coffee on the officers. Other passengers began obstructing federal officers," the DHS statement said.

Read More on News

Sofia Hernandez Mejia was arrested after throwing the coffee, DHS said, identifying her as "an illegal alien from Mexico and visa overstay." She will be charged with assaulting a federal officer, DHS said.

"Secretary Mullin has been clear: anyone who assaults or obstructs law enforcement will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the fullest extent of the law. Our brave law enforcement is facing more than a 1,600% increase in assaults, 3,300% increase in vehicular attacks, and an 8,000% increase in death threats against them. This violence must end," the DHS statement said.

Ferguson said it is violence by ICE agents that must stop.

"ICE is completely and totally out of control. Like many Americans, I’m outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities," the governor wrote. "Today’s actions at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport are just the latest example of ICE’s deeply un-American tactics."

In a separate X post, Ferguson reposted the video and wrote: "Absolutely outrageous."

Alaska Airlines told Newsweek that it recognizes how distressing this ICE activity was to employees and guests.

The airline said it was given prior notification of the action.

"We are working to understand the circumstances surrounding what occurred, including whether the proper protocols were followed. We will work with the Port of Seattle and government authorities to ensure the collaborative standards and practices that have kept our air system safe and secure for decades are respected moving forward," Alaska Airlines said.

In a statement to local station KOMO-TV, the Port of Seattle said it was outraged about the incident.

"Immigration enforcement actions at SEA are conducted without the Port’s participation or knowledge," its statement said. "The Port has continually asked, and local federal immigration authorities have previously agreed to protocols at SEA, and we are in conversation with DHS on whether any of these protocols were breached. However, the Port remains committed to the safety of all of our travelers and staff and airline team. This incident was not only distressing for the affected family but the passengers around them, and Port officials continue to engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred."

Senator Patty Murray echoed the governor's concerns, writing on X that she was "outraged by disturbing video."

"I'm demanding answers from DHS today & I’ll keep fighting to end this sick terror campaign. Trump answers to a Democratic Congress on January 3rd—there WILL be accountability," she wrote.

Michele Storms, executive director of the ACLU of Washington, said her organization condemns Saturday's arrest.

"The Trump administration’s practice of conducting immigration enforcement with masked and unidentifiable agents has resulted in civil rights violations at an unprecedented scale. Their cruelty turns everyday locations like schools, bus stops, grocery stores, and airports into sites of fear and chaos, and complicates holding agents accountable for abuses. ICE violence is intentional and will not stop unless Congress or the courts hold this rogue agency to account," the ACLU statement to Newsweek said.

The incident is the latest flashpoint in the Trump administration's escalating immigration enforcement crackdown. An analysis of government records obtained by the Deportation Data Project found 568 ICE arrests linked to airports between January 20, 2025, and March 10, 2026, compared with 108 that occurred at airports during the same period leading up to Trump’s second administration. The dataset covered 16 airports and did not establish whether every arrest occurred inside terminals or during boarding.

Nationwide, ICE carried out more than 491,000 immigration arrests during fiscal year 2026, the highest annual total in the agency's history, according to DHS data.

Immigration attorneys say the trend marks a significant shift for travelers, with domestic flights increasingly serving as a point of contact for enforcement—including for some noncitizens with work authorization or pending immigration applications. It remained unclear Saturday whether the Seattle operation was part of that broader strategy.

Princeton Student Also Arrested at Airport

On Thursday, Princeton University doctoral student Eva Yi Xie was detained by ICE at Ronald Reagan National Airport while returning from the Society for Neuroscience conference, where she had been a presenter.

In a statement to Newsweek late Friday, DHS said that it conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest the "illegal alien from China."

Xie was admitted to the United States on a temporary basis on March 16, 2016, with a required departure date of September 15, 2016, the statement said. A pending application would not confer legal status, the statement said, noting that Xie never held valid authorization to study in the United States.

“DHS reversed the horrendous Biden-era policy that allowed aliens in our country illegally to jet around our country. Under President Trump, DHS will no longer tolerate this. This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport," the statement said.

DHS noted that they offer those in detention a free flight and $3,000 to self-deport.

“Xie will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending her removal proceedings," the statement read.

text:
ICE said it arrested two “illegal aliens” from Mexico as agents were reported in Round Lake Beach, where a woman said her father was detained on his way to work and is now raising money to bring him home.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) identified the men as Marco Antonio Perez-Aguilar, 46, and Hector Perez-Martinez, 37, in a statement to Lake and McHenry County Scanner this week.

ICE said both men, whom the agency called “illegal aliens” from Mexico, were arrested Tuesday for being unlawfully present in the United States.

The agency provided the names after Lake and McHenry County Scanner asked about arrests in Round Lake Beach Tuesday, including the reported arrest of a man named Marcos Perez while he was on his way to work.

ICE’s statement did not say where the two men were arrested.

Community members on social media began reporting shortly after 8 a.m. Tuesday that ICE agents were in the area of Aldi on Rollins Road in Round Lake Beach.

One person said agents had been sitting since around 7 a.m. at the 19th Judicial Circuit Court’s North Branch Court on Nicole Lane, which is just behind the Aldi.

Residents reported agents throughout the morning at several businesses along Rollins Road, including a Grease Monkey, Burger King, O’Reilly Auto Parts and Petco, and at Rollins Road and Circuit Drive.

The vehicles observed included black Nissan Armada and Nissan Pathfinder SUVs, a silver Ford Explorer and a black Ford Explorer.

Residents said agents were still in the area shortly after 9 a.m.

Fatima Perez, of Round Lake Beach, said in a GoFundMe fundraiser she organized that her father, Marcos Perez, was detained by ICE agents in Round Lake Beach Tuesday morning while he was on his way to work.

“I last saw him that morning, and I never imagined he would be taken away,” Fatima Perez said.

She said her father is a hard worker who has helped many people and is “a truly good man.”

Fatima Perez said her son, Marcos Perez’s grandson, keeps looking for his grandfather.

“We want my father to come home; what we are going through right now is incredibly difficult,” she said.

The fundraiser, titled “Help me get my dad back home,” had raised $5,945 of its $8,000 goal from 63 donors as of Saturday afternoon.

ICE said Perez-Aguilar had previously entered the United States illegally and voluntarily returned.

Perez-Martinez had previously entered the United States illegally and voluntarily returned three times, ICE said.

It is unclear whether the two men were arrested together.

“Both individuals remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings and will receive due process under federal law,” ICE said. “Being in detention is a choice.”

The agency encouraged “all illegal aliens” to use the CBP Home App to leave the country and said the United States is offering $3,000 and a free flight to those who self-deport.

“If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return,” ICE said.

It was not immediately known where the men are being held.

The Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights (ICIRR) asks anyone who sees immigration enforcement activity or whose family member has been taken to call its Family Support Hotline at 855-435-7693.

The White House claimed that "Trump is ensuring that Americans' confidential information and national and homeland security work is protected, and that the executive branch is able to serve the American people efficiently and economically."

However, his move was widely seen as part of a broader effort by the president to limit Democrats' planned probes into not only the federal government and its contractors but also Trump and businesses that may have benefited from his return to power.

Acknowledging the anticipated Democrat-led investigations, the White House fact sheet says that "certain congressional leaders have threatened to intrude on these executive prerogatives by seeking confidential executive branch information from executive agencies and harassing private companies that contract with the federal government."

Lisa Gilbert, co-president of of the watchdog group Public Citizen, stressed in a Saturday statement that "contractors are paid with Americans' tax money and must be the best for the job, full stop."

"However, throughout the Trump administration we've seen widespread abuse of the contracting process, with lucrative contracts doled out to political allies, inexperienced startups, and flatly unqualified bidders, for everything from major ICE operations to Trump's vanity projects," she noted, referring to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. "No-bid and emergency awards have become the norm, circumventing rules designed to prevent corrupt contracting."

"The new Congress rightfully has its sites set on this obvious cronyism for investigation and oversight," she continued. "The American people have a right to know how their money is being spent, that it is going to capable contractors, and that is not be used to reward allies and punish perceived enemies."

Gilbert added that the new order, "dressed up in fancy talk about executive privilege and enhancing efficiencies, is nothing but a naked ploy to try and protect the perpetrators of this corruption. It will not succeed. Sunlight is coming and corrupt administration insiders and contractors, both, will have to face the American people."

As Reuters reported:

Friday's order follows a directive issued this week by White House Counsel Will Scharf requiring federal agencies to obtain White House approval before employees agree to testify before Congress. Scharf said certain Democratic investigations could amount to criminal conduct, a claim that has raised questions about the administration's attempts to limit congressional oversight."

The restrictions could face legal challenges, particularly if contractors are told to withhold information sought through congressional subpoenas. Executive privilege allows presidents to protect certain confidential communications, but courts can ⁠intervene in disputes over Congress' authority to obtain information.

Earlier this week Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), who is expected to lead the House Oversight Committee, sent document preservation letters to a dozen current and former Trump administration officials, and Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), likely the next House Judiciary Committee chair, sent similar notices to federal law enforcement agencies.

"Voters gave congressional Democrats a sweeping mandate to root out corruption and ensure that the government is accountable to the people," Garcia wrote in his letters, referring to the blue tsunami in the midterm elections earlier this month. "We intend to act on that mandate in the 120th Congress by conducting the critically important oversight essential for legislative reform."

Raskin—who managed Trump's historic second impeachment after his supporters stormed the US Capitol on January 6, 2021—said on social media Friday: "We will confront White House corruption and lawlessness with the full powers of Congress, the 'predominant' branch of government (Madison), the representatives of the people. Preserve all your records, Mr. President."

Trump has been widely condemned as "the most openly corrupt president in American history" and, during just his first year back in the White House, pocketed at least $2.2 billion—over half of it from his family’s cryptocurrency grift. Companies affiliated with the president's two eldest sons are have also scored key federal contracts during his second term.

In addition to Trump's sons, Elon Musk—a former member of the administration, leading Republican donor, and the world's richest person—could also be a key target of Democratic probes, as he leads multiple tech companies. Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, sent a Friday letter to Musk about SpaceX's role in the Starshield service disruptions in Ukraine last month.

Noting that inquiry on Musk's social media platform X on Saturday, Jonathan Cohn, political director of the group Progressive Mass, said that "contracts with Musk are a national security risk and should be treated as such."

This article has been updated with comment from Public Citizen.

She has interned at Meta, Microsoft, and IBM.

Rodney Priestley, dean of Princeton's graduate school, said in a statement that "news of Eva's detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community. The university has arranged for Eva to be represented by legal counsel, and we will remain in contact with her legal team, her family, and colleagues to provide support. We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton."

Neuroscience professor Carlos Brody, who advises Xie, told the student newspaper, The Daily Princetonian, that "it seems wildly unfair," adding: "Eva is a brilliant law-abiding student and wonderful person who has many talents to contribute to the United States. Detaining her, with the intent of deporting her, makes no sense whatsoever. It is cruel, and it is our country shooting itself in the foot."

Xie wrote on LinkedIn earlier this week that she was in Washington, DC to present at a Society for Neuroscience conference. The organization "is closely monitoring the detention" of Xie, it said Friday. "We are in close contact with Princeton University and stand ready to provide any support that may be needed. Our thoughts are with Eva, her family, and her colleagues."

The student's colleagues also weighed in, as did other academics and tech professionals. Ningshan Ma, who attended MIT with Xie, wrote on the platform X: "This is horrifying. Eva is an amazing classmate and friend. Please help in any capacity."

Brian Huang, an MIT alumnus who's now at Google DeepMind, said: "This woman was one of my labmates during undergrad.... absolute insanity from this administration."

The Brody Lab's official X account said that "she’s a brilliant neuroscientist, mentor, and friend. She went to a conference to present her work, and now she's in a detention center. She should be home."

Princeton student Conor McGrory wrote: "Just heard the news that a student in my PhD program was kidnapped by ICE earlier today. Eva is a great person and a gifted scientist, and the fact that these cruel, lawless people are subjecting her to this makes me sick with anger."

Another student at the university, Jorge Yanar, said that "Eva is one of the kindest and most brilliant people I've worked with during my PhD. It is shocking and deeply infuriating that this is happening. Please share! Call your representatives. Forward this to reporters."

Hood—who founded the Execution Intervention Project and has been present for 15 state killings—told the Tribune that "immediately, you’re supposed to... lose consciousness very quickly, and what happened, it was unquestionably botched."

Texas Department of Criminal Justice spokesperson Amanda Hernandez refuted Hood's characterization, telling The New York Times that “as far as this agency is concerned, it is 100% not a botched execution."

"This was a successful execution, and we did follow all of the proper protocols to do it correctly," she added.

Hood pushed back, telling the Tribune: “My hand was on Reinaldo’s shoulder the entire time I was in that chamber. I know what I saw... Texas does not get to tell a different story."

Dennes was convicted of capital murder in the 1996 shooting death of Houston jewelry store owner Janos Szucs. He maintained his innocence and argued in subsequent appeals that prosecutors had failed to disclose that a key witness was a police informant. His final appeals were rejected by the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals and the US Supreme Court.

Dennes' execution was the second recent American lethal injection procedure to be described as botched. In September, Tennessee officials twice injected Christa Pike with supposedly lethal doses of pentobarbital, but the 50-year-old woman survived. After regaining consciousness, Pike described suffering continuing physical and psychological pain.

Both cases involved the same execution drug, prompting renewed questions about the reliability—and humanity—of lethal injection. Texas, meanwhile, has drawn long-standing criticism for obtaining its pentobarbital from compounding pharmacies whose identities are shielded from public scrutiny, and for extending the expiration dates of its drug supplies.

The Eighth Amendment to the US Constitution's Bill of Rights prohibits the infliction of "cruel and unusual punishments."

"Lethal injection is torture—and Reinaldo Dennes was not sentenced to be tortured," Maya Foa, chief executive of the anti-death penalty advocacy group Reprieve, told The Guardian. "Even the most ardent supporters of capital punishment must recognize that the dominant method of execution in the US is broken and cannot be allowed to continue."

"People are being tortured. We need to stop, and take a hard look at why we are still doing this.”

Jonathan Groner, an execution expert and professor emeritus of clinical surgery at Ohio State University, called lethal injections a "medical charade."

“They imitate general anesthesia, which is done in hospitals across the country thousands of times a day, by people with expertise, but when it is done in the death chamber without necessary equipment or skills, people suffer," he told The Guardian.

Groner said that technicians' insertion of intravenous lines in Dennes' foot and shoulder indicated that they were struggling.

“Placing IVs in the neck is very painful and difficult, and a last resort; and the foot is not a top choice because there is a long way to the heart for the medication to be circulated," he said.

“It’s time for the medical profession to make a stand on executions," Groner added. "People are being tortured. We need to stop, and take a hard look at why we are still doing this.”

Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who has overseen 87 executions during his 11-year tenure.

In a letter to Hinojosa earlier this month obtained by Newsweek, Hood implored the governor-elect to do everything in her power to halt executions.

"You have one shot at being remembered for being the governor of Texas who walked into the mansion and said the killing stops here," he wrote. "There is no new era that includes the death penalty."

But as Newsweek's Khaleda Rahman explained:

The Texas governor does not have the authority to declare a moratorium on executions and can only commute a death sentence or a pardon if there is a written recommendation by a majority vote of the Texas Board of Pardons and Paroles. The governor can grant 30-day reprieves without the board's recommendation.

In capital cases involving an imminent execution since 1982, the board has only recommended sparing someone five times. Abbott has commuted just one death sentence, that of Thomas Bartlett Whitaker, an hour before his scheduled execution in 2018, to life in prison without parole.

Hood urged Hinojosa to use that power as often as possible to spare as many of the more than 160 people on Texas' death row from execution.

"Enough 30-day reprieves will slow the system down,” he wrote in his letter.

While Hinojosa has said she personally opposes capital punishment, she has stopped short of embracing abolition.

“I think it's terrible what has happened in this criminal justice system," Hinojosa said during a CNN interview last month before the election. "I think it is inhumane what has happened. I also believe that there should not be just blanket positions on these things. And so, as governor, I will take that responsibility seriously. Look at each case on a case-by-case basis.”

"I'm not going to sit here and make a blanket statement about what I will do, because I think every situation is unique and needs that special attention," she added.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, there have been 35 executions in the United States this year. Florida has put 19 inmates to death, Texas has killed seven, Alabama and Oklahoma three apiece, and Arizona, Indiana, and Tennessee have each executed one person.

States execute people by lethal injection, poison gas, electrocution, firing squad, and hanging.

Meanwhile, outgoing California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat widely believed to be preparing to run for president in 2028, announced earlier this month that he was commuting the death sentences of all 548 of the state's death row inmates to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.

The move, which did not abolish the death penalty as 23 states have done, was nevertheless hailed as an example for states retaining the ultimate punishment, which critics argue is inherently cruel and irreversible, disproportionately targets poor people and racial minorities, and—according to research from the National Academy of Sciences—has about a 4% error rate, meaning roughly 1 in every 25 people sentenced to death is likely innocent.

A Princeton University student was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement this week at Ronald Reagan National Airport in Washington, D.C., after attending a neuroscience conference, the school and her colleagues said.

Eva Yi Xie, a third-year Ph.D. student, was detained on Thursday night following a presentation she gave at the Society for Neuroscience, her colleague wrote on X.

"News of Eva's detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community," Rodney Priestley, the dean of the Princeton graduate school, said in a statement. "The University has arranged for Eva to be represented by legal counsel, and we will remain in contact with her legal team, her family, and colleagues to provide support. We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton."

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement that Xie was taken into custody during a "targeted immigration enforcement operation" at Reagan Airport.

Xie was admitted to the United States on a temporary basis on March 16, 2016, according to DHS, which said she is a Chinese national. DHS said Xie had been required to depart the U.S. by Sept. 15, 2016.

"Xie will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending her removal proceedings," DHS said in a statement. "Xie has NEVER held valid authorization to study in the United States. To be clear, a pending application does not confer legal status in the United States."

Carlos Brody, of the Princeton Neuroscience Institute, wrote on X that Xie sent her lab mates a Slack message for help before she was detained. She's being held in Chantilly, Virginia, according to Brody.

"Her lawyers are working on her release," Brody wrote. "She's a brilliant neuroscientist, mentor, and friend. She went to a conference to present her work, and now she's in a detention center. She should be home."

Xie's attorney, Kerry Doyle, said in a statement that her "arrest and detention is without legal basis."

"They cannot arrest people without a warrant if they are not a flight risk or danger to the community," Doyle said. "She is neither. She's a star rising scientist with permission to be in the US and they grabbed her because she is easy pickings at an airport where TSA and ICE are sharing information and targeting unsuspecting travelers with authorization to be in the US."

text:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton is abandoning several high-profile lawsuits against immigrant advocacy organizations, a Muslim civil rights group and the NCAA as he prepares to leave office following his failed U.S. Senate campaign.

The decisions mark a significant shift in a series of legal battles that attracted national attention and drew criticism from civil rights organizations. Several of the targeted groups had accused Paxton’s office of using state litigation to pressure organizations over their political activities and public positions.

Among the cases being dropped are lawsuits involving Annunciation House, a migrant shelter network in El Paso, Houston-based immigrant rights group FIEL, the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) and the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA).

The dismissals followed the November 3, 2026, election, in which Paxton lost his bid for the U.S. Senate. Democrat James Talarico defeated him in the race, while Democrat Nathan Johnson won the election to become Texas’ next attorney general.

Why Ken Paxton Is Dropping the Lawsuits

The withdrawals come after years of legal disputes involving organizations that had challenged Texas immigration policies, advocated for Muslim communities or criticized positions supported by Republican leaders.

Paxton’s office did not provide detailed explanations for several of the dismissals. Court filings generally recorded the state’s decision to stop pursuing the cases without outlining why the attorney general had changed course.

The timing has attracted attention because the decisions came shortly after the election and before a new administration takes control of the Texas attorney general’s office.

Johnson has said he intends to review cases initiated under Paxton and reconsider litigation he views as politically motivated. The incoming attorney general’s position has added another layer of significance to the outgoing administration’s decisions.

However, the available court filings do not establish that Paxton withdrew the lawsuits for a single political reason. His office had not publicly explained the broader strategy behind the withdrawals.

Annunciation House Lawsuit Ends After Years of Legal Disputes

One of the most closely watched cases involved Annunciation House, a nonprofit network operating migrant shelters in El Paso.

Paxton had accused the organization of illegally harboring undocumented immigrants and sought to shut down its operations. The lawsuit became a major point of conflict between the state and an organization providing assistance to migrants near the U.S.-Mexico border.

Annunciation House denied wrongdoing and challenged the state’s efforts in court. Its work included providing temporary shelter and assistance to migrants who had been processed and released by federal immigration authorities.

The attorney general’s office eventually abandoned its effort to close the organization. Ruben Garcia, Annunciation House’s founder and executive director, welcomed the decision after the lengthy legal fight.

The dismissal brought an end to a dispute that had consumed significant time and resources for the nonprofit.

Ken Paxton Drops Lawsuit Against Houston Immigration Group FIEL

Paxton’s office also withdrew its lawsuit against Familias Inmigrantes y Estudiantes en la Lucha, commonly known as FIEL.

The Houston-based organization works with immigrant families and students. The state had accused the nonprofit of violating restrictions governing its charitable status through social media activity opposing immigration policies supported by President Donald Trump and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott.

The lawsuit followed the group’s criticism of Texas Senate Bill 4, a state law that sought to give Texas authorities broader powers to arrest people suspected of entering the country illegally.

FIEL’s executive director, Cesar Espinosa, said the litigation had placed a substantial burden on the organization. He said the group could now return its attention and resources to protecting and supporting immigrant communities.

The state withdrew its claims with prejudice, meaning it cannot bring the same claims against FIEL again.

The decision was particularly significant for the nonprofit because the lawsuit had affected its ability to focus on its regular programs and community work.

CAIR Lawsuit Dropped After Attempt to Restrict Muslim Civil Rights Group

Another major development involved the Council on American-Islamic Relations, one of the largest Muslim civil rights organizations in the United States.

Paxton’s office had filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent CAIR from operating in Texas. The state also asked a judge to designate the organization as a foreign terrorist and transnational criminal organization.

The lawsuit, filed in February 2026, alleged connections involving the Muslim Brotherhood. CAIR rejected the allegations and challenged the state’s legal action.

The case attracted national attention because of the potential consequences for the organization’s activities and its ability to serve Muslim communities.

Paxton’s office filed a notice ending the lawsuit on November 16. CAIR welcomed the withdrawal, while its representatives criticized the decision to pursue the case in the first place.

The dismissal represented another retreat from a high-profile legal campaign launched by the Texas attorney general.

NCAA Lawsuit Over Transgender Athletes Also Abandoned

The NCAA was another major target of Paxton’s legal campaign.

In December 2024, his office sued the college sports organization, accusing it of misleading consumers by marketing competitions as women’s sports while allowing transgender athletes to participate under its policies.

The lawsuit was brought under the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act. Paxton argued that the NCAA’s descriptions of women’s competitions could mislead sports fans and consumers.

The NCAA disputed the allegations and maintained that its policies were clear regarding participation in women’s college sports.

In November 2026, Paxton’s office informed a Texas district court that it would no longer pursue the case.

The NCAA welcomed the decision, saying its policies already established who could compete in women’s college sports. The dismissal ended a legal dispute that had placed transgender participation in athletics at the center of another major Texas political controversy.

What Happens to the Other Cases Filed by Paxton?

The recent withdrawals do not mean that every controversial lawsuit initiated by Paxton has been abandoned.

His office has continued pursuing other legal matters, including a long-running Medicaid fraud lawsuit involving Planned Parenthood. That case remains separate from the dismissals involving immigrant organizations, CAIR and the NCAA.

Paxton also withdrew his support from an appeal involving Houston doctor Mary Talley Bowden and the Texas Medical Board. Bowden had been reprimanded after prescribing ivermectin to a COVID-19 patient at a hospital where she did not have practice privileges.

These developments show that the outgoing attorney general’s office has been reviewing or changing its position across several different legal disputes.

The cases also differ in their procedural status. Some withdrawals prevent the state from bringing the same claims again, while other dismissals may leave different legal options available.

Texas Politics Faces a Legal Shift After the 2026 Election

The changes come during a transition in Texas political leadership. Paxton’s defeat in the Senate race and Johnson’s victory in the attorney general election have raised questions about which legal priorities will continue under the next administration.

Johnson has indicated that he wants to examine lawsuits pursued by the current attorney general and reconsider cases that he believes were driven by political considerations.

That review could affect how Texas uses its legal authority in disputes involving immigration, civil rights organizations, education and public policy.

For the organizations involved, the dismissals offer relief from litigation that several leaders said had consumed money, staff time and organizational resources.

The broader political and legal implications will become clearer as the outgoing administration completes its remaining work and the incoming attorney general prepares to take office.

text:
APPLETON, MINN. (KARE) - Congress is now demanding answers from Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin about the federal government’s $495.6 million purchase of a shuttered Minnesota prison in Appleton, citing a KARE 11 investigation that revealed the same facility had been offered to the state for $75 million a year earlier.

A letter, led by Congresswoman Betty McCollum and Bennie G. Thompson, Ranking Member of the House Committee on Homeland Security, raises concerns about what the lawmakers call an overpayment of taxpayer dollars, the terms of the federal government’s agreement with CoreCivic, and the safety of people detained at the facility.

“This is just one more example of the Trump administration wasting taxpayer dollars on dubious projects,” said Congresswoman McCollum.

“DHS should not be wasting taxpayer funds to purchase – and grossly overpay for – private prisons to boost those corporations’ bottom line and expand the Trump administration’s grossly inhumane mass deportations,” Ranking Member Thompson said. ”DHS must answer for its actions.”

“We are deeply concerned”

The members of Congress cite KARE 11’s investigation, which uncovered a May 2025 email showing CoreCivic offered to sell the Prairie Correctional Facility to Minnesota for $75 million, including upgrades needed to reactivate it. The federal government ultimately paid nearly $495.6 million for the same facility.

“We are deeply concerned by this overpayment and the apparent misuse of taxpayer dollars,” the letter reads.

It also raises concerns about the facility’s medical infrastructure, staffing, emergency care, suicide prevention measures and whether it will detain both men and women.

Members of Congress are now requesting documents detailing the purchase agreement, the prison’s valuation and appraisal, and when the Department of Homeland Security learned CoreCivic had offered the facility to Minnesota for a fraction of the federal purchase price.

They are also questioning why the federal government is paying CoreCivic more than $536 million over five years to operate a facility it now owns, and whether the government considered operating the prison itself.

Congresswoman McCollum and Ranking Member Thompson were joined by Sen. Tina Smith, Rep. Ilhan Omar, Rep. Angie Craig, Rep. Kelly Morrison, Rep. Sara Jacobs, Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Rep. Veronica Escobar, Rep. Stephen Lynch, Rep. Madeleine Dean, Rep. Eleanor Holmes Norton, and Rep. Mike Quigley in demanding answers on the prison overpayment.

The letter requests written responses from Mullin by December 3.

This follows an investigation by the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, and a request that DHS and CoreCivic preserve all records dating back to January 1, 2025, and on an ongoing basis.

A $420 million gap

Minnesota declined CoreCivic’s $75 million offer in 2025, citing concerns about staffing and the services needed to operate a prison in a remote community roughly three hours from the Twin Cities. KARE 11 investigates uncovered the federal government’s purchase price was more than six times what CoreCivic had offered Minnesota for the same prison—a $420 million gap.

In a recent interview, Minnesota Corrections Commissioner Paul Schnell told KARE 11 he was stunned by the federal purchase price, saying he still couldn’t understand how the government could justify spending nearly half a billion dollars.

“Did Minnesota miss out on the real estate deal of the century, or are taxpayers potentially getting taken for a ride here?” KARE 11’s A.J. Lagoe asked.

“Well, I mean, that’s the only thing I can believe,” Schnell replied. “That the taxpayers - I don’t know how they could justify this amount.”

Financial windfall

CoreCivic has become a major financial winner during President Trump’s immigration crackdown.

The company’s then-CEO Damon Hininger told investors shortly after Trump returned to the White House that he anticipated significant growth opportunities, potentially the most significant in the company’s history.

Hininger said the administration’s immigration policies were creating enormous business opportunities by increasing demand for detention beds.

CoreCivic also donated $500,000 to the Trump-Vance inaugural committee. Hininger also made significant personal contributions to Trump-affiliated political committees.

When KARE 11 requested an interview, a company spokesperson declined an on-camera interview.

In a written statement, CoreCivic said independent appraisers used a cost-based methodology and that the federal government ultimately determined the sale price following its assessment process.

Multibillion-dollar prison buying spree

The Appleton prison was one of several facilities CoreCivic sold to the federal government this year.

The company also sold a facility in Kansas for $238 million and two prisons in California for a combined $1.5 billion.

The total price tag for the four facilities exceeded $2.2 billion.

Federal auditors raise concerns

The purchase comes amid broader questions about ICE’s detention facility expansion.

The nonpartisan Government Accountability Office recently warned ICE’s detention facility purchases have the potential to result in waste, finding the agency had not assessed the long-term affordability of owning the facilities.

The GAO’s September report called for urgent planning to avoid further waste of taxpayer dollars.

ICE also spent $1.07 billion purchasing 11 warehouses it planned to convert into detention centers. The agency later reversed course and planned to sell seven of them.

By then, the GAO found ICE had spent more than $20 million on unrecoverable costs, including utilities, security and other services.

Federal response

In October, a handful of officials with the Trump administration traveled to MN to discuss fraud; however, when asked by KARE 11’s Lou Raguse about the prison purchase, U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent claimed answering the question “was a waste of our time.”

“I don’t know anything about that,” Bessent responded when asked about the sale. “What we’re here to do is to prosecute criminal fraud and any question like that, that deflects away from it, I think, is a waste of our time.”

While not addressing KARE 11’s request for an on-camera interview or the questions submitted in writing, DHS provided the following statement on 11/02/26, attributed to an unnamed spokesperson:

“DHS acquired the Prairie Correctional Facility to strengthen America’s ability to enforce its immigration laws and carry out the American people’s mandate for mass deportations. The 1,600-bed site gives ICE immediate capacity to detain and remove those who have no legal right to remain, protecting American communities and restoring the integrity of our borders without waiting years for new construction. The purchase price was set through the standard federal appraisal process. Independent appraisers applied a replacement-cost method, current cost of equivalent secure space, adjusted for depreciation, land, and condition, including the security and fire upgrades required for ICE operations. The $75 million figure was a preliminary, non-binding indication offered during earlier discussions with the Minnesota Department of Corrections. Those talks never advanced to formal appraisal or agreed scope. The number was not based on replacement-cost analysis and did not reflect the intervening rise in construction costs or federal operational standards. Minnesota’s own estimate to replace Stillwater was roughly $1.3 billion.”

DHS Secretary Mullin has not directly responded to our questions.

text:
Video captured during an ICE arrest outside the Santa Clarita Sheriff’s Station Friday morning shows federal agents smashing a vehicle’s windows, shoving and pepper-spraying protesters, and taking a man into custody.

The confrontation unfolded shortly after 11 a.m. in the station’s parking lot, drawing protesters who recorded the encounter and questioned the agents’ actions.

Activist Ashley Calkins, with the Vote Up Advocacy Coalition, was among those documenting the incident.

"There’s nothing short of horrifying and brutal and dystopian," Calkins said, describing what she witnessed.

What we know:

According to activists who witnessed the incident, the man ICE agents were pursuing had been released from custody shortly before the confrontation. They say he approached a young couple in the parking lot and asked for a ride home. The couple agreed to help him. Their vehicle soon became the center of the confrontation.

Cellphone video shows protesters shouting at agents, repeatedly telling them they did not have a warrant as an agent smashed the vehicle's window. Shattered glass can be seen on the ground.

Calkins said she did not believe protesters had instigated the violence.

"At no point did any of the protesters instigate violence, but at every point, the ICE agents chose it," she said. Video also captures an agent approaching a protester who was holding a cellphone. The protester does not appear to be blocking the agents when the officer shoves him and sprays him with what appears to be pepper spray. Calkins can be heard yelling, "He did nothing to you! What are you doing?"

The confrontation also affected the couple who had offered the man a ride. Video shows the woman standing near her vehicle questioning why an agent sprayed her. "He sprayed me! Why did he spray me?" she can be heard saying. Her husband was also pepper-sprayed as he tried to get to his wife.

The man ICE agents were pursuing was eventually arrested and taken away.

What they're saying:

The Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department said its personnel were not involved in the federal immigration enforcement operation.

In a statement attributed to the Santa Clarita Valley Sheriff’s Station, the department said ICE agents did not notify station personnel before making the arrests and did not use any secured facilities connected to the station to stage or initiate the operation.

The department also said it did not notify ICE about the individuals’ impending release from custody and did not coordinate any transfer into federal custody.

According to the Sheriff’s Department, the arrests happened in a public area, after the individuals had been released from custody and outside any Sheriff’s Department facility. The department noted that federal immigration officials, like members of the public, have the right to access public areas of sensitive locations, as long as they do not disrupt county operations. The sheriff’s department emphasized that it does not participate in civil immigration enforcement and does not ask people about their immigration status when responding to calls for service.

It also acknowledged that immigration enforcement can create fear and uncertainty in the community, adding that everyone should be treated humanely.

What's next:

FOX 11 contacted the Department of Homeland Security seeking more information about the arrest, the man’s identity and the circumstances surrounding the confrontation.

The DHS has not responded.

text:
The Port of Seattle released a statement about a Saturday morning incident involving U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents and at least one passenger at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport.

In videos circulating on social media, two passengers can be seen being detained by masked ICE agents. Various social media pages have posted the video, which ranges from about 1 to 2 minutes.

Plenty of screaming can be heard in the video, which shows a woman and a man seated on the bridge before boarding a plane at the feet of two ICE agents. The woman in the video can be heard saying, "We have a work permit," to the person holding the camera before beginning to cry while screaming "no" multiple times.

The relationship between the man and the woman in the video is unclear at this time.

What they're saying:

The Port of Seattle said the passengers were preparing to board an Alaska Airlines flight to Los Angeles on Saturday when immigration enforcement agents conducted an operation without the Port's participation or knowledge.

"The Port has continually asked, and local federal immigration authorities have previously agreed to protocols at SEA, and we are in conversation with DHS on whether any of these protocols were breached," the agency said. "This incident was not only distressing for the affected family but for the passengers around them, and Port officials continue to engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred."

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson shared a statement on the incident as well, saying, "ICE is completely and totally out of control. Like many Americans, I’m outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities. Today’s actions at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport are just the latest example of ICE’s deeply un-American tactics. I’ll have more to say this afternoon."

The governor also posted a link to the video from his Facebook account, which can be seen below. The video posted by Ferguson is about 38 seconds long and shows three masked ICE agents walking with a woman while she is handcuffed. Other videos circulating social media show different portions of the interaction.

Alaska Airlines also released a statement on the incident, saying, "We understand that situations like this can be distressing. The law enforcement activity was not previously known to us, and we are actively reviewing the details and engaging with the appropriate contacts and authorities. The safety and well-being of our guests and employees remain our top priority."

Attorney General Nick Brown posted to social media later in the day, saying, "We are sick and tired of poorly trained masked federal agents vanishing people out of thin air. Washingtonians will never accept these stunts as legitimate or responsible law enforcement."

Mayor Katie Wilson also posted about the arrests, saying, "I am outraged by videos of masked ICE agents causing chaos and dragging a woman off the jetway at Sea-Tac airport. These tactics are unacceptable and un-American."

"Seattle will continue to stand as sanctuary city, and we are in active communication with the Port of Seattle and Governor Ferguson to hold the line against these abuses throughout our region," the mayor said.

Congressman Adam Smith said the situation was "absolutely unacceptable."

"ICE’s conduct across our country is putting people in harm’s way, undermining public trust, and stoking fear in our communities. I am incredibly concerned about the conduct of immigration enforcement and believe that ICE is operating as a paramilitary force that is a profound threat to our community. There is no question that this agency needs to be reined in before causing more chaos and fear," he wrote on social media.

SEA policy on federal immigration enforcement

Dig deeper:

On its website, SEA acknowledges that some travelers that use the airport have various pending immigration applications, but adds that it has no jurisdiction over U.S. Customs and Border Protection or ICE operations.

"Immigration enforcement actions at SEA are conducted without the Port’s participation or knowledge. For this reason, we encourage individuals to assess their individual circumstances before traveling. For additional transparency, we’ve answered some common questions about immigration enforcement activity at the airport," the airport says.

The airport adds that those who are traveling with an uncertain immigration status, share your travel itinerary and immigration attorney's contact information with a family member or friend. It also urges people facing these circumstances to memorize their immigration attorney's contact information and emergency contact information.

Previous ICE operations in Washington

Local perspective:

Saturday's incident marks the second known occurrence within the last month where ICE has arrested multiple people.

In late October, five Mexican men arrested by immigration agents while camping with their families in Washington’s Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest over Labor Day weekend.

The men, who spent about six weeks in immigration detention at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, returned home on Oct. 15. In FOX 13's report in October, all five were forced to wear ankle monitors as they awaited the next steps in their immigration cases.

Related

Additionally, earlier in the month of October, surveillance video from a Lynnwood tire shop showed the moments a 26-year-old employee walked outside and was taken into custody by masked federal agents.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested a Princeton University Ph.D. student at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Thursday as she was preparing to fly back to New Jersey after presenting her research at a conference, her adviser said.

Eva Yi Xie, a third-year neuroscience student from China, has had an asylum application pending for 10 years after her family came to the U.S. when she was 14, according to her attorney, Kerry Doyle. The Department of Homeland Security said Xie was in the country illegally, which Doyle disputed, saying she had permission to live, work and study in the country while her case was pending.

“Her arrest and detention is without legal basis as ICE and DHS are fully aware,” Doyle told NBC News.

DHS said in a statement about her arrest that Xie was admitted to the United States temporarily in March 2016 and was required to leave by Sept. 15 of that year. The agency said she stayed past that date.

“Xie has NEVER held valid authorization to study in the United States,” the statement said. “To be clear, a pending application does not confer legal status in the United States.”

Xie, 24, was being held at the Caroline Detention Facility in Bowling Green, Virginia, according to a detainee search on ICE’s website.

Doyle filed a habeas corpus petition in federal court in Virginia challenging the legality of Xie’s arrest. She argued that ICE had no grounds to arrest Xie without a warrant because Xie was not a flight risk or a danger to the community.

Doyle said people with pending asylum cases “have permission to be here” while their cases are decided.

“It’s their over-the-top enforcement used as a way to scare people,” Doyle said. She called Xie’s arrest “an incredible waste of time and resources — to what end?”

The Trump administration has detained asylum-seekers and others with pending immigration applications as part of its broader immigration crackdown.

In its statement on Xie’s arrest, DHS repeated a warning it issued in recent press releases, saying it was working to prevent people it considered to be in the country illegally from flying domestically.

Xie’s adviser, Carlos Brody, described the research she presented at the conference in an emailed statement.

“There, Eva described her work discovering and researching an unexpected link between how brains make decisions and how they navigate through space,” Brody said.

Brody said Xie mentors undergraduates and sent messages to colleagues from the detention center “to make sure that her experiments could move forward and the grant applications she is part of could be submitted.”

“Eva is a gentle, kind, caring person who is contributing enormously to the United States,” Brody added. “She belongs back home in Princeton, doing the science that she loves, and helping our country excel and grow.”

Princeton’s graduate school dean, Rodney D. Priestley, said that Eva’s arrest “is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community.”

“The University has arranged for Eva to be represented by legal counsel, and we will remain in contact with her legal team, her family, and colleagues to provide support,” Priestley said in a statement. “We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton.”

Xie’s attorney did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Saturday.

According to Xie’s professional biography page, she graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2024 with degrees in computer science and mathematics. She was helping to plan a cognitive computational neuroscience conference in the U.K. in 2027, according to the page.

text:
GRAHAM, N.C. -- As he ran for sheriff in North Carolina against a longtime incumbent who had joined forces with the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, Shannon Long found his campaign van was an obstacle with some voters.

The trust between law enforcement and Alamance County's growing Latino community was so fractured, Long said, that the vehicle emblazoned with “sheriff” made it a struggle to get some people to speak with him.

“They’ve been living in fear. They feel like they don’t have a voice. They have been suppressed, oppressed; a lot of them are depressed. So they feel that they live in a community where they don’t belong,” Long, a pastor, business owner and former sheriff’s deputy, told The Associated Press two weeks after defeating Republican Sheriff Terry Johnson in a campaign that some activists, voters and local officials say turned partly on questions about immigration enforcement and the treatment of Latino residents.

Johnson is one of a few sheriffs around the country who were ousted by challengers critical of their cooperation with President Donald Trump’s push for mass deportations of people in the country illegally. While only a smattering, the results could spell trouble for other sheriffs who are seen as participants in Trump’s crackdown and possibly hinder agreements that have become a cornerstone of the administration's efforts.

Johnson was among the first sheriffs to allow his deputies to enforce federal immigration laws under what’s known as a 287(g) agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Long, who ran as an independent, promised to curtail cooperation with ICE, which continues to rely on the cooperative pacts to boost arrest numbers despite a one-time infusion of $75 billion from Congress and hiring about 12,000 officers.

The administration has more than 2,700 such pacts with state and local agencies, up from 135 when Trump began his second term. The agreements, predominantly in the South, have deputized over 29,000 local law officers and resulted in more than 6,600 arrests in July, about 15% of all ICE arrests, according to government data obtained by the Deportation Data Project that was analyzed by the advocacy group fwd.us.

The AP reviewed about 250 elections held this month for sheriffs whose offices had 287(g) agreements, identifying races in Indiana, Maryland, North Carolina, Wisconsin and elsewhere in which ICE pacts played a role in a candidate's defeat. Many sheriffs who ran this year were unopposed. But the ICE agreements could become a focus again in two years, when sheriffs from Florida, Texas and other states with large numbers of 287(g) agreements are up for election.

Alamance County is a longtime Republican stronghold of just under 200,000 residents that sits between Greensboro and the Research Triangle metropolitan area that includes Raleigh, Durham and Chapel Hill. It has become more politically competitive as its population has grown increasingly diverse — from 750 residents who identified as Hispanic in the 1990 census to nearly 25,000 in 2020. The sheriff's office currently participates in the 287(g) program, a spokesman confirmed, though last year it ended an agreement to house ICE detainees.

Johnson, who is white, was first elected in 2002 and has been a prominent and polarizing figure. He has insisted he welcomes lawful immigrants and denied persistent allegations — including in a Justice Department lawsuit over a decade ago that ended with a settlement — that his office racially profiled minority residents.

The county acquired the moniker “No Chance Alamance” because of a perceived sense of unjust policing and a lack of political representation among Black and Latino residents, school board member Seneca Rogers said.

Johnson initially said in a phone call that immigration policy could have contributed to his loss. But in a brief interview later, he said it likely didn't and laid blame with his long tenure and a national political environment that was brutal for Republicans, acutely so in North Carolina, where Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper flipped a U.S. Senate seat, winning by nearly 20 percentage points. He said he always followed the law and protected public safety.

Activists and longtime residents said the Latino community — and to some extent, the Black community — feared engaging with the sheriff's office and described a sense that non-white residents were far likelier to be pulled over or detained after a traffic stop. Some people were afraid to call 911 or even go to work, said community organizer Leslie Arevalo.

Voter Renee Russell said the sheriff’s cooperation with ICE gave a false impression of Alamance as unwelcoming. She was excited to see fresh leadership. Long will be the county’s first Black sheriff, local media reported.

But Republican state Sen. Amy Galey, whose district includes the county, defended Johnson's record. She said he had worked to improve training opportunities and mental health services. Although Galey didn't think immigration played a big role in the race, she wondered if hard-line ICE tactics elsewhere could have contributed to simmering concerns about law enforcement more broadly.

The sheriff’s office in Frederick County, Maryland, northwest of Washington, D.C., was another longtime participant in the 287(g) program. Since 2008, the county detained and turned over 1,884 people to ICE, Republican Sheriff Chuck Jenkins said. But that came to a halt this year when Democratic Gov. Wes Moore signed a law banning immigration enforcement pacts with the federal government.

Public sentiment also turned against Jenkins, who said the program made the community safer but acknowledged it likely cost him reelection. U.S. District Judge Randy Crane granted the federal government's motion to dismiss a lawsuit brought by a Donna, Texas family, in an order signed November 9, 2026. The case was dismissed without prejudice after the court found the family had not shown a real and immediate threat of future injury.

Why it matters

The ruling means the family's claims over the January 9 entry into their home will not proceed in this case, though the dismissal is without prejudice. It also shows how standing requirements can determine whether challenges to immigration enforcement actions reach the merits in Texas federal courts.

The court ruling is a federal order signed November 9, 2026, granting the government's September 3, 2026 motion to dismiss. Whether the family will refile or appeal is not yet known, and the allegations have not been decided on the merits.

The players

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement

The federal agency responsible for immigration enforcement within the United States, including arrests and home visits in the interior.

Randy Crane

A U.S. District Judge in the Southern District of Texas who presided over the case and granted the government's motion to dismiss.

The details

The lawsuit, filed February 18, 2026, accused ICE officers of entering the family's home on January 9, 2026, using an administrative warrant. A video obtained by Channel 5 News shows agents jumping a fence into the family's yard around 7 a.m. The parents are noncitizens in the process of obtaining lawful permanent resident status, and the mother was later deported to Mexico.

Timeline

January 9, 2026: ICE enters the family's home in Donna around 7 a.m.

February 18, 2026: The family files suit in federal court.

September 3, 2026: The government moves to dismiss the case.

November 9, 2026: Judge Randy Crane signs the order dismissing the lawsuit without prejudice.

Related coverage

Immigration

Government

Nov. 19

Law

Nov. 7

Justice Department Joins Texas Suit Against Planned Parenthood

Legal Context

The dismissal turns on the Article III standing requirement that plaintiffs demonstrate a real and immediate threat of future injury, a test that has repeatedly shaped whether challenges to federal enforcement actions reach the merits. The outcome fits that pattern even though the family's past injury from the January entry was alleged.

Texas residents, especially mixed-status families, may see that a federal court found a family lacked standing to sue over an in-home enforcement entry, leaving that route closed for now. The dismissal being without prejudice means the family could potentially bring a new case if circumstances change.

Families facing immigration enforcement at home should consult an immigration attorney promptly, since standing rules can determine whether a lawsuit proceeds at all. Documenting any entry, including video and timing, can matter for any later claim.

text:
GRAHAM, N.C. (AP) — As he ran for sheriff in North Carolina against a longtime incumbent who had joined forces with the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, Shannon Long found his campaign van was an obstacle with some voters.

The trust between law enforcement and Alamance County's growing Latino community was so fractured, Long said, that the vehicle emblazoned with “sheriff” made it a struggle to get some people to speak with him.

“They’ve been living in fear. They feel like they don’t have a voice. They have been suppressed, oppressed; a lot of them are depressed. So they feel that they live in a community where they don’t belong,” Long, a pastor, business owner and former sheriff’s deputy, told The Associated Press two weeks after defeating Republican Sheriff Terry Johnson in a campaign that some activists, voters and local officials say turned partly on questions about immigration enforcement and the treatment of Latino residents.

Johnson is one of a few sheriffs around the country who were ousted by challengers critical of their cooperation with President Donald Trump’s push for mass deportations of people in the country illegally. While only a smattering, the results could spell trouble for other sheriffs who are seen as participants in Trump’s crackdown and possibly hinder agreements that have become a cornerstone of the administration's efforts.

Johnson was among the first sheriffs to allow his deputies to enforce federal immigration laws under what’s known as a 287(g) agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Long, who ran as an independent, promised to curtail cooperation with ICE, which continues to rely on the cooperative pacts to boost arrest numbers despite a one-time infusion of $75 billion from Congress and hiring about 12,000 officers.

The administration has more than 2,700 such pacts with state and local agencies, up from 135 when Trump began his second term. The agreements, predominantly in the South, have deputized over 29,000 local law officers and resulted in more than 6,600 arrests in July, about 15% of all ICE arrests, according to government data obtained by the Deportation Data Project that was analyzed by the advocacy group fwd.us.

The AP reviewed about 250 elections held this month for sheriffs whose offices had 287(g) agreements, identifying races in Indiana, Maryland, North Carolina, Wisconsin and elsewhere in which ICE pacts played a role in a candidate's defeat. Many sheriffs who ran this year were unopposed. But the ICE agreements could become a focus again in two years, when sheriffs from Florida, Texas and other states with large numbers of 287(g) agreements are up for election.

A new sheriff is coming to ‘No Chance Alamance'

Alamance County is a longtime Republican stronghold of just under 200,000 residents that sits between Greensboro and the Research Triangle metropolitan area that includes Raleigh, Durham and Chapel Hill. It has become more politically competitive as its population has grown increasingly diverse — from 750 residents who identified as Hispanic in the 1990 census to nearly 25,000 in 2020. The sheriff's office currently participates in the 287(g) program, a spokesman confirmed, though last year it ended an agreement to house ICE detainees.

Johnson, who is white, was first elected in 2002 and has been a prominent and polarizing figure. He has insisted he welcomes lawful immigrants and denied persistent allegations — including in a Justice Department lawsuit over a decade ago that ended with a settlement — that his office racially profiled minority residents.

The county acquired the moniker “No Chance Alamance” because of a perceived sense of unjust policing and a lack of political representation among Black and Latino residents, school board member Seneca Rogers said.

Johnson initially said in a phone call that immigration policy could have contributed to his loss. But in a brief interview later, he said it likely didn't and laid blame with his long tenure and a national political environment that was brutal for Republicans, acutely so in North Carolina, where Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper flipped a U.S. Senate seat, winning by nearly 20 percentage points. He said he always followed the law and protected public safety.

Activists and longtime residents said the Latino community — and to some extent, the Black community — feared engaging with the sheriff's office and described a sense that non-white residents were far likelier to be pulled over or detained after a traffic stop. Some people were afraid to call 911 or even go to work, said community organizer Leslie Arevalo.

Voter Renee Russell said the sheriff’s cooperation with ICE gave a false impression of Alamance as unwelcoming. She was excited to see fresh leadership. Long will be the county’s first Black sheriff, local media reported.

But Republican state Sen. Amy Galey, whose district includes the county, defended Johnson's record. She said he had worked to improve training opportunities and mental health services. Although Galey didn't think immigration played a big role in the race, she wondered if hard-line ICE tactics elsewhere could have contributed to simmering concerns about law enforcement more broadly.

text:
The arrest of a man in the parking lot of the Santa Clarita Valley Sheriff’s Station on Friday escalated following a standoff involving U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers and local protesters, culminating in a car window being shattered and at least two protesters being pepper sprayed while trying to disrupt the arrest.

The Santa Clarita Valley Sheriff’s Station was not coordinating with federal agents, who were there conducting their own operation independent of sheriff’s personnel, according to Sgt. Jerome Gage.

It was unclear at the scene who was being arrested by the agents, or what charges the person has faced or will face. Public affairs officers from the Los Angeles office for Immigration and Customs Enforcement have not yet responded to a request for comment Friday regarding the arrest.

Federal agents present during the operation gave no comment.

The activity, which occurred in the station’s parking lot on Golden Valley Road, began at 8:30 a.m., according to Gage.

Castaic resident Dan Chapman said he spotted unmarked vehicles occupied by federal agents in the local station parking lot as early as 6:50 a.m. Friday. Chapman is a volunteer with Valley Defensa, which is comprised of people who monitor immigration enforcement activity and organize protests against ICE.

Chapman said he witnessed federal agents attempt to take one person into custody from the sheriff’s station gate where people are released after detainment.

“ICE was at the gate, waiting for them to come out, and then they didn’t come out. They’re still inside,” he said at the time.

About a dozen protesters gathered once word spread about a possible ICE presence at the station.

“They want to come and help out,” Chapman said. “There’s a lot of talk about reforming ICE or getting them to take their masks off, but there’s nothing short of abolishment that is going to change this situation.”

Chapman noted that local sheriff’s station officials may not be happy with the protesters’ presence but “this is what’s going to happen every time ICE comes here,” he said.

At approximately 11:30 a.m., a confrontation between federal agents and protesters escalated outside the SCV Sheriff’s Station.

Federal agents instructed the occupants of a white vehicle attempting to exit the parking lot to lower their windows and identify themselves as protesters shouted and recorded the interaction.

After the occupants did not comply with the instructions, federal agents broke the rear driver’s side window of the vehicle, removed a man and took him into custody.

At least two people, including Chapman, were pepper sprayed during the confrontation.

The incident comes after two others were taken into custody on Nov. 5 following their release from the SCV Sheriff’s Station.

After the Nov. 5 incident, Nicole Nishida, a spokeswoman for the L.A. County Sheriff’s Department, stated in an email that the operations in the station’s parking lot did not violate L.A. County’s “Sensitive Locations Policy,” which the county Board of Supervisors approved in November 2025.

“ICE agents did NOT notify the station prior to the arrests. It appears that they used the public parking lot in front of the station (emphasis hers). The arrests occurred after the individuals had been released from custody and outside any Sheriff’s Department facility. Station personnel did NOT notify ICE of their impending release and did NOT coordinate any transfer of the individuals into ICE custody,” Nishida wrote in an email after the Nov. 5 incident.

She reiterated those statements on Friday.

To read about the two previous ICE detainments, go to signalscv.com/2026/11/two-detained-by-ice-outside-scv-sheriffs-station.

text:
Rights organizations and legal aid groups are preparing amicus briefs and other filings ahead of case before the Supreme Court next month over the Trump administration’s so-called third country deportations.

The process sends immigrants and asylum seekers to countries they have no ties to though a series of binational agreements.

More than 25,000 people have been sent to countries other than their own since the practice began last year.

Alma David is compiling their stories as a consultant with the National Immigration Litigation Alliance.

She says among those arrested is a Honduran woman who was working as a pastor in Texas for years. She has what’s called withholding of removal for than a decade — it’s a status given by an immigration judge that prevents someone from being sent back to their home country because of specific threats they’d face.

Recipients of the status have to do regular check-ins with ICE. David says the pastor was arrested during a check-in this summer.

“She was taken into custody, and within a few days had been deported to Mexico, and from Mexico was then basically right away deported onward to Honduras,” David said.

They can often get a work permit and are legally allowed to remain in the U.S., but have no path to U.S. citizenship or permanent legal status.

David says up until this year, people with withholding-of-removal status were rarely deported.

“They were told, you know, welcome to the United States, as long as you don’t commit any serious crimes you can live here, you can get your work permit every year.

But now, under agreements with at least 31 countries, many are being sent to places where they have no ties.

The pastor is one of at least 310 deportees with protective orders from U.S. judges, according to rights groups.

Some, like the pastor, are then sent back to the country they fled.

The Supreme Court hears the case Dec. 9.

The AP reviewed about 250 elections held this month for sheriffs whose offices had 287(g) agreements, identifying races in Indiana, Maryland, North Carolina, Wisconsin and elsewhere in which ICE pacts played a role in a candidate's defeat. Many sheriffs who ran this year were unopposed. But the ICE agreements could become a focus again in two years, when sheriffs from Florida, Texas and other states with large numbers of 287(g) agreements are up for election.

A new sheriff is coming to ‘No Chance Alamance'

Alamance County is a longtime Republican stronghold of just under 200,000 residents that sits between Greensboro and the Research Triangle metropolitan area that includes Raleigh, Durham and Chapel Hill. It has become more politically competitive as its population has grown increasingly diverse — from 750 residents who identified as Hispanic in the 1990 census to nearly 25,000 in 2020. The sheriff's office currently participates in the 287(g) program, a spokesman confirmed, though last year it ended an agreement to house ICE detainees.

Johnson, who is white, was first elected in 2002 and has been a prominent and polarizing figure. He has insisted he welcomes lawful immigrants and denied persistent allegations — including in a Justice Department lawsuit over a decade ago that ended with a settlement — that his office racially profiled minority residents.

The county acquired the moniker “No Chance Alamance” because of a perceived sense of unjust policing and a lack of political representation among Black and Latino residents, school board member Seneca Rogers said.

Johnson initially said in a phone call that immigration policy could have contributed to his loss. But in a brief interview later, he said it likely didn't and laid blame with his long tenure and a national political environment that was brutal for Republicans, acutely so in North Carolina, where Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper flipped a U.S. Senate seat, winning by nearly 20 percentage points. He said he always followed the law and protected public safety.

Activists and longtime residents said the Latino community — and to some extent, the Black community — feared engaging with the sheriff's office and described a sense that non-white residents were far likelier to be pulled over or detained after a traffic stop. Some people were afraid to call 911 or even go to work, said community organizer Leslie Arevalo.

Voter Renee Russell said the sheriff’s cooperation with ICE gave a false impression of Alamance as unwelcoming. She was excited to see fresh leadership. Long will be the county’s first Black sheriff, local media reported.

But Republican state Sen. Amy Galey, whose district includes the county, defended Johnson's record. She said he had worked to improve training opportunities and mental health services. Although Galey didn't think immigration played a big role in the race, she wondered if hard-line ICE tactics elsewhere could have contributed to simmering concerns about law enforcement more broadly.

Candidates who ba

cked ICE cooperatio

n lost elsewhere

The sheriff’s office in Frederick County, Maryland, northwest of Washington, D.C., was another longtime participant in the 287(g) program. Since 2008, the county detained and turned over 1,884 people to ICE, Republican Sheriff Chuck Jenkins said. But that came to a halt this year when Democratic Gov. Wes Moore signed a law banning immigration enforcement pacts with the federal government.

Public sentiment also turned against Jenkins, who said the program made the community safer but acknowledged it likely cost him reelection. He was defeated by Democrat Karl Bickel, a retired U.S. Department of Justice employee who had lost four previous elections to Jenkins and pledged not to cooperate with ICE.

“In general, people are fed up with the sheriff’s negativeness about immigrants,” said retired social worker Carol Antoniewicz, who distributed emails, social media posts and campaign literature in support of Bickel.

In Wisconsin’s Winnebago County, ICE’s arrest and detention of a schoolteacher weeks before Election Day sparked backlash against anyone seemingly supportive of immigration officers, including a Republican vying to replace a retiring sheriff.

“Any kind of perceived alignment definitely is considered a liability at this point,” said Molly Smiltneek, a local advocate and immigration lawyer who attended a vigil for the teacher.

Though the sheriff’s department had nothing to do with the teacher’s arrest, its 287(g) agreement became central to the campaign, boosting Democrat Jason Rippl, who promised to end it.

A newly elected sheriff seeks a better community partnership

Long, who formerly worked as a deputy in a neighboring North Carolina county, said he will uphold the law in his new role and hold offenders accountable. But he said he won't participate in the 287(g) program.

He has set up meetings with the Latino community in the hopes of building new relationships.

“I want them to see the sheriff’s office in the community, creating a partnership, letting them know that they have a voice. … There’s no need to operate in fear,” he said.

___

Schuettler reported from Phoenix and Lieb from Jefferson City, Missouri. Associated Press journalist Allen G. Breed contributed from Graham.
