text:
Among its findings was that more than 3,500 ICE recruits with prior law enforcement experience were allowed to complete their basic training virtually.

“Previously, the training was done fully in person at a training center over the course of a month. Using the online option, some officers completed the training in less than a day,” the Times reported.

Noem, whose 14-month tenure at DHS earned her the nickname “ICE Barbie” for her fondness for dressing up in tactical gear, was ousted by President Donald Trump in March following a string of controversies, including the fatal shootings of two American citizens in Minneapolis.

According to the Times, it wasn’t just the 3,500 recruits with prior law enforcement experience who benefited from the relaxed requirements.

The draft report also revealed that DHS scrapped a policy giving recruits just two chances to pass a training test, instead allowing unlimited attempts as it raced to bolster ICE’s ranks.

One recruit needed 32 tries to pass, according to the Times.

The report acknowledged that current DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin reinstated stricter training standards in July but warned that significant gaps remain.

“Despite increasing training hours and days for future recruits, ICE has not fully addressed training gaps born of the reductions and revisions,” it stated.

The 19-page draft report, prepared by the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Inspector General, has yet to be finalized or made public. The Times described it as “a sweeping critique” of Noem’s rush to hire and deploy 10,000 new officers, backed by tens of billions of dollars in funding approved by the then-Republican-controlled Congress.

One ICE training instructor quoted in the report called the rollback of training standards a “catastrophic failure.”

Although the report did not examine whether the training cuts contributed to deadly confrontations between ICE agents and civilians, at least one officer involved in a recent fatal incident was hired while the relaxed standards were in place.

David Brouillette was hired in December 2025, and fatally shot Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old Colombian immigrant, in Maine during a vehicle stop in July.

DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but an ICE spokesperson told the Times that “a significant portion of officers brought on during the hiring surge have law enforcement experience and have already successfully completed a law enforcement academy.”

DHS Inspector General Joseph V. Cuffari told the Times that his office strongly condemned “the premature release of draft reports before the department has had the opportunity to complete its review and provide formal comments.”

“Such disclosures undermine the integrity of the oversight process, risk presenting incomplete or misleading information, and compromise the fairness and accuracy essential to credible oversight,” he added.

The DHS inspector general’s office, Noem, and the White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

text:
EL PASO, Texas (KTSM) -- An El Paso family who was detained for a month at an Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in South Texas were released and arrived home late Friday night, Nov. 20 in El Paso.

Michell German, her 11-year-old sister and parents had been in ICE custody since October. Michell German is a senior at El Paso High School and a member of the school's dance team.

Human rights group rallies for El Paso High student in ICE custody

The family had been held at the immigration detention facility in Dilley, Texas near San Antonio.

State Rep. Vince Perez, D-El Paso, was at the airport when the German family arrived back in El Paso late Friday night.

"We're very happy to have Michell and her sister, Paola, and their parents back home in El Paso," Perez said. "They were in detention for nearly a month at the Dilley facility outside of San Antonio. You know, it's a terrible experience. You know what they went through."

Perez added: "It is, in my opinion, just morally wrong to detain children this way for nearly a month. And I think the people of Texas are also seeing just how wrong it is to put people through these situations."

The case first gained notoriety when U.S. Rep. Joaquin Castro posted about the family online and called on the federal government to release them.

Others including U.S. Rep. Veronica Escobar, a Democrat who represents the El Paso area, have also called on the federal government to release the family. Friday, a group of more than 50 Democratic members or members-elect to the Texas House of Representatives also joined the chorus.

57 Texas House Democrats push for release of El Paso teen, family held in ICE custody

Tuesday, the Border Network for Human Rights held a rally where El Paso turned out to show support for the family.

Here is a statement from the attorney who represents the German family:

"There is real beauty in this family, in the community that supports them, and in the leaders who stood by them: Congressman Castro, Congresswoman Escobar, Representative Vince Perez, and Beto O'Rourke. Along with everyone who rallied around them, they show the positive side of a situation like this. This family finally gets to come home to a community that stood for them in their absence.

"But we cannot ignore the injustice and the horror of what has happened to this family, and what happens to families like them. It is never OK to detain children, and the Dilley detention center needs to be closed immediately.

"Pablo and Dolores came to this country with their daughters, seeking a safer and better life. They followed the rules. They had valid work permits. And yet they were treated like criminals and detained on their way to school one day. That is not something that should happen in this country, or anywhere in the world.

"We are thankful to everyone who cared about this family and helped amplify their story. I will continue to fight for families like this one until we see an end to family detention, and to the detention of children under any circumstances."

Rochester, N.Y. (WHAM) — Demonstrators outside Rochester's Keating Federal Building Friday called for an end to the expansion of an ICE detention facility in Batavia while welcoming news that federal officials had withdrawn plans for a detention facility in downtown Rochester.

BACKGROUND: Trump admin no longer planning detention center in downtown Rochester, Democrats say

Sens. Chuck Schumer and Kirsten Gillibrand and Rep. Joe Morelle announced Friday that U.S. Customs and Border Protection was no longer seeking to build a small detention facility inside the Keating Federal Building.

The General Services Administration, which manages the building, notified the federal court that CBP had withdrawn its request for space, according to the lawmakers' joint statement. A court representative said the notification was communicated verbally.

"CBP has an ongoing operational requirement in Rochester," a spokesperson for the agency said. "After evaluation, CBP determined that the proposed GSA-owned space in the Keating Federal Building does not meet our operational requirements. CBP is currently evaluating alternative courses of action to meet our facility operational requirements in the area."

"It's been and will continue to be a long fight," one demonstrator said outside the building Friday.

"The Trump administration's cruel immigration agenda is tearing families apart and treating human beings as little more than numbers in a detention system," said Marcia Glenn, an activist with Indivisible Outreach.

"This is what happens when the people of Rochester Stand ROC Solid," Mayor Malik Evans said in a statement. "The Federal Administration did not cancel its plan to install cages in Downtown Rochester because they came to their senses and concluded it was a good idea. They backed down because we fought back from day one..."

Despite the announcement, dozens of demonstrators gathered outside the building Friday to oppose the ongoing expansion of the Buffalo Service Processing Center, an ICE detention facility in Batavia. The project includes a new 100-bed facility.

13WHAM reported in February that the facility was holding nearly 100 more detainees than its 650-bed capacity. Immigration advocates said the growing population raised concerns about overcrowding and conditions inside.

"Expanding the ICE detention facility in Batavia would put even more of our neighbors at risk," Glenn said.

"These activists should be thanking our law enforcement for removing dangerous criminals from the United States — NOT vilifying law enforcement," an ICE spokesperson said in response to the demonstrations. "While these people smear ICE, law enforcement is arresting criminals and saving countless American lives."

"The Trump Administration is utilizing all lawful options to carry out the largest deportation operation in history, just as President Trump promised," the spokesperson added.

"It's a testing ground for authoritarianism," said Carlton Huff, an activist with Metro Justice. "It's the administration seeing how much they can get away with, and we know the others that they'll target."

text:
A federal judge on Friday declined to release from custody a man who was shot and wounded by immigration officers as they arrested him in New York in October.

The US district court judge Hector Gonzalez said in a written ruling that agents may have made a procedural error in serving an arrest warrant on Oscar Belgal before he was given a notice to appear in immigration court. However, he wrote, that was merely a technical error that does not require Belgal to be released from federal custody pending deportation proceedings.

Belgal, a 28-year-old Dominican national, entered the US illegally in 2021, and about two years later he was arrested on robbery and other charges and eventually pleaded guilty to grand larceny. He was given a sentence of probation, and in 2025 he was arrested again, this time on allegations that he attempted to sell controlled substances. That case remains pending.

On 8 October, amid the Trump administration’s ongoing immigration crackdown, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents found him as he was driving his five-year-old son home from school.

Security camera footage released by the New York City police shows an officer dressed in plainclothes running up to the car with his gun pointed at Belgal, then immediately using the barrel of his gun to bash in the driver’s side window. A second officer then draws his gun as Belgal pulls out, away from the two officers. The chase ends moments later, with Belgal’s bullet-riddled car coming to rest.

Belgal was struck in the shoulder and neck. His son was not injured. His attorneys said he didn’t learn the men were ICE officers until he awoke later in the hospital.

“It is unconscionable that Mr Belgal should have to endure another day in detention, separated from his family, particularly given everything he has already suffered,” said a written statement from the Legal Aid Society, a non-profit law firm that represents him.

Federal officials maintained that ICE officers fired their weapons because they believed their lives were in danger. They said Belgal smashed his car into two government vehicles and “accelerated toward other officers”.

His attorneys said the agents did not have a valid warrant and never identified themselves before running up to Belgal’s car, smashing a window and firing several shots inside. The lawyers also argued in their filings that Belgal’s due process rights were violated because he was subjected to “unreasonable use of extreme force” during his arrest.

The judge disagreed that the agents did not have a valid warrant. And the petition Belgal filed for release from custody was not an appropriate venue for arguing that the agents used excessive force, he said.

Gonzalez noted that Belgal can still ask the immigration court to release him on bond.

The federal government has acknowledged that an Austin man deported to Mexico following a Central Texas traffic stop in April is a U.S. citizen, reversing its earlier position as it seeks to dismiss a lawsuit accusing immigration agents of violating his constitutional rights.

Brian José Morales García, 25, was born in Denver and is a dual citizen of the United States and Mexico, federal attorneys said in a motion filed Friday in U.S. District Court in Austin. The acknowledgment comes nearly seven months after U.S. Border Patrol agents sent him to Mexico despite his repeated claims that he was American.

In the same filing, federal attorneys asked U.S. District Judge Robert Pitman to dismiss Morales García's lawsuit, arguing that federal immigration officers are protected from certain civil claims arising from their enforcement of immigration laws. The government maintains that Morales García voluntarily agreed to return to Mexico and disputes his allegations that agents pressured him into doing so.

The admission is a reversal of the government's previous position. In April, U.S. Customs and Border Protection told the American-Statesman that it had not arrested a U.S. citizen, saying records showed Morales García was in the country illegally.

Morales García returned to Texas on Aug. 30 after his attorneys provided additional documentation supporting his citizenship and reached an agreement with the Justice Department. His lawsuit, which seeks monetary damages and other relief, remains pending.

How an Austin man was deported after a traffic stop

Morales García was riding in a pickup truck with coworkers near Fredericksburg on April 3 when a Texas Department of Public Safety trooper pulled over the vehicle for an alleged window tint violation.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Morales García, who speaks Spanish and was not carrying identification, told officers that he was born in Colorado and had a birth certificate and Social Security card at his Austin home, according to his lawsuit. Authorities contacted federal immigration agents, and Morales García was taken to the Gillespie County Jail before being transferred to Border Patrol custody.

Four days later, he was sent to Mexico.

The American-Statesman previously reviewed copies of Morales García's Colorado birth certificate, hospital documents and baptismal records and independently confirmed the existence of records supporting his birth in Denver.

His citizenship became a central dispute in the lawsuit he filed May 1 against federal immigration officials and state and local law enforcement officers.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

At a June hearing, Pitman declined to immediately order Morales García's return, citing conflicting birth records from the United States and Mexico. The judge instead directed both sides to gather additional evidence.

Morales García's attorneys subsequently obtained further documentation, including hospital records and witness statements, before the federal government agreed to permit his return in August.

Federal attorneys defend agents' actions

The government's latest filing provides a detailed account of how Border Patrol agents concluded Morales García was born in Mexico, even as federal attorneys now acknowledge his American citizenship.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

According to the motion, Border Patrol Agent Robert Gil Jr. questioned Morales García at the Gillespie County Jail and checked a Mexican government identification database after Morales García said he did not have his birth certificate.

Gil found a Mexican registration record identifying Morales García as having been born in Zacatecas, Mexico. The agent said Morales García also told him he was born there after being warned that providing false information could result in criminal charges.

Based on that information, Gil concluded Morales García was in the United States illegally, according to the filing.

Federal attorneys contend that the agent explained Morales García's options, including appearing before an immigration judge or voluntarily returning to Mexico. They said Morales García chose to return and signed immigration forms confirming his decision.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Morales García has offered a different account.

In his lawsuit, he alleges agents repeatedly accused him of lying about his citizenship and threatened him with imprisonment. He said he eventually falsely claimed to have entered the country illegally because he feared prolonged detention and believed agreeing to leave was his only realistic option.

His attorneys also allege that family members and friends tried unsuccessfully to provide documents proving his citizenship while he was detained.

The federal government disputes those allegations, maintaining that Gil did not threaten Morales García or force him to sign the documents.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The motion does not explain what specific evidence ultimately resolved the conflicting birth records or whether immigration authorities reviewed that evidence before allowing Morales García to return.

Government seeks dismissal despite citizenship acknowledgment

Federal attorneys argue that Morales García cannot pursue damages against individual immigration agents under a legal doctrine stemming from a 1971 Supreme Court decision known as Bivens, which allows certain lawsuits against federal officers for constitutional violations. The government contends that federal courts have declined to extend those protections to similar claims involving civil immigration enforcement.

Federal attorneys also argue that sovereign immunity prevents Morales García from pursuing his constitutional claims against the federal officials named in their official capacities because he has not established that the government waived its immunity from such lawsuits.

text:
JUBA, South Sudan -- Migrants deported by the Trump administration to countries other than their own have endured hunger, thirst and other deprivations while being detained indefinitely in places with poor human rights records and little oversight.

For those expelled to South Sudan, and their families, the ordeal has come at an additional cost.

Guards have solicited and received thousands of dollars from detainees' families, who were told the money would be used to improve conditions for their loved ones. Instead, the guards pocketed most of the money, families said, while detainees went for days without food or clean water, and months held incommunicado.

"They used our desperate situation," said Ngoc Phan, a U.S. citizen whose husband Tuan Phan had been detained in South Sudan for nearly a year before he was repatriated to Vietnam in June. "If that's not exploitation, I don't know what is."

It is the inevitable outcome, she said, of a U.S. immigration policy that places deportees in the custody of countries struggling with poverty and corruption, then looks the other way.

Five deportees remain in custody in South Sudan, a country in East Africa where millions face severe hunger and poverty after years of civil conflict and devastating floods. The economy is in tatters, and government workers rarely receive wages.

In all, Ngoc Phan said she forked over roughly $4,000 intended for food, water and a cellphone. She sent several hundred dollars on multiple occasions and each time, her husband said, guards would give him a few bananas and apples, and some peanuts.

Tuan Phan, 44, said he lost 20 pounds while under confinement at a gated three-story building in Juba, the capital, and that tensions grew between detainees and guards as living conditions worsened. One detainee who wanted a window open for fresh air was struck in the face by a guard, and another who complained about a lack of soap was locked in his room for days and only let out to eat, he said.

In addition to the Phans, The Associated Press interviewed six other people familiar with the treatment of detainees in South Sudan, including relatives and lawyers. Most spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation against the detainees.

AP also reviewed money-transfer receipts and messages between guards and four detainees' relatives.

When asked about AP's findings, a spokesperson from South Sudan's Foreign Ministry said detainees are given adequate food, water and medical care, and are allowed regular contact with relatives and lawyers while it works to resolve their individual cases. The spokesperson said the government pays for all the associated costs.

Under a series of murky agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to more than 30 countries that are not their own, advocates say. Many were asylum seekers with U.S. court orders protecting them from being returned to their home countries because they could face persecution or torture.

The countries taking deportees have struck deals to receive millions of dollars in payments from the U.S., or have sought goodwill in negotiations over trade, migration or aid, documents show.

In July 2025, after a legal battle that ended with a Supreme Court ruling, Phan and seven other migrants with criminal convictions -- including for murder and sexual assault -- were deported to South Sudan.

All eight had completed their sentences in the U.S. before being taken into immigration custody. One more deportee has been detained in South Sudan.

The Trump administration defends its policy as a means of quickly deporting migrants who have final removal orders, but whose home countries refuse to accept them.

The first time Ngoc Phan sent money to a guard was in November 2025, after hearing from a lawyer that several detainees in Juba had complained about food shortages. She sent $300. After that, requests for money started coming in more frequently.

Whenever food ran out, guards would instruct Tuan Phan to call his wife and tell her to send money. Occasionally, a guard would contact her directly, requesting cash without indicating what it was for, messages show.

Three other detainees had similar experiences, their relatives and a lawyer said.

Relatives and lawyers for detainees still stuck in South Sudan say they have little faith the detention will end or conditions will improve without pressure from the U.S. government or international organizations.

But the Trump administration has signaled it has no intention of getting involved, and U.N. agencies say they are unable to help.

Johnson was among the first sheriffs to allow his deputies to enforce federal immigration laws under what’s known as a 287(g) agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The administration has more than 2,700 such pacts with state and local agencies, up from 135 when Trump began his second term. The agreements, predominantly in the South, have deputized over 29,000 local law officers and resulted in more than 6,600 arrests in July, about 15% of all ICE arrests, according to government data obtained by the Deportation Data Project that was analyzed by the advocacy group fwd.us.

The AP reviewed about 250 elections held this month for sheriffs whose offices had 287(g) agreements, identifying races in Indiana, Maryland, North Carolina, Wisconsin and elsewhere in which ICE pacts played a role in a candidate's defeat. Many sheriffs who ran this year were unopposed. But the ICE agreements could become a focus again in two years, when sheriffs from Florida, Texas and other states with large numbers of 287(g) agreements are up for election.

A new sheriff is coming to ‘No Chance Alamance'

Alamance County is a longtime Republican stronghold of just under 200,000 residents that sits between Greensboro and the Research Triangle metropolitan area that includes Raleigh, Durham and Chapel Hill. It has become more politically competitive as its population has grown increasingly diverse — from 750 residents who identified as Hispanic in the 1990 census to nearly 25,000 in 2020. The sheriff's office currently participates in the 287(g) program, a spokesman confirmed, though last year it ended an agreement to house ICE detainees.

Johnson, who is white, was first elected in 2002 and has been a prominent and polarizing figure. He has insisted he welcomes lawful immigrants and denied persistent allegations — including in a Justice Department lawsuit over a decade ago that ended with a settlement — that his office racially profiled minority residents.

The county acquired the moniker “No Chance Alamance” because of a perceived sense of unjust policing and a lack of political representation among Black and Latino residents, school board member Seneca Rogers said.

Johnson initially said in a phone call that immigration policy could have contributed to his loss. But in a brief interview later, he said it likely didn't and laid blame with his long tenure and a national political environment that was brutal for Republicans, acutely so in North Carolina, where Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper flipped a U.S. Senate seat, winning by nearly 20 percentage points. He said he always followed the law and protected public safety.

Activists and longtime residents said the Latino community — and to some extent, the Black community — feared engaging with the sheriff's office and described a sense that non-white residents were far likelier to be pulled over or detained after a traffic stop. Some people were afraid to call 911 or even go to work, said community organizer Leslie Arevalo.

n lost elsewhere

Wes Moore signed a law banning immigration enforcement pacts with the federal government.

He was defeated by Democrat Karl Bickel, a retired U.S. Department of Justice employee who had lost four previous elections to Jenkins and pledged not to cooperate with ICE.

In Wisconsin’s Winnebago County, ICE’s arrest and detention of a schoolteacher weeks before Election Day sparked backlash against anyone seemingly supportive of immigration officers, including a Republican vying to replace a retiring sheriff.

Though the sheriff’s department had nothing to do with the teacher’s arrest, its 287(g) agreement became central to the campaign, boosting Democrat Jason Rippl, who promised to end it.

A newly elected sheriff seeks a better community partnership

Long, who formerly worked as a deputy in a neighboring North Carolina county, said he will uphold the law in his new role and hold offenders accountable. But he said he won't participate in the 287(g) program.

He has set up meetings with the Latino community in the hopes of building new relationships.

“I want them to see the sheriff’s office in the community, creating a partnership, letting them know that they have a voice. … There’s no need to operate in fear,” he said.

text:
Five EU countries have unveiled this week a deal to deport rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda.

Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece will kick off this plan in 2027, with around 100 single men who cannot be deported directly to their home countries being sent to Rwanda.

The agreement is enabled by the EU return regulation, which entered into force last month. This marks the first time a group of EU member states have used the framework to send irregular migrants to a so-called “return hub.”

Article 14 of this law says that deals to deport migrants can only be made with countries that respect human rights, and many have expressed doubts about whether that is the case for Rwanda.

Freedom House, a US-based organisation which measures freedom around the world, gives the country a score of 7 points out of 40 in political rights and 14 out of 60 in civil liberties. Overall, they label Rwanda as “not free.”

The country also received a score of 0 out of 4 on judicial independence, raising questions about whether migrants not receiving proper treatment in Rwanda would be able to challenge their situation in court freely.

The United Nations Human Rights Council has also said this year that Rwandan authorities “suppress opposition and dissent, prosecuting political opponents, journalists and human rights defenders.”

Meanwhile, Amnesty International notes that Rwanda may be implicated in war crimes because of its support of M23, an armed group in the Democratic Republic of the Congo that is allegedly responsible for summary killings and gang rape. War crimes are amongst the worst possible human rights violations.

The EU Parliament itself has proposed to suspend agreements with Rwanda because of these allegations.

Opponents also point to a precedent: a deal between the UK and Rwanda to send people there while their asylum requests were being processed (so not the same as the EU-Rwanda deal, but similar) was blocked by the UK Supreme Court because it found a real risk that Rwanda would send refugees back to the countries they had fled, which is forbidden by international law.

Rwanda’s government has pushed back and says that human rights are respected in the country and that an independent monitoring mechanism, to which the 5 EU countries have committed, will ensure that.

The parties also say that the UN Refugee Agency will have a role in making sure human rights are protected.

Former Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton was long the tip of President Donald Trump’s spear for pressing culture war lawsuits against liberal enemies, particularly those on the bad side of Paxton’s war on the trans community and immigration, among others. But a blue sweep in Texas cost Paxton his AG spot after he surrendered his seat to pursue a failed spot on the U.S. Senate.

After his brutal November defeat, the Houston Chronicle reports Trump’s legal attack dog has not only lost its teeth, he’s apparently surrendered the whole doghouse and slunk off.

“It's not at all normal,” said Rob McKenna, former Republican attorney general for the state of Washington. “I can't think of another example of an AG doing that.”

The Houston Chronicle reports Ruben Garcia was at his wit’s end battling Paxton’s allegations that his shelter for immigrants, Annunciation House, harbored undocumented immigrants and participated in human smuggling, among other accusations.

“So when the office suddenly dropped its suit last week, without explanation, Garcia felt immense relief. … [H]e said the litigation had cost the organization a lot, from lawyer fees to lost donors. It’s now one of a handful of headline-grabbing cases that outgoing Attorney General Ken Paxton has backed out of in the last few weeks,” reports the Chronicle.

“The case was very much alive,” Garcia said. “I can't help but believe that this was an acknowledgement of the writing on the wall.”

But that wasn’t all. Paxton’s office also abruptly surrendered another lawsuit this month against Houston-area immigrant activist group FIEL. And it dropped its support for a MAGA-leaning doctor who got reprimanded for prescribing ivermectin during the Covid pandemic. Without warning, Paxton also dropped and ran from another lawsuit against the NCAA for allowing transgender athletes to participate in events, and the Chronicle says his office is no longer pursuing a lawsuit against Muslim civil rights group CAIR.

Paxton’s office and the conservative courts in Texas have long acted in tandem as a springboard for culture war, Trump-friendly lawsuits to appeal their way up to the conservative Supreme Court — which often sided with Paxton’s arguments. Paxton defended controversial Texas laws, including “tight abortion restrictions and an immigration law” giving local police the power to arrest migrants, which was reserved for federal officials. The Supreme Court allowed both of those cases to go into effect.

But critics say the AG’s sudden abdication of all legal fights undermines the argument that they were legitimate cases to begin with.

“For the state to dismiss a series of cases is humiliating,” said James Tierney, a former Democratic attorney general for Maine. “The lawsuits have no merit, and he knows it.”

Some of the cases dropped were done so “with prejudice,” which means the agency has forfeited the right to pursue the organization on similar charges in the future, like in the lawsuits against Annunciation House and FIEL.

Democrat Nathan Johnson is set to take over, and Johnson has made clear he has no intent of letting his office serve as a taxpayer-funded adjunct for MAGA lawsuits.

“The MAGA movement looked at Texas as their own private law firm, which happens to have been publicly funded, which I would call corrupt,” Johnson said. “My approach will be quite different.”

Johnson also had his own suspicion for why Paxton was dropping every case.

text:
Chautauqua County is now represented in a lawsuit challenging the state’s “Local Cops, Local Crimes Act.”

The law bans state law enforcement agencies from entering or maintaining 287(g) agreements with ICE, which can deputize local law enforcement to make immigration-related arrests. Initially, 15 New York sheriffs signed onto the suit. On Thursday, Chautauqua County Sheriff Jim Quattrone was added to the list along with Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, who recently lost in his attempt to unseat Gov. Kathy Hochul, and the Nassau County sheriff and police commissioner.

"The proposed amendments could not have been made earlier," attorney Mateo Forero-Norena of the Federation for American Immigration Reform (FAIR) in his memorandum of law supporting adding the new plaintiffs, including Quattrone. "The capacity allegations are being added in light of the concerns articulated in the court's Nov. 4 order. Meanwhile, adding Sheriff Quattrone and the Nassau County parties required completing the necessary arrangements with undersigned counsel and assembling supporting materials after the original complaint was filed. Plaintiffs elected not to seek to add them while the preliminary injunction briefing was underway so as not to complicate that emergency proceeding. This motion is being filed promptly after the Nov. 4 order and before defendants' response to the complaint is due. No discovery has occurred, and the case remains at the pleading stage. Defendants do not contend that the timing of this motion constitutes undue delay. They have taken no position on the proposed amendments."

Under the 287(g) program led by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, police officers can interrogate immigrants in their custody and detain them for potential deportation. Since President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, ICE had expanded the number of signed agreements it has with law enforcement agencies across the country. That prompted Democrats in the state Legislature, with support from Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James, to enact the Local Cops, Local Crimes Act. Hochul and James have defended the law as a way to protect public safety. The state has since taken legal action against Rensselaer County, the lead plaintiff in the suit, to force compliance with the new law.

Prior to 2025, only one of New York’s 62 counties had a 287(g) agreement with ICE. As of July, there were 12 local law enforcement agencies with 287(g) contracts with ICE. In July James sent letters to the 12 local law enforcement agencies in New York that had 287(g) agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), informing them that state law requires they unwind the agreements by August 25, 2026.

"Here in New York, we need local police focused on keeping our communities safe--not serving as de-facto ICE agents, not conducting civil immigration enforcement, and not carrying out the Trump Administration's callous immigration agenda," Hochul said in July. "That's why I championed our new law banning 287(g) agreements and ensuring local cops remain focused on real crime in our communities. Starting today, ICE can no longer commandeer locally-funded police to aid an out-of-control federal agency with an $85 billion budget."

The federal lawsuit to which Quattrone is now attached asks the U.S. District Court to declare that the Local Crimes, Local Cops Act is unconstitutional under the Contracts Clause of the U.S. Constitution, the 10th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution and the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution as well as under multiple sections of the New York State Constitution. FAIR is also asking the court to find that the state’s Executive Law Section 63-E, as applied to the sheriffs and counties, is unconstitutional under both the state and federal constitutions. Attorneys are also asking for an injunction keeping the state from enforcing the Local Crimes, Local Cops Act.

The lawsuit argues that New York is tearing up valid contracts the sheriffs already signed with the federal government, coercing independent elected officials into a statewide policy of non-cooperation, and overriding the constitutional authority of the Office of Sheriff. Several of the plaintiff sheriffs maintain long-standing 287(g) agreements and federal housing contracts that let them identify and transfer criminal aliens already in their jails. Albany has now declared those agreements illegal, set hard deadlines to kill them, and created a new investigative office to police any sheriff who refuses to comply.

"New York's law does not merely decline to cooperate with immigration enforcement priorities. It actively dismantles existing, congressionally authorized partnerships that sheriffs lawfully entered to protect their communities," said Dale L. Wilcox, executive director and general counsel of FAIR, when the lawsuit was filed in August. "Independently elected sheriffs should not be forced by Albany to abandon tools that keep dangerous criminal aliens from walking back onto their streets. This lawsuit seeks to restore the status quo and vindicate the independence of the Office of Sheriff."

text:
PRINCETON, New Jersey (WABC) -- A Princeton University doctoral student was detained by federal immigration authorities while returning from a neuroscience conference in Washington, D.C., according to the university and members of her research lab.

Eva Yi Xie, a neuroscience Ph.D. student at Princeton University, was detained Thursday at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport after attending the annual Society for Neuroscience conference, where she presented her research.

Members of the Brody Lab said Xie sent a message seeking help on Nov. 19 before communication with her stopped.

"On Nov 19, Eva sent a call for help to her lab mates on Slack, then we lost contact," the lab wrote in a social media post. "Her lawyers are working on her release. She's a brilliant neuroscientist, mentor, and friend. She went to a conference to present her work, and now she's in a detention center. She should be home."

She is being held at the Caroline Detention Center in Virginia. A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said Xie was admitted to the United States on a temporary basis in 2016 but later overstayed her visa.

"Xie has NEVER held valid authorization to study in the United States," the spokesperson said. "To be clear, a pending application does not confer legal status in the United States."

On Friday, a federal judge in Virginia blocked the government from removing Xie from the state and ordered the parties to submit filings by Nov. 25.

In a statement, Rodney D. Priestley, dean of the Graduate School at Princeton University, said the university has arranged legal representation and is supporting Xie, her family and colleagues.

"News of Eva's detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community," Priestley said. "The University has arranged for Eva to be represented by legal counsel, and we will remain in contact with her legal team, her family, and colleagues to provide support. We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton."

description:
Surveillance Videos Document Two Arrests The footage captures incidents on September 9 and September 25 outside the Whipple Federal Building, which houses ICE's St. Paul field office and an immigration court.
Federal Judges Reach Different Conclusions The re-arrests have divided federal judges in Minnesota.
The Colorado ruling does not settle the legal questions in Minnesota, where federal judges have issued differing decisions.
With surveillance footage now publicly documenting two incidents and federal judges continuing to examine the practice, the question is no longer whether immediate re-arrests have occurred in Minnesota.
The unresolved issue is when, if ever, the government may carry them out without violating the authority of a federal court.
text:
At least eight men have been re-arrested shortly after federal judges ordered their release. Conflicting judicial rulings have intensified questions about the government's authority to detain them again.

FORT SNELLING, MN (November 21, 2026).

Newly published surveillance footage showing federal immigration officers re-arresting men immediately after their court-ordered release has intensified scrutiny of Immigration and Customs Enforcement practices at the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building in Minnesota.

The footage, reported Friday by MPR News, documents two incidents in September in which officers waited outside the building and detained men moments after they emerged from federal custody.

MPR News has confirmed at least eight instances of immediate re-arrest at the Whipple building, including one man who was detained again on two separate occasions.

The cases have produced conflicting federal court decisions, with some judges finding that the re-arrests violated their release orders and others concluding that the government had not established grounds requiring another release.

The dispute raises questions about the meaning of a judicial release order and the circumstances under which immigration authorities may lawfully initiate a new detention.

Surveillance Videos Document Two Arrests

The footage captures incidents on September 9 and September 25 outside the Whipple Federal Building, which houses ICE's St. Paul field office and an immigration court.

In both cases, officers dressed in civilian clothing waited near the entrance as men who had been ordered released left the facility.

The officers detained them almost immediately.

One of the men, Pablo Hernandez Franco, said in a sworn statement that his shoulder was dislocated during his September 9 re-arrest.

An ICE deportation officer involved in the incident disputed that account in a sworn statement, saying Hernandez had not expressed pain or discomfort to him.

Court records identify the officer, Mitchell T. Olson, as having participated in at least four immediate re-arrests.

The September footage shows Olson displaying a document to Hernandez shortly before the detention.

Hernandez, a 32-year-old Mexican national living in Minnesota, had challenged his detention through a federal habeas corpus petition.

According to court records, he entered the United States in 2024 on a tourist visa and remained after it expired. His petition also stated that he was engaged to a United States citizen and expecting a child with her.

U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Bryan subsequently ordered his immediate release, finding that the manner of the re-arrest had effectively prevented the government from carrying out the earlier release order.

Hernandez was released again on September 25.

That same day, another man, Alejandro Corro Guzmán, was re-arrested outside the building.

Corro, also a Mexican national, had a work permit and a pending asylum claim when immigration authorities detained him in May, according to the reporting and court records. His asylum claim was later denied, and an appeal remained pending.

Chief U.S. District Judge Eric Tostrud declined to order Corro's release again, finding that the arguments presented did not establish an adequate legal basis for that remedy.

The differing outcomes illustrate the unsettled legal questions surrounding the practice.

Federal Judges Reach Different Conclusions

The re-arrests have divided federal judges in Minnesota.

Judges Jeffrey Bryan and John Tunheim have found that immediate re-arrests violated their release orders in cases before them.

Judge Jerry Blackwell reached a different conclusion in another case, while Chief Judge Tostrud rejected requests for renewed release involving two men.

The decisions turn on the language of particular court orders, the circumstances of each detention and the legal authority asserted by immigration officials.

A judicial order releasing someone from custody does not necessarily prohibit all future arrests.

The legal dispute concerns whether an immediate re-arrest based on the government's renewed assertion of detention authority satisfies the original court order or effectively circumvents it.

In two release orders issued earlier this week, Judge Tunheim included additional restrictions requiring adequate notice and a bond hearing before immigration authorities could detain the individuals again.

Those provisions reflect an effort to address the possibility of renewed detention before it occurs.

ICE Defends Its Authority

Immigration authorities have defended their ability to initiate a new arrest when they believe the action complies with applicable law and a court's decision.

In a November statement to MPR News, an unnamed ICE official said the agency could take further action after addressing legal deficiencies identified by a court, including re-arresting an individual.

The Department of Homeland Security has similarly maintained that a new arrest may be lawful if the agency follows the requirements established by the relevant judicial ruling.

The government's position is that an order invalidating one detention does not necessarily eliminate its underlying immigration enforcement authority.

Critics of the practice argue that immediately detaining someone after a judge orders release can undermine judicial oversight and deny individuals the practical benefit of a court decision.

The courts have not reached a uniform conclusion.

Colorado Case Adds to Scrutiny

The controversy has extended beyond Minnesota.

In Colorado, immigration officials carried out at least 18 immediate re-arrests between October 27 and November 4, according to court records reviewed by MPR News.

An ICE official testified that he had authorized the practice after learning that Minnesota officers were conducting similar re-arrests.

On November 18, U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney held the federal government and an immigration official in contempt over one such detention.

The judge declined to impose additional measures after an ICE official testified under oath that the practice had stopped in Colorado.

The Colorado ruling does not settle the legal questions in Minnesota, where federal judges have issued differing decisions.

It nevertheless demonstrates the broader significance of a practice that has prompted judicial scrutiny in multiple jurisdictions.

Families and Due Process

The immediate re-arrests have practical consequences for individuals challenging immigration detention.

People seeking release may spend weeks or months pursuing habeas corpus petitions, which require the government to justify continued custody.

A favorable ruling can allow a person to return to family, employment or legal proceedings outside detention.

When immigration officers initiate another arrest immediately after release, the individual may face additional detention and another round of litigation.

The cases also create uncertainty for families and attorneys attempting to determine whether a court order will result in a person's actual release.

The Whipple Federal Building has become a central location in that dispute.

With surveillance footage now publicly documenting two incidents and federal judges continuing to examine the practice, the question is no longer whether immediate re-arrests have occurred in Minnesota.

The unresolved issue is when, if ever, the government may carry them out without violating the authority of a federal court.

text:
An El Paso High School student and her family have been released from Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody, according to their immigration attorney.

In a statement to KFOX14/CBS4, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch's office confirmed that 17-year-old Michell Germán and her family have been released from ICE custody after they were detained at the Dilley Immigration Detention Processing Center, just outside San Antonio.

Germán and her family were previously detained on Oct. 22 in El Paso for entering the U.S. illegally in 2022, according to an ICE spokesperson.

ICE said agents arrested Pablo Jose Guerrero-Pimentel from Venezuela and that he “admitted he was in the U.S. illegally and had no documentation to remain in the U.S. legally.”

Guerrero-Pimentel was arrested along with “a 17-year-old female passenger also in the country illegally," identified as German, an El Paso High School student.

RELATED: El Paso High student, family held in ICE custody at Dilley pending immigration hearing

Since the family's detainment, many local officials have called for Germán and her family to be released, including U.S. Rep. Joaquin Castro and Congresswoman Veronica Escobar.

On Friday, Texas state Rep. Vince Perez announced that 57 Texas House Democrats sent a letter to the Department of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and acting ICE Director David Venturella, calling for the release of Germán and her 11-year-old sister and their parents.

Their release also comes after the El Paso High School community gathered on Tuesday to speak about their classmate and what her absence means to them, stating that her absence is being felt across the campus, missing milestones at school, including Senior Night, and rehearsing for a dance competition.

Community members, including representatives from the Border Network for Human Rights, Rep. Perez, and the family's immigration lawyer, also joined the rally urging members of Congress to step in and bring the family back home to El Paso.

Organizers said the family agreed to share their story to show the community "this is still happening," and asked members of Congress to take action to help bring families home, adding that for Michell, that means returning in time for her dance competition, and for Paola, it means getting back to her classroom and friends.

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents made an announced visit to a construction site in Amherst County on Tuesday morning, Nov. 17.

David Wall, owner of Wall Construction LLC, said ICE agents arrived at his job site at the corner of Dillard Road and Elon Road around 8 a.m., taking a site worker away without warning. “Where’s my dad going? He’s got work papers. What is going on?” Wall said, describing the reaction from his crew, including his two sons.

Wall said the agents "bodyslammed" one worker to the ground before they “put him in handcuffs and they carried him into the vehicle.”

But Wall said the worker did not remain in custody for long. “From what he told me, he was riding down the road and asked why he was apprehended and, and they stated, 'You're illegal,'" said Wall. "And, he goes, 'I got a work visa in my back pocket if you'd like to see it.'"

Wall said ICE then dropped the worker off down the road in Madison Heights, and the worker walked back to the job site. He said the worker is in the process of applying for formal citizenship, and close to completion.

SEE ALSO: Court documents reveal information about Amherst County cockfighting investigation

"It's shocking that they would just show up and without any real warrant, due process, probable cause," said Wall. "Just take somebody down like that. You know, you see it on the national news. But, I was not expecting that to happen on Tuesday morning in Amherst."

“We did not know that was going to happen,” Amherst County Sheriff Jimmy Ayers said.

Shortly after the incident, Wall gave Sheriff Ayers a call from the site to try to determine what had happened. “I told him I knew nothing about it," said Ayers. "I had to make some phone calls to find out, you know, what it was. And it was a group of ICE agents out of the Roanoke area had come in, and made a visit to that site, and that's pretty much the extent I know of it."

Sheriff Ayers did confirm that the Amherst County Sheriff's Office does have an active memorandum of understanding with ICE, meaning they partner with the agency. But Ayers said that none of his officers were involved.

Wall said the agents showed no arrest warrant and provided little explanation. “It just doesn't make any sense,” he said.

Even after the worker returned, Wall said the incident disrupted work at the site, with some workers not returning to their jobs, forcing him to look for additional labor.

“We need to have a fair and safe place for our employees to work, which means I can't have people being attacked illegally because of the color of skin,” Wall said.

ABC13 reached out to ICE with questions about what led to the arrest and whether it was a mistake, but at this time, no answers were provided.

Wall says he's still waiting for answers too.

"You don't come on a job site and just body slam people and make assumptions," said Wall. "It's just unconstitutional. And that's why I want people to see what's going on. So, hopefully we can all come together and work on a policy that works for everybody."

name: Litigation
title: ICE is using New Mexico courts to apprehend immigrants. Lawyers are pushing back.
authors: André Salkin, Jim Weber, New Mexican file photo
description: Amid a national surge in immigration enforcement, cases of ICE using criminal justice systems to make arrests have emerged in Santa Fe.
text:
Snowy winter

The project is already stirring opposition from landowners i…



Federal agents search a man in a parking lot on the south side of Santa Fe in August. The activity appeared to be part of a sweeping surge of immigration enforcement nationwide.

A row of Spanish-speaking men sat in the back of a Santa Fe courtroom one recent day, awaiting their hearings and peering out the window through the blinds, wondering who might be waiting in the parking lot.

One of them, appearing for a plea hearing in a drunken-driving case, said his public defender had warned him the day before that federal immigration agents might be waiting outside the court to make an arrest.

He was trembling, he said: " Temblando ."

A staffer from the Law Offices of the Public Defender walked the men to their cars without incident that day at Santa Fe County Magistrate Court.

However, amid a national surge in immigration enforcement, cases of federal agents using state criminal justice systems to make arrests have emerged across the country and in Santa Fe. The rise in courthouse arrests — and the appearance of potential collaboration between state and local government workers in New Mexico with immigration officers — has prompted advocates, including public defenders, to push for changes to laws and procedures to increase protections for immigrants.

Some point to a potential loophole allowing some government officials in New Mexico to cooperate with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, despite laws prohibiting such practices.

"The activity by ICE around the courthouses and places of law, I think, tends to be on an upswing like in most places," District Defender Julie Ball said in a recent interview.

Ball oversees the legal representation of all indigent defendants in the state’s First Judicial District — which includes Santa Fe, Rio Arriba and Los Alamos counties — for the New Mexico Law Offices of the Public Defender. She also serves on the city of Santa Fe’s Immigration Committee.

"If this upswing continues, then we … will be instituting more motions for our clients to appear virtually,” she said. “And it's important to remember, this affects all immigrants, even those who are here legally in the United States."

Rob Leutheuser joins a crowd of demonstrators in August as New Mexico State Police circle the block during a protest at the Roundhouse against a surge in recent Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests.

Ball recounted a “ruse” ICE used to detain a Santa Fe client of the Public Defender’s Office who had a case in state District Court.

The man was on pretrial release with an ankle monitor, she said. He received a call at his home one day from someone from the electronic monitoring company — or someone pretending to be — who told him his ankle monitor had lost connection. The person instructed him to exit his house, she said.

Immigration agents were waiting outside to apprehend him when he opened the door.

"Fortunately, we knew about it immediately and were able to call in the resources of the Santa Fe Immigration Committee to assist this person who was in ICE custody and his family,” Ball said. "Criminal justice partners in Santa Fe "all closed ranks" to condemn the incident.

"It was just overwhelming, the assistance that the community poured out for this person," she added.

Barry Massey, a spokesperson for the Administrative Office of the Courts, which oversees the state's district and magistrate courts, wrote in an email Friday that after a review by his agency and the First Judicial District Court, "the judiciary found no indication that court staff were involved" in the arrest of the man with the ankle monitor.

"Court documents are public records, including court orders that require certain defendants to wear a GPS location tracking device," he added, suggesting ICE is using public information to track defendants without the help of court staff.

Santa Fe County Magistrate Judge David Segura said he has not seen or heard about ICE agents targeting immigrants through the local courts.

"There has been none of that activity that we have been made aware of — no law enforcement doing that whatsoever," Segura said.

The First Judicial District Attorney’s Office also denied knowledge of ICE arrests or an ICE presence in state district courts — though the agency acknowledged the concerns, and a spokesperson said it “is well aware of the potential complication.”

“Our judicial system is built on the fundamental principle of due process, and ICE involvement in or around courthouses has the potential to complicate court proceedings and discourage participation by victims, witnesses, and defendants,” spokesperson Catherine Lynch said in a statement.

She added, “Our concern remains ensuring that everyone can participate in the judicial process without fear or intimidation, allowing our office to pursue justice and protect public safety.”

Demonstrators march to the Santa Fe Plaza during a protest in August against a surge in recent Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests.

Ball noted many of the ICE arrests at courthouses violate the Fifth and 14th amendments of the U.S. Constitution and the right of due process for "anyone present within the borders of the United States" by interceding in the criminal justice system.

"We're criminalizing the state of being an immigrant, and using deportation as a punishment without due process of law," she said. "What gives law enforcement, as only one branch of the government, the right to be the judge, jury and executioner?"

The intervention by federal immigration agents has also helped some suspects skirt legal consequences by being deported. In one California case, immigration agents deported a suspect in what authorities called the largest jewelry heist in U.S. history to Ecuador in December 2025 before he could be tried, the Los Angeles Times reported .

"The threat of arrest by ICE has a chilling effect on due process and deters all immigrants — not just defendants, but also witnesses and victims — from participating in the justice system," Ball said.

"ICE arrests occur when one is simply accused of a crime, even minor crimes or traffic offenses, regardless whether that person is in the U.S. legally or not," she added.

In one high-profile local case in August, immigration agents arrested a father with legal status in the parking lot of a medical clinic as he brought his daughter to an appointment. The man spent 23 days in the Torrance County Detention Facility in Estancia before federal immigration authorities released him.

A deportation officer later admitted in a court filing agents had mistaken the father, whom the agency had labeled a "criminal illegal alien," for someone else.

Immigration attorneys presented another example of a courthouse arrest to state lawmakers earlier this month. A person with only a traffic citation exited a Carlsbad courthouse, "and ICE just happened to know the moment that he was walking out," Teague González, executive director of the New Mexico Immigrant Law Center, told the interim legislative Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee.

González and attorneys from the legal nonprofit Contigo Immigrant Justice and immigrant advocacy group Somos Un Pueblo Unido presented lawmakers with a slate of cases to demonstrate how, despite state laws barring local agencies from formal cooperation with ICE and restricting state employees from sharing information, a gap in the statute still permits local agencies to informally collaborate with ICE.

"No law prohibits that right now from happening," González said, citing other examples, including an alleged practice by Sandoval County sheriff's deputies of turning over immigrants they arrest to ICE agents in a store parking lot.

Senate Bill 36, enacted in 2025, prohibits state employees from sharing most sensitive information with federal agencies. Albuquerque Democratic Sen. Antoinette Sedillo Lopez and Rep. Cristina Pajarón indicated they would sponsor a bill to extend that prohibition to local employees as well.

State agencies have faced legal consequences as a result of staffers’ alleged violations of the 2025 law.

The State Ethics Commission filed a lawsuit against the New Mexico Corrections Department in September 2025 over allegations of multiple probation and parole employees in Santa Fe and Albuquerque working with federal agents to lure immigrants to their arrests under the guise of a routine check-in.

Corrections Secretary Alisha Tafoya Lucero told a legislative committee last month her agency was moving toward a settlement in the case.

Employees of municipal courts are under local government oversight and would be affected by the new proposal to be considered by lawmakers in the upcoming legislative session.

Ball said she would support such legislation "to close these loopholes."

"Fortunately, the legislative session is a full session this year," she said, speaking of the 60-day session that starts in January. “The Santa Fe Immigration Committee will not only be taking its viewpoints to the mayor … but also lobbying the Legislature."

Staff writer Nicholas Gilmore contributed to this report.

André Salkin is an education and immigration reporter for The New Mexican .

title: Attorneys, family express fears of reduced oversight after ICE purchase of Tacoma detention center
description:

GEO Group has previously denied reports of abuse and complaints about its standards of care.
GEO Group reports it will receive approximately $340 million in net proceeds from the sale.
Bob Ferguson called the use of taxpayer dollars and continued collaboration with GEO Group "disappointing."
Boyd expressed hope that members of Congress might be more likely to be able to access and receive tours of the detention center under the new federal ownership.
text:
Months of speculation ended this week as ICE bought the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, sparking fears amongst immigration attorneys and detainees' families that the sale could further conceal conditions detainees are facing.

On Wednesday, owner GEO Group and ICE announced that the federal government had purchased the facility for $453 million, while allowing GEO Group to continue operating it. The facility currently has a capacity of nearly 1,600 and is one of the largest detention centers in the country, according to the Northwest Immigrant Rights Project.

Immigration advocates and attorney have long expected the facility could be sold to the federal government by GEO Group, as other private detention facilities have been before. Now that speculation has become reality, immigration attorneys say what happens next is unclear.

"I think one of the biggest concerns that advocates have is that it will make it harder for oversight of the facility," said Kristin Kyrka, a Seattle-based immigration attorney.

The Tacoma facility has faced years of complaints and lawsuits that it mistreats migrants, with concerns ranging from reports of inedible food and health standards not being met to abuse.

GEO Group has previously denied reports of abuse and complaints about its standards of care.

"If the federal government now owns the facility, that might make it harder for state oversight, which would allow more abuses to go on unchecked," Kyrka said.

Immigration attorney Adam Boyd said the move by ICE to purchase the facility was an effort to avoid liability or regulatory enforcement from local authorities, including by the State of Washington, by using the legal shield of the federal government. The facility is currently in litigation with Washington state.

Boyd also raised red flags about the high price of the purchase, which he described as an "absurd figure" that the land "cannot possibly" be worth. GEO Group reports it will receive approximately $340 million in net proceeds from the sale.

Gov. Bob Ferguson called the use of taxpayer dollars and continued collaboration with GEO Group "disappointing."

"We have received thousands of reports of sickness, poor water quality, contaminated food, and allegations of sexual abuse at the Tacoma facility," Ferguson said in a statement. "Washington state is fighting to get state health inspectors into this facility — the Department of Health has attempted to access the facility 10 times to investigate complaints of serious mistreatment and medical neglect."

Attorneys KING 5 spoke with said they did not expect immediate changes in day-to-day operations, such as detainees' ability to contact their lawyers, because GEO Group will continue to operate the detention center.

Families worry that's exactly the problem.

"How they treat them in there, I wouldn't wish it on anybody," said Johnell, whose husband Jerome, an immigrant from the Bahamas, has been detained since July.

After driving ten hours from Bozeman, Montana and waiting for hours at the facility with her three young children, Johnell was told on Thursday afternoon that her husband's appearance had been postponed. The appearance was supposed to determine whether Jerome would be sent back to the Bahamas.

"Every time we feel like we're getting closer to the end, it's - they just push us out some more," Johnell said.

Jerome missed the birth of their twins, who were born prematurely a week after he was detained. In addition to the stress of caring for her children, Johnell is now grappling with fears for her husband, who faces recurring health challenges in the detention center.

The news that the facility has been sold to ICE provides no comfort.

"I don't feel like anything will change with Trump being in power," Johnell said.

Boyd expressed hope that members of Congress might be more likely to be able to access and receive tours of the detention center under the new federal ownership.

KING 5 contacted ICE about the concerns from immigration attorneys regarding conditions inside the facility.

ICE did not respond to the specific concerns, but said in part that it "is regularly audited and inspected by external agencies to ensure that all ICE facilities comply with performance-based national detention standards."

text:
An estimated 12 people were reportedly detained Friday morning in what immigration organizers called a "mass ICE enforcement" operation in the North Bay.

In a statement sent out Friday afternoon, Sonoma County officials confirmed that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents took custody of multiple people around the county.

"The county has activated Phase 1 of our emergency contingency plan related to immigration enforcement impacts," said the statement. Sonoma County staff also said the U.S. Department of Homeland Security called Friday's detentions "targeted."

At least one detention was confirmed in Sebastopol along with two in Petaluma, with reports of nine more awaiting confirmation by the North Bay Rapid Response Network, which serves as a legal aid resource for immigrants and as a hotline for reporting sightings and detentions by ICE.

"We've seen immigration enforcement activity in various parts of Sonoma County since 6 a.m.," the rapid response network said. "According to our protocols, this is a mass ICE enforcement."

In a statement Friday, the Santa Rosa Police Department maintained that its officers would not assist in any ICE operations, and that the department received no communication from the agency about the detentions. "We want every resident to know that when they call the Santa Rosa Police Department for help, our priority is their safety and wellbeing regardless of their immigration status," police said.

Civilian observers are reporting multiple ICE arrests and a strong presence of federal Immigration and Customs officers around Sonoma County Friday.

The North Bay Rapid Response Network said its confirmed three ICE arrests, one in Sebastopol, and two in Petaluma which took place before 7 A.M. this morning.

The legal observer network said its received unconfirmed reports of additional arrests, and reports of vehicles used by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Rohnert Park.

One legal observer with the group says observers and bystanders documented multiple ICE vehicles and agents staged at the Sutter Urgent Care Parking lot on State Farm Drive in Rohnert Park.

"Around 8:10 this morning Rapid Response sent out a notification that there was possible ICE presence here, and a lot of folks ended up just coming here," said a legal observer who asked to remain anonymous for safety reasons. "We saw the vehicles, there weren't any agents here, and by their license plate numbers we were able to verify that they were ICE vehicles."

The observer said other North Bay Rapid Response Network observers and bystanders confronted ICE agents as they returned to retrieve the vehicles in a 15 to 20 minute span around noon.

"We filmed, we took pictures, we tried to document best we could what they looked like," said the observer. "They were all masked, and in tactical gear so we weren't really able to get a good look at their faces, but they didn't have anyone detained with them when they came back."

The North Bay Rapid Response Network has documented multiple ICE detentions across the North Bay this week, including three arrests in Sonoma Valley on Tuesday, November 17th.

In the wake of Friday's I.C.E. activity, Santa Rosa Police Chief John Cregan said his department has received multiple reports of I.C.E. activity, and reiterated that Santa Rosa police are not involved in any arrests, enforcement, or information sharing with federal immigration agents.

You can find Cregan's full statement here.

The Sonoma County Sheriff's Office released a statement on Friday afternoon:

"The Sonoma County Sheriff’s Office is aware of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) activity in Sonoma County today, November 20. Our office does not participate in immigration enforcement activities, and we had no prior knowledge of ICE’s presence or planned activity in Sonoma County today. We understand that reports of immigration enforcement activity may cause concern and uncertainty within our community. Our commitment remains to serving all Sonoma County residents, regardless of immigration status, and ensuring that everyone feels safe accessing law enforcement services when they need them."

Alex Mensing, of the California Collaborative for Immigrant Justice, issued a joint statement with the North Bay Rapid Response Network, saying in part, "The North Bay Rapid Response Network is aware of at least 12 detentions, including one incident in which a minor was left behind. The people affected are our neighbors, coworkers, friends, and family members. Their families deserve immediate support, and their rights deserve a vigorous defense. The community members arrested by ICE today were taken to the San Francisco, Stockton, and Bakersfield ICE field offices. Attorneys with multiple organizations have been swiftly deployed to provide emergency legal response."

Read the full statement here.

Redwood Empire Food Bank President and CEO Allison Goodwin issued a statement for those concerned about accessing food, saying, "Our proxy system allows someone you trust to pick up groceries on your behalf and bring them to you. This option is available to everyone—not just those with concerns about immigration status. You do not need to explain why you need to use it."

The full statement can be found on the Redwood Empire Food Bank Facebook page here.

"I'll tell you, it's deeply saddening to see how fear is affecting our community, especially, just a week before Thanksgiving," Gore said in the video. "There are families who are afraid to send their children to school, people who fear going to work, and neighbors who feel they cannot leave their homes. If you need information, guidance, or wish to report any activity, please contact the Rapid Response Network at 707-800-4544. Our community is stronger when we support one another."

text:
A Chinese-born Princeton University doctoral student was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement after attending a neuroscience conference in Washington, prompting her lawyers to challenge the detention in federal court despite her pending asylum application and valid work authorization.

Eva Yi Xie, a 24-year-old neuroscience researcher who has lived in the United States since 2016, was taken into custody Thursday at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia, while preparing to board a domestic flight.

Her attorney, Kerry Doyle, told The Daily Princetonian Friday that immigration authorities had not explained the reason for her arrest.

Xie's legal team has filed a habeas corpus petition in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, challenging the lawfulness of her detention.

According to Doyle, Xie entered the United States legally as a minor and later applied for asylum with her family. Her case remains pending, with an immigration court hearing scheduled for January 2028.

Doyle told The Washington Post that Xie also has valid employment authorization and no criminal history.

The attorney said the student's original visa had expired but that her pending asylum case permitted her to remain in the United States while immigration proceedings continued.

The precise legal basis for ICE's decision to detain her remained unclear Friday. The Department of Homeland Security had not responded to requests for comment from news organizations covering the case.

Xie's lawyers argue that immigration officers detained her without a warrant despite the absence of circumstances that would justify an immediate arrest.

They maintain that she did not pose an imminent risk of leaving the country and had experienced no recent change in circumstances requiring detention.

The case has drawn attention because Xie was returning from an academic conference where she had presented scientific research rather than attempting to enter the country from abroad.

She attended the Society for Neuroscience's annual meeting in Washington, which concluded Wednesday.

A third-year doctoral student at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute, Xie studies how different regions of the brain interact to support decision-making.

According to The Daily Princetonian's initial report, she presented research examining how neural activity associated with spatial navigation may also help organize information used in cognitive decisions.

Xie's academic adviser, Princeton neuroscience professor Carlos Brody, publicly criticized her detention and called for her release.

"She went to a conference to present her work, and now she's in a detention center," Brody wrote in a social media post. "She should be home."

Members of Brody's research laboratory said Xie contacted colleagues through Slack shortly before losing contact with them Thursday.

According to her attorney, she was subsequently taken to an ICE holding facility in Chantilly, Virginia, where she remained Friday.

The detention has also prompted a response from Princeton University.

University spokesperson Michael Hotchkiss confirmed that Princeton arranged legal representation for the student.

Rodney Priestley, dean of Princeton's Graduate School, said the university was maintaining contact with Xie's family, attorneys and colleagues.

"News of Eva's detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community," Priestley said in a statement reported by WHYY.

"We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton."

The Society for Neuroscience issued its own statement Friday, saying it was monitoring the situation and had been communicating with Princeton.

"We are in close contact with Princeton University and stand ready to provide any support that may be needed," the organization said.

Xie moved to the United States from Shanghai in 2016 and attended the Bronx High School of Science in New York before enrolling at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

She graduated from MIT in 2024 with degrees in computer science and mathematics before beginning her doctoral research at Princeton.

Her detention has attracted the attention of elected officials in New Jersey.

Sen. Andy Kim's office confirmed to The Daily Princetonian that it was in contact with Xie and working on her case.

Sen. Cory Booker said his office had contacted ICE seeking an explanation but had not received a response.

"I expect a prompt and full explanation of the circumstances surrounding her detention," Booker said.

The case comes as immigration enforcement at American airports draws growing scrutiny.

Immigration attorneys and advocates have reported additional cases involving people detained while boarding domestic flights, raising questions about how information is shared between federal transportation and immigration authorities.

According to The Washington Post, attorneys representing Xie are seeking her release while the underlying asylum proceedings remain pending.

As of Friday, no court ruling on her detention had been announced.
