text:
Seven months after removing him to Mexico, the federal government now calls Brian José Morales García a U.S. citizen, in the same filing that asks a judge to end his lawsuit.

The Justice Department has conceded in federal court that a deported U.S. citizen, Brian José Morales García of Austin, is an American, while asking a judge to dismiss his damages suit over the removal. A motion to dismiss filed Friday, Nov. 20, by U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons describes the Denver-born 25-year-old as “a dual citizen of the United States and Mexico,” the Texas Tribune reported, calling it the first time a Trump administration official has acknowledged his citizenship in plain terms. The motion argues the government is immune from suit for immigration enforcement. U.S. District Judge Robert Pitman has not ruled.

The concession matters because it closes the factual dispute that defined this case. In April, federal officials publicly insisted that “CBP did NOT arrest a U.S. citizen,” according to the Tribune, and said Morales García had admitted he was a Mexican national who entered illegally. The government’s position now is narrower: he may be a citizen, but the United States should not have to pay for what happened to him. The case is now about accountability, not facts.

Five days from a window-tint stop to Mexico

Morales García was a passenger in a pickup with coworkers headed to an air-conditioning job when a Texas Department of Public Safety trooper stopped the truck near Fredericksburg on April 3, the Tribune reported in April. He told the trooper he had a birth certificate and a Social Security card. Immigration officers were called, ICE asked that he be held, and Border Patrol took custody after he was booked into the Gillespie County jail. He says agents accused him of lying and warned he could go to prison, so he told them he had entered illegally. He signed papers, and DHS says he was removed on April 7.

His lawyers later filed hospital records, witness affidavits and a certified Colorado birth record. A Mexican ID spells his name “Bryan” and lists a different birth date, an error his mother blames on a clerk. The government let him reenter on Aug. 30 under an agreement with his attorneys, according to the Tribune.

Legally, the citizenship question was never close once the birth record held up. A person born in Denver is a citizen under the Fourteenth Amendment and 8 U.S.C. 1401(a), Mexican nationality changes nothing, and removal powers reach only “aliens.” Under 8 U.S.C. 1481 and Afroyim v. Rusk, citizenship ends only through a voluntary act intended to give it up, never through a statement made in custody. The practical lesson is how much weight an on-the-spot admission carried against documents sitting at his home.

The immunity fight now at the center

The suit against ICE, DPS and the Gillespie County Sheriff’s Office seeks unspecified damages. Public reporting has not said which legal theories it rests on, and the motion was not available for review, but the terrain is well mapped. Tort claims against the United States go through the Federal Tort Claims Act, which waives sovereign immunity but excludes “discretionary functions” under 28 U.S.C. 2680(a). Damages claims against individual federal officers have been sharply limited since Egbert v. Boule (2022), in which the Supreme Court refused to extend a Bivens remedy against a Border Patrol agent. Claims against state and county officers raise qualified immunity.

The local layer is where the case reaches beyond one family. DPS and the Gillespie County Sheriff’s Office both take part in ICE’s 287(g) program, the Tribune has reported. Whether officers working under such an agreement are treated as federal or state actors could decide which immunity rules apply. That question will matter more as Texas sheriffs face a Dec. 1 deadline under the state’s 287(g) mandate.

A problem the government barely counts

No federal agency publishes a current count of citizens arrested or removed by immigration officers. A 2021 Government Accountability Office report found that from fiscal 2015 through the middle of fiscal 2020, ICE arrested 674 potential U.S. citizens, detained 121 and removed 70. GAO recommended that ICE track these cases better, and DHS agreed. ProPublica counted more than 170 citizens held by immigration agents from January 2025 through early October 2025, a figure it called almost certainly incomplete.

If immunity defenses defeat a suit by a citizen the government admits it removed, the main remaining checks on such errors are agency policy and congressional oversight. The case joins other challenges to fast-moving arrests, from a class action over warrantless arrests in Virginia to detentions of work-permit holders at Alabama traffic stops and airport arrests on domestic flights.

What to watch

The response: Morales García’s lawyers will answer the motion to dismiss in the Western District of Texas.

Pitman’s ruling: whether any claim survives immunity, and against which defendants.

DHS and DPS: neither had responded to the Tribune about the filing; any public statement would be the first since the government’s concession.

This article is for general information and is not legal advice.

title: US deportees in South Sudan went hungry as guards pocketed money from relatives, families say
description:
Five deportees remain in custody in South Sudan, a country in East Africa where millions face severe hunger and poverty after years of civil conflict and devastating floods.
In addition to the Phans, the Associated Press interviewed six other people familiar with the treatment of detainees in South Sudan, including relatives and lawyers.
AP also reviewed money-transfer receipts and messages between guards and four detainees’ relatives.
South Sudan sought sanctions relief and other concessions, though details of the arrangement remain unclear.
A spokesperson for the UN’s International Organization for Migration said the agency is unable to step in without a request from South Sudan.
text:
“They used our desperate situation,” said Ngoc Phan, a US citizen whose husband Tuan Phan had been detained in South Sudan for nearly a year before he was repatriated to Vietnam in June. “If that’s not exploitation, I don’t know what is.”

It is the inevitable outcome, she said, of a US immigration policy that places deportees in the custody of countries struggling with poverty and corruption, then looks the other way.

Five deportees remain in custody in South Sudan, a country in East Africa where millions face severe hunger and poverty after years of civil conflict and devastating floods. The economy is in tatters, and government workers rarely receive wages.

In all, Ngoc Phan said she forked over roughly $4,000 intended for food, water, and a cellphone. She sent several hundred dollars on multiple occasions and each time, her husband said, guards would give him a few bananas and apples, and some peanuts.

Tuan Phan, 44, said he lost 20 pounds while under confinement at a gated three-story building in Juba, the capital, and that tensions grew between detainees and guards as living conditions worsened. One detainee who wanted a window open for fresh air was struck in the face by a guard, and another who complained about a lack of soap was locked in his room for days and only let out to eat, he said.

“I feared for my life every day I was there,” he said.

In addition to the Phans, the Associated Press interviewed six other people familiar with the treatment of detainees in South Sudan, including relatives and lawyers. Most spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation against the detainees.

AP also reviewed money-transfer receipts and messages between guards and four detainees’ relatives.

When asked about AP’s findings, a spokesperson from South Sudan’s Foreign Ministry said detainees are given adequate food, water, and medical care, and are allowed regular contact with relatives and lawyers while it works to resolve their individual cases. The spokesperson said the government pays for all the associated costs.

Under a series of murky agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to more than 30 countries that are not their own, advocates say, all part of the broad US crackdown on immigration. Many were asylum seekers with US court orders protecting them from being returned to their home countries because they could face persecution or torture.

The countries taking deportees have struck deals to receive millions of dollars in payments from the United States, or have sought goodwill in negotiations over trade, migration, or aid, documents show. South Sudan sought sanctions relief and other concessions, though details of the arrangement remain unclear.

In July 2025, after a legal battle that ended with a Supreme Court ruling, Phan and seven other migrants with criminal convictions — including for murder and sexual assault — were deported to South Sudan. In a press release heralding their expulsion, the Trump administration referred to the men — originally from Mexico, Cuba, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar, and South Sudan — as “barbaric criminal illegal aliens.”

All eight had completed their sentences in the United States before being taken into immigration custody. One more deportee has been detained in South Sudan.

The Trump administration defends its policy as a means of quickly deporting migrants who have final removal orders, but whose home countries refuse to accept them.

Alma David, a lawyer representing one of the detainees still in Juba, said her client has been arbitrarily held for over a year despite not being charged with a crime.

“These are people who had lives and friends and families and who were scooped up and flown to a faraway country and locked up,” she said.

The first time Ngoc Phan sent money to a guard was in November 2025, after hearing from a lawyer that several detainees in Juba had complained about food shortages. She sent $300. After that, requests for money started coming in more frequently.

Whenever food ran out, guards would instruct Tuan Phan to call his wife and tell her to send money. Occasionally, a guard would contact her directly, requesting cash without indicating what it was for, messages show.

Three other detainees had similar experiences, their relatives and a lawyer said. Payments made on their behalf to four individuals identified as guards ranged from $100 to $1,000 at a time, money-transfer receipts show. A $1,000 payment was made after a guard demanded money for suits, shirts, and shoes that he said a detainee needed to travel back to his home country, according to text messages and a money-transfer receipt.

Food and other supplies were depleted quickly, Tuan Phan said, as up to a dozen guards lived and ate alongside the detainees. Sometimes the men ate only bread or rice, or went days without eating.

When they had no drinking water, some detainees collected rainwater, he said. “They give you a jug of water and say it needs to last a week. But then when it runs out it can be another 10 days before you get more.”

Fuel shortages led to weekslong blackouts, and when the plumbing stopped working, the smell of feces filled the building, he said.

In September, one detainee called his niece in the United States to tell her to stop sending money after an earlier payment never reached him.

Relatives and lawyers for detainees still stuck in South Sudan say they have little faith the detention will end or conditions will improve without pressure from the US government or international organizations.

But the Trump administration has signaled it has no intention of getting involved, and UN agencies say they are unable to help.

The staff at the US Embassy in Juba has been instructed by the Trump administration not to visit the detainees or follow up on their treatment, according to a US congressional aide who discussed the subject with embassy staff during a visit in August 2025. The aide spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.

The US Embassy referred questions to the State Department, where a spokesperson did not address whether the embassy had received such instructions.

A spokesperson for the UN’s International Organization for Migration said the agency is unable to step in without a request from South Sudan.

In a statement, South Sudan’s Foreign Ministry said the United States “fully relinquished responsibility and no longer has any legal jurisdiction over, or ties to, these individuals.”

A federal appeals court has temporarily blocked a mandate requiring the U.S. government to immediately bring a deported Minnesota immigrant back to the United States.

Stuck in Africa

Big picture view:

The Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals has granted the government's request to temporarily pause the case. This blocks a lower court judge's order that required the U.S. to immediately pay for and arrange Kenis Lopez Gonzalez's return from the Central African Republic (CAR)."

Lopez Gonzalez, a Nicaraguan immigrant who operated a construction business in Minnesota, had previously been granted protection from being deported to Nicaragua due to the risk of torture. His attorneys contend that he was arrested by ICE in January and eventually flown to the CAR without a hearing. The lower court recently found that the government likely violated his due process and ordered his immediate return.

However, with the Eighth Circuit's stay now in place, Lopez Gonzalez will remain stranded in the CAR—a country under a Level 4 "Do not travel" advisory by the U.S. State Department—while the government's appeal plays out in court. A process that some legal experts say could take months.

Feds believe district judge went too far

Dig deeper:

In their court filings leading up to Thursday's appellate decision, federal attorneys pushed back against the lower court's mandate, arguing that the judge overstepped his authority.

The government claimed that forcing the U.S. to seek the return of a deported noncitizen from a foreign government "impermissibly interjects the court into the United States' diplomatic discussions with a foreign sovereign nation," which irreparably harms U.S. foreign policy. They further argued that Lopez Gonzalez's risk of injury is overstated because the U.S. had received "diplomatic assurances" from the CAR that deportees would not be tortured or persecuted.

Malaria diagnosis

What they're saying:

Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, an attorney representing Lopez Gonzalez, expressed confidence that they will ultimately win the appeal, but issued a bleak update on his client's health.

"The Eighth Circuit’s order only holds things in place during the appeal, and we’re confident the law is on Mr. Lopez Gonzalez’s side," Sandoval-Moshenberg said in a statement to FOX 9. "The government granted him protection from torture in Nicaragua, then ICE arrested him without telling him why, shot him with rubber bullets, and flew him to Central Africa without a hearing; a judge ordering him brought back is hardly interference."

"He has now been diagnosed with malaria, and every day this order stays in place, the government is choosing to leave a sick man in a country it warns its own citizens not to visit," Sandoval-Moshenberg added.

text:
Formerly detained Georgetown University researcher Badar Khan Suri urged the U.S. Supreme Court to leave intact the appellate decision that kept him out of immigration detention in a Nov. 20 petition.

The legal filing comes two months after the Trump administration appealed Khan Suri’s case to the Supreme Court, arguing federal courts cannot free noncitizens from immigration detention. The U.S. 4th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in Khan Suri’s favor in July, 14 months after a district court freed him from federal detention.

The Supreme Court will now decide whether or not it will hear the case, weighing the brief alongside the federal government’s original appeal. It is not required to do so, but the 4th Circuit’s decision split with two other federal appeals courts — making a Supreme Court battle more likely.

Khan Suri’s lawyers argued that the 4th Circuit was right to allow noncitizens to challenge the legality of their immigration detention in federal court.

“That review is in line with our bedrock constitutional guarantee that an individual claiming he is subject to unlawful executive detention can call on a federal court to consider his claim and afford him the remedy of release,” the lawyers wrote in the petition.

When immigration authorities detained Khan Suri in March 2025, they drew on a rarely-used statute to allege he threatened U.S. foreign policy. The district court found that the government likely violated the First Amendment by targeting Khan Suri for protected speech and familial associations.

In internal memos justifying the removal order, federal officials accused Khan Suri of spreading “Hamas propaganda” and cited his Georgetown faculty profiles and conservative watchdogs’ posts about him.

A federal judge released him 58 days later, but the Trump administration argued Khan Suri and other noncitizens could only petition immigration courts — not federal courts — regarding his detainment. Unlike the independent federal judiciary, political appointees in the U.S. Department of Justice oversee immigration courts.

In the 4th Circuit’s decision, Judge DeAndrea Benjamin wrote that “no provision within the immigration code deprived” federal courts of jurisdiction over immigration detention.

Two other circuit courts, however, agreed with the Trump administration’s interpretation in similar cases. In one of these decisions, the 3rd Circuit ruled against former Columbia University student Mahmoud Khalil, who recently appealed his case to the Supreme Court.

Khan Suri remains embroiled in a bifurcated legal battle — the Supreme Court appeal contesting his detention, and a parallel immigration case to determine if he can remain in the United States. He is currently awaiting an immigration judge’s decision after his trial concluded in late October.

Khan Suri’s lawyers in the federal case said immigration courts — whose processes are lengthy and opaque — are not a sufficient venue for noncitizens’ constitutional challenges.

“Forcing Dr. Suri to wait to challenge his unlawful detention on First Amendment grounds would be ‘absurd,’” the lawyers wrote.

text:
Democrats and the White House are already in a showdown over alleged document destruction — and the party hasn't even taken control of Congress yet.

Democratic lawmakers and investigators are increasingly concerned that the Trump administration is destroying documents and not adhering to preservation record laws before they take control of Congress, setting off a flurry of letters across the federal government demanding officials properly save documents and turn off auto-delete settings on encrypted messaging applications.

The White House has said that Democrats are making claims over document destruction by the administration without evidence, but has also indicated it sees no obligation to comply with their demands to preserve or turn over documents before they gain control of committee gavels in January.

The high-stakes standoff is laying the groundwork for a legal fight, as Democrats prepare for far-reaching investigations into the Trump administration and fear that document destruction could hinder their ability to conduct oversight.

"What I think you're seeing in Congress with these document preservation letters is Congress is drawing a line in the sand and maintaining a record so that if people do destroy records they could potentially be prosecuted in a future administration for obstruction of Congress," Jim Secreto, who worked in the Obama White House Counsel's office on congressional investigations and compliance with the Presidential Records Act, told CNN.

Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, who is in line to chair the House Judiciary Committee, is particularly concerned about the use of Signal by federal employees as a way to circumvent future Democratic oversight.

In a series of preservation letters sent to the Department of Justice, Federal Bureau of Investigation, Department of Homeland Security, Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Bureau of Prisons, Raskin raised concerns about the potential for document destruction.

A White House official told CNN, "We comply with all federal record retention laws and regulations."

A Justice Department official told CNN that the department "follows all legal requirements for the management of federal records involving its official functions and decisions." They added that the DOJ employees "who work tirelessly to arrest and prosecute criminals will not be intimidated."

A DHS spokesperson similarly said the department "complies with all applicable federal laws, including as it relates to document retention. DHS responds to official correspondence through official channels."

Raskin said in the letters that "there is significant evidence that Trump Administration officials have engaged in the widespread destruction, mutilation, and concealment of government records, seemingly with the express purpose of circumventing federal record preservation laws."

"This attempt to evade transparency extends to the highest levels of federal agencies, including top-ranking law enforcement officials," he continued.

In the letters, Raskin said that a Signal conversation between the general counsel of the FBI and an associate of Donald Trump Jr. appeared to have been set for messages to auto-delete after a week. The Democratic lawmaker said that the conversation concerned "a potential or ongoing investigation involving an individual wanted by federal authorities on health care fraud and related charges."

"This incident, just one of many that have already been reported to our Committee, raises significant concerns that DOJ and FBI officials are openly flouting federal law when it comes to the preservation of official government records," Raskin said.

The panel declined to provide other examples of alleged document destruction with CNN.

Judiciary Committee staffers plan to rely on whistleblowers and third parties to help them get the information they seek, but are hoping that the preservation letters sent Friday will put a stop to the use of Signal and auto-delete settings for official work by federal employees.

"We want them to be on notice that this behavior is wrong. And if they are doing it, and especially if they continue doing it, we will draw inferences from your destruction of evidence. That's something that every litigate is familiar with, both in the civil and criminal context," a Democratic source familiar told CNN.

Other Democrats are also raising concerns of alleged document destruction and federal employees using encrypted messaging applications without properly storing them.

Congressional sources preparing investigations into Trump's construction projects around Washington told CNN whistleblowers have warned that key paperwork has already been destroyed before Democrats take power.

Democratic Rep. Gregory Meeks warned in his preservation letters earlier this week of document destruction and specifically noted that Signal messages must be properly stored and not subject to automatic deletion.

By law, federal employees are required to preserve all records. Federal employees can use encrypted messaging applications like Signal but must correctly store the conversations in compliance with the law.

White House Counsel Will Scharf sent letters earlier this week to Democratic committee leaders saying the Trump administration's position is that no official has to comply with their demands to preserve or turn over documents and information because Democrats do not yet chair the committees, according to a copy of the letter obtained by CNN.

On Thursday, Raskin received a preservation letter of his own from US Attorney Aaron Reitz, who accused the Maryland Democrat of weaponizing his investigative efforts without a legislative purpose to go after Trump associates and the administration.

Scharf wrote that the purpose of the letters sent by Democrats "is not legitimate oversight but to harass and aggrandize."

"In the days since the November 3, 2026 election, several Ranking Members have sent letters to the Executive Branch demanding documents or information. Some of these letters imply, without evidence, that thousands of United States government employees are conspiring to destroy documents in violation of the Federal Records Act," he said.

In addition to calling on agencies to preserve their documents, Raskin is demanding Attorney General Todd Blanche and other Trump officials open an inquiry into what documents may have been deleted and attempt to recover those records.

Even though Democrats don't yet have the authority to compel document production with subpoena power, these preservation letters serve as a preview of what's to come, particularly if Democrats regain control of the White House in 2028.

"It's the type of thing that a future Department of Justice could use as evidence in court of intent to destroy records," Secreto told CNN.

This story has been updated with additional details.

title: After November 20: Why Venezuelan TPS Remains Terminated and What Holders Must Do Now
description:
Hours after Sauer filed, the Ninth Circuit issued an order in National TPS Alliance v. Mullin, No.
With the Ninth Circuit having acted, the Supreme Court application had no remaining purpose.
By securing an extended stay at the circuit level, the administration kept Venezuelan TPS terminated without expending political and legal capital at the Supreme Court ahead of a circuit ruling that has not yet been issued.
Employment Authorization Documents issued under Venezuelan TPS are not receiving any new extension from this order.
No court order currently in force guarantees re-entry rights for terminated TPS holders who travel abroad.
text:
The November 20 deadline came and went without changing anything for the more than 348,000 Venezuelans covered by the country's 2023 Temporary Protected Status designation. The Ninth Circuit extended its freeze on the district court order that would have restored Venezuelan TPS, leaving the termination in effect until seven days after the appeals court publishes its decision on the appeal.

The legal maneuvering that produced that outcome unfolded in roughly 24 hours — and it included a Supreme Court application that was filed and then pulled before the justices had any chance to act on it.

How the Legal Sequence Unfolded in Less Than a Day

On November 18, Solicitor General D. John Sauer filed an emergency application at the Supreme Court, assigned docket No. 26A714, asking the justices to freeze the summary-judgment order issued by U.S. District Judge Edward Chen of the Northern District of California. Judge Chen's order had blocked the government from carrying out the termination of Venezuela's 2023 TPS designation.

Hours after Sauer filed, the Ninth Circuit issued an order in National TPS Alliance v. Mullin, No. 25-5724, extending its prior 14-day administrative stay — which had been set to expire after November 20 — until seven days after the panel issues its decision, keeping the district court's ruling on hold.

With the Ninth Circuit having acted, the Supreme Court application had no remaining purpose. Sauer submitted a withdrawal letter to the Court's clerk the following day, confirming the emergency request was no longer necessary. The government's own filings had described the situation as "a remarkable third trip to this Court in the same case."

The Strategic Logic Behind the Withdrawal

The move reflected a clear calculation. By securing an extended stay at the circuit level, the administration kept Venezuelan TPS terminated without expending political and legal capital at the Supreme Court ahead of a circuit ruling that has not yet been issued. The government made its next step equally clear: should the Ninth Circuit rule against it on the merits, it would immediately return to Washington for further relief from the justices.

The Human Numbers Behind the Case

The legal filings in this case deal in abstract procedural categories, but the population affected is concrete. According to Immigration Analytics, DHS's own court submissions put the total number of individuals registered under Venezuela's 2023 designation at 348,202. In its Supreme Court filing, the government warned that letting the lower-court order take effect could force DHS to release roughly 1,800 Venezuelan nationals from immigration detention and halt removal efforts for hundreds of individuals subject to deportation.

Work Permits: What the Stay Does — and Does Not — Do

The Ninth Circuit's extended freeze does not create new work authorization for anyone. It simply prevents the district court's restoration order from going into effect while the appeal proceeds. Employment Authorization Documents issued under Venezuelan TPS are not receiving any new extension from this order. Holders whose EADs have expired or are approaching expiration should consult an immigration attorney immediately to determine whether any prior DHS administrative extension notices still apply to their specific document class.

Asylum Cases: A Separate Legal Process

A pending asylum application runs on an entirely independent legal track from the TPS dispute. The court's stay order does not pause any asylum deadlines, alter individual hearing schedules, or change how immigration judges evaluate pending claims. Venezuelan nationals with cases before an immigration court should continue attending every scheduled hearing and maintaining close contact with their attorneys. Whatever the Ninth Circuit ultimately decides about TPS will have no retroactive effect on an asylum case that has already been granted or denied.

International Travel: The Risk Remains Severe

Leaving the United States while TPS-terminated and without another valid immigration status carries a risk of permanent displacement. No court order currently in force guarantees re-entry rights for terminated TPS holders who travel abroad. Until the Ninth Circuit issues a full merits decision and that decision survives any further action at the Supreme Court, international travel should be treated as a potentially permanent departure from the country.

What the Ninth Circuit Must Decide Next

The case now returns to the appeals court for a full ruling on whether the Trump administration's termination of Venezuela's 2023 TPS designation was lawful — a question the Ninth Circuit has not yet answered on the merits. The legal backdrop has shifted significantly since the litigation began. In June 2026, the Supreme Court issued its ruling in Mullin v. Doe, 609 U.S. 324 (2026), holding that the TPS statute bars judicial review of non-constitutional challenges to TPS termination decisions. The Court had previously vacated the Ninth Circuit's earlier judgment in this case and remanded it for reconsideration in light of that ruling.

Community advocates in Doral — home to one of the country's most concentrated Venezuelan diaspora communities — and in Houston's expanding Venezuelan corridor are warning holders not to read the November 20 non-event as a sign of stability. The legal fight is unresolved, the timeline is open-ended, and the administration has openly signaled it will escalate the moment it faces an adverse ruling from the circuit court.

For the more than 348,000 Venezuelans whose status is at stake in this case, one fact remains unchanged: nothing is restored until a court orders it.

title: What US Immigration Courts Now Expect From Country Evidence | The Ritz Herald
description:
When an asylum case reaches an immigration judge in the United States, the dispute is rarely about whether something happened.
Counsel who once attached a handful of news clippings now file structured country evidence, and adjudicators increasingly expect it.
The result is uneven: well-resourced applicants arrive with detailed country evidence, and others arrive with a printout from a news site.
This is why country evidence has become a service rather than a side task.
As filings grow more structured, the absence of country evidence becomes more conspicuous.
text:
When an asylum case reaches an immigration judge in the United States, the dispute is rarely about whether something happened. More often, it is about what the record shows regarding the country the applicant left: who holds power in a particular state or municipality, whether the police there can or will protect anyone, and whether the risk described in the application still exists today.

That shift has been visible in filings over the past two years. Counsel who once attached a handful of news clippings now file structured country evidence, and adjudicators increasingly expect it.

Why general reporting is no longer enough

Human rights reporting is written for a general audience. It summarises a country over a year, names the worst incidents, and moves on. An immigration judge is asked a narrower question: does this particular applicant, with this profile, in this place, face a real risk now.

The gap between the two is where most claims are lost. A report may state that violence in a region is widespread without saying whether the authorities there investigate complaints. It may describe a criminal group without explaining whether that group operates in the applicant’s home municipality or two states away. It may be eighteen months old, which in some regions is a long time.

Country evidence prepared for a case closes that gap. It takes the questions in the file and answers them one by one, citing the underlying sources rather than summarising them.

Mexico as the clearest example

Mexican claims illustrate the problem well, and they make up a large share of the docket. The Department of Justice has reported that Mexico is consistently among the top nationalities in immigration court proceedings.

The difficulty in these cases is not a shortage of information. It is that the information is national when the question is local. Control of territory varies between municipalities. A group dominant in one state may be absent in the next. Protection available in a large city may not exist in a rural district three hours away. Internal relocation, which the government often raises, turns entirely on these details.

A judge asked to decide whether a family can safely move within Mexico needs to know what the record shows about that specific route and that specific destination, not what it shows about the country as a whole. Lawyers preparing such a file usually need a structured summary of country conditions in Mexico before they can decide which experts and which documents the case actually requires.

What a tribunal needs on country conditions.

What adjudicators look for

Practitioners who work on these cases describe a consistent set of expectations.

Sources that can be checked. Each assertion should trace to a document the other side can open: a government report, a UN body, a court decision, a named organization. Unsourced assertions carry little weight and can undermine the rest of the report.

A stated method. A report should say what was reviewed, what was not available, and what the author could not establish. Candor about limits tends to strengthen rather than weaken the document.

Currency. Conditions change. A report that relies on material from two years ago without saying whether the situation has shifted invites the question of whether the risk persists.

Separation of fact and opinion. The factual record and the expert’s assessment should be distinguishable on the page. Judges are entitled to accept one and question the other.

The practical problem for smaller firms

Large firms maintain their own country research. Solo practitioners and small immigration practices rarely can, and they handle a substantial share of asylum work in the United States.

For them, the obstacle is not willingness but time. Assembling current, sourced material on a region takes days that a practice running thirty active matters does not have. The result is uneven: well-resourced applicants arrive with detailed country evidence, and others arrive with a printout from a news site.

This is why country evidence has become a service rather than a side task. Specialist providers maintain regional coverage, work with named experts, and produce reports written to the standards courts expect. If you are working out who covers a particular region, a directory of country experts lists specialists by country and sets out their backgrounds.

How a report is usually commissioned

The process is more routine than practitioners expect. Counsel sends the questions the case turns on, the applicant’s profile and the relevant dates. The provider confirms which expert covers the region and gives a timescale and a fee before any work starts. A standard report takes one to two weeks; shorter opinions on a single question are faster.

Two points matter at that first stage. The questions should be the ones the judge will have to answer, not general requests for background, because a report written to a vague brief tends to read as a country summary rather than evidence. And the instruction should state the deadline, since a report delivered after the filing date is of no use regardless of its quality.

Cost is the other recurring question. It varies with the scope and the region, and a short opinion on one issue is considerably cheaper than a full report. For a practice weighing whether to commission one at all, the useful comparison is not the fee in isolation but the cost of losing a hearing on an evidential gap that was identifiable months earlier.

What this means for the year ahead

Two developments are worth watching.

The first is procedural. As filings grow more structured, the absence of country evidence becomes more conspicuous. A file without it does not merely lack support; it stands out against the files that have it.

The second concerns expertise itself. Courts have become more attentive to who is writing these reports: whether the author has direct knowledge of the region, whether their background is documented, whether they have given evidence before. A report from a named specialist with a verifiable record carries weight that an anonymous summary does not.

Neither development is dramatic on its own. Together they point in a clear direction. Country evidence is moving from something that helps a case to something a case is expected to contain, and practitioners who build that into their preparation early are better placed than those who reach for it in the final weeks before a hearing.

Alvarez described appearing before a female judge on a video screen, along with an immigration enforcement official. Two other participants did not identify themselves, she said, and their screens remained dark.

Asked whether she had an attorney, Alvarez said: “My lawyer is the Lord.”

The new proceedings are part of an effort to dispose of long-pending immigration cases, with judges, government lawyers and interpreters appearing remotely while immigrants must appear in person.

Fairness questions

The accelerated hearings are the latest change to immigration courts under the Trump administration, which has also stepped up arrests at courthouses and increased the number of cases judges are expected to handle.

Similar arrangements elsewhere have drawn objections from immigration attorneys and advocates, who say moving hearings up with little notice and routing immigrants without lawyers into makeshift courtrooms threaten their right to a fair hearing.

“When people have cases set way far out and then the court gives them seven days’ notice, that could be a due process issue,” said Paul Hunker, a Dallas immigration attorney who served as Immigration and Customs Enforcement's chief counsel in Dallas.

Sarah Ellison Hernandez, a former Dallas immigration judge, told The News that the new hearings are specifically for immigrants without attorneys, leaving them to navigate a complex legal system on their own.

“These people who are in proceedings have limited understanding of rules or their rights, and so they’re really left very vulnerable,” she said.

John Martin, a spokesperson for the Executive Office for Immigration Review, the agency overseeing the court system, said Friday there’s “nothing novel” about trying to find more court space.

The goal, he said, is to ensure cases “do not languish” and migrants “receive their day in court in a timely manner.”

The Dallas hearings, which were scheduled to run from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., involve preliminary proceedings, not necessarily final decisions on whether immigrants can remain in the United States.

Related: Former Dallas ICE supervisor says agency got off track under Trump

A shifting schedule

A July report by the Government Accountability Office found that remote hearings were widely used and generally viewed favorably by judges and attorneys, although some reported problems with technology and language interpretation.

“It’s constantly changing,” said Gretchen Peterson, a Dallas public observer with Vecinos Unidos DFW, an immigrant advocacy group.

Johany Beltran, a Venezuelan immigrant, said she received notice Nov. 12 to appear in court Friday, giving her just over a week to prepare. After her hearing, she was given a change-of-address form and a new court date of June 2, 2027.

title: What do we know about Rwanda return hubs and how effective will they be?
description:
Today's Euronews Verify episode takes a closer look at the measure.
Those moved to Rwanda will be free to live and work there or return to their home countries.
There's still a lot we don't know, however, and critics are concerned about the lack of detail given in the announcement of the Rwanda plan.
While both the EU countries in question and Rwanda itself assure that the hubs will comply with EU, international and human rights law, critics and experts are less convinced.
Watch Euronews Verify
text:
Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands have announced plans to set up a return hub in Rwanda, which they say will allow the EU to secure control of its borders.

The group of five want to start deporting rejected asylum seekers — and those who have exhausted all appeal options against their removal — to Rwanda in 2027. Today's Euronews Verify episode takes a closer look at the measure.

The details of the return hubs are still being ironed out, but the first is expected to accommodate around 100 people with no legal right to stay in the EU at a time, in a pilot run of the model.

Those moved to Rwanda will be free to live and work there or return to their home countries.

Announcing the plan on 16 November, Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said that the move will serve as a strong deterrent for anyone looking to enter the EU illegally.

"The signal that we are sending, that you can no longer enter the European Union illegally and think that you can just stay around ... will prevent a lot and ensure that thousands of people will think it through before starting their journey into Europe," she said.

Rwanda has also hailed the plan as a way to "protect the right to asylum while treating migrants with dignity at every stage".

What don't we know and what are the concerns?

There's still a lot we don't know, however, and critics are concerned about the lack of detail given in the announcement of the Rwanda plan.

"We don't know how much it will cost; we don't know what Rwanda has been offered in exchange; we don't know what guarantees exist for people; we don't know how the courts will intervene; we don't know what protections will be in place; and we don't know who's legally responsible if something goes wrong," Olivia Sundberg, EU advocate on migration and asylum at Amnesty International, told Euronews Verify.

While both the EU countries in question and Rwanda itself assure that the hubs will comply with EU, international and human rights law, critics and experts are less convinced.

They've also raised concerns about the hubs' ability to even deter illegal immigrants, as such measures, they say, only force people to take more dangerous trips to Europe rather than giving up the plan entirely.

Can nuclear play a part in Europe's energy transition?

Also on today's episode of Euronews Verify is a look at whether Europe is heading for a nuclear revival.

As the COP climate summit in Turkey wraps up, nuclear energy has been a particularly big elephant in the room, complete with nuclear-related events on the sidelines.

From calls to triple capacity by 2050 to countries reconsidering their phase-outs, there is a growing push to bring nuclear back to the table as a low-carbon source.

Soaring energy bills in Europe are also presenting the industry with an opportunity to turn political momentum into climate legitimacy.

"If you want to have cheap energy, it's going to be very, very difficult to do it without nuclear power," Damien Erst, electromechanics professor at the University of Liège, told Euronews Verify.

"Especially in a context where gas is becoming extremely expensive, and in a context where foreign powers also use our dependency on energy imports to threaten and weaken the EU."

Several countries are already weighing up their options, with Italy giving the strongest indication that it's time for change: the government just passed new legislation this year to pave the way for a return to nuclear energy after decades without it.

Spain and Belgium, meanwhile, have postponed reactor shutdowns; the Netherlands is planning new units; and Poland and Estonia are laying the groundwork for their first nuclear plants.

text:
El Paso High School senior Michell Germán and her family returned to El Paso on Friday night after being freed from Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody at the Dilley detention center.

Michell, her 11-year-old sister Paola and their parents, Pablo Jose Guerrero-Pimentel and Dolores Emilia Zarraga-Colina, were expected to arrive at El Paso International Airport late Friday, where a handful of community members who had advocated for their release waited to greet them.

The family had been detained at the South Texas Family Residential Center, also known as the Dilley detention center, since a day after being arrested by ICE agents in El Paso on their way to school on Oct. 22.

Michell, 17, who is on the school’s dance team, had been crowned lady-in-waiting at homecoming celebrations this fall. Paola, a student at Lamar Elementary School, is a dedicated student who looks up to her big sister, family friends said.

The family, originally from Venezuela, came to the United States in August 2022. ICE officials have said neither parent had documentation to remain in the U.S. legally. But attorneys for the family said they are seeking asylum and have been undergoing “valid immigration proceedings.” The parents have work permits and no criminal records, according to the attorneys.

The family’s release comes after an outpouring of support from community members and lawmakers, including a rally at El Paso High School on Tuesday night where many of Michell’s classmates chanted, prayed and cried as they stood on the marble steps at the school’s main entrance.

“It’s one thing to miss someone and it’s another to miss them worrying about their well-being while they’re away in ICE detention. It’s hard to imagine what she’s going through,” Ana Talavera, 16, who is on the Tigerettes dance team with Michell, said through tears.

Talevera described her friend as “strong, independent and very sweet.”

LEARN MORE: She should be celebrating Senior Night. Instead, this El Paso teen is in Dilley ICE detention.

The family on Wednesday was scheduled for a master calendar hearing, where court dates for future immigration hearings are set. But that was postponed to Dec. 9.

Austin immigration attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, who is representing the family, told El Paso Matters through a spokesperson that she submitted another request this week for their release, citing the Flores settlement. That’s the 1997 federal court ruling that set standards for the detention of children – including establishing a 20-day limit for their detention in U.S. immigration custody.

“There is real beauty in this family, in the community that supports them, and in the leaders who stood by them,” Goldfinch said in a statement Friday. “This family finally gets to come home to a community that stood for them in their absence.”

“But we cannot ignore the injustice and the horror of what has happened to this family, and what happens to families like them,” she said. “ It is never OK to detain children, and the Dilley detention center needs to be closed immediately.”

Goldfinch said the family came to the United States “seeking a safer and better life. They followed the rules. They had valid work permits. And yet they were treated like criminals and detained on their way to sc

Goldfinch criticized the administration of President Donald Trump and its mass detention and deportation efforts that she said are targeting hardworking families who have been living and working in the country with authorization for years.

In July 2026, Senate Judiciary Committee staff reported that while most families at Dilley were detained an average of 20 days, some had been held for months – and one for more than 10 months.

The controversial Dilley center has been the focus of protests and calls for closure over alleged human rights violations, particularly following the detention of 5-year-old Liam Conejo Ramos in January.

About 70 miles southwest of San Antonio, Dilley first opened in December 2014 under President Barack Obama and was closed in June 2023. ICE reopened the facility last year under a $160 million annual contract with CoreCivic. The 50-acre site comprises about 80 cottages and has a capacity to hold up to 2,400 people.

Community leaders, civil rights groups and elected representatives, including San Antonio Congressman Joaquin Castro and El Paso Congresswoman Veronica Escobar, had petitioned that Michell and her family be released – and demanded that Dilley be shut down.

On Tuesday, Escobar, Castro and a group of more than a dozen current and incoming Democratic members of Congress sent a letter to Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Acting ICE Director David Venturella urging them to release the family from Dilley. That was followed by a similar letter from El Paso state Rep. Vince Perez and more than 50 sitting and incoming Texas House Democrats.

Escobar in a statement Friday thanked those who fought for Michell and her family to be released, adding that “no family should have to endure the trauma of being held in detention while separated from their community.” She said she will continue fighting for an immigration system that treats every person with dignity and to close down Dilley and other for-profit ICE detention facilities.

Perez at the Tuesday rally praised students for their advocacy and encouraged them to remain involved, telling them to recognize the power they have.

“Michell and her family are going to come home,” he said. “But we cannot stop when she comes home. There are thousands of other people who are detained unjustly and going through similar situations.”

One of Michell’s friends on Tuesday held back tears as she read off her cellphone in Spanish, “It’s strange not seeing her in the hallways, in our English class, or at practice every day.”

“Esta familia no solo son nombres, números o un caso de inmigracion más. Estas personas son seres humanos, son familia, son personas con sueños, amistades, metas y vidas que importan,” she said.

“This family is not only names, numbers or just another immigration case. They are people, they are human beings, they are family. They are people with dreams, friendships, goals and lives that matter.”

This is a developing story and will be updated.

text:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton dropped a lawsuit late Friday that sought to shutter Jolt Initiative, a nonprofit group that aims to increase civic participation among Latinos.

In a court filing shared by Jolt, Paxton dismissed the suit that targeted the nonprofit’s corporate rights and privileges to effectively dissolve its charter. The attorney general’s office had opened a probe into Jolt following August 2024 claims leveled by Fox News host Maria Bartiromo — who had previously promoted conspiracy theories concerning the 2020 election — that organizations in the state were illegally registering migrants to vote.

“After more than two years of facing attacks designed to undermine our organization and threaten our ability to serve Texans, the State of Texas has now dismissed its entire case against us,” Jackie Bastard, executive director of Jolt Initiative, said in a statement Friday night. “Our mission has always been to ensure that young Latinos and historically underrepresented Texans have the resources, opportunities, and power to participate in our democracy. No intimidation will change that commitment.”

Paxton’s office, which has been dropping suits all week, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

After Bartiromo’s comments, an undercover agent dispatched by Paxton’s office investigated by trying to register a fake daughter to vote. A Jolt volunteer instructed the agent on how to register her, despite her absence, according to previous filings from Paxton’s office. The filings did not provide evidence of Jolt registering noncitizens to vote, a practice that remains rare if nonexistent. There’s no evidence that large numbers of noncitizens vote or are registered to vote.

Following the stunt, Paxton’s office filed a suit in state court to shut down Jolt. In response the nonprofit filed a federal lawsuit to stop the state.

In January, a federal judge ruled that Paxton had failed to offer “any plausible proof” that Jolt was breaking the law.

Three weeks ago Paxton, a hardline Republican and MAGA firebrand, lost his bid for U.S. Senate to James Talarcio, an Austin state representative who became the first Democrat to win a Senate election in Texas since 1988.

“This fight was never just about Jolt,” Bastard said. “It was about whether Latino-led organizations can organize, engage their communities, and help people make their voices heard without facing intimidation retaliation. We stood our ground because our communities deserve nothing less.”

title: Democrat-controlled Congress faces task of reforming Trump's immigration agenda | U.S.
description:
Arizona Senator Ruben Gallego, who was also present at the Capitol event last Wednesday, stressed the intent to push for immigration reform but expressed little hope it would happen quickly.
The initiative emerged from collaboration between Democratic Representative Veronica Escobar of Texas and Republican María Elvira Salazar of Florida.
I have very aspirational dreams and hopes for immigration reform.
So any comprehensive immigration reform must be bipartisan.
Speaking to Fox News about how he would work with a Democratic Congress, Trump said: “They are in control, but they’re really not in control.
text:
After the economy, the aggressive immigration policy implemented by the administration of Donald Trump was the main reason U.S. voters punished the Republican Party and gave the Democrats a historic victory in the midterms.

The Democratic Party will hold a majority in the United States Congress starting January 3. In the House of Representatives it will occupy at least 256 of the 435 seats after taking 42 seats from the Republicans. In the Senate it will hold 55 seats, eight more than before. The victors face the arduous task of changing an immigration system widely regarded as broken and that Congress has been unable to reform for decades. Amid Democratic euphoria over the win, ending Trump’s anti-immigrant crusade has emerged as one of their legislative priorities. Whether they succeed will not depend solely on them.

A Democrat-controlled Congress will coincide with the last two years of Trump’s term. The president, as is typical for him, has sent mixed signals about how he wants to address immigration. Just a week ago he admitted in an interview on CBS’s 60 Minutes that his immigration policy had been too harsh and that people who were taxpaying workers had been deported.

Hours after the interview was recorded, however, he promoted the architect of the administration’s most hardline immigration stance, Stephen Miller, to White House chief of staff. In later remarks, Trump clarified that there would be no amnesty and that his policy had not changed.

“We’ve seen this time and again. Trump says something moderately reasonable on immigration and then Stephen Miller gives him a dressing-down, after which he comes out with a new commitment to maximalist positions,” says Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, senior researcher at the American Immigration Council and one of the immigration experts who has testified in Congress about the administration’s abuses in this area.

But the reality is that the landscape has changed with the Democrats taking control of Congress. Markwayne Mullin, secretary of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), said Trump encouraged him to work with the Democrats on immigration reform after telling him he had received many calls about the issue.

Democratic lawmakers have confirmed the same. “We’ve had some conversations and, without going into details, I think there are common ground points that will allow us to reach an agreement,” said Representative Henry Cuéllar of Texas at a pro-immigration reform event held last week in front of the Capitol.

‘Dreamers’ top the list

Among the immigration bills that have so far failed in the House of Representatives, one stands a better chance of succeeding: the Dream Act, a bill that grants legal residency and opens a path to citizenship for foreigners who arrived undocumented as children. Many are beneficiaries of the DACA program (Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals) and have grown up, studied, worked and formed families in the only country they consider home. Trump has tried to end the program, created under the Barack Obama administration, during his two terms, but courts have blocked him. The so-called “dreamers” are the migrants with the broadest support across the political spectrum.

The bill needs only one more Republican representative’s signature to be brought to the floor of the House. “My American Dream and Promise discharge petition has 217 signatures. 214 Democrats and three Republicans. We just need one more Republican signature to get it to the finish line and force a vote. We cannot wait any longer,” Representative Sylvia García, co-author of the Dream Act, wrote on social media after attending the same event in front of Congress on November 11.

The administration has shown some willingness to engage. “If we want to have an immigration reform where we can look at DACA and figure out a way that these individuals can become maybe legal permanent citizens or something like this, that’ll be up to Congress to do that. I’ll be open to talk to anything,” Mullin told reporters at an event in Maryland last Monday.

Arizona Senator Ruben Gallego, who was also present at the Capitol event last Wednesday, stressed the intent to push for immigration reform but expressed little hope it would happen quickly. “We want to get it done before the end of the year and, if that’s not possible, we will keep trying throughout the next year. Protecting families is our priority. We are fully committed to making this happen,” he said.

A bipartisan bill

In addition to the Dream Act, there is another legislative proposal with broad bipartisan support: the Dignity Act, which provides for the legalization of undocumented migrants who have lived in the country for years, while also strengthening border security and reforming visa programs.

The initiative emerged from collaboration between Democratic Representative Veronica Escobar of Texas and Republican María Elvira Salazar of Florida. Salazar was narrowly reelected on November 3 after distancing herself from Trump and his immigration policy in a video that went viral on social media.

“I am a progressive Democrat. I have very aspirational dreams and hopes for immigration reform. But I am also a pragmatist. And as we continue to have Donald Trump in the White House and without a super majority in the Senate, we need Republican support. So any comprehensive immigration reform must be bipartisan. I am deeply committed to ensuring that the Dignity Act is reintroduced in 2027,” Escobar said last Wednesday. The representative addressed lawmakers who do not support the bill and asked them to communicate their reservations because it will be modified in the coming weeks. “If you want to be a part of bipartisan, comprehensive immigration reform compromise so that we can get a bill to the president’s desk in 2027, we welcome you with open arms.”

Even if the bills pass both chambers, uncertainty remains over whether Trump — who has the power to veto them — will sign them.

Speaking to Fox News about how he would work with a Democratic Congress, Trump said: “They are in control, but they’re really not in control. They can send over 50 different, great bills that they’re all excited about, and I send them back with a nice stamp veto.” On election night, upon learning of the Republican defeat, he posted on his social network, Truth, an image of a red cap with one word printed on it: “VETO.”

ICE yes, ICE no

Another issue Democrats have announced for the next legislative session concerns the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE). Views differ within the party. Those on the left, such as socialists, advocate for abolishing the agency responsible for detaining and deporting migrants. Others, more moderate, are content to cut the exorbitant budget allocated to the immigration agenda, which stands at about $240 billion.

Representative Cuéllar, who is likely to chair the House Appropriations subcommittee that funds the DHS, said last Wednesday: “I’m not going to abolish ICE, but I will put serious railguards on ICE. We’ve got to put ICE the way it was before January of 2025, and we will get that done.”

Investigations into abuses by ICE and DHS after two years without accountability are another priority announced by Democratic lawmakers.

The brutality of detentions, deportations without due process, family separations, and falsehoods coming from the government have carried scarcely any consequences. Investigations into deaths caused by fire from immigration agents — of U.S. citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti, of Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and of Colombian Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero — remain unresolved. With the majority they will hold, Democrats can subpoena key officials and compel them to testify under oath before Congress.

Possible subjects of investigation include border czar Tom Homan; former Homeland Security secretary Kristi Noem; former Border Patrol chief Gregory Bovino; and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, among others.

Democratic Representative from Maryland Jamie Raskin — who is poised to chair the House Judiciary Committee — told public radio network NPR four days after the elections that Congress will use “every tool” at its disposal to investigate ICE and that the time has come for the agency to “start answering to the American people.”

“Do not let us down”

Victory at the ballot box is not free, and voters will demand action from the Democrats. “Do not let us down,” Mario Guerrero, president of the South Texas Builders Association, warned Democrats last week while campaigning for legalization of migrant workers.

The aggressive immigration policy has also affected the economy because deportations and detentions have left many sectors — such as hospitality, agriculture, caregiving, and healthcare — short on labor. Business owners who identified as Republicans voted for Democrats in the midterms. Guerrero is one such example: after voting for Trump in three elections, he withdrew his support in the midterms. He now expects results.

Pressure for Democrats to act quickly to reverse the damage caused by the immigration agenda is coming from several fronts. One week after the elections, the country’s leading Latino organizations sent a joint letter to Democratic leaders demanding accountability for abuses committed during the anti-immigrant campaign that targeted this community for arrest quotas. The support of Latino voters who distanced themselves from Trump after backing him in 2024 determined the Democratic victory.

“At this critical moment, you have the power to deliver accountability and change, and we stand ready to help,” the letter — signed by Voto Latino, UnidosUS, America’s Voice and We Are CASA, among others — states. They ask that those responsible for the immigration agenda be investigated and that ICE funding be frozen. “The American people have given you the power to hold the architects of mass deportation accountable. Use it on day one, and we will be with you until the job is done,” the letter concludes.

text:
The Trump administration admitted it deported a U.S. citizen in court documents filed Friday in an ongoing federal lawsuit, stemming from a Texas Department of Public Safety traffic stop earlier this year near Fredericksburg.

Brian José Morales García, who was born in Denver and raised in Mexico before he moved to Austin, had told the trooper that he had a birth certificate and a Social Security card that proved he was a U.S. citizen before the officer called immigration enforcement officers.

Morales García “is a dual citizen of the United States and Mexico,” U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons wrote in a motion filed in the case before U.S. District Judge Robert Pitman in Austin.

It’s the first time a Trump administration official has admitted in no uncertain terms Morales García is a U.S. citizen after initially insisting he was in the country illegally. Morales García was the passenger in a pickup truck with coworkers on his way to install an air conditioning system, a job he recently had started after not finding stable work in Colorado where his brother lives.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security and Texas DPS didn’t immediately answer questions in emails from The Texas Tribune seeking comment about the latest court filing.

In May, Morales García’s attorneys filed a lawsuit against Immigration and Customs Enforcement, DPS and the Gillespie County Sheriff’s Office, which had responded to the initial traffic stop.

As part of the lawsuit, Morales García is seeking an unspecified amount of money for being deported.

The federal government’s admission that Morales García, who has since returned to the country, is a U.S. citizen is part of a motion to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the federal government has immunity in immigration enforcement. The judge has not made a ruling.

In an April statement to the Texas Tribune, shortly after Morales García’s removal, a U.S. Customs and Border Protection spokesperson cast doubt about his citizenship and insisted he was in the country illegally.

“CBP did NOT arrest a U.S. citizen,” the agency spokesperson said in a statement. “Agents determined Morales García was illegally in the U.S. through record checks. Morales García also admitted he is a Mexican national and he entered the country illegally.”

In previous interviews with the Tribune, Morales García said he told agents that he had entered the country legally through El Paso’s port of entry and had proof at home. The agents responded by accusing him of lying “and they told me I could go to prison, so I just told them I entered illegally,” he said.

Now that he’s back at home and working, he said he remains concerned.

“Am I supposed to just accept that if I get pulled over again, it’ll be the same thing?” Morales García said in September upon returning to Austin. “Will it be the same treatment?”

Morales García’s mother, María del Socorro García, previously said she and her sister moved from Mexico to Denver in 1999. She had two children, including Morales García and his younger brother, Miguel. Socorro García said she returned to Mexico with her sons in 2002 because she wanted them to meet their grandfather, who had been struggling with diabetes. Her husband followed them later, and they agreed to stay and raise their sons in Mexico.

In January 2025, a family friend who also has relatives in Denver drove Morales García from Aguascalientes to the border city of Ciudad Juárez, where they drove across the bridge into El Paso. Morales García said he showed the U.S. Customs and Border Protection his birth certificate and they let them through.

“I wanted to come to the U.S. because I wanted to work and help provide for my wife who was three months pregnant at the time,” Morales García said.

When the federal government and Morales García’s lawyers reached an agreement in August to allow his return into the country, U.S. Department of Homeland media officials told the Tribune they were working on a response about the development. Then, they stopped answering inquiries and never said anything about García’s return — after questioning his citizenship for months.

His arrest and removal renewed attention on the eagerness among many Texas law enforcement agencies to help the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. The state is home to roughly 1.7 million undocumented citizens and hundreds of police agencies have signed up to work with federal immigration agents.

The scrutiny over the state’s role in the president’s mass deportation effort has only increased after an ICE agent shot to death a man, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, in Houston in July and another agent shot and wounded another man in Austin in September.

There is no authoritative accounting of deported citizens. From 2015 to 2020, immigration agents arrested 674, detained 121, and removed 70 potential U.S. citizens, according to a congressional watchdog.

description:
Rwanda has once again offered to partner with Europe on migration.
British officials developed a plan to send asylum seekers to Rwanda in 2022.
But the UK’s Supreme Court ruled that the central African nation wasn’t a safe destination for migrants.

text:
Joins coalition of 20 AGs in recommending inquiries into accountability of immigration officers, detention practices, and DHS waste and corruption

RICHMOND, Va. — Virginia Attorney General Jones joined a coalition of 20 attorneys general in encouraging leaders of the incoming majorities in Congress to hold hearings on Trump Administration abuses in immigration enforcement. In a letter to congressional leadership — including the incoming chairs of House and Senate committees with responsibility over the judiciary, homeland security, and government oversight and accountability — Attorney General Jones and the coalition encourage Congress to hold hearings on the accountability of immigration officers, detention practices, and waste and corruption in the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

Attorney General Jones and the coalition also encourage the incoming chairs of these committees to feature testimony at the hearings from Americans directly harmed by immigration enforcement abuse, advocates for immigrant communities, and from state Attorneys General who have been using the tools at their disposal to fight against this abuse and for the rule of law. State officials and community leaders have important insights to share gathered through truth councils, accountability commissions, and other community engagement.

“Across the country communities are living in fear because of this administration’s lawless actions. It’s time to hold those who have terrorized and targeted our neighbors, with no respect for the law, accountable,” said Attorney General Jones. “Virginians are fighting to scrape by while DHS is pouring money into the pockets of Trump donors, violating the law and people’s rights, and tearing families apart.”

Donald Trump’s DHS and its agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and Customs and Border Protection (CBP), have operated as if they are exempt from accountability and the rule of law. In 2025, DHS began a months-long campaign of lawlessness across multiple American cities. Since the beginning of Trump’s second term, DHS agents have shot at least 25 people across the United States.

Use of force by immigration agents has also increased dramatically. In just the first three months of the current administration, there was a nearly fourfold increase in reported ICE use-of-force incidents. Independent researchers have subsequently documented more than 400 incidents of misuse of crowd-control weapons in 16 cities across the country in just 12 months, resulting in over 200 injuries to demonstrators, bystanders, and journalists attempting to cover the events.

Attorney General Jones and the coalition write to Congressional leaders: “In the face of immigration enforcement conduct that is both immoral and unlawful, the outgoing House and Senate majorities were content to look the other way. The incoming majorities need to confront this head-on. The American people voted for real, serious oversight — with teeth and consequences for any agency or individual who would ignore the rule of law.”

Immigration detention practices are in dire need of reform and oversight as well. By ICE’s own accounting, close to 60 people have died in ICE custody in the past two years, enough to make 2025 the deadliest year in immigration detention in over two decades.

DHS has also wasted significant sums of money in its rushed and ill-conceived efforts to rapidly expand immigration detention. DHS spent approximately $1 billion purchasing warehouses in a grossly inhumane effort to house people in them before shifting course. Now DHS has purchased four prisons from CoreCivic, a significant donor to President Trump’s inaugural committee and his PACs, for the extraordinary sum of $2.2 billion. DHS paid CoreCivic $495 million for a prison in Minnesota that CoreCivic offered to the State of Minnesota for just $75 million in 2025. Americans deserve to know whether DHS is inflating the purchase price of these facilities and diverting their tax dollars into the coffers of the President’s supporters.
