description:
samael1986/Depositphotos A major court setback A federal appeals court has ruled against the Trump administration in a dispute over New York's commercial driver's licensing practices under earlier federal regulations.
The ruling centers on commercial driver's licenses issued in New York and a dispute over how long those licenses could remain valid.
The agency had accused New York of improperly issuing certain commercial driver's licenses.
Depositphotos New York's licensing policy New York issued nondomiciled commercial driver's licenses that were generally valid for five years after initial approval.
How do you think federal commercial driver's licensing requirements should balance road safety, regulatory consistency, and state responsibilities?
text:
samael1986/Depositphotos

A major court setback

A federal appeals court has ruled against the Trump administration in a dispute over New York's commercial driver's licensing practices under earlier federal regulations. The ruling centers on commercial driver's licenses issued in New York and a dispute over how long those licenses could remain valid.

The decision overturns a federal funding penalty of more than $73 million imposed on New York. The case raises important questions about state licensing rules and federal transportation authority.

Depositphotos

Appeals court backs New York

A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit ruled in favor of New York on November 13, 2026. The state had challenged a decision by the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration, known as FMCSA.

The agency had accused New York of improperly issuing certain commercial driver's licenses. However, the appeals court found that federal regulations in effect at the time did not contain the specific requirement the agency wanted to enforce.

Depositphotos

Millions in funding at stake

The federal government had imposed a $73,502,543 highway funding penalty on New York for fiscal year 2027. That amount represented 4% of the state's federal-aid highway funding covered by the decision.

The money supports important transportation projects, including road repairs, bridge improvements, and other infrastructure work. New York Attorney General Letitia James argued that withholding the funding would threaten resources needed to repair roads and bridges across the state.

Mehaniq/Depositphotos

What are nondomiciled CDLs?

Nondomiciled commercial driver's licenses are issued to individuals who meet specific federal eligibility requirements and are domiciled outside the issuing state or jurisdiction under qualifying circumstances. These licenses allow qualified drivers to operate commercial vehicles, including large trucks.

Depending on their immigration status, eligible applicants have included DACA recipients, refugees, and people granted asylum under earlier rules. The licensing system has become a major focus of federal efforts to change how immigrant truck drivers are approved.

Depositphotos

New York's licensing policy

New York issued nondomiciled commercial driver's licenses that were generally valid for five years after initial approval. Renewed licenses could remain valid for up to eight years. The state allowed these licenses to extend beyond the expiration dates of some drivers' immigration documents.

Applicants still had to provide documentation showing lawful presence when applying. This difference between immigration document expiration and license expiration eventually became the center of the federal dispute.

Little-known fact: Commercial driver's licenses are issued by state governments, not the federal transportation agency.

Mehaniq/Depositphotos

Thousands of licenses affected

New York had approximately 32,600 holders of nondomiciled commercial driver's licenses and learner's permits as of July 2025, according to the court's opinion. That represented around 7% of the state's active commercial licenses and permits.

The number helps explain why the federal review attracted so much attention. Changes to the licensing system could affect thousands of drivers and employers who depend on commercial transportation workers.

Depositphotos

Federal review raises concerns

FMCSA began reviewing New York's licensing program in July 2025. The agency examined whether the state was following federal requirements when issuing licenses to drivers with temporary immigration documents.

In a sample of 200 licenses and permits, officials identified 101 that remained valid beyond the expiration dates of the immigration documents presented by applicants. The findings led the agency to question the state's licensing practices and demand changes.

Fun fact: New Class A and Class B CDL applicants must complete approved entry-level driver training before taking their skills tests.

Mehaniq/Depositphotos

Federal officials demand changes

After its review, FMCSA directed New York to pause issuing certain nondomiciled commercial licenses and withdraw licenses it considered noncompliant. The agency later issued a final determination in April 2026.

It warned that the state could lose 4% of its federal highway funding if it did not meet the agency's interpretation of the rules. Continued noncompliance could have resulted in subsequent annual funding penalties of up to $147 million, representing 8% of the applicable federal highway funding.

Depositphotos

The court explains its decision

New York argued that the federal rules in effect when the licenses were issued did not require commercial licenses to expire alongside immigration documents. The appeals court agreed with the state's interpretation.

The judges said applicants had to show valid immigration documents when applying, but the regulations did not require the license itself to expire on the same date. The court concluded that the government could not withhold federal money over a requirement that did not exist at the time.

Depositphotos

Administration rejects state's approach

Federal transportation officials argued that the older rules implied a requirement to match license expiration dates with immigration documents. They said this would help prevent people whose permission to remain or work in the country had expired from operating commercial vehicles.

The appeals court rejected that interpretation. The court found that the wording, structure, and history of the earlier regulations did not support the agency's interpretation.

thenews2.com/Depositphotos

New York celebrates the ruling

New York Attorney General Letitia James and Governor Kathy Hochul welcomed the decision. In a joint statement, they described the ruling as a victory for New York residents who rely on safe roads and the drivers who support the state's economy.

They also argued that the decision would protect people who rely on safe roads and the workers who support New York's economy. The ruling gives the state relief from the threatened funding penalty in this particular dispute.

palinchak/Depositphotos

New federal rules change eligibility

A separate federal rule that took effect on March 16, 2026, introduced much tighter eligibility requirements for nondomiciled commercial driver's licenses. It generally limits eligibility to foreign nationals with H-2A, H-2B, or E-2 immigration classifications.

The rule also generally limits license validity to one year or the expiration of the driver's authorized stay in the United States, whichever comes first. These newer restrictions were not decided in the New York appeals court case.

Why is California's Medi-Cal program facing growing debate over costs and immigrant coverage? Discover what is driving the discussion and how coverage decisions could affect the state's healthcare budget and residents.

Depositphotos

Another legal battle continues

The newer federal licensing restrictions are facing a separate legal challenge before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. That case focuses on the legality of the updated federal requirements.

On May 5, 2026, the court declined to suspend the final rule while the legal challenge continued. For now, the New York ruling addresses the older regulations and the threatened funding penalty, not the legality of the newer restrictions. The two legal disputes remain separate.

text:
Joins federal lawsuit with FTC and bipartisan coalition of 30 AGs against Dollar General for routinely charging consumers more at the register than the products advertised and shelf prices

November 20, 2026 (SAINT PAUL) — Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison has joined the Federal Trade Commission and a bipartisan coalition of 30 attorneys general in filing a federal lawsuit against Dollar General, alleging that the company has engaged in a long-running and widespread deceptive pricing scheme where it has routinely charged customers more at the register than the prices Dollar General displays on its shelves, on its price tags, and in its advertisements, resulting in consumers being overcharged millions of dollars.

“It’s my job to protect Minnesotans’ wallets and help them afford their lives,” Attorney General Ellison said. “Minnesotans visit Dollar General’s stores everyday believing it’s a place that they can stretch their hard-earned money to buy the things they need to get by. Dollar General has abused that trust by routinely overcharging them at the register despite promising lower prices, all in the name of padding their corporate profits. I’m joining with my fellow AGs and the FTC to put a stop to these unlawful pricing practices that are harming Minnesotans.”

Dollar General is a Tennessee-based, publicly traded company with more than 21,000 stores nationwide that has attempted to position itself as “America’s neighborhood general store.” In Minnesota, Dollar General has at least 226 store locations, most of which are located in rural communities. The first amended complaint, filed today in U.S. District Court in the Middle District of Tennessee, alleges that for years, Dollar General has repeatedly mislabeled prices, overcharged consumers, and failed to correct the issue despite extensive corporate knowledge of the problem. It has done so despite promising lower prices on its website, app, and print advertising, in-store price tags, and shelf prices. These widespread deceptive pricing practices have cost consumers millions in overcharges.

The lawsuit accuses Dollar General of violating the FTC Act, the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, and state consumer protection laws, including Minnesota’s Prevention of Consumer Fraud Act and Deceptive Trade Practices Act. Attorney General Ellison, the bipartisan coalition of attorneys general, and the FTC ask the court to end Dollar General’s deceptive pricing practices, and grant equitable monetary relief, civil penalties, and attorney fees, among other remedies.

Joining Attorney General Ellison and the FTC in the lawsuit are the bipartisan attorneys general of Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Michigan, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, and Wisconsin.

A British far-right anti-immigration activist has been jailed for 15 months for criminal damage for slashing a small boat which had brought migrants from France to the United Kingdom.

Daniel Thomas, also known as “Danny Tommo”, is the founder of the British anti-migrant Patriot Platform group, which mobilised hundreds of protesters earlier this year. He pleaded guilty to criminal damage earlier this month, after slashing the inflatable vessel while a French emergency responder was on board.

Sentencing Thomas on Friday, judge James Newton-Price said the offence “amounted to flagrant interference and a deliberate disruption” of French and British authorities’ important activities in the English Channel.

“They do necessary, highly sensitive and difficult jobs, and which should not be disrupted by a publicity-seeker slashing with a knife a boat they were attempting to recover,” he added.

Thomas livestreamed himself on September 22 as he followed a small boat ⁠⁠carrying migrants across the Channel, who were transferred ⁠⁠onto another vessel and taken ashore.

The 37-year-old later approached the dinghy and slashed it with a knife, soon after a French rescue worker had stepped on board. British police arrested him shortly after the incident.

Prosecutor Joel Smith told Portsmouth Crown Court that Thomas had shouted “get off the boat, you’ve got time to get off the ⁠⁠boat … take them back, no more ⁠⁠of these”.

‘Thuggish’

Thomas appeared in court via videolink from prison, with his head bowed and rarely looked up as footage of ‌‌the incident was played.

Judge Newton-Price accepted that “there was no immediate danger to the rescue worker”, but said Thomas’s actions were a deliberate ‌‌attempt ‌‌to disrupt rescue efforts.

The far-right activist had built a large online following and organised gatherings of protesters on the UK’s southern coast in response to the arrivals of small boats.

A government minister described the demonstrations as “thuggish”.

The court heard that Thomas had five previous convictions, including in 2016 for kidnapping.

Separately, he is set to stand trial in London next June accused of multiple offences, including entering a restricted zone at a migrant processing centre in Dover in March.

UK government data shows the number of people arriving in small boats to British shores has fallen, though the crossings remain a prominent political issue which has dogged successive governments. Right-wing opposition parties and anti-immigration activists have called for more action.

text:
This article was updated at 6:07 p.m. on Nov. 20.

A federal judge ordered U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement late Friday to not remove Eva Yi Xie GS from the Eastern District of Virginia barring a further court order. The judge, Anthony Trenga ’71, also ordered ICE to respond to a petition for habeas corpus filed by Xie’s lawyers by 5 p.m. on Wednesday.

Xie is a third-year Princeton neuroscience Ph.D. student who was detained by ICE at an airport in Virginia on Thursday after departing the Society for Neuroscience’s annual conference in Washington, D.C. She is being held at an ICE holding facility in Chantilly, Va. Xie, who was born in China, came to the United States in 2016 on a visa, when she was a minor. Though her original nonimmigrant status has expired, she has a pending asylum claim and an immigration court date set for early 2028, according to her lawyer, Kerry Doyle.

Trenga did not immediately respond to a request for comment. ICE did not respond to multiple requests for comment on Thursday and Friday.

During the current Trump administration, ICE has frequently moved detainees away from the districts in which they were detained, but Trenga’s order prohibits that from happening to Xie.

Mahmoud Khalil, who was detained in New York in March 2025 as a recent Columbia University graduate, was transferred to a detention facility in Jena, La. as his case was being heard. Khalil was a prominent organizer of the pro-Palestine encampments at Columbia.

Rümeysa Öztürk, a Tufts University student detained by ICE in March 2025, was also brought to Louisiana from Massachusetts. Öztürk’s student visa was revoked by the U.S. government largely due to an op-ed she co-authored in The Tufts Daily, the university’s student newspaper, that was critical of the university’s response to the Gaza war.

Xie does not appear to have been outspoken on political issues at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where she was an undergraduate student, nor at Princeton.

THIS IS A BREAKING NEWS UPDATE. The Daily Princetonian’s original story follows below.

Eva Yi Xie GS, a third-year Princeton neuroscience Ph.D. student who was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Virginia on Thursday, is an asylum seeker who has an immigration court date set for early 2028, her lawyer Kerry Doyle told The Daily Princetonian on Friday afternoon. A habeas corpus petition has been filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia by Xie’s lawyers.

Xie was detained at the Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Va., after departing from the Society for Neuroscience annual conference, where she presented a poster on Wednesday. Rupert Li, a mathematics Ph.D. student at Stanford University who Xie is in a relationship with, told the ‘Prince’ that Xie was planning to board a domestic flight to the San Francisco International Airport to visit him.

Doyle, who was arranged to represent Xie by the University, said ICE has not informed her of a reason for the arrest. ICE did not respond to multiple requests for comment on Thursday and Friday.

The law office of Parastoo Golesorkhi Zahedi, based in Virginia, is also representing Xie. Doyle previously served as a principal legal adviser for ICE and as deputy general counsel of the Department of Homeland Security during the Biden administration. She is a partner at the law firm Green & Spiegel.

Xie is currently being held at an ICE holding center in Chantilly, Va. She has been there since she was detained Thursday afternoon, according to Doyle. Holding centers are not fully equipped detention facilities, and they are meant to be a temporary holding location.

Xie arrived in the United States from China in 2016, when she was a minor, and attended the Bronx High School of Science. She later attended the Massachusetts Institute of Technology as an undergraduate. Doyle said that Xie’s family applied for asylum within a year of arriving. The asylum claim was referred to immigration court, though Doyle said she does not yet know when that referral occurred.

In the habeas corpus filing, according to Doyle, Xie’s lawyers argued that ICE detained her without a warrant. They claimed that because Xie did not have a recent change in circumstances or pose an imminent risk of leaving the country that would make a warrantless arrest necessary, Xie should be released.

According to Doyle, holding facilities like the one in Chantilly don’t have accommodations like readily accessible beds and showers, making them incompatible for long-term detention. She called it “completely inhumane” to hold people at processing facilities for extended periods.

In August 2026, immigration advocacy organizations reported poor conditions at the Virginia facility. The American Civil Liberties Union reported that up to 80 people were held in a single room for longer than a week without access to lawyers, medical care, or basic hygiene.

Since Xie’s detention, members of the University community have advocated for her release. Princeton graduate students and Xie’s lab have called for people to send messages to politicians in New Jersey and Virginia about the case.

New Jersey Senator Andy Kim’s office is directly in touch with Xie, according to Kim’s press secretary Katey Sabo. She added that his office is “working on the case” in a statement to the ‘Prince.’

Sen. Cory Booker, the other New Jersey senator, wrote in a statement to the ‘Prince’ that ICE has not responded to his outreach on Xie’s detention. Kim and Booker are both Democrats.

“My office has contacted U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) regarding the detention of Eva Yi Xie and has not yet received a response. I expect a prompt and full explanation of the circumstances surrounding her detention,” Booker wrote.

Wynne Stagnaro GS, a member of Xie’s lab, shared in an interview with the ‘Prince’ that Xie’s advisor, Carlos Brody, has said she is remaining calm about the situation.

“‘She’s amazing, steady as a rock,’” Stagnaro said Brody wrote after speaking with Xie. “I really want Eva to be able to be back and to be able to live her life and to be able to celebrate the holiday. It’s really jarring and something that I don’t think should be happening,” Stagnaro added.

İnci Çetin GS, who serves on the policy subcommittee of the Faculty Committee on the Graduate School alongside Xie, had been on a call with other graduate students right before she spoke with the ‘Prince.’ She shared in an interview that Xie has been a strong leader for the graduate student body.

“She’s a really engaged person. She always brought up important issues … to the community, and she was vocal about it,” Çetin said.

The Society for Neuroscience, which organized the conference Xie was attending, wrote in a statement that it was “closing monitoring the detention.”

“We are in close contact with Princeton University and stand ready to provide any support that may be needed. Our thoughts are with Eva, her family, and her colleagues,” the Society added.

“News of Eva’s detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community,” Dean of the Graduate School Rodney Priestley wrote in a statement to the ‘Prince.’ “We will remain in contact with her legal team, her family, and colleagues to provide support.”

“We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton,” Priestley added.

Xie is the first MIT graduate or student detained by ICE

Reddit

US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detained Eva Yi Xie ’24, a third-year neuroscience Ph.D. candidate at Princeton University, at Reagan National Airport on Thursday, Nov. 19. She is being held in a detention center in Chantilly, Va., The Daily Princetonian first reported.

Xie was returning from the Society for Neuroscience’s annual conference in Washington, D.C., where she presented a poster on how brain cells long known for tracking physical location might also track the information used to make decisions. Her co-authors included MIT professor Ila Fiete, whose lab Xie worked in as an undergraduate.

In a statement to The Daily Princetonian, Princeton Professor Carlos Brody, Xie’s Ph.D. advisor, wrote that detaining Xie was “wildly unfair” and was not in the best interest of the United States.

“Eva is a brilliant law-abiding student and wonderful person who has many talents to contribute to the United States,” Brody told the Princeton student newspaper. “Detaining her, with the intent of deporting her, makes no sense whatsoever. It is cruel, and it is our country shooting itself in the foot.”

According to a post on X from the Brody Lab, Xie sent a “call for help from her lab mates on Slack” before losing contact.

“Her lawyers are working on her release,” the post states. “She went to a conference to present her work, and now she’s in a detention center. She should be home.”

Xie graduated from MIT in 2024 with a double major in 6-4 (AI and Decision Making) and 18 (Mathematics). In addition to doing research in Professor Fiete’s lab, Xie also worked with Professors Earl Miller, Tomaso Poggio, and Aleksander Madry during her time at the Institute as an undergraduate.

Xie emigrated from Shanghai, China to the United States in 2016, where she attended the Bronx High School of Science and was a Regeneron Science Talent Search Finalist.

This is the first case of ICE detaining an MIT graduate or student. In 2017, MIT custodian Francisco Rodriguez was released from ICE detainment after being held for five months.

Sophie Liu ’27, a friend of Xie, told The Tech that she learned of the detention through a friend’s Instagram story.

“I’ve been crying ever since [I found out],” Liu said. “I know her ranking of boba shops. We played board games together in Simmons, debated if subs are secretly tacos, and now she’s in the news for this awful, tragic reason.”

Liu urged others to “help us get her home” by sharing the news on social media and calling their representatives.

According to fellow Princeton graduate student Wynne Stagnaro, members of the Brody Lab have been in touch with the office of Senator Andy Kim (D-NJ), media, and other elected officials to arrange her release. A Princeton spokesperson has said that Princeton has secured legal counsel to represent Xie.

Amid recent policy changes towards international students, including new limits on how long they can stay in the U.S. and proposed restrictions on student work programs, MIT has been navigating an increasingly uncertain landscape for its international community.

In a May video message sent to the MIT community, MIT President Sally Kornbluth noted that federal policy changes are discouraging international applicants.

“I’ve said many times that MIT is in the talent business. Which means we’re very alert to changes in our talent pipeline,” Kornbluth said. “We’ve already seen clear signs that policy changes affecting international students and scholars are discouraging extremely talented individuals from applying to join our community.”

The Institute has also launched initiatives such as “The World at MIT,” a series of videos featuring foreign-born professors, including economics Nobel laureate Daron Acemoglu and CSAIL director Daniela Rus.

Last year in April, nine MIT community members had their visas abruptly revoked and restored. And in May of last year, the MIT Office of the General Counsel released a bulletin to the MIT community on navigating immigration and law enforcement interactions on campus.

This is a developing story and may be updated. Please send tips to tt-news@mit.edu.

text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani proposed Friday to delay the closure of Rikers Island until 2032, five years beyond the deadline established under a 2019 city law. The plan, announced November 20, 2026, would require City Council approval to extend the August 31, 2027 deadline while the city builds four replacement jails and reduces the number of people in custody.

City Council Speaker Julie Menin has expressed support for extending the timeline, citing years of construction delays. Brooklyn Council Member Sandy Nurse is expected to sponsor legislation revising the closure requirement, with possible interim deadlines for construction and jail population reductions. Lawmakers are expected to examine the proposal at an oversight hearing in December.

Under the new schedule, Brooklyn's replacement jail would open in 2029, followed by facilities in the Bronx and Queens in 2031 and Manhattan in 2032. The completed system would provide approximately 4,500 beds, requiring New York City to reduce its jail population from roughly 6,600 people to no more than 4,100 by the end of 2032.

Attorney Advertising

An intermediate target calls for reducing the population to 5,500 by the time the Brooklyn facility opens. City officials plan to achieve those reductions through expanded alternatives to detention, faster criminal case processing, mental health services and changes to bail procedures.

The closure requirement dates to legislation adopted under former Mayor Bill de Blasio in 2019, when the city committed to replacing Rikers with smaller facilities closer to courts, public transportation and the communities where people in custody live. Construction setbacks, rising costs and an increase in the jail population have pushed the transition years beyond its original schedule.

Mamdani's proposal comes as Rikers operates under federal court supervision following years of litigation over excessive force, unsafe conditions and violations of court-ordered reforms.

In February, U.S. District Judge Laura Taylor Swain formally appointed Nicholas Deml as remediation manager in Nunez v. City of New York, granting him authority to direct changes to jail operations, staffing, investigations and accountability procedures. Deml began his role on February 23 after the court found that earlier oversight and reform orders had failed to correct longstanding constitutional violations.

Attorney Advertising

Federal supervision remains in place as the city prepares to replace Rikers. Deml's responsibilities include addressing unsafe conditions in existing facilities and overseeing operational reforms that will affect the transition to the new jails.

The administration plans to invest $146 million next fiscal year in mental health care, substance use treatment, education, vocational training and services for crime victims. Additional funding through fiscal year 2030 would support programs intended to reduce detention and help people return to their communities.

Hospital-based treatment is another part of the transition. The city plans to add 236 therapeutic beds at hospitals in Brooklyn and the Bronx, bringing its total planned capacity to 340 beds for incarcerated people with serious mental illnesses or complex medical needs. A 104-bed unit opened at Bellevue Hospital in April.

Criminal case delays are also a target. The city's closure plan identifies approximately 1,470 people who have spent more than a year in pretrial detention, including hundreds awaiting resolution of serious felony charges.

Officials intend to establish an interagency task force involving prosecutors, defense attorneys, courts and law enforcement agencies to accelerate case processing and the exchange of evidence. The effort would address delays that extend detention for people awaiting trial under New York's speedy trial laws.

Other proposed changes include expanding pretrial advocacy teams to challenge unaffordable bail, increasing supervised release options and restoring online bail payments so families can arrange release without traveling to correctional facilities.

The administration has already closed the North Infirmary Command on Rikers and transferred the building, along with portions of two other facilities, to the Department of Citywide Administrative Services. Further transfers are planned as replacement jails open, allowing the city to consider renewable energy and other uses for the island.

title: Are immigration agents targeting people of color in Northern California? The ACLU is investigating
description:
A Sacramento-area man says he was driving to a landscaping job with a longtime friend when federal immigration agents followed their truck into a grocery store parking lot.
Julio, whose real name is being withheld because he fears retaliation, said several agents approached the vehicle and identified themselves as immigration officers.
The organization has also been documenting vehicles left behind after reported encounters with immigration agents.
The Department of Homeland Security rejected allegations that immigration agents are targeting people based on race or ethnicity.
Last month, a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction barring immigration agents from conducting detentive stops based on racial stereotyping in seven Southern California counties.
text:
A Sacramento-area man says he was driving to a landscaping job with a longtime friend when federal immigration agents followed their truck into a grocery store parking lot.

Julio, whose real name is being withheld because he fears retaliation, said several agents approached the vehicle and identified themselves as immigration officers.

Julio said the agents eventually handcuffed him and held him in a vehicle for about 15 minutes before releasing him. His friend was taken into custody.

“You don’t feel as safe anymore,” Julio said in Spanish. “Sometimes you don’t feel safe going out because you think they could arrest you at any moment, even though you haven’t done anything.”

Julio has lived in the United States for over 25 years and works as a landscaper. He said the encounter has changed how he goes about his daily life, even as he continues working and caring for his family.

(Gerardo Zavala/CapRadio)

Giselle Garcia with NorCal Resist, a mutual aid-organization and immigrant-rights group, said agents never told Julio why they had approached the truck. The paperwork he later received instructing him to report to ICE for a check-in also did not give a reason for the encounter.

Garcia explained that Julio has no criminal history and had no legal immigration status at the time. He had entered the country without inspection and recently applied for a U visa, a form of immigration relief available to certain victims of crimes who cooperate with law enforcement.

That’s significant because under a May federal court ruling, ICE generally cannot arrest, detain or deport individuals with a pending U visa application.

“It doesn’t seem like they actually had that reasonable suspicion to pull him over,” Garcia said.

Garcia added that Julio’s friend later signed paperwork agreeing to leave the country, which she says is common among people the organization hears from.

“The majority of these individuals have unfortunately signed voluntary departure after being detained,” she said. “And there’s a lot of different factors. One, they come from very hard working class families that don’t have the funds to hire an attorney… others have expressed they felt forced to sign that document because of ICE officers saying ‘You have to, you have to, you have to.’”

Garcia said accounts like Julio’s are part of a broader pattern of federal immigration enforcement they are trying to document.

NorCal Resist’s rapid-response network has flagged nearly 80 cases for possible racial profiling since Oct. 25, according to Garcia. The nonprofit has sent those cases to the ACLU of Northern California for review.

The groups have not announced a lawsuit over the recent enforcement activity, but the ACLU says it’s gathering accounts and looking for evidence of broader patterns.

Looking for patterns in traffic stops

Emilia Garcia, an investigator with the ACLU of Northern California, said the organization is interviewing people who have been stopped to understand what happened and whether agents gave a reason for the encounter.

She said the goal is to learn whether officers appeared to know anything about someone before stopping them, or whether the person was approached seemingly at random.

“ICE is pulling people over either because they see that they’re a person of color or they see a vehicle that looks like it might be driven by a person of color,” the ACLU investigator said. “We’ve been seeing huge numbers of work trucks with either construction or landscaping materials, maybe pulling trailers or with racks on the back, being pulled over.”

NorCal Resist is helping identify potential cases and connect people with the ACLU. Programs Director Giselle Garcia said the organization has been flagging and referring cases it believes warrant further scrutiny.

The referrals include cases the group believes may involve racial profiling or other potentially unlawful enforcement practices.

“Our role is providing the real human stories that prove these abuses are happening,” Garcia said, describing how NorCal Resist’s Migra Watch observers find abandoned vehicles and make door-to-door visits to alert families that someone has been taken.

Garcia added that NorCal Resist has completed intakes for more than 140 detainments since Oct. 6. The organization has flagged about 80 of these cases so far as potentially involving racial profiling.

These cases have not all been independently verified as instances of profiling by the ACLU.

Garcia also said many of the reported encounters have happened during the morning commute between 5:30 a.m. and 9 a.m. and that most in the reports have been men of color.

“With the exception of two or three women out of these 73, they’ve all been men. Brown men,” she said in an earlier interview.

Garcia said another pattern is that many of the people being detained have had little or no prior contact with the immigration system have no criminal record.

“They don’t even have A-numbers assigned when we talk to their families,” she said, referring to Alien Registration Numbers, unique identifiers used in immigration records.

The organization has also been documenting vehicles left behind after reported encounters with immigration agents. In one case near Marysville, Garcia said an employer contacted the group after four workers failed to show up.

“Our observers through Migra Watch found that vehicle on the side of the highway,” Garcia recounted. “We saw coffee cups and lunches throughout the car so we knew it was at least four people.”

Garcia said the employer didn’t know their full names so they weren’t able to track them all down to get them help.

“How many of these kinds of detainments are going unaccounted for and people being eaten up by the system?” she added.

The Department of Homeland Security rejected allegations that immigration agents are targeting people based on race or ethnicity.

“Allegations that DHS law enforcement engages in ‘racial profiling’ are disgusting, reckless, and categorically FALSE” a department spokesperson said in a statement. “What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is if they are illegally in the U.S. — NOT their skin color, race, or ethnicity.”

The spokesperson said ICE officers use reasonable suspicion to investigate immigration status and probable cause to make arrests, consistent with the Fourth Amendment. However, they did not elaborate on what constitutes “reasonable suspicion” when asked.

DHS also declined to discuss specific enforcement operations citing security and officer safety concerns.

What counts as racial profiling?

UC Davis law professor and immigration law expert Kevin Johnson said immigration officers generally need reasonable suspicion that someone is in the country unlawfully before making an investigative stop.

“And the Supreme Court has said that the officers are required to consider the totality of the circumstances, which includes attire, location of the stop, Mexican appearance and a variety of other factors,” he said. “But the court left it pretty open to the officers to consider what they want to consider in an immigration stop.”

Johnson is referring to a 1975 Supreme Court ruling that found apparent Mexican ancestry alone cannot justify an immigration stop, but that it could be considered alongside other factors.

The legal debate has resurfaced in Southern California where the ACLU and other groups sued over immigration raids and alleged that federal agents were stopping people based on their perceived Latino identity and other characteristics.

Last month, a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction barring immigration agents from conducting detentive stops based on racial stereotyping in seven Southern California counties.

But the ruling was not a final decision and the Trump administration has appealed. The injunction applies to Southern California, not the Sacramento region.

Johnson said a separate lawsuit in Northern California could potentially lead to similar restrictions if investigators document evidence that agents are relying on racial appearance, language or work attire to make stops.

Investigators would need to establish common patterns to prove federal immigration officers are racial profiling individuals in the region.

“You’d look at who is being apprehended and whether they were almost exclusively Latino,” he said. “You’d want to look at data of who’s being stopped, indicators like Spanish surname… You’d want to look at as much data as you can about the kinds of stops, where the stops are and what the officers when confronted say are the basis for the stop.”

“It’s hard to get that kind of information in advance of a lawsuit, but you certainly can collect data and talk to people who’ve been apprehended by ICE either on the streets or in workplaces or in arrests, including immigration check-ins.”

Johnson added that while he believes ICE officers are engaging in similar practices in the greater Sacramento area as in Southern California, the outcome of any potential case would depend on the facts gathered.

Still gathering evidence

Emilia Garcia said the ACLU is still in the fact-gathering stage and has not announced a lawsuit over the recent enforcement activity in Northern California.

Investigators are speaking with individuals who have been stopped and their families to learn whether the encounters point to a broader pattern.

“Myself and my co-workers interview them to understand ‘What did ICE say when they stopped you?” she said. “‘Did they have any reason to stop you? Did they know who you were before they stopped you or did they just sort of randomly stop you on the street, or in your work truck as you were going to a job?’”

The ACLU investigator said NorCal Resist’s rapid-response network is helping them connect with individuals who have been arrested or detained — and their families — so the ACLU can follow up with them.

For Julio, the encounter has left him feeling less secure in his daily life.

“You go to the store without thinking twice,” he said in Spanish. “You think, ‘I haven’t done anything wrong. I’m just going to pick something up.’ And then, after getting your groceries, suddenly they’re right there behind you. It’s unjust, honestly.”

And the experience has also made him think about his family and the possibility of being separated from his children.

“Leaving your children, not knowing whether you’ll make it back to them or not,” he said in Spanish. “All of this is very difficult.”

. . .

About the data: The data analyzed for this story was collected by NorCal Resist, an immigrant-rights organization that documents immigration enforcement activity reported by affected individuals and their families. It is not a comprehensive record of ICE arrests or operations in Northern California. Many enforcement actions may go unnoticed or unreported, meaning the dataset represents only a portion of the activity taking place in the region.

ICE is the only agency with comprehensive records of its own enforcement operations. CapRadio requested this information from the agency and DHS but did not receive the requested data. As a result, the analysis reflects the incidents documented and verified by NorCal Resist and should not be interpreted as a representative sample of all immigration arrests or enforcement activity.

Data verification: Each individual mentioned in this dataset starts out as a call from a family member or a member of the community. NorCal Resist and its partners — which include legal attorneys — verify individuals’ names and dates of birth to find them in the detainee locator system. Individuals who voluntarily depart are confirmed through volunteer attorneys who can check whether someone has signed voluntary departure forms within the EOIR system. Dispatches are not added to this list until NorCal Resist confirms the individual or individuals have been arrested or detained.

text:
On Nov. 3, 2026, Distinguished Professor Helen Norton argued before the U.S. Supreme Court in the case of St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a pivotal case at the intersection of religious freedom, LGBTQ+ rights and constitutional law.

For Norton, a 20-year Colorado Law professor and the Ira C. Rothgerber Jr. Chair in Constitutional Law who has served as Colorado’s Deputy Solicitor General for Constitutional and Civil Rights since 2020, the experience was a landmark moment within a storied legal career.

Listen to the oral arguments

Although Norton has sat at the Supreme Court counsel’s table three times previously, this was her first time arguing before the court.

Only a tiny percentage of attorneys will advocate at the nation’s highest court in their lifetimes—even fewer are women. Several Colorado Law professors have made Supreme Court arguments before or after their faculty appointments, but Norton is believed to be the first since Stephen F. Williams in 1983 to argue before SCOTUS while simultaneously serving on the faculty.

The occasion drew dozens of students, faculty and staff to Wolf Law for a listening session hosted by the Byron R. White Center, where Director Deep Gulasekaram and students provided an overview of the case. Cheers and applause erupted as Norton began speaking.

“I think it’s special to be at a law school connected enough to have professors doing things like this,” said 1L student Mikaela Gantz.

Read more about Norton’s experience:

Michelle Penn contributed research to this article.

How did you prepare to argue before the Supreme Court?

I’m part of a terrific team of legal professionals from Colorado’s Office of the Attorney General assigned to this case. Our first priority was writing our brief. After filing that in August, we had what turned out to be a little over two months before the oral argument.

I had been keeping a list of possible oral argument questions since I argued this case before the Tenth Circuit in March 2025, and we built on this template substantially—identifying areas of likely questioning, doing additional question-specific research, developing and test-driving and improving possible answers.

We added to this as we did a series of increasingly challenging moot courts—starting with moots by folks within the Attorney General's office and then expanding to moots with highly-experienced SCOTUS litigators and with scholars and lawyers who are subject matter experts.

I also listened to dozens of recordings of SCOTUS oral arguments.

Did anything surprise you about the process?

The very first time I sat at counsel’s table for a SCOTUS oral argument, I remember being startled by how close the justices are to the arguing counsel. If anybody sneezes…

Across your career you have published two books and dozens of articles, worked as deputy assistant attorney general for civil rights in the U.S. Department of Justice, and served on President-elect Barack Obama’s transition team. How does this compare to other career milestones?

It has been definitely a career highlight from start to finish: being part of a terrific team; the intellectual challenges of briefing and prepping for the oral argument; the experience of exchanging views with the justices.

And just as my work on this effort was informed in part by my writing and teaching about First Amendment and antidiscrimination law, I know going forward that my writing and teaching will be informed in part by this experience.

The argument is finished. What happens now?

Mostly we wait for the opinion.

But I’m a big believer in taking time after big projects (and sometimes smaller projects, too) to reflect and identify key lessons learned. So our team has dedicated time to discussing what worked and what we want to make sure to repeat and institutionalize in the future—and what we can do differently and improve going forward.

We did this after the trial three years ago, after the Tenth Circuit briefing and argument 18 months ago, after the SCOTUS briefing this past summer, and again after the oral argument.

What advice do you have for others preparing for high-stakes moments in their personal or professional life, whether in law or any other field?

Focus on what you can control: your effort, your curiosity, your empathy, and patience. Let go of what you can’t control. Your time is your most precious resource; spend it intentionally and wisely. Spend it on what matters.

text:
The “Cut Ties With ICE!” package would restrict the City from colluding with ICE and from using city resources to funnel New Yorkers into detention and deportation

NEW YORK CITY – Today, following the New York City Council’s immigration hearing, elected officials, immigrants’ rights advocates, and impacted communities rallied at City Hall in support of the “Cut Ties With ICE!” legislative package – three bills (Intros. 1078-A, 1077-A, and 209) that would cut off New York City’s deportation pipeline by restricting the City from colluding with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and from using city resources to funnel people into detention and deportation.

After years of advocacy to protect New York’s immigrant communities, New York City currently boasts strong, bipartisan sanctuary laws that have protected countless New Yorkers. But gaps exist, and the “Cut Ties With ICE” package would strengthen our laws by establishing judicial warrant requirements for ICE; a mechanism for City accountability when local laws are violated; and an assurance that local tax dollars are used for local needs, not to assist ICE operations.

Today’s action follows the horrific ICE violence in the Bronx earlier this fall. On October 8, ICE officers wearing street clothes and masks stopped Oscar Belgal and fired multiple rounds into his car, hitting him in the neck as his five-year-old son watched. Since then, advocates, electeds, and communities impacted by ICE have demanded the City take immediate, decisive action to cut ties with ICE.

Quotes from organizations, electeds, and impacted communities are as follows:

“ICE is a violent, rogue, unaccountable agency that has no place in New York City,” said Donna Lieberman, Executive Director of the New York Civil Liberties Union. “New York communities have been built by generations of immigrant love, ingenuity, creativity, and resilience — and ICE cannot scare, brutalize, or beat that out of us. We call on Mayor Mamdani and the City Council to pass the ‘Cut Ties With ICE’ package so every New Yorker can live with freedom, safety, and dignity.”

“New Yorkers have made it clear that we refuse to be complicit as ICE’s violent terror tactics tear families apart. We welcome the call from a growing number of elected officials to abolish ICE, and yet we must go further than calling for it to be abolished: we must cut off the sources that funnel our neighbors to ICE in the first place,” said Yasmine Farhang, Executive Director of the Immigrant Defense Project. “The Cut Ties with ICE legislative package is critical to strengthen current sanctuary laws that have not been updated in over a decade and will take meaningful steps in this moment to ensure New Yorkers can trust their city agencies not to funnel them to ICE’s deadly hands.”

“If we really believe New York is a city for immigrants, then city agencies should not be aiding ICE operations,” said Ben Brodsky, a member of Jews For Racial & Economic Justice (JFREJ). “If NYC wants to stay true to our sanctuary laws, it is imperative that this Council codify these protections with regard to the NYPD and the Department of Correction, to prevent these agencies from exploiting loopholes any further. Countless Jewish New Yorkers, including my great-grandparents, were given safe haven in New York when they arrived in the United States. Today, we call on our city to cut ties with ICE for good and ensure NYC remains a beacon of freedom.”

“For five years, we have shared stories with the City Council about New Yorkers who were funneled into ICE custody by the NYPD and DOC because of loopholes that exist in our laws,” said Rosa Cohen-Cruz, Immigration Policy Director at The Bronx Defenders. “They are the stories of New Yorkers who don’t make the headlines, but for their families and communities, the fact that the City was involved is eroding trust and creating fear. By passing these laws and completely cutting ties with ICE, the City can convincingly reassert that it refuses to participate in ICE’s campaign of terror.”

“ICE’s actions are taking an enormous toll on our communities with every neighbor they intimidate and every family they separate,” said Randy Ali, CEO of the Arab-American Family Support Center. “We refuse to accept that a federal agency can come into our city and our homes, break families apart, and tear at our social fabric. The City must do its part to ensure that public resources are used to protect our communities, not facilitate detention and deportation. Let’s send a clear signal that New York City stands with our immigrant neighbors.”

“Every New Yorker deserves due process no matter their race, background or immigration status,” said Murad Awawdeh, President & CEO, New York Immigration Coalition. “As ICE continues to escalate its attacks against our immigrant neighbors, New York City must strengthen its protection of all New Yorkers and ensure our tax dollars are invested in our communities – not used to tear families apart. ICE should not be able to rely on our local agencies to do its dirty work for it. If ICE wants to arrest a New Yorker, they should get a warrant signed by a judge. New York City cannot be an extension of ICE’s mass detention and deportation machine. By passing this legislative package, New York City can close loopholes in its sanctuary laws and hold City agencies accountable when they violate those protections. The City can lead and show the rest of the country what it means to strengthen due process protections for all New Yorkers.”

“When ICE agents shot Oscar Belgal in Marble Hill in front of his five-year-old son, they made clear how little regard this administration has for the safety of New Yorkers,” said Brad Hoylman-Sigal, Manhattan Borough President. “Our City has a responsibility to do everything in its power to protect our immigrant neighbors. That’s why I’m calling on the City Council to pass the Cut Ties With ICE package, which would ensure the City does not unduly facilitate the detention of immigrants, hold City agencies accountable when our sanctuary laws are violated, and keep New Yorkers’ tax dollars from funding ICE operations. New York is a city of immigrants, and we will use every tool at our disposal to keep our neighbors safe.”

“As ICE escalates its violent targeting of New Yorkers, it’s critical that the City Council take serious steps to protect our immigrant neighbors,” said Council Member Lincoln Restler. “We need to start by passing this legislative package, which would limit the NYPD’s ability to help ICE arrest New Yorkers, limit the Department of Correction’s communications with ICE, and create a pathway for immigrant New Yorkers harmed by immigration detainers to seek justice.”

“We must close the loopholes that allow for ICE to terrorize our communities,” said Council Member Alexa Avilés. “NYC is a sanctuary city because we are an immigrant city. Every person who lives here should feel safe to go about their daily lives and access our public services. Any failing of our sanctuary laws to provide that dignity and justice is a problem we must resolve as the City Council. Thank you to the organizers of the ICE Out! Coalition who have kept the safety and health of New Yorkers at the heart of their legislative package.”

“New York City cannot help an agency that shoots a father in front of his child,” said Council Member Julie Won. “On October 8, masked ICE officers in street clothes shot Oscar Belgal in the neck as his five-year-old son watched from the car. Immigrant families must be able to share personal information with city agencies without fear that ICE will get it. Our sanctuary laws need to catch up to how ICE operates now. City Council must pass Intros 1078-A, 1077-A, and 209, and Mayor Mamdani must sign them.”

“New York City has some of the strongest sanctuary laws in the country, and they’ve protected countless families,” said Majority Leader Shaun Abreu. “This package builds on that foundation, updating protections and clarifying our rules to make sure we are meeting the moment and protecting our neighbors. I’m proud to stand with my colleagues and our city’s advocates to ensure our city’s resources serve New Yorkers, not deportation.”

“State protections for immigrant families are only as strong as the local policies that support them. When city rules fall short, federal agents and the agencies that assist them find room to operate in the cracks. That is unacceptable,” said Assemblymember Karines Reyes, RN, Assembly prime sponsor of the New York for All/Dignity Not Detention Laws. “Due process is a right that belongs to every New Yorker, and we have a responsibility to ensure it is granted, regardless of status. Accountability ought to be enforced on authorities who so often violate local laws. Assurances that our tax dollars are used to support our needs, not to aid operations that put our communities in danger. New York City must be firm in its opposition to ICE and pass these council protections immediately.”

“When city agencies still find ways to assist ICE in kidnapping and deporting our neighbors, our sanctuary laws are rendered meaningless. I have seen firsthand how this collaboration impacts families in my district, including the detention of parents in front of their children and the loss of community members’ trust in the very institutions that are supposed to protect and serve them,” said Assemblywoman Catalina Cruz. “No New Yorker should fear that reaching out to their local government for help may tear their family apart. The Cut Ties With ICE package would make it plain that city agencies must respect our sanctuary laws and close the loopholes that allow collaboration to continue. Public resources should serve New Yorkers, not help ICE carry out its deportation agenda. We have a responsibility to make sure every New Yorker, regardless of immigration status, trusts the city they call home.”

“Our immigrant neighbors should be able to turn to their city for help without fearing that doing so could get them separated from their families,” said Council Member Christopher Marte. “Every city dollar and every city agency should serve the people who live here. We have no business helping ICE terrorize our communities, and we cannot leave loopholes in our laws that allow that cooperation to continue. Let’s pass this package and make good on the protection we’ve promised New Yorkers.”

“New York City’s long-standing sanctuary laws protect immigrant communities from being detained and deported without due process. Today, the Council has the opportunity to strengthen these vital protections to ensure that ICE officers adhere to the law before depriving someone of their liberty,” said Deborah Lee, Attorney-in-Charge of the Immigration Law Unit at The Legal Aid Society. “ICE has shown that it will use any pretext to carry out mass deportations. The Council must close the detainer law loopholes and protect all of Legal Aid’s clients from being funneled into our cruel, inhumane immigration system.”

“No part of our City should collaborate with ICE,” said Council Member Sandy Nurse. “Their very presence puts all New Yorkers – not just immigrants – at risk of physical harm and having their constitutional rights further eroded under this President. While our ultimate goal is to abolish ICE, we can help prevent any part of our city from aiding and abetting their behavior by passing this legislation.”

“NYC has long been recognized as a sanctuary city for immigrants, and its sanctuary laws are an essential tool to protect immigrant New Yorkers from the increasingly cruel harms of ICE arrest and detention,” said Josh Epstein, the Director of the Immigration Practice at Brooklyn Defender Services’ (BDS) Queens Office. “The Cut Ties With ICE legislative package would close dangerous gaps in the law that allow the NYPD and DOC to funnel New Yorkers into the deportation machine. We call on the Council and Mayor to take action to protect the rights of immigrant New Yorkers by enacting these bills immediately.”

“When city agencies violate our sanctuary laws, lives are destroyed,” said Scott Foletta, Managing Director of the Immigration Defense Team at the Neighborhood Defender Service of Harlem. “It is more important than ever for New York City to draw a clear line: we will not be complicit in ICE’s violent, racist attacks on our immigrant communities.”

“ICE’s presence in New York City harms immigrant youth in our community. So many young New Yorkers and their families have been detained and deported through ICE’s cruel actions,” said Beth Baltimore, Interim Managing Director of The Door’s Legal Services Center. “ICE has torn apart families and has shown that they will do anything to carry out its mass deportation agenda. The Council must close the gaps in the detainer laws to protect The Door’s young members and their families.”

“To stand idly by while Federal ICE Agents continue to terrorize our friends, families, and neighbors only further degrades the trust New Yorkers place in their government officials who they elected to enact policies that protect them. If we do not act now, New York remains an accomplice to criminal, unjust, and inhumane attacks on Immigrant New Yorkers,” said Council Member Amanda Farías. “As a sponsor and supporter of the full Cut Ties With ICE package, I’m proud to be a part of the crew of policymakers in the city council prepared to bring balance back to the scales of justice with strategic legislative action against ICE.”

“With ICE raiding streets and shooting up blocks from Minneapolis to Marble Hill, our immigrant communities have been forced back into the shadows. But in The World’s Borough, where half of us were born abroad, we uplift and defend our immigrant neighbors, both with our voices and with critical legislation like this package of bills,” said Queens Borough President Donovan Richards Jr. “Not only does ICE need to get the hell out of town, ICE needs to be defunded and abolished once and for all. But until that day comes, we’ll keep fighting to hold agents accountable for law-breaking and to further prevent city agencies from cooperating with this rogue agency.”

“The tragic shooting of Oscar Belgal is a devastating reminder that we can’t afford to leave anyone behind when it comes to keeping New Yorkers safe,” said State Senator Andrew Gounardes. “Our local government shouldn’t be deputized to carry out ICE’s mass deportation agenda, and no New Yorker should have to fear that the city agencies tasked with protecting them might instead put them in harm’s way. The Cut Ties With ICE package can help us close legal loopholes to prevent federal immigration authorities from exploiting local resources and tearing immigrant families apart. By passing these laws, we can send a clear message that New Yorkers stick together—whether our families came here generations ago or just last week.”

text:
Eva Yi Xie, a Princeton University neuroscience graduate student who was detained yesterday by U.S. immigration officials, is “brilliant and incredibly talented,” according to her mentor, Carlos Brody, professor of neuroscience at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute. The detention “grinds her science to a screeching halt,” he says.

“My first reaction was shock and pain, and horror and disbelief that this could be happening. Eva is a gentle, kind, caring person who is contributing enormously to the United States,” Brody says. “She belongs back home in Princeton doing the science that she loves.”

Xie, a third-year Ph.D. student in Brody’s lab, was traveling yesterday from the Society for Neuroscience annual meeting in Washington, D.C., to Philadelphia when she was stopped by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, near Washington, D.C., Brody says. “It was an absolute shock.”

Xie presented a poster on the cognitive functions of the entorhinal cortex on Wednesday at the Society for Neuroscience meeting. Her research focuses on the science of decision-making, in which she combines theoretical, computational and experimental neuroscience. As an undergraduate student in Ila Fiete’s lab at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, she developed a model of how the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex make decisions, which suggested these regions have a joint representation of cognitive evidence and physical space. Experimental work in Brody’s lab showed that “that model ended up being correct,” Brody says. Someday, Brody says, Xie hopes to continue doing basic research at an academic institution. “She is absolutely fearless in taking on new things.”

Xie is a caring mentor for undergraduates, as well as being a “brilliant Ph.D. student with unstoppable energy and enthusiasm,” Brody says. She is “driven simply by having a good problem to solve, and genuinely cares about giving back to her community.”

Xie immigrated to the United States from China in 2016. Her visa was expired, but her asylum application allowed her to remain in the country legally, Xie’s lawyers told The New York Times. Her lawyers have challenged the legality of her detention, court records show.

X

ie is being held in a temporary processing and holding facility in Chantilly, Virginia, which does not have beds, showers or infrastructure to feed detainees, Brody says Xie told him in a phone call yesterday.

Jorge Yanar, a graduate student in Brody’s lab, says that he was “blindsided” by Xie’s detention. Like many international students at Princeton, Xie had expressed concerns about traveling internationally but not domestically, Yanar says.

“I honestly couldn’t say anything negative about working with Eva,” Yanar says. “She’s brilliant. She came already knowing how to hit the ground running with projects, so I’ve just been really amazed to be able to witness and contribute in some small part to her studies.”

Princeton University has arranged legal representation for Xie, Princeton University spokesperson Michael Hotchkiss wrote in a statement to The Daily Princetonian. Princeton University did not respond to The Transmitter’s request for comment.

ICE and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not respond to The Transmitter’s emailed requests for comment.

“She’s incredibly broad and ambitious,” says Nathaniel Daw, professor of computational and theoretical neuroscience at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute and Xie’s co-adviser. Xie studies perceptual discrimination in rodents, and combines both theoretical and experimental techniques, Daw says. “It’s incredibly disruptive,” to her work, he says of her detention. “I’m sure she would have been at work on Monday or Tuesday.”

“She is one of us. She is one of the best of us. And this shouldn’t be happening to any of us” in the neuroscience community, Brody says.

text:
The Mamdani administration closed the last remaining migrant shelter, a Mott Haven facility that was the target of an ICE subpoena seeking the names and birthdays of men residing there.

Lawyers for the city filed a letter in court late Thursday night arguing the South Bronx shelter’s closure rendered the subpoena moot since there are no current residents to identify, a copy of the filing shared with Gothamist shows.

“There will be no more residents living inside of Bruckner, and the site is officially closed,” Mamdani said in a statement. “Our administration believes that every homeless New Yorker should not only have access to shelter but to spaces that are safe, humane and truly livable. We cannot accept a system that treats people without dignity or stability.”

The megashelter on Bruckner Boulevard, which once housed as many as 2,000 migrant men, was slated to shut down by the end of the year under an executive order signed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani. The order directed city agencies to phase out its remaining emergency migrant shelter and bring other facilities into compliance with city rules, such as capping the number of residents at 200.

A federal judge earlier this month ordered the Mamdani administration to hand over the personal information of certain residents staying in the shelter. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement argued the information was needed to investigate whether anyone inside the facility was subject to deportation.

The agency did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Under the judge’s November ruling, ICE agreed to the appointment of a special master who would identify shelter residents with serious criminal histories and arrange for their information to be turned over.

Under the Trump administration, ICE had tried at least four times to obtain information about shelter residents. But the city fended off those requests.

It’s not clear how many residents were living in the facility in the weeks before it closed. But as recently as this summer, the shelter was still home to 1,500 residents, many of whom were migrants from Latin America or West Africa.

City officials said some of the residents had left and found housing or were staying with friends. Others were relocated within the city’s municipal shelter system.

The Bruckner location was operated by the Mayor’s Office of Housing Recovery Operations and first opened in February 2025. It was one of about 250 sites propped up under the former Adams administration to accommodate the influx of asylum seekers in 2024.

Many of those sites skirted stringent rules imposed on traditional homeless shelters. For example, they did not provide kitchens for homeless families with children, and they ignored rules about how far apart the beds should be. The migrant population has declined in recent years, allowing the city to close these sites,

Several residents inside Bruckner had previously complained about poor conditions, like bad food and bug infestations.

This story has been updated.

title: US deportees in South Sudan went hungry as guards pocketed money from relatives, families say
description:
For those expelled to South Sudan, and their families, the ordeal has come at an additional cost.
Five deportees remain in custody in South Sudan, a country in East Africa where millions face severe hunger and poverty after years of civil conflict and devastating floods.
In addition to the Phans, The Associated Press interviewed six other people familiar with the treatment of detainees in South Sudan, including relatives and lawyers.
South Sudan sought sanctions relief and other concessions, though details of the arrangement remain unclear.
One more deportee has been detained in South Sudan.
text:
JUBA, South Sudan (AP) — Migrants deported by the Trump administration to countries other than their own have endured hunger, thirst and other deprivations while being detained indefinitely in places with poor human rights records and little oversight.

For those expelled to South Sudan, and their families, the ordeal has come at an additional cost.

Guards have solicited and received thousands of dollars from detainees’ families, who were told the money would be used to improve conditions for their loved ones. Instead, the guards pocketed most of the money, families said, while detainees went for days without food or clean water, and months held incommunicado.

“They used our desperate situation,” said Ngoc Phan, a U.S. citizen whose husband Tuan Phan had been detained in South Sudan for nearly a year before he was repatriated to Vietnam in June. “If that’s not exploitation, I don’t know what is.”

It is the inevitable outcome, she said, of a U.S. immigration policy that places deportees in the custody of countries struggling with poverty and corruption, then looks the other way.

Five deportees remain in custody in South Sudan, a country in East Africa where millions face severe hunger and poverty after years of civil conflict and devastating floods. The economy is in tatters, and government workers rarely receive wages.

In all, Ngoc Phan said she forked over roughly $4,000 intended for food, water and a cellphone. She sent several hundred dollars on multiple occasions and each time, her husband said, guards would give him a few bananas and apples, and some peanuts.

Tuan Phan, 44, said he lost 20 pounds while under confinement at a gated three-story building in Juba, the capital, and that tensions grew between detainees and guards as living conditions worsened. One detainee who wanted a window open for fresh air was struck in the face by a guard, and another who complained about a lack of soap was locked in his room for days and only let out to eat, he said.

“I feared for my life every day I was there,” he said.

In addition to the Phans, The Associated Press interviewed six other people familiar with the treatment of detainees in South Sudan, including relatives and lawyers. Most spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation against the detainees.

AP also reviewed money-transfer receipts and messages between guards and four detainees’ relatives.

When asked about AP’s findings, a spokesperson from South Sudan’s Foreign Ministry said detainees are given adequate food, water and medical care, and are allowed regular contact with relatives and lawyers while it works to resolve their individual cases. The spokesperson said the government pays for all the associated costs.

Migrants deported to a country beset by severe poverty and corruption

Under a series of murky agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to more than 30 countries that are not their own, advocates say, all part of the broad U.S. crackdown on immigration. Many were asylum seekers with U.S. court orders protecting them from being returned to their home countries because they could face persecution or torture.

The countries taking deportees have struck deals to receive millions of dollars in payments from the U.S., or have sought goodwill in negotiations over trade, migration or aid, documents show. South Sudan sought sanctions relief and other concessions, though details of the arrangement remain unclear.

In July 2025, after a legal battle that ended with a Supreme Court ruling, Phan and seven other migrants with criminal convictions — including for murder and sexual assault — were deported to South Sudan. In a press release heralding their expulsion, the Trump administration referred to the men — originally from Mexico, Cuba, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar and South Sudan — as “barbaric criminal illegal aliens.”

All eight had completed their sentences in the U.S. before being taken into immigration custody. One more deportee has been detained in South Sudan.

The Trump administration defends its policy as a means of quickly deporting migrants who have final removal orders, but whose home countries refuse to accept them.

Alma David, a lawyer representing one of the detainees still in Juba, said her client has been arbitrarily held for over a year despite not being charged with a crime.

“These are people who had lives and friends and families and who were scooped up and flown to a faraway country and locked up,” she said.

Worried families sent money as detainees’ food and water ran out

The first time Ngoc Phan sent money to a guard was in November 2025, after hearing from a lawyer that several detainees in Juba had complained about food shortages. She sent $300. After that, requests for money started coming in more frequently.

Whenever food ran out, guards would instruct Tuan Phan to call his wife and tell her to send money. Occasionally, a guard would contact her directly requesting cash messages show, without indicating what it was for.

Three other detainees had similar experiences, their relatives and a lawyer said. Payments made on their behalf to four individuals identified as guards ranged from $100 to $1,000 at a time, money-transfer receipts show. A $1,000 payment was made after a guard demanded money for suits, shirts and shoes that he said a detainee needed to travel back to his home country, according to text messages and a money-transfer receipt.

Food and other supplies were depleted quickly, Tuan Phan said, as up to a dozen guards lived and ate alongside the detainees. Sometimes the men ate only bread or rice, or went days without eating.

When they had no drinking water, some detainees collected rainwater, he said. “They give you a jug of water and say it needs to last a week. But then when it runs out it can be another 10 days before you get more.”

Fuel shortages led to weekslong blackouts, and when the plumbing stopped working, the smell of feces filled the building, he said.

In September, one detainee called his niece in the U.S. to tell her to stop sending money after an earlier payment never reached him.

South Sudan says the US has ‘relinquished’ responsibility

Relatives and lawyers for detainees still stuck in South Sudan say they have little faith the detention will end or conditions will improve without pressure from the U.S. government or international organizations.

But the Trump administration has signaled it has no intention of getting involved, and U.N. agencies say they are unable to help.

The staff at the U.S. Embassy in Juba has been instructed by the Trump administration not to visit the detainees or follow up on their treatment, according to a U.S. congressional aide who discussed the subject with embassy staff during a visit in August 2025. The aide spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.

The U.S. embassy referred questions to the State Department, where a spokesperson did not address whether the embassy had received such instructions.

A spokesperson for the U.N.’s International Organization for Migration said the agency is unable to step in without a request from South Sudan.

In a statement, South Sudan’s Foreign Ministry said the U.S. “fully relinquished responsibility and no longer has any legal jurisdiction over, or ties to, these individuals."
