title: Transgender Migrants: The Overlooked Voices in Two National Debates - DPG Law
description:
Something discussed far less often is the experiences of those who exist at the intersection of these two identities: transgender migrants.
Against this backdrop, the experiences of transgender migrants remain too often overlooked.
Transgender migrants are frequently housed alongside individuals from the very communities or countries they have fled.
[13] Conclusion These issues highlight the particular vulnerabilities faced by transgender migrants and asylum seekers.
To learn more about the experiences and challenges facing transgender migrants, please see the resources linked below.
text:
In today's political climate, both transgender rights and immigration have become highly visible and frequently debated topics. They dominate newspaper headlines, social media discussions, political campaigns, and television debates. Something discussed far less often is the experiences of those who exist at the intersection of these two identities: transgender migrants. For this group, the challenges associated with being transgender and the difficulties of navigating the immigration system do not exist separately, they often compound one another.

Today (20 November 2026) is Transgender Day of Remembrance and in light of recent legislation and case law affecting both transgender people and migrants, it is especially important to recognise and reflect on the experiences of those who belong to both communities.

Deighton Pierce Glynn has long been committed to standing alongside those who are marginalised and disadvantaged in our society. To this end, we have represented transgender people, individuals navigating the UK's complex immigration system, and those that fall within the intersection. Through our casework, we have seen first-hand the challenges faced by these groups and the barriers they often encounter when seeking safety, dignity, and equal treatment.

Recent developments in the UK include the UK Supreme Court's decision in For Women Scotland Ltd v The Scottish Ministers [2025] UKSC 16, which held that the terms "woman", “man” and "sex" in the Equality Act 2010 refer to biological sex at birth. By the Immigration and Asylum Bill 2026, which is currently in the House of Lords, the Government is also proposing major reforms to the UK’s immigration laws including seeking to introduce more stringent requirements for those seeking asylum and requiring successful asylum seekers to repay certain government support. Against this backdrop, the experiences of transgender migrants remain too often overlooked. Their stories, challenges, and resilience deserve far greater recognition than they currently receive. This month’s blog post seeks to highlight those experiences and explore the realities faced by transgender migrants in the UK and around the world today.

For the purpose of this blog post, the phrase ‘Transgender’ and ‘Trans’ will be used interchangeably and will define those who do not fall within the gender binary assigned to them at birth, including non-binary and non-gender-conforming individuals as well.

Prominent issues at this intersection

Identity documents and Legal Gender Recognition

One of the greatest challenges facing transgender migrants and asylum seekers is obtaining identification documents that reflect their identity. While many cisgender people rarely think twice about passports, birth certificates, or other forms of ID, these documents can become significant barriers for transgender individuals.

Immigration systems, including in the UK, often rely heavily on identity documents to establish a person's legal status, treating inconsistencies as signs of fraud or grounds for refusing assistance. For transgender migrants, however, official documents may display a name, photograph, or gender marker that no longer matches who they are.[1]

In the cases of JT (Cameroon) v Secretary of State for the Home Department[2], R (S and others) v Secretary of State for Home Department[3], and Ramesh Gurung v SSHD[4], we can see examples of where inconsistencies in identification documents has caused significant delays and issues for migrants. Although these cases resulted in methods to justify inconsistencies with “reasonable explanations” and “credibility tests”, this still demonstrates an additional barrier that many migrants and, by extension, transgender migrants have to face.

In many cases, this mismatch is one of the reasons individuals flee their countries of origin. Without accurate identification, transgender people can face barriers to employment and education, as well as discrimination, violence, and exclusion from legal protection. In some instances, identity documents effectively "out" their holder as transgender, increasing their vulnerability.

These difficulties stem largely from the absence of legal gender recognition in many parts of the world. In his 2018 report on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, Victor Madrigal-Borloz noted that transgender people across much of the world still lack access to effective legal gender recognition. Many countries either have no process, or deliberately restrictive procedures, for changing the gender a person was assigned at birth, leaving countless individuals unable to obtain official recognition of their identity.[5]

Even once an individual has been awarded refugee status in a country, these issues with identity documents are often carried over and present new problems in an unfamiliar setting. For example, in the cases of R (Castellucci) v Gender Recognition Panel[6] and R (Elan-Cane) v Secretary of State for the Home Department[7], we see examples of where the UK courts have ruled against sufficient legal gender recognition for people who did not identify with the gender binary, something that may apply to certain trans migrants as well.

Unsafe Accommodation and Violence

Many people seeking asylum in the UK spend significant periods of time in Home Office asylum accommodation. Through our work at DPG, we have seen repeated concerns that the Home Office often fails to consider, and provide accommodation adequate for, residents' specific needs. For transgender asylum seekers, these shortcomings can create serious risks to their safety and wellbeing.

Transgender migrants are frequently housed alongside individuals from the very communities or countries they have fled. They may also be placed in single-sex accommodation based on the sex they were assigned at birth rather than their gender identity. As a result, some are unfortunately exposed to harassment, discrimination, and violence.

In the case of ACN v SSHD 2026, it was argued that the Home Secretary had breached the PSED (provided for by section 149 of the Equality Act 2010) by failing to undertake statistical monitoring in relation to the experiences of LGBT+ asylum seekers who were provided with accommodation in “large sites” (such as Napier Barracks), and in accommodation involving room sharing (for example in hotels). The claim was, however, dismissed with the Court concluding that in the context of the function which the Secretary of State was performing (allocating asylum accommodation), the PSED did not require such monitoring.[8]

Research by the University of Birmingham in 2024 has nonetheless documented numerous accounts of abuse against LGBTQ+ individuals within asylum accommodation due to their identity. Transgender asylum seekers have reported being harassed, followed, and threatened by other residents. In one case, a transgender asylum seeker in Wales was threatened with a knife by a fellow resident. After attempting to seek help, their phone was smashed, yet the accommodation provider reportedly dismissed the incident as a "household spat" and failed to take protective action.[9] DPG recently helped secure compensation for a gay man, refugee and victim of torture, who experienced life-changing attacks whilst living in asylum accommodation.[10]

In another case a trans woman was detained in a male immigration centre in the UK for prolonged periods in 2014 and 2015, where she experienced harassment from both detainees and staff. She described avoiding showers for weeks because she felt unsafe and suffering significant physical and psychological harm after being denied access to gender-affirming medication.[11]

These experiences are not unique to the UK. Across Europe, transgender asylum seekers are unfortunately experiencing similar violence. In Denmark, a young trans woman was reportedly raped after being housed in the men's section of an asylum facility.[12] In Norway, a trans woman awaiting the outcome of her asylum appeal was also assaulted by a man who had gained her trust before attacking her in her asylum accommodation.[13]

Conclusion

These issues highlight the particular vulnerabilities faced by transgender migrants and asylum seekers. Inadequate accommodation, barriers to gender recognition and healthcare, poor safeguarding, and dehumanising procedures can expose individuals to significant harm at a time when they are seeking safety and protection.

This blog post has focused on a handful of key challenges faced by this group, but they represent only part of a much broader reality. Across the world, transgender people continue to flee discrimination, violence, and persecution, including from countries often considered safe, such as the United States.

To learn more about the experiences and challenges facing transgender migrants, please see the resources linked below.

This blog post was prepared with contributions from members of our legal team including: Dante Williams, Megan Smith and Emily Soothill. It is for general information and is not intended to be used as legal advice.

text:
Democratic lawmakers on Wednesday pressed the Tennessee Department of Homeland Safety & Security for details about its role in cooperating with immigration enforcement and in implementing a new policy to deny driver’s licenses to immigrants with valid federal work permits.

They received few answers. Department leaders, testifying before a legislative subcommittee, cited ongoing court challenges against them in declining to publicly respond to pointed questions.

Rep. John Ray Clemmons, a Nashville Democrat, sought an explanation for the department denying licenses to certain categories of immigrants.

“Apparently a lot of individuals who are legal residents of the state are being denied licenses in an inconsistent manner,” Clemmons said. “Can you speak to that?”

In recent months, the department began rejecting applications for driver’s licenses and license renewals from immigrants with valid work permits, citing state law. Hundreds of immigrants statewide, including so-called “Dreamers” who were brought to the country as children and are protected from deportation were turned away at driver’s license offices despite being issued Tennessee licenses for many years.

A Nashville judge earlier this month ordered the department to resume issuing licenses to immigrants authorized to work in the country while litigation against the state agency continues.

Russell Shoup, assistant commissioner at the department, cited the ongoing litigation in declining to respond, drawing an immediate rebuke.

“So you can’t speak or reassure the people of Tennessee right now who are legal residents that they are not going to be unlawfully denied their licenses, unable to work, unable to take their children to school, get to church in any way whatsoever now,” Clemmons said.

“We are very limited on what we can say,” Shoup responded.

Clemmons also questioned the Tennessee Highway Patrol’s decision to enter into a cooperative agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, giving state troopers the authority to enforce federal immigration law. “Public school absenteeism has spiked as families fear to venture out for fear of detention by ICE or cooperating agencies, including the Tennessee Highway Patrol,” Clemmons said.

“A lot of legal residents, law-abiding citizens in my district were targeted, pulled over. It’s not uncommon for the Tennessee Highway Patrol to be on some of these streets….I do not appreciate (immigration enforcement) giving the state of Tennessee I love and that I’m proud of a bad name and instilling fear in children,” Clemmons said. “Please be mindful of the impact you have on people’s lives, whether you’re asked to do it or not asked to do it.”

Col. Matt Perry of the Tennessee Highway Patrol cited ongoing litigation in responding more broadly to the professionalism of state troopers.

“I assure you that Commissioner (Jeff) Long and I love Tennessee in the same way you do,” Perry responded. “Without speaking to something being litigated, troopers make — in every operation — probable cause traffic laws…We are trained for that. We are for every operation we’ve taken part in.”

State Sen. Sara Kyle, a Shelby County Democrat, questioned the Tennessee Highway Patrol’s presence in Memphis as part of a multi-agency law enforcement presence convened by President Donald Trump that has made thousands of traffic stops and detained hundreds of immigrants.

Kyle noted there was community anger in her district stemming from the presence of hundreds of federal and state law enforcement officers and the detention of immigrants who live there.

“The anger that has been brought by stopping and taking or kidnapping immigrants, it has just changed our city,” Kyle said. “We are getting a bad rap. I want you to be aware the economy is failing because people are not taking jobs. They won’t drive to certain areas.”

“When we’re trying to improve our city, whoever you all need to talk to, the higher ups, the administration…this has got to come to an end,” she said. “The message is, ‘please stop.’”

But Kyle’s comments drew a rebuke from Rep. Justin Lafferty, a Knox County Republican. “I know you guys can’t talk about some of the stuff going on because of the legal status or what have you, but the mischaracterization that you all are kidnapping people is appalling to me,” he said.

title: ICE roughs up lawyer — then DHS demands she wipe Facebook post exposing it: complaint
description:
“I was back in the office where I had been assaulted by the ICE officer, with the ICE officer that assaulted me,” Medina told Raw Story.
“The DHS official that coerced Ms. Medina into taking her Facebook post down violated her First Amendment rights,” Lauren Bonds, a lawyer with the National Police Accountability Project who represents her on the complaint, told Raw Story.
“When the interaction with the ICE officer happened, I thought I was going to die,” Medina told Raw Story.
“Claims that the individual was assaulted, harassed or surveilled by ICE are FALSE,” an ICE spokesperson told Raw Story.
Medina told Raw Story she fears that the U.S. government could attempt to denaturalize her in retaliation for speaking out about ICE’s practices.
text:
Lawyer Yovana Lopez Medina says she was shoved by an immigration officer in Oklahoma City earlier this year as she asked to speak with his supervisor while trying to prevent him from taking her client into custody.

Ordered to leave ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations office and shaken by the experience on March 16, the 33-year-old lawyer went to her car and made a Facebook post about the alleged assault.

When Medina returned to the ICE office the following day, she said a Department of Homeland Security official was waiting for her. She claimed he demanded that she delete the Facebook post.

Medina complied with the demand, although she declined a suggestion that she make a new post detailing “how her actions” against the ICE agent “were wrong,” according to a complaint for personal injury she filed last month with the Department of Homeland Security.

“I was back in the office where I had been assaulted by the ICE officer, with the ICE officer that assaulted me,” Medina told Raw Story. “I felt that I didn’t have a choice. I was there by myself. There were no other attorneys, no people in the lobby. Quite honestly, I was afraid to get hurt.”

Medina said the immigration officials told her that social media posts like the one she had published were “why their officers were in danger and had to wear protective vests.” She said they also named a local community organizer known for making social media posts about the presence of ICE agents in Oklahoma City as a source of aggravation.

“The DHS official that coerced Ms. Medina into taking her Facebook post down violated her First Amendment rights,” Lauren Bonds, a lawyer with the National Police Accountability Project who represents her on the complaint, told Raw Story.

“Government employees cannot censor a person because they don’t like what they are saying. Ms. Medina’s post was protected speech on an issue of public importance, and the official used intimidation and the authority of his position to silence her. It’s a textbook First Amendment violation.”

Medina’s experience mirrors a visit by federal agents to a polling place in Syracuse, New York, in June in which they confronted a poll worker about a social media post. PaigeLynn Gonyea, the worker, had written on Facebook about the ICE agent who fatally shot Renee Good in Minneapolis, while stating that it was “a great day” for him “to be indicted.”

Gonyea, is suing the Department of Homeland Security for failing to release records about its efforts to monitor her social media.

In her complaint, Medina alleged that when she accompanied a client to a routine check-in at the Enforcement and Removal Office in Oklahoma City in March, an ICE officer informed her that he was taking her client into custody. Medina said the officer became angry when she asked to speak with his supervisor. A second officer entered the room and, when the two officers grabbed her client, Medina said one of them pushed her.

The first officer “shoved Ms. Medina as he escorted her client outside the room and threatened her with arrest,” according to the complaint. Later, the officers’ supervisor told her she could be charged with assault and battery of a federal agent, though no charges ever materialized.

“When the interaction with the ICE officer happened, I thought I was going to die,” Medina told Raw Story. “I don’t think anybody should feel that way when interacting with a federal agent or agency. That comes from someone with a law degree, a law license, someone who speaks the language. Despite all that, I still felt that way.”

When she returned to the facility over the next two months to advocate for other clients, Medina said she was subjected to stepped-up security measures. Her complaint alleges that security staff at the building “made joking references to her being a risk to their safety, raising their hands in mocking surrender when she enters the building.”

She also said ICE officers surveilled her at her home and while she traveled around Oklahoma City. She told Raw Story she observed black SUVs with barriers between the front and back seats that are typically used to transport detainees parked at either end of her street, and also speeding past her when she traveled around the city.

“Claims that the individual was assaulted, harassed or surveilled by ICE are FALSE,” an ICE spokesperson told Raw Story.

Medina is a naturalized citizen from Mexico who graduated from law school in 2022, the same year she took the oath of citizenship. She resigned from her position at the law firm in August, in part because she said her supervisors didn’t have her back against ICE. She opened her own practice 10 days later.

Medina told Raw Story she fears that the U.S. government could attempt to denaturalize her in retaliation for speaking out about ICE’s practices. It’s particularly stressful when she travels out of state to represent clients. Oklahoma doesn’t have its own immigration court, so she must travel to Aurora, Colorado, for detention cases and to Dallas for non-detained immigration cases.

“When I do travel to Dallas for a court hearing, I go with my U.S. passport because I don’t feel safe,” Medina said. “Even though I’m a naturalized U.S. citizen, I know that if there is an interaction, they may not take that for what it is.”

Medina said she hopes her complaint, which will turn into a lawsuit if the Department of Homeland Security fails to resolve it first, brings public awareness.

“In the community at large, you don’t think of a naturalized U.S. citizen in Oklahoma, but we are here and we are fighting the fight,” Medina said. “We want people to know this is what’s happening. This machine is going to continue to do what they want. I hope this can prevent any incident of intimidation, not only against professionals but with the individuals ICE interacts with on a day-to-day basis.”

text:
ICE spent an estimated $13 million a month for empty beds at five recently acquired detention centers and overpaid by more than 50% for nine megawarehouses — most of which the immigration enforcement agency is now trying to offload, according to a new report from the government’s watchdog.

In total, ICE spent more than $1 billion in taxpayer money on the warehouses. According to the report, ICE paid more than triple the assessed value for three of the warehouses.

In Michigan, ICE bought a warehouse for more than $34 million, which the Government Accountability Office calculated was nearly five times the assessed value.

ICE did not respond to NBC News’ request for comment. The immigration agency responded to the GAO within the report and agreed with the report’s recommendations that it should keep its spending plans updated and evaluate the full cost of a detention facility’s cost before purchase.

In its letter to the watchdog, DHS wrote that the agency “remains committed to ICE strengthening the necessary processes, policies, procedures, and safeguards to ensure the continual oversight and management of ICE’s financial resources as it carries out its mission.”

Roughly a year ago, ICE began exploring a plan to buy massive empty warehouses to house up to 8,000 immigrant detainees each, but the plan quickly ran into roadblocks when local leaders, immigrant advocates and some GOP members of Congress expressed sharp opposition.

Plans for one ICE warehouse in the Atlanta suburb of Social Circle, Georgia, sparked a lawsuit in which town officials said the new facility would exceed the capacity of the town’s sewage system and result in “dry taps and raw human waste spills.”

Contractors from private prison companies also expressed concern about housing more than 1,500 detainees in one location.

After then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem’s departure from the agency in late March, the agency paused the warehouse plan. Now at least seven warehouses are for sale, according to the report.

The authors of the GAO report wrote that the warehouse initiative was an example of a “major investment that was implemented rapidly and will likely result in significant waste.”

ICE has roughly doubled the number of detention facilities it manages but is facing a shortfall in staff who oversee and manage those facilities. Fifty-five out of 87 positions are currently vacant, according to the report.

On average, ICE paid for more than 9,000 empty beds per day across facilities with guaranteed-payment agreements, the report found.

ICE began purchasing new detention capacity after the July 2025 passage of President Donald Trump’s “big beautiful bill,” which gave the agency $45 billion through 2029.

ICE also faced scrutiny for paying $495 million for a former prison in western Minnesota, a year after its owner offered to sell the same facility to the state for $75 million, according to documents obtained by KARE 11.

name: Human Rights
title: U.S. deportees in South Sudan went hungry as guards pocketed money from relatives, families say
description:
For those expelled to South Sudan, and their families, the ordeal has come at an additional cost.
Five deportees remain in custody in South Sudan, a country in East Africa where millions face severe hunger and poverty after years of civil conflict and devastating floods.
In addition to the Phans, The Associated Press interviewed six other people familiar with the treatment of detainees in South Sudan, including relatives and lawyers.
South Sudan sought sanctions relief and other concessions, though details of the arrangement remain unclear.
A spokesperson for the U.N.’s International Organization for Migration said the agency is unable to step in without a request from South Sudan.
text:
JUBA, South Sudan — Migrants deported by the Trump administration to countries other than their own have endured hunger, thirst and other deprivations while being detained indefinitely in places with poor human rights records and little oversight.

For those expelled to South Sudan, and their families, the ordeal has come at an additional cost.

Guards have solicited and received thousands of dollars from detainees’ families, who were told the money would be used to improve conditions for their loved ones. Instead, the guards pocketed most of the money, families said, while detainees went for days without food or clean water, and months held incommunicado.

“They used our desperate situation,” said Ngoc Phan, a U.S. citizen whose husband Tuan Phan had been detained in South Sudan for nearly a year before he was repatriated to Vietnam in June. “If that’s not exploitation, I don’t know what is.”

It is the inevitable outcome, she said, of a U.S. immigration policy that places deportees in the custody of countries struggling with poverty and corruption, then looks the other way.

Five deportees remain in custody in South Sudan, a country in East Africa where millions face severe hunger and poverty after years of civil conflict and devastating floods. The economy is in tatters, and government workers rarely receive wages.

In all, Ngoc Phan said she forked over roughly $4,000 intended for food, water and a cellphone. She sent several hundred dollars on multiple occasions and each time, her husband said, guards would give him a few bananas and apples, and some peanuts.

Tuan Phan, 44, said he lost 20 pounds while under confinement at a gated three-story building in Juba, the capital, and that tensions grew between detainees and guards as living conditions worsened. One detainee who wanted a window open for fresh air was struck in the face by a guard, and another who complained about a lack of soap was locked in his room for days and only let out to eat, he said.

“I feared for my life every day I was there,” he said.

In addition to the Phans, The Associated Press interviewed six other people familiar with the treatment of detainees in South Sudan, including relatives and lawyers. Most spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation against the detainees.

AP also reviewed money-transfer receipts and messages between guards and four detainees’ relatives.

When asked about AP’s findings, a spokesperson from South Sudan’s Foreign Ministry said detainees are given adequate food, water and medical care, and are allowed regular contact with relatives and lawyers while it works to resolve their individual cases. The spokesperson said the government pays for all the associated costs.

Migrants deported to a country beset by severe poverty and corruption

Under a series of murky agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to more than 30 countries that are not their own, advocates say, all part of the broad U.S. crackdown on immigration. Many were asylum seekers with U.S. court orders protecting them from being returned to their home countries because they could face persecution or torture.

The countries taking deportees have struck deals to receive millions of dollars in payments from the U.S., or have sought goodwill in negotiations over trade, migration or aid, documents show. South Sudan sought sanctions relief and other concessions, though details of the arrangement remain unclear.

In July 2025, after a legal battle that ended with a Supreme Court ruling, Phan and seven other migrants with criminal convictions — including for murder and sexual assault — were deported to South Sudan. In a press release heralding their expulsion, the Trump administration referred to the men — originally from Mexico, Cuba, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar and South Sudan — as “barbaric criminal illegal aliens.”

All eight had completed their sentences in the U.S. before being taken into immigration custody. One more deportee has been detained in South Sudan.

The Trump administration defends its policy as a means of quickly deporting migrants who have final removal orders, but whose home countries refuse to accept them.

Alma David, a lawyer representing one of the detainees still in Juba, said her client has been arbitrarily held for over a year despite not being charged with a crime.

“These are people who had lives and friends and families and who were scooped up and flown to a faraway country and locked up,” she said.

Worried families sent money as detainees’ food and water ran out

The first time Ngoc Phan sent money to a guard was in November 2025, after hearing from a lawyer that several detainees in Juba had complained about food shortages. She sent $300. After that, requests for money started coming in more frequently.

Whenever food ran out, guards would instruct Tuan Phan to call his wife and tell her to send money. Occasionally, a guard would contact her directly, requesting cash without indicating what it was for, messages show.

Three other detainees had similar experiences, their relatives and a lawyer said. Payments made on their behalf to four individuals identified as guards ranged from $100 to $1,000 at a time, money-transfer receipts show. A $1,000 payment was made after a guard demanded money for suits, shirts and shoes that he said a detainee needed to travel back to his home country, according to text messages and a money-transfer receipt.

Food and other supplies were depleted quickly, Tuan Phan said, as up to a dozen guards lived and ate alongside the detainees. Sometimes the men ate only bread or rice, or went days without eating.

When they had no drinking water, some detainees collected rainwater, he said. “They give you a jug of water and say it needs to last a week. But then when it runs out it can be another 10 days before you get more.”

Fuel shortages led to weekslong blackouts, and when the plumbing stopped working, the smell of feces filled the building, he said.

In September, one detainee called his niece in the U.S. to tell her to stop sending money after an earlier payment never reached him.

South Sudan says the U.S. has ‘relinquished’ responsibility

Relatives and lawyers for detainees still stuck in South Sudan say they have little faith the detention will end or conditions will improve without pressure from the U.S. government or international organizations.

But the Trump administration has signaled it has no intention of getting involved, and U.N. agencies say they are unable to help.

The staff at the U.S. Embassy in Juba has been instructed by the Trump administration not to visit the detainees or follow up on their treatment, according to a U.S. congressional aide who discussed the subject with embassy staff during a visit in August 2025. The aide spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.

The U.S. embassy referred questions to the State Department, where a spokesperson did not address whether the embassy had received such instructions.

A spokesperson for the U.N.’s International Organization for Migration said the agency is unable to step in without a request from South Sudan.

title: ICE courthouse arrests continue despite Massachusetts PROTECT Act
description:
Immigration advocates report that ICE agents are still making arrests in Massachusetts courthouses despite the new PROTECT Act.
The PROTECT Act, signed by Gov.
Maura Healey, is meant to limit ICE arrests in sensitive locations like courts without a federal criminal warrant.
ICE arrests continue at Massachusetts courthouses Ramachandran said there have been several documented incidents of violations in courthouses throughout the state, including in Framingham and Marlborough.
Court officers are not supposed to assist ICE agents under the provisions of the PROTECT Act.
text:
Immigration advocates report that ICE agents are still making arrests in Massachusetts courthouses despite the new PROTECT Act.

The PROTECT Act, signed by Gov. Maura Healey, is meant to limit ICE arrests in sensitive locations like courts without a federal criminal warrant.

Advocacy groups claim these courthouse arrests are causing some individuals, including witnesses and those seeking restraining orders, to avoid court appearances.

Protestors gathered at the State House to urge Gov. Healey to enforce the PROTECT Act more strictly.

Despite the passing of the recent PROTECT Act, immigration enforcement officers are still going into courthouses and taking people into custody, the head of a Framingham-based non-profit agency that advocates on behalf of immigrants and for human rights.

The actions of ICE officers continuing to go into court is scaring people from going to court because they’re afraid they’ll be taken into custody and deported, said CASA MetroWest Worker Center co-Director Leela Ramachandran said.

“Folks are doing their best to follow through and go to court and get whatever method of justice they can,” she said.

Gov. Maura Healey in August signed the PROTECT Act, which, in part is designed to prevent ICE agents from arresting people in “sensitive” locations, such as hospitals and schools with just a civil warrant. That includes courts. ICE can still arrest those who have federal criminal warrants.

ICE arrests continue at Massachusetts courthouses

Ramachandran said there have been several documented incidents of violations in courthouses throughout the state, including in Framingham and Marlborough. She said there have been at least five incidents locally.

Just on Wednesday, an unidentified person was taken into custody in Marlborough District Court. Ramachandran did not have any details on the person who was taken into custody.

A spokesperson for ICE did not return a call and email seeking comment. Marlborough District Court Clerk Magistrate Jennifer Lennon also could not be reached for comment.

ICE concerns are changing how people approach court

Ramachandran said there was a recent example of a man who was living out of state who had a warrant in Framingham. He rented a vehicle, drove here, found out ICE was in the courthouse and did not go in. He waited all day before driving back home because he was afraid to go to court.

He returned the following day on a bus and again found out ICE was in the courthouse and left again with an outstanding warrant for his arrest.

“He was weighing what could happen and left,” she said. “He was trying to do the right thing.”

Although court officials are not supposed to interfere with ICE activity under the PROTECT Act, Ramachandran said court officials can enforce the same court rules they have for everyone else, but they do not. She said ICE agents are constantly seen in courtrooms using their phones and texting people, which is not allowed in court.

Ramachandran said those in court to observe ICE are not allowed to text, just like others in the courthouse. She also alleged that court security officers show security footage to ICE agents. Court officers are not supposed to assist ICE agents under the provisions of the PROTECT Act.

Framingham District Court Clerk Magistrate Robert Jubinville could not be reached for comment on Thursday, Nov. 19.

Ramachandran was among a large group of people who protested outside of the State House on Wednesday, Nov. 18 seeking to have Healey order stricter enforcement of the PROTECT Act.

A spokesperson for Healey could not be reached for comment on Thursday.

The fear of ICE in courts are making some people skip court, Ramachandran said. This is more than those who have criminal cases, she said. They include people obtaining restraining orders or witnesses for cases.

“Now, all of these folks are having concerns if they go to court, they’ll be taken,” she said. “They’re choosing to stay home.”

title: As Big Bend border wall condemnation proceedings escalate, landowners hold the line
description:
Alvarado and David Keller lead No Big Bend Wall's coalition of more than 200 area landowners.
Conserve Big Bend, the parent organization of No Big Bend Wall, announced it and a handful of landowners were suing the federal government over the project in September.
Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa told The Texas Tribune this week that she met with President Trump to discuss border security and told him Big Bend residents would prefer technology over physical barriers.
A judge could slow down the process by requiring an "order of possession" before allowing survey access, Brandys said.
Landowners react to potential court filings No Big Bend Wall's landowner coalition continues to advise its members not to sign anything, Keller said.
text:
The Trump administration is moving ahead with efforts to gain access to privately owned property along the Rio Grande for its $7.5 billion Big Bend border wall project. The move follows a recent U.S. Supreme Court ruling allowing construction to continue.

Landowners up and down the river, from Hudspeth to Val Verde counties, are receiving letters from U.S. Customs and Border Protection, the Department of Justice and even private real estate acquisition firms urging them to cooperate or face legal action.

The letters mark a new escalation in the government's efforts to acquire land for the project.

"Overall — they still have this money allocated," said landowner Yolanda Alvarado. "There's still an imminent threat to the land."

Alvarado and David Keller lead No Big Bend Wall's coalition of more than 200 area landowners. Keller believes their refusal to cooperate has helped delay the effort, including a pause on an entire section of the project.

"If we had all been compliant, they'd already be building right now," Keller said.

Landowners hold out hope that the wall can be stopped

Despite the government's insistence that they cooperate or be taken to court, a number of landowners told Marfa Public Radio they are continuing to refuse to sign anything. The true status of the project seems uncertain, they said, even in the wake of the Supreme Court ruling.

"If there's a glimmer of hope that things could get resolved in your favor, why sign?" landowner Esteban Mesa said.

The various construction pauses — including one ordered by CBP itself — ongoing lawsuits, and shifting political tides in Texas and Congress are making landowners hesitant to cooperate, they said.

Conserve Big Bend, the parent organization of No Big Bend Wall, announced it and a handful of landowners were suing the federal government over the project in September. That lawsuit is ongoing.

Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa told The Texas Tribune this week that she met with President Trump to discuss border security and told him Big Bend residents would prefer technology over physical barriers.

"Who knows what's going to happen in January," landowner Diana Valles said.

"I just wish it was something we could wake up from," she added.

But changing political leadership in Texas might not be enough to stop the border wall project. CBP has repeatedly asserted that the barriers are needed to secure the southern border, and Congress has allocated $46.5 billion towards border wall construction nationwide.

CBP threatens to take legal action against landowners for survey access

Recent letters indicate that CBP plans to take some Big Bend landowners to court over survey access, a typical next step in the eminent domain process, according to Roy Brandys, an eminent domain attorney assisting area landowners.

"That's not the condemnation proceeding to actually acquire their land. It's just to acquire the right to survey," Brandys said. "I think there's a lot of confusion regarding that."

The government typically needs surveys to establish property boundaries before acquiring land through eminent domain, he said.

It is unclear exactly when the government will file those initial complaints. But documents reviewed by Marfa Public Radio warn some landowners they could be taken to court for survey access "within 90 days" of letters dated in late October.

CBP declined to comment on when it might file complaints or how many landowners could face legal action. "Releasing that information could affect ongoing legal, real estate, procurement, and construction activities," a CBP spokesperson said.

Brandys estimated that "hundreds, if not thousands" of property owners could be impacted, potentially creating a slow path through courts.

"This volume of cases does require a lot of attorneys and support personnel to file them and get them across the finish line," Brandys said.

CBP said the agency would prefer to obtain property rights voluntarily rather than through eminent domain.

"If CBP is unable to acquire the necessary access voluntarily within a reasonable timeframe, CBP refers the matter to the Department of Justice to acquire any necessary property interest(s) through eminent domain," the spokesperson said in a statement to Marfa Public Radio. "Regardless of the manner in which the property is acquired, the landowner is provided just compensation for the property."

Some landowners have maintained that no amount of money is worth what they stand to lose — the ability to farm, raise cattle, recreate and visit family cemeteries — if their properties are cut off from the river.

Government's messaging becomes more urgent

Though construction was halted under an October 2 injunction, letters obtained by Marfa Public Radio show that the federal government continued pursuing land rights during the pause.

The government began contacting landowners in February, followed by meetings and site visits in the spring. In October, CBP began sending new letters threatening court action over survey access.

Other landowners have received letters from the DOJ urging them to contact its attorneys within seven days to discuss the acquisition process. In Val Verde County, letters from Bowman, a private real estate acquisition company, invite landowners to attend property appraisals under what the company called an "accelerated schedule."

Landowners directly in the path of the wall are not the only ones facing eminent domain. The government is also seeking land along important access roads, including Chispa Road and roads off of Highway 90 near Langtry, according to landowners who spoke with Marfa Public Radio.

CBP letters state the government will file a "Declaration of Taking and Complaint in Condemnation" in the U.S. District Court of the Western District of Texas against landowners they are seeking survey access from.

Brandys said the government typically deposits a nominal amount of money along with the filing, giving it the right to enter people's land to conduct surveys.

A judge could slow down the process by requiring an "order of possession" before allowing survey access, Brandys said. But an influx of cases could also strain the already crowded dockets of the federal court.

Appraisals and purchase offers typically follow the survey, Brandys said. Landowners often have just 30 days to consider an offer before an eminent domain case is filed.

Landowners react to potential court filings

No Big Bend Wall's landowner coalition continues to advise its members not to sign anything, Keller said. But it also encourages them to tell the federal government about concerns, such as avoiding archeological sites or installing gates for irrigation equipment — even if there is no guarantee that special accommodations will be made.

"Holding off as long as you can has been an ongoing tactic. But at some point, if it continues to progress, we do recommend that landowners begin to engage so at least that their concerns are logged," Keller said.

What exactly CBP is planning to build and where has been in flux since the project's inception. Maps show a mix of 30-foot-high steel bollard walls, vehicle barriers, patrol roads and technology currently planned for the region. But federal contracting documents recently revealed in a lawsuit show secondary barriers were also planned for a roughly 70-mile stretch of the project in Presidio County.

Raymond Skiles, a landowner in Langtry, said he recently met with CBP and Bowman representatives to discuss the impact on his family property, but not to sign over any permissions.

It is his understanding, he said, that land acquisition in that area appears to be focused on larger properties, with the government offering incentives like wells to "sweeten the deals" and encourage cooperation.

Henry Quintela, whose family owns land near Redford, received a letter threatening court action over survey access in October. He said his family is still hanging tight, refusing to give survey access, and will wait to be taken to court.

" As long as everybody holds together and tells them no, I think it'll serve as a good strong point," Quintela said.

title: Security videos show instant ICE re-arrests at Whipple Federal Building - MPR News
description:
Previously unpublished security camera footage shows two men being instantly re-arrested by immigration officers steps outside the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building after judges ordered their release.
ICE deportation officer Mitchell T. Olson was involved in at least four instant re-arrests, according to court records.
ICE agents brought them from one of the county jails that are paid to hold detainees for ICE to the Whipple building for processing.
Others were brought out a back door or said they didn't make it outside at all before ICE re-arrested them.
ICE instantly re-arrested at least 18 people in Colorado in about a week, according to court records.
text:
Previously unpublished security camera footage shows two men being instantly re-arrested by immigration officers steps outside the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building after judges ordered their release.

The videos show instant re-arrests made on Sept. 9 and Sept. 25, a tactic several judges have found Immigration and Customs Enforcement has used to circumvent their release orders. MPR News has confirmed at least eight men have been instantly re-arrested this way. One man was re-arrested twice.

In both videos, ICE officers in plain clothes wait outside the front doors of the Whipple building and instantly arrest the men as soon as they step outside. Pablo Hernandez Franco said in a sworn statement that his shoulder was dislocated during his Sept. 9 re-arrest.

ICE deportation officer Mitchell T. Olson was involved in at least four instant re-arrests, according to court records. Court records confirm that Olson carried the new arrest warrant when Hernandez was re-arrested. The video shows Olson holding a piece of paper in front of Hernandez for about a second.

In response to Hernandez’s claim that his shoulder was dislocated, Olson said in a sworn statement that Hernandez “did not express any displeasure or pain to me.”

ICE officials in Minnesota have said their lawyers analyze release orders for candidates for re-arrest. For example, if the judge ruled the original arrest was warrantless and unlawful, ICE has interpreted that to mean it gets a do-over.

In a Nov. 10 statement to MPR News, an unnamed ICE official wrote: “When appropriate, ICE will address the issues identified by the court and take further action consistent with applicable law and court orders, which can include rearresting an offender.”

An unnamed Department of Homeland Security spokesperson wrote on Oct. 27 that ICE “may seek to rearrest the alien in a way that complies with the judicial decision. To suggest that ICE cannot do this is nothing short of sabotage.”

Hernandez is a 32-year-old man from Mexico, who lives and works in Minnesota. According to court records, he came to the United States in 2024 and overstayed a tourist visa. He’s engaged to a U.S. citizen and expecting a child with her, according to his habeas petition, filed Sept. 3.

U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Bryan wrote a scathing order in response to the re-arrest and required ICE to “immediately” release Hernandez. Bryan wrote that a habeas release order does not preclude the government from ever re-arresting someone, but because ICE officers “immediately swarmed” Hernandez steps outside the Whipple building, he “was not released from custody.”

ICE re-released Hernandez at about 9 a.m. Sept. 25, according to court records.

That same morning, Alejandro Corro Guzmán was instantly re-arrested at the front doors of Whipple. Corro is a 34-year-old man also from Mexico who had a valid work permit and a pending asylum claim when ICE detained him in May. The claim was later denied and an appeal is pending, according to Corro’s lawyer.

Chief U.S. District Judge Eric Tostrud did not find that the government violated his release order by re-arresting Corro and denied Corro’s request to be released again.

Tostrud found Corro and another man who was instantly re-arrested did not make strong enough legal arguments that re-release would remedy the actions ICE took against them.

Corro had previously requested MPR News only refer to him by his first name because he feared retaliation. Now that his habeas case has concluded, Corro agreed his full name could be published.

How the re-arrests work

The re-arrests come as the paths for immigrants to gain release from ICE detention have narrowed under the second Trump administration.

Previously, immigrants were commonly released on bond if they were detained at all. They would continue to live and work in between regular check-ins with ICE as their immigration case made its way through the court.

Now, many immigrants are being denied bond or even the chance at a bond hearing. Many challenge their detention by filing what’s known as a petition for habeas corpus requiring the government to justify why it's holding someone.

In many cases, federal judges are granting habeas petitions and ordering the government to provide a bond hearing or ordering the person’s release outright.

In each of the eight cases confirmed in Minnesota, an immigrant was ordered released by a federal judge. ICE agents brought them from one of the county jails that are paid to hold detainees for ICE to the Whipple building for processing.

The Whipple building is located in Fort Snelling and houses ICE’s St. Paul field office and the immigration court.

The men were told they were being released, signed release papers and were given back their belongings. However, some men reported belongings were missing. Then the men were pointed toward a door.

Sometimes, the men made it steps outside the building’s front doors. Others were brought out a back door or said they didn't make it outside at all before ICE re-arrested them.

Sometimes ICE told the court what happened. Sometimes it didn’t. Some men had lawyers who could quickly alert the court to the re-arrest. Some didn’t.

For example, a Cambodian man named Tha Im was instantly re-arrested on Oct. 19. He is representing himself in court and is still in custody a month later at Kandiyohi County Jail.

Judges split on re-arrests

Federal judges in Minnesota are split on the issue. Bryan and U.S. District Judge John Tunheim found the re-arrests violated their release orders.

U.S. District Judge Jerry Blackwell found a re-arrest did not violate his release order. Tostrud denied re-release requests from two re-arrested men and wrote he found Corro’s argument that he had never been released at all “not persuasive.”

In two habeas release orders issued Monday, Tunheim proactively wrote “Respondents SHALL NOT re-detain Petitioner” without “adequate notice” and a pre-detention bond hearing, citing reporting about instant re-arrests by MPR News.

An ICE official in Colorado testified he ordered similar re-arrests there after speaking to “colleagues” in Minnesota. ICE instantly re-arrested at least 18 people in Colorado in about a week, according to court records.

Colorado U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney held the government in contempt for an instant re-arrest and said she wouldn’t take further action only because the ICE official had said under oath that he had stopped the re-arrests.

text:
HOUSTON – The family of a Houston man who has been in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody for 40 days says they have been unable to visit him for about two weeks and are increasingly concerned about his physical and mental health.

Miguel Parra Hernandez’s family, attorney Kim Bruno and representatives from the Houston immigrant rights organization FIEL held a news conference Friday, Nov. 20, calling for his immediate release and greater transparency about his medical care.

Parra was injured during an immigration enforcement operation in northwest Houston on Oct. 10. He has remained in custody while recovering from his injuries at a rehabilitation facility.

His brother, Rodolfo Parra, said the family’s last visit with Miguel was about 15 days ago. During that visit, which lasted approximately 45 minutes, he said his brother expressed deep frustration and despair about his situation.

“He told me that he didn’t want to live, that he no longer wanted to fight for the case,” Rodolfo Parra said, describing the visit as one of the most painful experiences he has had with his brother.

He said Miguel also complained about back and knee pain and told him the days felt endless.

Rodolfo Parra said the family is now unable to see his brother and is asking for help obtaining his medical records to better understand his condition and whether he is receiving the care needed to recover.

“We need to know if he’s having the best care,” he said.

FIEL says requests for release have been denied

FIEL Executive Director Cesar Espinosa said the organization and Parra’s legal team have submitted multiple requests seeking his release, but have encountered obstacles.

Espinosa said one challenge is that Parra is not being held in a traditional detention center, making it difficult for his legal team to determine where certain requests should be filed.

He also said a recently filed deferred action request has not been signed by ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO).

Espinosa said the family and attorney have also faced increasing restrictions on visiting Parra.

According to Espinosa, attorney Kim Bruno last saw her client about a week before Friday’s news conference.

Espinosa called the situation unfair, saying the same agency whose agents were involved in the incident that left Parra injured has the authority to make decisions about his continued detention.

Family questions medical care at rehabilitation facility

The family also raised concerns about the medical treatment Parra is receiving at Avere, a rehabilitation facility near West Orem Drive and Highway 288.

Espinosa said the family has not received a complete medical report detailing Parra’s condition, the surgeries he has undergone or his recovery progress.

He said the family has requested additional testing, including an MRI, to determine whether Parra has internal injuries.

Rodolfo Parra also recalled concerns about his brother’s hygiene during an earlier visit, saying he appeared unwashed and had an unkempt beard.

He said he was later told that conditions had improved, including that his brother was receiving assistance with bathing. However, the family has not been able to verify those improvements during a more recent visit.

“We don’t know if they’ve done all the necessary studies or not,” Rodolfo Parra said.

FIEL calls on Sen. John Cornyn to intervene

With Thanksgiving approaching, Espinosa urged elected officials to intervene and specifically called on outgoing U.S. Sen. John Cornyn to contact ICE about Parra’s detention.

Espinosa said FIEL has reached out to members of Congress and other elected officials, as well as immigration agencies, but has not secured Parra’s release.

He said the organization is also considering an initiative to bring more attention to the case, including potentially traveling to Washington, D.C.

“Some people say that with the change in government, things might change in January, but Mr. Miguel Parra cannot wait a single day longer,” Espinosa said.

FIEL is asking for Parra’s immediate release so he can reunite with his family and continue his recovery.

text:
Chanting, "Hey, hey, what do we say? ICE out of Dublin, out of the Bay," a coalition of groups gathered Thursday amid gloomy weather outside Santa Rita Jail, braving the elements and what they called intimidation.

ICE-free zone

What they're saying:

"We have an ICE-free zone policy," Alameda County District 5 Supervisor Nikki Fortunato Bas said. "That means ICE cannot conduct immigration enforcement activities on county property without a judicial warrant."

That policy and the presence of ICE agents are under greater scrutiny following an incident last week.

Video obtained exclusively by KTVU shows agents and activists exchanging shoves in the lobby of Santa Rita Jail.

In an earlier interview, Alameda County Sheriff Yesenia Sanchez acknowledged an increase in ICE activity in the parking lot is spilling over to actions inside the facility – and the activity got physical.

"There were some interactions that became escalated where there was physical contact between ICE agents and advocates," Sanchez said. "And I can't have that happening in my jail. Our jail has to be a safe operation. I want to make sure it is a safe facility."

Last week, the Alameda County Board of Supervisors sent a letter to the Department of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, stating, "...This conduct violates County policy and creates significant safety risks to members of the public, ASCO personnel and other employees..." The letter goes on to bar ICE agents from conducting operations at the facility unless they have a judicial warrant.

ICE continues to be in parking lot

The other side:

Organizers and activists said they are calling for the removal of all ICE agents from Alameda County, the Bay Area, and the state of California.

Despite the cease-and-desist, ICE officers have continued to wait in the parking lot of the jail to detain people. In fact, activists pointed out that they were there during Thursday's rally as well.

The Department of Homeland Security told KTVU in an email they won't adhere to the ICE-free zone policy, stating they have a right to enforce federal immigration policy wherever and whenever they want.

But Sanchez stressed that there is no way her deputies are going to engage in a physical fight with ICE.

"There was this unrealistic expectation of having an ICE-free zone. Who's going to enforce that?" Sanchez asked. "Are we asking for deputies to physically engage with another law enforcement entity? That's just not going to happen. There's this expectation that we're going to go to war with one another. That is not going to happen."

Sanchez added that the ICE-free zones may make some in the community feel like they're in a safe bubble, that there's this "safety zone that can be protected."

"And that's not just realistic," Sanchez said.

text:
Sen. Bernie Sanders urged Democrats preparing to take control of Congress in January to repeal nearly $75 billion in funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement and pass immigration reform with a path to citizenship, citing shootings by federal immigration agents, home raids, and the detention of young children.

"ICE agents have shot Americans, broken down doors and sent 5-year-old children to detention centers," Sanders wrote Friday on X, calling the actions "immoral and unconstitutional." He did not outline a specific immigration bill or say how he would structure a path to citizenship.

The shootings include the deaths of two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis. Renee Good, 37, was fatally shot by an ICE agent on Jan. 7. Alex Pretti, also 37, was killed by Border Patrol agents on Jan. 24. Pretti's killing involved Customs and Border Protection, not ICE. Federal authorities turned over evidence in both cases to Minnesota prosecutors in July, after a dispute over access to the investigations.

Sanders' reference to agents breaking down doors also reflects a documented Minneapolis case. On Jan. 11, federal immigration officers used a battering ram to enter the home of Teyana Gibson Brown and arrest her husband, Garrison Gibson. The officers used an administrative warrant signed by an ICE supervisor, rather than a warrant issued by a judge. A federal judge later ordered Gibson released, finding that ICE had violated his civil rights and its own rules.

The 5-year-old Sanders referenced was Liam Conejo Ramos, who was detained with his father in Minnesota on Jan. 20 and taken to a family detention center in Dilley, Texas. At the time, the family had a pending immigration case and no deportation order, according to records reviewed by CBS News. The government said agents were targeting Liam's father, not the child. A federal judge ordered both released on Jan. 31.

Sanders characterized the practices as unconstitutional, but the cases have produced narrower, individual court rulings. The judge in the Gibson case found a civil rights violation tied to that home entry. Liam's release order did not amount to a blanket ruling that detaining children in immigration cases is unconstitutional.

The money Sanders wants to repeal was included in the 2025 reconciliation law, Public Law 119-21, signed July 4 of that year. The Congressional Research Service puts ICE's allocation at $74.85 billion, commonly rounded to $75 billion. That includes $45 billion for detention capacity and $29.85 billion for operational and procurement costs. The funds are available for obligation over multiple years, through fiscal 2029.

Sanders sought to repeal the same funding in January, proposing to redirect the money to Medicaid. The Senate rejected his amendment, 49-51, short of the 60 votes required for approval.

The political landscape has since shifted. Democrats won control of both the House and Senate in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, and will take over when the new Congress convenes in January. President Donald Trump has vowed to veto Democratic legislation, setting up a likely clash over any attempt to reverse the ICE funding.

Sanders' post renews a demand he has made for months: cut ICE's expanded funding and use immigration reform to create a path to citizenship. The post does not specify which immigrants would qualify or what enforcement changes would accompany such a measure.

text:
Washington, D.C. — Today, Congresswoman Norma Torres (CA-35), a member of the House Appropriations Committee, requested that Department of Homeland Security Inspector General Joseph Cuffari investigate ICE’s $950 million purchase of the Adelanto ICE Processing Center from GEO Group, including whether taxpayers were left responsible for infrastructure failures identified before the sale.

“Taxpayers should not be on the hook for infrastructure and repair costs that were known before ICE signed this deal,” said Congresswoman Torres. “Before spending nearly a billion dollars, ICE owes the public a full accounting of the repair costs, who would pay them, and whether the purchase served a legitimate public purpose. If an investigation proves illegal or corrupt actions influenced this purchase, then DHS must pursue every available legal remedy to unwind the deal and recover taxpayer dollars, seeking a full refund to the extent permitted by law. Anyone who violates the law must be held accountable.”

The letter cites a September 2026 Government Accountability Office report finding that ICE expanded detention capacity without necessary planning and analysis. Torres asked whether ICE addressed those recommendations to prevent waste of taxpayer dollars before buying the Adelanto facility and whether ICE evaluated its long-term repair, maintenance, and operating costs.

Torres also requested scrutiny of the purchase price, procurement integrity, and whether ICE Acting Director David Venturella, a former GEO Group executive who committed to recusing himself from matters involving the company, participated in the transaction.

Rep. Norma Torres' office has conducted more than 20 oversight visits to Adelanto this Congress. The letter describes persistent failures in medical care and living conditions, questions whether federal ownership was intended to evade oversight, and notes that GEO Group will continue operating the facilities.

“Changing ownership does not erase dangerous conditions or the obligation to comply with court orders,” Torres added. “Congress and the public deserve to know who approved this purchase, who benefits, and what it will ultimately cost taxpayers.”

text:
The Senate rejected a war powers resolution on Thursday that would have directed President Trump to seek congressional approval before resuming attacks on Iran. The resolution failed on a vote of 51-48. Three Republicans voted in favor, while Pennsylvania Democratic Senator John Fetterman voted in opposition. The House approved the resolution in September. Both the House and Senate previously approved a war powers resolution back in June, but President Trump largely ignored it. Thursday’s failed vote in the Senate came after Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries suggested he would not block funding for attacks on Iran in the government funding package due by December 11. Meanwhile, a Pentagon official said Thursday the cost of the war on Iran has topped $48 billion. That figure does not include damage to U.S. bases, the cost of providing healthcare to hundreds of injured troops or the tens of billions of dollars in higher fuel costs triggered by the war.

The Senate has approved a permitting reform bill that would weaken environmental laws to speed approval of new housing, roads, energy projects and other infrastructure. While the bill would make it easier to build new transmission lines and wind and solar farms, it would also speed construction of fossil fuel power plants and new data centers, including on public lands. Meanwhile, Native leaders and advocacy groups strongly opposed the legislation, saying it would weaken tribal sovereignty and threaten cultural and sacred sites. This is Oregon Democratic Senator Jeff Merkley, who voted “no.”

Sen. Jeff Merkley: “First, it makes it a lot easier to build data centers. Did anybody notice data centers were a big issue in this most recent election? Here we come right in after the election, and we’re going to pass a bill that makes it easier to do data centers by striking down tools that states have when they decide they do not want to have a data center because it threatens key clean air or clean water issues.”

Despite those objections, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known as BAAJA, passed on a vote of 62-33 with 14 Democrats in favor, including Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer. In a statement, Food & Water Watch said, “Sen. Schumer’s alignment with Republicans over a majority of his own Democratic caucus in voting to advance this terrible pro-polluter, pro-data center permitting bill is all the reason needed to demand that Schumer step down as leader of the Senate Democrats.” The bill now goes to the House and is expected to be voted on the week after next.

Here at the COP31 U.N. climate summit, negotiators published a “slimmed-down” draft text on Thursday that stripped out any reference to fossil fuels, or ending their use. Instead, the document promotes carbon capture and storage, an unproven technology that critics say will never have a meaningful impact on the climate crisis. Activists at the COP are demanding more financing to help poorer countries adapt to a warming world. This is Iona Stewart of the climate action group Global Witness.

Emily Iona Stewart: “Mentions of human rights, especially human rights and environment defenders, which had previously been introduced by the Brazilians, are now being walked back in this cover decision. So that’s really worrying for us. Another thing: fossil fuels, still not in there. Where is the text on phasing out fossil fuels and having a concrete roadmap for all of the parties? We need that now. And then, finance. There’s not enough momentum on making sure that countries who have already signed up and pledged to give climate finance actually deliver on those pledges.”

In Ukraine, officials say eight people were killed and dozens injured overnight, as Russia launched a massive drone and missile attack. In Kyiv, Russian bombs struck three ⁠bridges over the Dnipro River. Meanwhile, in Kharkiv, a Russian drone damaged a hospital, wounding four people.

The Russian attacks came after Ukraine bombed the Kerch Bridge, the only link between mainland Russia and Russian-annexed Crimea. Engineers say it could take years for Russia to repair the damage.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky defended the bridge strike and warned of further action.

President Volodymyr Zelensky: “We have long been telling Russia: Enough of striking bridges, our cities and villages, Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, railways and grain ships. Enough of this war. But every time, Russia chooses a new escalation.”

Meanwhile, Poland’s military said it was investigating a suspected violation of its airspace by Russia near Poland’s border with Ukraine, after an unidentified object crash-landed this morning.

In Minnesota, a Somali American Uber driver is fighting for his life after he was allegedly run over multiple times with his own vehicle by a passenger who disliked his Muslim name. Mohamed Yusuf remained in critical condition Thursday with life-threatening injuries following Saturday’s attack. It follows last month’s raid on the D.C. home of Somali American Minnesota Congresswoman Ilhan Omar by federal agents. And it follows president Trump’s repeated racist attacks demonizing Somali American communities. Trump has called Somalis “garbage” and “low-IQ people” who “contribute nothing.” Just weeks ago, Trump wrote on social media, “Fight back Minnesota, fight back!”

In Huntsville, Texas, a man on death row repeatedly moaned out in pain during a botched execution that took over an hour. Reinaldo Dennes remained strapped to a gurney as prison officials struggled to locate a vein to administer a lethal dose of pentobarbital. After more than an hour Thursday evening, vein lines were ultimately found in his neck and one of his feet. Seventy-year-old Dennes reportedly exclaimed that his leg felt like it was on fire. This comes just over a month after the botched execution attempt of Christa Pike in Tennessee that drew widespread condemnation. Pike survived two lethal injections and was left hospitalized in critical condition and unconscious for nearly a week. She’s now back in prison.

The White House has picked Eric Ueland to run the Government Accountability Office, Congress’s independent watchdog, for a 15-year term. Ueland is a longtime Republican operative who served as a Big Pharma and fossil fuel lobbyist before joining the Trump administration in 2016. Senate Republicans are skipping the bipartisan process used for every GAO head since 1980, in which top lawmakers submit a short list of candidates. Twenty-one inspectors general are urging congressional leaders to reject Ueland’s confirmation, writing, “the credibility of any oversight institution depends on two pillars: strict adherence to statutory safeguards designed to protect its independence, and leadership defined by proven, nonpartisan fidelity to objective evidence. Mr. Ueland’s nomination fails on both counts.”

Following a preliminary injunction blocking implementation of DHS’s new rule (scheduled to take effect on Sep. 15, 2026), the court has now set aside the F-1/J-1/I status rule in its entirety. The rule would have replaced “Duration of Status” admission for students (F-1), exchange visitors (J-1), and journalists (I) with fixed periods of admission of up to four years. It also would have imposed additional restrictions on grace periods and changes to programs or majors. A detailed discussion of the rule’s impact is available here.

On Nov. 16, in an action brought by several organizations representing colleges, universities, and educators, together with four labor organizations, the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts vacated the rule in its entirety as “arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, and otherwise not in accordance with law.”

Although DHS may appeal the decision, the current F-1/J-1/I rules remain in effect: Individuals in these categories will retain their current grace period and will continue to be admitted to the United States for “Duration of Status,” without the need to apply for an extension of status when extending their studies, changing degree programs or majors, or applying for OPT/STEM OPT (F-1) or Academic Training or Medical Residency (J-1). description:

American families are paying an ICE Tax and the mass deportation agenda is making this holiday season more expensive for everyone.
