text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Thanksgiving dinner is getting more expensive, and farmers warn that the Trump Administration’s targeting of long-time immigrant workers is putting additional pressure on the workforce the nation relies on to produce America’s food.

Turkey prices increased 24% per pound, going from $1.04 last year to $1.29 per pound this year, according to a November 2026 analysis by Auburn University and the Alabama Cooperative Extension System. The increase means a 15-pound turkey went from $15.53 last year to $19.35 this year.

“The wholesale arrest and deportation of long-term, law-abiding immigrants puts America’s food supply and agricultural businesses at risk,” said Rebecca Shi, CEO of the American Business Immigration Coalition (ABIC). “Targeting hard-working immigrants working on American farms, in food processing plants and at dairies threatens farmers’ ability to operate and makes our Thanksgiving meals more expensive, hurting all Americans.

Lawmakers should give Americans more to be grateful for this year and grant legal pathways for long-term immigrants now.”

“Immigration is a pocketbook issue and the mass deportation agenda is making it harder for Americans to afford their Thanksgiving meal. Instead of deporting hard working people, we should be focused on creating a path to legality for the workers that keep food on our tables through good times and bad. American families are paying an ICE Tax and the mass deportation agenda is making this holiday season more expensive for everyone. Congress must rein in ICE and protect the workers who feed this country,” said Vanessa Cárdenas, Executive Director of America’s Voice.

These price increases come as farms, dairies and poultry processors are struggling to find enough employees amid spiking immigration arrests and fear spreading throughout their existing workforce, including workers who have proper documentation in place. The absence of workers staying home due to fear or who are arrested is compounding existing challenges farmers face, including increased fuel and fertilizer costs, tariffs and shrinking profits.

The majority (68%) of U.S. crop workers are foreign-born, and 42% are undocumented immigrants, according to an October report released by America’s Voice.

Researchers connected immigration enforcement and the loss of workers as contributing to rising food prices and found that foods that rely more heavily on immigrant workers have grown more in price than groceries overall since January 2025. For example, apple prices rose 7.2% between Jan. 2025 and August 2026, but grocery prices as a whole grew by 3.4%.

Consequences of losing agricultural workers reach beyond grocery pricing, though, as another study found that, due to the time-sensitive nature of planting and harvesting, farmers risk losing all of their annual profits if workers aren’t available when they need them, according to research by the American Enterprise Institute.

That’s because the Trump administration has increased interior immigration enforcement by 151% since January 2025, according to the Migration Policy Institute.

ICE enforcement raids targeted long-term, law-abiding workers on jobsites, with around 80% of ICE arrests in Trump’s second term involving people with no criminal history, according to MPI.

Pennsylvania ICE raids came at the worst time for turkey producers

Poultry processing’s busy season starts in the late summer and fall as producers ramp up production for Thanksgiving and Christmas. Enforcement has decimated this specialized workforce, forcing existing employees to work longer hours in different jobs to make up for the absences.

“These raids targeting long-term immigrant workers are driving up the cost of your Thanksgiving meal,” said Chris Herr, Executive Vice President of PennAg Industries Association. “President Trump and Congress have the opportunity to get a historic win for affordability, our communities, farmers and the American people if they are finally able to create legal pathways for long-term immigrant workers. I guarantee no one in the administration or Congress could do the jobs these workers are doing.”

Mashed potatoes the hero of your Thanksgiving meal? Not without immigrants

The price of milk, used in many Thanksgiving dishes to add texture and flavor, has increased 19% since 2025, according to the analysis by Auburn University and the Alabama Cooperative Extension System.

“In order for Americans to sit down for a Thanksgiving meal that includes creamy mashed potatoes, green bean casserole, buttermilk biscuits and pumpkin pie, they need the immigrants who staff Americans’ dairy farms,” said Hans Breitenmoser Jr., a second-generation dairy farmer who owns Golden Dawn Farm, a Merrill, Wisconsin farm with 460 milk cows. “We’re dealing with living, breathing creatures that rely on us. When even employees with legal status are bullied and afraid and concerned and stressed out about ICE, it’s difficult to show up for work. Less employees means less cows milked and higher prices at the store.”

“When it comes to the Thanksgiving meal, it’s not all gravy. The very workers who ensure there’s food on your table are the ones being ruthlessly and cruelly deported. As a result, Americans spend more on holiday meals, while many immigrants won’t even get to spend the holidays in their homes or with their families,” said Kathy Davis, a seventh-generation owner at Ayers Farms Inc., in Perrysville, Ohio. “Additionally, providing workable, realistic, and pragmatic immigration reform will help sustain the American food chain — from the farm family carefully raising their livestock and crops, through processors and transportation, and ultimately to the consumer, while maintaining the high quality and safety standards we’ve come to expect and enjoy. It’s time for thoughtful immigration reform, not more barbaric enforcement.”

Fresh green beans went up 70% per pound, from $1.92 per pound in 2025 to $3.26 per pound this year.

Overall, fresh vegetables increased 5.7% from January 2025 to August 2026, according to America’s Voice. Canned vegetables rose 6.3% and apples went up 7.2%.

“Thanksgiving is the biggest week of the year for mushroom producers and sales, and it is the time of the year when we are reminded that when people come together to grow and share the bounty, everyone benefits,” said Rachel Roberts, president of the American Mushroom Institute. “It’s unacceptable that any farm should have to worry about whether any of their valued employees sustaining their operations are going to show up to work because there is a risk of being pulled over and detained. Without legal pathways for long-time immigrant employees, the food they produce and the American jobs and economics they sustain will cease to exist.”

As Americans gather for Thanksgiving meals produced in large part by immigrants, agricultural producers say policymakers must recognize the essential role immigrant workers play in keeping the nation’s food supply stable and affordable.

President Trump and Congress must work together to advance practical immigration reform that provides legal pathways for long-term workers, protects American businesses and strengthens the agricultural workforce.

text:
The federal government has agreed to remove Immigration and Customs Enforcement vehicles from a city-owned parking garage and relocate them elsewhere, according to emails obtained by Mission Local.

The move comes three weeks after Mission Local first reported that ICE vehicles were using dozens of parking spaces at a downtown garage owned by the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency. Those vehicles were presumably active in enforcement operations across the Bay Area.

The federal government hopes to remove the ICE vehicles by Monday, Nov. 23, according to a Friday email from Jason Cawthorne, a director at the Government Services Administration, the federal entity that has assigned spots to ICE at the garage for over a decade.

In the email, which was sent to the San Francisco Municipal Transportation on Nov. 20 and reviewed by Mission Local, Cawthorne wrote that the federal government will forfeit its 147 spaces at the garage and negotiate a new lease elsewhere.

From: Kirschbaum, Julie B

Sent: 11:13 AM

To: Jason Cawthorne – PMBC, +2

Subject: RE: GSA Parking Lease at 250 Clay Street

Dear Mr. Cawthorne,

Thank you for your response to my letter and for understanding that the use of a city garage by ICE vehicles is inconsistent with the City’s laws and policies.

We appreciate your commitment to remove all vehicles from the Golden Gateway Garage on Monday, November 23.

We see the removal of these vehicles as urgent and will reach out immediately.

Sincerely,

Julie Kirschbaum

Julie Kirschbaum

Director of Transportation

San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency

From: Jason Cawthorne

Subject: GSA Parking Lease at 250 Clay Street

Good Morning,

I’m reaching out to share GSA’s current plan related to the parking lease at 250 Clay Street and its use by ICE vehicles.

GSA is currently negotiating a new lease to move the 147 spaces out of the 250 Clay Street garage. We are finalizing pricing and costs to install security gates and card readers for the new location. Once signed, it would then take approximately 3-4 weeks for the work to be completed.

As an interim solution, we plan to move the vehicles before that work is completed. We are targeting Monday, November 23 to make that move, and are waiting for confirmation from the new lessor that this will be possible; we hope to have that confirmation today.

GSA understands the concerns raised and wants to work with you to determine a path forward that works for both groups. We’re available to meet to discuss in more detail.

Thanks,

Jason

Jason Cawthorne

Director

Central Pacific Coast Service Center

Office of Facilities Management

U.S. General Services Administration

A source close to the matter said Mayor Daniel Lurie had called the General Services Administration multiple times since the city became aware in late October that ICE was using the city-owned garage. The mayor asked the agency to remove the ICE vehicles, the source said.

Mission Local first reported the garage’s use by ICE on Oct. 30. The SFMTA on Nov. 2 wrote the federal government urging it to “immediately and permanently cease parking ICE vehicles” in the Golden Gateway Garage at 250 Clay St.

On Thursday, Mission Local reported that SFMTA staff had knowingly signed off an “ICE Lease” deal for parking spots in the garage, an act that half a dozen attorneys said was a plain violation of the city and state sanctuary laws prohibiting cooperation with immigration enforcement.

One SFMTA staffer had written, “If we have the space, I don’t mind taking the money.”

The federal government’s decision Friday ends an at-least 16-year history of federal immigration vehicles parking in the garage, according to contracts.

Cawthorne, the General Services Administration staffer, wrote that the ICE vehicles would be relocated and that finalizing a lease and installing “security gates and card readers for the new location” would take about a month, but “we plan to move the vehicles before that work is completed.”

“We are targeting Monday, November 23 to make that move, and are waiting for confirmation from the new lessor that this will be possible; we hope to have that confirmation today.”

Julie Kirschbaum, the director of transportation at SFMTA, thanked Cawthorne for his response and for “understanding that the use of a city garage by ICE vehicles is inconsistent with the City’s laws and policies,” according to the emails.

She wrote that she “appreciates” his commitment to remove the ICE vehicles. “We see the removal of these vehicles as urgent,” she wrote.

Mission Local previously reported that the SFMTA retained “sole discretion” to cut its contract with the private parking operator that subleased spaces to the federal government. That contract governs more than a dozen garages, however, and the SFMTA had sought a way to remove the ICE vehicles without affecting the larger contract.

The garage lies in close proximity to the ICE field office at 630 Sansome St., where hundreds of immigrants have been detained or taken to after being arrested in and around the Bay Area.

Agents used the garage to store vehicles, which helped the federal government transport detained immigrants, including to and from arrests at homes, workplaces, and traffic stops, according to activists who have been monitoring the garage for months.

title: Federal judge blocks CT law that sought to regulate ICE agents - CT Mirror
authors: Andrew Brown, Mark Pazniokas, Andrew Brown Investigative
description:
[RELATED: ICE agents appear to be wearing masks in CT. Is that legal?]
Masked ICE agents made an arrest at a courthouse in Meriden in September, raising questions about the law and whether ICE agents acted beyond their authority.
[The law] was meant to hold federal law enforcement officers to the same standards of accountability as local and state police.
“We warned that the law violates the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause by attempting to regulate federal officers while they carry out their official duties.
Lo and behold, a federal judge right here in CT agrees with what we had warned about,” they said in a statement.
text:
A federal judge issued a ruling on Friday blocking Connecticut officials from enforcing a 2026 law that sought to regulate the actions of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents and to stop federal agents from wearing masks and other face coverings.

U.S. District Judge Vernon Oliver determined that several sections of S.B. 397, which was passed by state Democratic lawmakers earlier this year, is likely to violate the U.S. Constitution.

As a result, Oliver, a former state Superior Court judge who was appointed to the federal bench by President Joe Biden in 2023, issued an injunction blocking four sections of the law from being enforced as the lawsuit continues to play out in court.

Three of those sections sought to empower Connecticut’s Inspector General, who is responsible for investigating state and local police shootings, to also examine and criminally prosecute federal agents operating in the state.

And the fourth section sought to prevent ICE agents from wearing face coverings by making it misdemeanor for officers to wear a mask “while interacting with the public” while performing their official duties.

In his written order, Oliver said those portions of the law likely violate the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution. And he said President Donald Trump’s Department of Justice was likely to win the lawsuit the federal government filed in May.

The state law, Oliver wrote, “plainly imposes conditions on how federal officers must conduct and present themselves during the course of their federal duties, and it subjects them to criminal and civil penalties if they do not abide by those state-imposed conditions.”

“But the Supremacy Clause ensures that federal operations are not chilled by state prosecution and that federal officers are immune from state prosecution when acting within the scope of their federal authority,” he added.

The injunction is a significant setback for Connecticut Democrats who sought to rein in ICE agents, who have drastically stepped up their enforcement practices across the country during Trump’s second term.

[RELATED: ICE agents appear to be wearing masks in CT. Is that legal?]

Masked ICE agents made an arrest at a courthouse in Meriden in September, raising questions about the law and whether ICE agents acted beyond their authority.

Gov. Ned Lamont, who signed the bill into law in May, urged the new Congress to protect immigrants.

“We are disappointed by today’s ruling and condemn ICE’s treatment of Connecticut residents,” Cathryn Vaulman, Lamont’s communications director, wrote on Friday. “Masked, armed agents without visible badges have surrounded cars in traffic and stormed homes and workplaces, rounded up parents dropping kids off at school and picked up a Cheshire high school student whose father aided troops in Afghanistan. ICE has terrorized and traumatized our communities. [The law] was meant to hold federal law enforcement officers to the same standards of accountability as local and state police. Gov. Lamont urges the new Democratic majorities in Congress to strengthen oversight of DHS and help us protect our immigrant communities from abuses of power.”

Reached for comment Friday, a representative for the office of Attorney General William Tong responded briefly: “We are reviewing the decision and evaluating next steps.”

Meanwhile, state Republican lawmakers in Connecticut celebrated the ruling. In a statement, several members of the state’s Republican caucus noted that they warned their Democratic colleagues the law was likely to face opposition.

“We warned that the law violates the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause by attempting to regulate federal officers while they carry out their official duties. Lo and behold, a federal judge right here in CT agrees with what we had warned about,” they said in a statement.

The statement, which was issued by Sen. Rob Sampson of Wolcott, Sen. Eric Berthel of Watertown and outgoing Senate Minority Leader Stephen Harding of Brookfield, blamed Democrats for passing unconstitutional laws for the sake of “scoring political points.”

“When one party controls nearly every lever of power in Hartford, the temptation to ignore constitutional constraints in pursuit of political theater becomes far too common,” the Republicans wrote.

Rep. Steven Stafstrom, D-Bridgeport, a key backer of the law as co-chair of the legislature’s Judiciary Committee, said he did not believe the judge adequately weighed the Supremacy Clause against the inherent police powers of the states.

“There was very robust debate over where Supremacy Clause begins and ends and where inherent police power begins and ends,” Stafstrom said.

“I respect the court, but I fear today’s ruling leaves Connecticut less safe, because it blocks the tools S.B. 397 gave us to investigate deaths involving federal officers and to make sure people know who is exercising police power in their communities,” said Stafstrom, a practicing attorney.

“The court did not find that any act of Congress overrides our law, and whether an officer acted within federal authority is a question that belongs in a real case with real facts, not one that should be decided before any case exists. This ruling is preliminary, and I will work with my colleagues and the attorney general’s office on next steps, because accountability is how we keep our communities safe,” he added.

text:
HARTFORD, CT — Gov. Ned Lamont is urging the new Democratic majorities in Congress to strengthen oversight over the Department of Homeland security after a federal judge temporarily blocked some provisions of Public Act 26-14. The law had aimed to hold federal officials to the same standards as state law enforcement by banning them from carrying out their duties while masked, requiring visible badges and limiting access to certain places.

“We are disappointed by today’s ruling and condemn ICE’s treatment of Connecticut residents,” Lamont said in a statement. “Masked, armed agents without visible badges have surrounded cars in traffic and stormed homes and workplaces, terrorizing and traumatizing our communities.”

State Rep. Steve Stafstrom, D-Bridgeport, said that the ruling was preliminary and that he would work with his legislative colleagues and Attorney General William Tong on next steps.

“The court did not find that any act of Congress overrides our law, and whether an officer acted within federal authority is a question that belongs in a real case with real facts, not one that should be decided before any case exists,” he said. He added that “accountability is how we keep our communities safe.”

On Friday, Judge Vernon Oliver ruled that portions of the state’s law violated the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause that places the federal government above the states when federal and state law conflict.

Senate Republicans agreed, with Senate Minority Leader Stephen Harding of Brookfield and Minority Leader-elect Rob Sampson of Wolcott issuing a statement calling the state law anti-law enforcement and unconstitutional.

“Democratic leaders pushed this bill knowing the constitutional problems. They prioritized scoring political points and sending a message over respect for the rule of law and the Constitution’s limits on state power,” Harding and Sampson wrote. “When one party controls nearly every lever of power in Hartford, the temptation to ignore constitutional constraints in pursuit of political theater becomes far too common.”

text:
LANSING – Attorney General Nessel today joined a coalition of 20 attorneys general in encouraging leaders of the incoming majorities in Congress to hold hearings on Trump Administration abuses in immigration enforcement. In a letter to congressional leadership (PDF) — including the incoming chairs of House and Senate committees with responsibility over the judiciary, homeland security, and government oversight and accountability — Attorney General Nessel and the coalition encourage Congress to hold hearings on the accountability of immigration officers, detention practices, and waste and corruption in the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

Attorney General Nessel and the coalition also encourage the incoming chairs of these committees to feature testimony at the hearings from Americans directly harmed by immigration enforcement abuse, advocates for immigrant communities, and from state Attorneys General who have been using the tools at their disposal to fight against this abuse and for the rule of law. State officials and community leaders have important insights to share gathered through investigative councils, accountability commissions, and other community engagement.

“These new Congressional majorities were built by the American people, and they expect their votes will drive meaningful change in Washington,” said Attorney General Nessel. “Americans deserve not only oversight, but accountability, over DHS, CBP, and ICE and the way they’ve antagonized and terrorized communities across the country. Our federal legislators should hold broad public hearings on the conduct of these agencies and the harms brought about by cruel and failing politics and policies.”

President Trump’s DHS and its agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and Customs and Border Protection (CBP), have operated as if they are exempt from accountability and the rule of law. In 2025, DHS began a months-long campaign of terror across multiple American cities. Since the beginning of Trump’s second term, DHS agents have shot at least 25 people across the United States.

Use of force by immigration agents has also increased dramatically. In just the first three months of the current administration, there was a nearly fourfold increase in reported ICE use-of-force incidents. Independent researchers have subsequently documented more than 400 incidents of misuse of crowd-control weapons in sixteen cities across the country in just 12 months, resulting in over 200 injuries to demonstrators, bystanders, and journalists attempting to cover the events.

Attorney General Nessel and the coalition write to Congressional leaders, “In the face of immigration enforcement conduct that is both immoral and unlawful, the outgoing House and Senate majorities were content to look the other way. The incoming majorities need to confront this head-on. The American people voted for real, serious oversight — with teeth and consequences for any agency or individual who would ignore the rule of law.”

Immigration detention practices are in dire need of reform and oversight as well. By ICE’s own accounting, close to 60 people have died in ICE custody in the past two years, enough to make 2025 the deadliest year in immigration detention in over two decades.

DHS has also wasted significant sums of money in its rushed and ill-conceived efforts to rapidly expand immigration detention. DHS spent approximately $1 billion purchasing warehouses in a grossly inhumane effort to house people in them before shifting course, including a warehouse in Romulus that DHS planned to convert into an immigration detention center. The State of Michigan and the City of Romulus sued the federal government over the plan, and DHS has since abandoned its plans for the site. Now DHS has purchased four prisons from CoreCivic, a significant donor to President Trump’s inaugural committee and his PACs, for the extraordinary sum of $2.2 billion. DHS paid CoreCivic $495 million for a prison in Minnesota that CoreCivic offered to the State of Minnesota for just $75 million in 2025. Americans deserve to know whether DHS is inflating the purchase price of these facilities and diverting their tax dollars into the coffers of the President’s supporters.

Joining Attorney General Nessel in the letter to Congressional leaders are the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawai‘i, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, and Washington.

title: Rebuked in court, ICE stops immediate rearrest tactics in Colorado - CSMonitor.com
authors: Sarah Matusek, The Christian Science Monitor
description:
After spending more than half a year in an immigration detention center, Emmanuel thought he was free.
A federal judge in Colorado had ordered his release, but Immigration and Customs Enforcement had other plans.
“As soon as I stepped outside, there were five ICE officers waiting,” says Emmanuel, who asked to use only that name due to privacy concerns.
“The whole system is set up to break you.” A federal judge on Wednesday found an ICE official in civil contempt in a similar re-detention case in Colorado.

text:
After spending more than half a year in an immigration detention center, Emmanuel thought he was free. A federal judge in Colorado had ordered his release, but Immigration and Customs Enforcement had other plans.

“As soon as I stepped outside, there were five ICE officers waiting,” says Emmanuel, who asked to use only that name due to privacy concerns.

The immigrant says he was handcuffed, put in a van, and driven to the back. From there, he was brought back into the Aurora detention center as if he were a new detainee.

“I wasn’t too surprised,” says Emmanuel, who had heard about this tactic. “The whole system is set up to break you.”

A federal judge on Wednesday found an ICE official in civil contempt in a similar re-detention case in Colorado. Beginning in late October, ICE’s Denver office subjected at least 18 immigrants to the practice, according to court records. Officers staged a release after a court ordered someone free, followed by re-detention within 12 hours.

“Sometimes, behavior stuns and renders a listener speechless,” wrote U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney. She described “unconstitutional behavior that runs top to bottom.”

Immigrant advocates had decried the immediate re-detention practice on due-process grounds. Before the contempt order against his colleague this week, Nathan Rasper, the acting field office director for ICE in Denver, told the judge he had halted the practice that he believed was legal.

Meanwhile, similar arrests have cropped up elsewhere, at least in Minnesota, and the Department of Homeland Security, which includes ICE, has left the door open for more. The revelations in Colorado come as other federal judges rebuke ICE practices here.

Courts weigh in

After major midterm election losses for Republicans, President Donald Trump said his immigration crackdown might have been “too tough.”

Yet he has also elevated immigration hard-liner Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff. Mr. Miller had previously explored suspending the constitutional right of habeas corpus, which allows people to challenge their detention in court. Immigrants recently rearrested in Colorado had been previously ordered released by federal judges on habeas petitions.

Detention is key to the deportation pipeline. It’s easier for ICE to remove people under its control. Yet as the government claims record-high ICE arrests of more than 50,000 a month, the agency has struggled to keep many in custody due to historic filings of habeas petitions.

Mr. Rasper, who assumed his post in Colorado mid-October, said he’d heard of rearrests from ICE’s office in Minnesota. He saw the practice as lawful if the second arrest was based on fixing the government’s own paperwork errors, such as around issuing what’s called a “notice to appear.” That charging document starts someone’s process in immigration court.

Rearrests were meant to target “public safety concerns,” Mr. Rasper said in a hearing Nov. 9. Given the judge’s concerns, he said he directed the practice to stop and for those rearrested to be released. Through an ICE spokesperson, Mr. Rasper declined an interview.

The American Civil Liberties Union of Colorado, which appeared as a friend of the court, rejected Mr. Rasper’s arguments as lawful grounds for rearrest.

What ICE described as a technical violation is a “fundamental violation of law,” said Tim Macdonald, the group’s legal director. “We’re seeing it repeatedly.”

The judge sided with the immigrant advocates.

“It is a due process violation,” said Judge Sweeney. “ICE is not in a position to monitor its own conduct in terms of legality.”

A week after his release from re-detention, another man recounts how officers drove him from the ICE detention center in Aurora to another ICE office nearby, then back to Aurora.

“Very confused. I was scared,” says the man, who requested not to publish his name due to fear of retribution. He recalls a fellow detainee asking ICE officers why they were doing this, and one responding: “We just want to try something.”

The White House referred the Monitor to the DHS.

Break from tradition

Asked by the Monitor if the re-detention directive came from Washington, and where else officers have been ordered to follow it, the DHS sent an unsigned statement that didn’t directly address those points. “ICE complies with all lawful court orders,” the email said.

“When an illegal alien is ordered released by a judge, that does not immunize the alien from immigration enforcement,” the statement said. “Instead, if ICE does not appeal the ruling, it may seek to re-arrest the alien in a way that complies with the judicial decision.”

Three former ICE attorneys, whose combined careers spanned more than three decades at the agency, told the Monitor they question the legality of the tactic.

To rearrest someone, such as someone released on bond by an immigration judge, there need to be “changed circumstances,” such as new criminal activity on the part of the person released, says Paul Hunker, former longtime chief counsel for ICE in Dallas. “They can’t just arrest the person for no good reason.”

ICE is taking a “maximalist approach,” says Ryan Schwank, an assistant chief counsel at ICE who resigned in February, as a whistleblower on officer training. “They really do interpret things in the way that’s most favorable to themselves. And that’s not good-faith behavior.”

Kerry Doyle, general counsel for ICE under the Biden administration, also says she’s “dubious” of immediate rearrests without a change in circumstances.

Even if the government had a “creative argument,” says Ms. Doyle, the policy adds to the “ongoing undermining of the judiciary ... and the relationship between the federal government and these judges.”

In a separate case before a federal appellate court, the government is appealing a preliminary injunction meant to ensure ICE’s warrantless arrests are lawful, an order that a district judge said ICE defied.

Emmanuel’s immigration case, meanwhile, continues.

He legally entered the United States over two decades ago. But his status expired, and an immigration judge ordered him deported at a hearing that Emmanuel says he didn’t know he needed to attend. As he adjusts back to life with his family, for now, he says he still fears arrest.

In detention, he recalls, an officer asked if he hated this country now.

No, Emmanuel said. His American children were born here.

“If I love my children, I cannot hate where they’re from.”

text:
From Camden and Cherry Hill to Trenton and the Jersey Shore, what about life in New Jersey do you want WHYY News to cover? Let us know.

A doctoral student at Princeton University was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement as she was returning home to New Jersey from a conference in Washington, D.C. late Thursday.

Eva Yi Xie, a third-year student studying neuroscience, was taken into custody by federal immigration officers while waiting for her flight at Reagan National Airport in Arlington, Virginia, according to a social media thread from Carlos Brody, one of her academic advisers.

“She went to a conference to present her work, and now she’s in a detention center,” Brody wrote in a post. “She should be home.”

Xie was attending the Society for Neuroscience annual conference where she made a presentation.

In a social media post, Brody Lab, where Xie does her work, said that she is being held at a facility in Chantilly, Virginia, and that her colleagues have since lost contact with her after she reached out to them for help through the communication app Slack.

Brody wrote that her colleagues have been in contact with U.S. Sen. Andy Kim. He encouraged others to reach out to Kim, U.S. Sen. Cory Booker and New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill.

Kim’s office has confirmed that they have been in contact with Xie and are working on her case. They declined to provide more details, citing confidentiality rules.

“Eva is an brilliant computational and experimental systems neuroscientist,” Brody wrote in a post. “She is also a valued colleague, mentor, and friend, and we are privileged that she chose our labs for her thesis research.”

University spokesperson Michael Hotchkiss said in a statement that Princeton has arranged legal counsel to represent Xie.

Requests for comment from the Department of Homeland Security and ICE were not returned.

Rodney D. Priestly, dean of the Princeton Graduate School, notified students in the neuroscience institute late Thursday about the incident, according to the Daily Princetonian, which first reported Xie’s detention. He said that he will stay in close contact with Xie’s family, legal team and colleagues until the situation gets resolved.

In a statement to WHYY News, Priestly said Xie’s detention “is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community.”

“We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton,” he said.

Xie emigrated to the U.S. from Shanghai, China, according to the Science Survey, the student newspaper of Bronx High School of Science, which she attended. She holds degrees in computer science and mathematics from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Her doctoral research seeks to understand the neural basis of decision-making, according to her website.

text:
"The Department of Homeland Security transferred $169 million from other agencies to Immigration and Customs Enforcement for the detention and removal of migrants this year, according to a document sent to Congress by DHS. Many of the transfers came from key national security programs, including $1.8 million from the Domestic Nuclear Detection Office, $9.8 million from FEMA, $29 million from the U.S. Coast Guard and more than $34 million from several TSA programs. DHS also transferred $33 million from other ICE programs to pay for detention and removal, making the total amount of money transferred $202 million. The department has the authority to move funds around internally with the approval of Congress and transfers are not unusual. The total DHS budget for fiscal 2018 was $65 billion; FEMA's total budget was $15.5 billion. DHS spokesperson Tyler Houlton tweeted Tuesday night that, "Under no circumstances was any disaster relief funding transferred from @fema to immigration enforcement efforts. This is a sorry attempt to push a false agenda." He also said that the transferred money came from routine operating expenses and "could not have been used for hurricane response due to appropriation limitations." On Wednesday, FEMA director Brock Long told Andrea Mitchell, chief foreign affairs correspondent for NBC News, that none of the $10 million transferred from FEMA to ICE came from the Disaster Relief Fund, saying that Merkley was "playing politics" ahead of Hurricane Florence. "Right now, that money has nothing to do with what you see behind us," he said in an interview from the FEMA response center in Washington. However, money was taken from the response and recovery, preparedness and protection and mission support operations budgets, which are used to prepare for emergencies like Florence. Those FEMA budgets are for "training for all hazards, preparing our warehouses, making sure we have things ready to go so that we can pre-deploy like you see FEMA doing now," Moira Whelan, FEMA's former chief of staff for the office of Gulf Coast rebuilding, told Maddow on Wednesday. "Taking money away from that operation doesn't just harm [FEMA's hurricane response], it harms us with any disaster we face." DHS stated in the document that the transfers to ICE were made due to "increasing operational demands." The transfers were requested so ICE could add more than 2,000 detention center beds on top of 38,000 adult beds it predicted it would need in its initial budget request for the year. Those beds cost an additional $93 million above the allocated budget, according to the document provided to Congress."

We Shall Rise Again · 6 comments

ICE is melting our tax money.... ICE to offload 7 warehouses it bought for $700M Decision a shift from DHS’ rapid expansion of deportation capacity. By Hamed Aleaziz. The New York Times The idea was meant to supercharge President Donald Trump’s mass deportation plan. Immigration and Customs Enforcement would purchase more than a dozen empty warehouses across the United States to massively expand its capacity to detain people deemed to be in the country illegally, which in turn would spike deportations. A year into Trump’s term, it had bought 11 facilities at a cost of $1 billion. But in a major turnabout, the agency is planning to offload seven warehouses purchased for more than $700 million by either giving them to other federal agencies or selling them outright, according to documents obtained by The New York Times. The decision to sharply scale back the warehouse plan is a rejection of a signature initiative under previous Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, who pushed the boundaries of what the government can do to aggressively round up potential deportees. The new secretary, Markwayne Mullin, who had privately expressed skepticism about the plan, has said publicly that he wants the agency to be quieter about how it carries out immigration enforcement. “From Day 1, DHS has remained singularly focused on removing the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens from the United States and is always evaluating the best methods to do so,” the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement for this article. “These heinous criminals, once arrested, should be removed at lightning speed, not housed on American soil at the taxpayer’s expense. DHS is moving swiftly to utilize EXISTING detention space with our state and county partners.” The move comes months after Noem’s agency, flush with cash, pursued an idea to fundamentally change immigration detention in the country by not only expanding it to unprecedented levels but placing ownership in the federal government’s hands, rather than contractors’. The shift also raises questions about the original decision-making behind the plan to buy the warehouses — a costly undertaking that involved converting industrial space into places that could house thousands of people, with water and sewer capacity and proper ventilation, and created almost immediate conflict with local communities across the United States. ICE has been battered by lawsuits over a lack of environmental checks, and the Department of Homeland Security’s inspector general is investigating the purchases. The warehouses that ICE plans to hand off or sell are in Romulus, Mich.; Social Circle and Flowery Branch, Ga.; Hamburg and Tremont, Pa.; Salt Lake City; and Roxbury, N.J. The agency appears to still be moving forward with four of the warehouses purchased for detention purposes, in San Antonio and Socorro, Texas; Surprise, Ariz.; and Hagerstown, Md. However, a federal judge has blocked work on the Maryland facility. It was not immediately clear why the agency decided to proceed with those four spaces for detention. ICE also plans to buy immigrant detention facilities from private prison companies that it already contracts with, according to documents. But the move to offload most of the warehouses raises questions about the agency’s ability to deport high numbers of immigrants. Immigrants set for deportation are typically arrested, processed and then detained by ICE before being flown out of the country. For an agency whose budget jumped from $8 billion annually to $28 billion through funding by Congress, detention was always going to be a priority. Without more beds, any conversation of deportation on the scale of what Trump discussed on the campaign trail would be out of the question. The passage of Trump’s signature domestic policy law turned what was a key challenge — a lack of detention beds — into a suddenly easy problem to solve. And Trump administration officials were confident. After the bill’s passage, White House border czar Tom Homan told the Times that ICE hoped the administration would have 100,000 beds by the end of 2025. The agency topped out at holding around 70,000 immigrants in custody earlier this year. The lack of detention space had already caught up with ICE as it sought to meet the White House’s goals to detain thousands of people a day. A federal judge ruled that the agency needed to cut down the number of people it was detaining in an office in a New York City building last year. But the reality of creating a new detention apparatus has been challenging, much like how the promises of mass deportation have run into the complicated bureaucracy of trying to remove large numbers of people. ICE targeted warehouses for purchase because so many were empty, and they could be bought up and turned into detention sites. In particular, the agency wanted some of the warehouses for processing purposes — to take immigrants who were arrested, process their information and quickly move them to areas where they could detain them for longer periods. “The warehouses were a quick concept to scale up mass deportation,” said John Fabbricatore, a former Trump administration official who until recently worked as a senior adviser on immigration issues at the Department of Health and Human Services. “Unfortunately, because of the scale and footprint, the left was able to throw up immediate roadblocks. Immigration detention is necessary for a successful deportation plan, and this was the easiest point for the Democrats to attack and stop that effort.” As soon as the agency bought the warehouses, communities began to rebel, including in conservative areas that worried about the toll on utilities and the economy, and the potential to draw protests. Even Republican politicians wrote to DHS urging it to turn away from the idea in their communities. Obstacles mounted when the department’s inspector general announced its investigation. Some of the sites cost upward of $145 million — before costly renovations. “Clearly the warehouses have caused some serious headaches, with pauses due to state litigation, an IG investigation and no opening date in sight with close to a billion dollars spent,” said Claire Trickler-McNulty, a senior ICE official in the Biden administration. “This plan seemed questionable from inception, and the only thing saving it is probably the endless blank check ICE has for detention.” But the biggest challenge has been the proliferation of lawsuits across the country. For months, ICE has faced serious legal challenges over whether the agency adhered to a federal law that requires federal agencies to examine the impact of its projects on the local environment. The lawsuits have set the agency back significantly. A judge in Maryland blocked ICE from taking any action at a warehouse in the state that it purchased for around $100 million. ICE also told a federal judge in New Jersey the agency would take no action at a warehouse there until it conducted further environmental tests. The agency promised the same in a Michigan federal court as well. Justice Department officials have expressed concern to ICE that the lack of reviews has left the agency vulnerable to more legal roadblocks.

text:
A Princeton University doctoral student has reportedly been taken into custody by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after traveling to Washington DC, for a neuroscience conference.

Eva Yi Xie, a third-year PhD candidate at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute, was detained Thursday at a Washington-area airport, according to university officials and her colleagues.

The Daily Princetonian, the university’s student newspaper, reported that Xie is believed to be held at an immigration detention facility in Chantilly, Virginia.

The Brody Lab, a Princeton neuroscience research group, identified Ronald Reagan National airport as the location of her detention in a post on X. According to the lab, Xie had been returning from the Society for Neuroscience conference, where she presented a research poster, when immigration authorities detained her.

Princeton has since secured legal representation for Xie, university spokesperson Michael Hotchkiss confirmed to the Daily Princetonian.

The detention also prompted a late-night message to graduate students from Rodney Priestley, dean of Princeton’s graduate school. Priestley sent the email to students at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute late Thursday night, acknowledging the situation and outlining the university’s response.

“We hope she is able to soon resume her studies at Princeton,” the email, obtained by the Daily Princetonian, read. “Please be assured that we will stay in close contact with the student’s family, her legal team, and her PNI colleagues as this situation is resolved.”

Xie’s current immigration status has not been publicly disclosed.

Xie moved to the US from China in 2016. She earned degrees in computer science and mathematics from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2024, alongside a concentration in economics, according to her portfolio.

Her professional experience includes internships at Meta, Microsoft AI and IBM Research, among other organizations. At Princeton, her doctoral work focuses on the “neural basis of decision-making,” according to the Daily Princetonian.

The Guardian has reached out to ICE and Princeton for comment.

Xie’s detention comes amid an aggressive nationwide immigration enforcement campaign under Donald Trump, whose administration has made mass deportations a defining priority.

Department of Homeland Security (DHS) figures show that ICE deported 483,200 people and conducted more than 491,000 immigration arrests during fiscal year 2026, setting new annual records for the agency.

The Trump administration maintains that its enforcement efforts are intended to uphold immigration laws and remove dangerous offenders from the country. However, federal figures and independent reviews indicate that substantial numbers of people kept in ICE detention have no criminal convictions.

The enforcement campaign has affected international students and immigrants who originally entered the US legally. Xie’s detention now joins a string of prominent immigration cases that have drawn worldwide scrutiny and raised serious questions about the administration’s tactics.

Among those cases is Rümeysa Öztürk, a Tufts University student detained by immigration agents in Massachusetts last year. Videos of Öztürk’s arrest spread rapidly online, drawing widespread attention to the administration’s treatment of international students.

She was among numerous foreign students targeted over pro-Palestinian expression and protest during demonstrations against Israel’s military campaign in Gaza. Those protests have been particularly prominent on American university campuses.

Another high-profile case involved Mahmoud Khalil, a 30-year-old Palestinian permanent resident and Columbia University graduate student who emerged as a leading figure in campus protests last year.

Khalil was arrested without due process in front of his pregnant wife and subsequently detained at an immigration facility. Authorities denied him permission to leave detention to attend the birth of his child.

text:
A group of public housing tenant and housing rights organizations have sued the Trump administration in Boston federal court to stop a new rule that could cause hundreds of immigrant families to lose housing or divide families.

The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development issued a new rule on Nov. 12 that will prevent families whose members have different immigration statuses from getting prorated housing benefits. Advocates say the changes will force low-income immigrant families have to choose between splitting up or leaving their current housing.

“The new rule would force those families to either remove the ineligible individual or give up the subsidy,” said Joey Michalakes, deputy managing attorney of the housing unit at Greater Boston Legal Services, in an interview with GBH News.

“For many families, it’s not actually a choice, because the ineligible individual or individuals are parents, and the eligible members are U.S. citizen children who are minors. That is the circumstance of most affected families. So in effect, what that means is, these families have to leave the housing,” Michalakes said. Housing authorities will be mandated to implement the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development’s changes.

Plaintiffs in the lawsuit, filed Thursday, say the new rule violates both the Administrative Procedure Act and the Fifth Amendment’s due process clause, and that HUD violated its duty under the Fair Housing Act to eradicate discrimination.

Additionally, the lawsuit says the rule was put out in tandem with the Trump administration’s effort to “push the bounds” of the Supreme Court’s birthright citizenship ruling this summer.

This changes a 30-year-old practice of allowing families with mixed-immigration status to live together even if a member is undocumented or has a status not approved for federally subsidized housing. In those cases, the family member without the appropriate legal status would not receive the housing subsidy, so the other family members would pay more.

Three anonymous plaintiffs in the lawsuit are from mixed-status families. One of them lives in Massachusetts, has been in the U.S. since 2015, and is currently authorized to live and work in the state, but her immigration status isn’t among the categories with eligibility, according to the lawsuit. Three of her children are U.S. citizens (her eldest, age 12, is not). They all live together in an apartment with the assistance of federal subsidies.

Other plaintiffs include the Mass Union of Public Housing Tenants; Fall River Housing Authority Joint Tenants’ Council; Border Workers United; and Smith Houses Resident Association. The federal class action lawsuit was filed by the National Housing Law Project, The Legal Aid Society, LatinoJustice PRLDEF, Winston Taylor, Greater Boston Legal Services and Massachusetts Law Reform Institute.

The new rule would require all federal public housing recipients, including US citizens, to file what the plaintiffs claim is an “unreasonable” amount of extra paperwork, particularly for senior citizens.

“They’re going to ask to be chased down copies of birth certificates, of financial records. A lot of them are elderly, a lot of them are disabled,” said Dave Underhill, Mass Union’s Board Chair and a public housing tenant in Fall River. He’s a 19-year tenant of his complex, and the city has nearly 4,000 public housing residents.

“They don’t leave their buildings or their developments on a regular basis. That’s going to take a lot of work on behalf of the staff of the housing authority, which is going to take away from the day-to-day operations of what they have to do.” HUD didn’t include any funding mechanism for local housing authorities to hire more staff to implement the changes.

The Trump administration tried to advance a similar rule in its first term. This time, the proposed changes got more than 13,000 public comments nationwide, and was opposed by Massachusetts lawmakers and over a dozen local tenant organizations. It’s set to go into effect on Dec. 14.

After that, local housing authorities will issue notices requiring mixed-status families to verify eligibility of every person in a household within 90 days.

Green card holders, asylees, refugees, certain human trafficking victims, and immigrants with a few other statuses are eligible for federally subsidized housing. Immigrants who are undocumented or have temporary statuses or are in the process of attaining the previously mentioned statuses, are not.

The government estimates that 62,000 people could be displaced. The changes will require more complicated verification requirements for all tenants in federally subsidized housing — over 8.5 million people.

Michalakes said the lawsuit seeks to delay the effective date, and eventually prevent the rule change permanently after more thorough oral arguments are heard.

“What we do not want to see is families self-evicting on the basis of a proposal that has not meaningfully gone into effect yet,” he said.

text:
Records Obtained by Judiciary Democrats Reveal FBI’s Top Lawyer Discussed a Federal Investigation in a Signal Chat Set to Auto-Delete After One Week, Likely Violating Federal Law

Washington, D.C. (November 20, 2026)—Rep. Jamie Raskin, Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Committee, demanded that the heads of the Department of Justice (DOJ), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and Bureau of Prisons (BOP) preserve agency records, determine whether officials improperly deleted government communications from Signal and other messaging apps, and take immediate steps to recover any such records.

In the letters, Ranking Member Raskin disclosed a Signal exchange between FBI General Counsel Samuel Ramer and Drew Lynch, an associate of Donald Trump Jr. They discussed a potential or ongoing investigation involving an individual wanted by federal authorities on health care fraud and related charges. The exchange appears to show that the participants set their messages to disappear after one week. The exchange is one of many incidents already reported to the Committee.

“The FBI’s top lawyer should be ensuring that all 35,000 FBI employees are preserving government and law enforcement records; instead, he has conducted official business on a platform specifically configured to erase communications,” wrote Ranking Member Raskin.

Federal recordkeeping requirements apply to official communications on third-party messaging apps, including those sent from personal accounts. The National Archives has warned that automatic deletion can violate those requirements when it prevents officials from identifying and preserving federal records.

Ranking Member Raskin’s preservation demands cover official records on government and personal devices used for agency business, including records sought by the Judiciary Committee’s Chair or Ranking Member since January 20, 2025. He called on each agency head to open an inquiry into improperly deleted records and begin recovering them, including any available backups and associated metadata. Ranking Member Raskin asked all five agency heads to certify compliance by December 3 and detail the steps they have taken to determine whether officials used messaging apps to evade federal recordkeeping requirements and to prevent future violations.

text:
Sign up for The Brief, The Texas Tribune’s daily newsletter that keeps readers up to speed on the most essential Texas news.

This article is co-published with KXAN and ProPublica as part of an initiative to report on state and federal efforts to restrict local control.

Last spring, the police chief in a tiny North Texas suburb called Pantego went before his town council with what might have sounded like an audacious pitch to bring in more money for policing.

His department could accept the federal government’s offer to get into the business of immigration enforcement.

“I won’t say there’s unlimited funding, but there’s quite a bit of money in the fund,” Pantego Police Chief Robert Rife said during the April meeting in which council members approved an agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

He was right. After a single immigration arrest this past June, Pantego received $100,000.

It stands to earn much more.

Rife predicted in his presentation to the council that federal grants could bring in an additional $720,000 for the 2,500-resident town a few miles east of Fort Worth. For perspective, combined with the money it had already received, that’s roughly equivalent to 40% of the town’s $2.1 million police budget last year.

Pantego is one of 429 law enforcement agencies in the state as of mid-September that have entered into agreements with ICE as part of President Donald Trump’s efforts to accelerate deportations. Texas leads the nation in these partnerships, known as 287(g) agreements, which authorize local officers to make immigration arrests during their normal course of duty. A key incentive for local governments across the country has long been the funding that comes with participation.

The federal program funnels millions of dollars to local law enforcement while requiring few measurable results and little tracking of how the money is spent. KXAN reviewed minutes from nine local government meetings and found that, over and over again, Texas law enforcement officials sold the program to their local elected leaders as a boon for their cash-strapped departments.

The same month Pantego decided to join the program, for example, the police chief in the small suburb of Hollywood Park near San Antonio made a similar pitch to his city council. The city “actively profits on payroll for the time spent,” he said.

And in Smith County in East Texas, Sheriff Larry Smith told county commissioners that “equipment, use of fuel, mileage and things of that nature” could all be reimbursed, plus there would be $100,000 for two new vehicles and money for overtime.

“How often do the feds offer us money for anything?” Smith County Commissioner John Moore asked.

“Not very often,” the sheriff responded. He declined to speak with KXAN.

Austin-based immigration attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch worries that local law enforcement will become dependent on the financial incentives, making it difficult to pull away from the program in the future.

“I’m concerned about what this money is going to be doing to the mindset of these small police departments,” she said.

In the Texas Panhandle, Hartley County Sheriff Chanze Fowler said nearly all the federal funding his department receives supports its regular operations, in addition to immigration work.

The sheriff’s office recorded 54 arrests under 287(g) authority from January to early July, most for minor traffic and vehicle violations, according to records obtained by KXAN. It received more than $205,000 during that time. By this past summer, it had spent about $30,000 on things like wages, extra pay for officers who became 287(g) certified, payroll taxes, retirement funds and “fleet purchases.”

Almost all of the 287(g)-related funds “go towards items needed for our everyday job,” Fowler said.

Other local city and law enforcement officials said the additional funds help officers protect their communities and carry out core duties. ICE did not respond to a request for an interview for this story but instead provided a statement that explained the program. Its website says the program targets dangerous criminal offenders.

Pantego officials have declined to answer KXAN’s questions about the department’s involvement with the program since August, despite repeated attempts to reach the mayor, town council, city manager and police chief by phone, email and in person.

“We are not interested in interviewing at this time,” said City Manager Leslie Galloway, the only official to respond.

Ammon Blair, a senior fellow for the Texas Public Policy Foundation, a conservative think tank that supports the program, acknowledged the money can help departments operating on thin budgets, including helping to pay for overtime. But he said there should be more oversight of how the federal money is spent.

KXAN obtained service agreements between ICE and the Smith County Sheriff’s Office and the police department in Bullard, Texas, a town of about 5,300 people in East Texas. The agreements allow either party to terminate with 60 days’ notice. None indicate that the federal government can reclaim funding if an agreement is terminated.

That was one of the selling points in Pantego. The department could get federal funding and eventually drop out of the program without penalty and keep the equipment already purchased, the police chief told town council members. All it had to do was make at least one immigration arrest.

Between the end of April and mid-June, it made two.

“Are you a U.S. citizen?”

Local law enforcement agencies that join forces with ICE can choose among three models, two of which focus on identifying people already in jail who may be subject to deportation.

Trump revived the third kind, called the task force model, at the beginning of his second term. Task force agreements often worry civil and immigrants’ rights groups because of the model’s problematic track record: ICE started phasing them out in 2012, after Department of Justice investigations revealed that sheriff’s offices participating in the model had committed civil rights violations.

But task force agreements can also be lucrative.

Agencies can receive federal reimbursement for salaries, overtime and benefits for “conducting purposeful and intentional” immigration enforcement activities once the contract starts, according to a service agreement obtained by KXAN.

They can also get recurring quarterly incentive payments and one-time stipends for equipment, technology and vehicles, though federal memoranda and agreements obtained by KXAN don’t specify what agencies can purchase.

The Department of Homeland Security stopped renewing task force model agreements during the Obama administration after federal investigations revealed civil rights violations involving sheriffs’ offices in Arizona and North Carolina.

Since Trump’s return to office, the model has become the most common of the three agreement types. At least 241 task force model agreements were signed in Texas in 2026 alone, compared to just 30 combined for the other models in that time period, according to ICE participation data from September.

Smith County was among the first in Texas to sign on after the president reinstated the task force model in early 2025.

Moore, the only member of Smith County’s Commissioners Court who agreed to speak with KXAN, explained why he thought the commissioners wanted to partner.

His first word: “budgetary.”

“Any kind of training that any of our departments need to have, or are required to have, costs money, and it’s rare that we get an opportunity to get funding for training from outside county taxes,” Moore said. “Any time we can save the taxpayers money, I’m all for it.”

Smith County got more money than any other of the 93 Texas law enforcement agencies whose funding KXAN reviewed. The sheriff’s office received nearly $2.2 million in federal 287(g) funding from January 2025 to June 2026, according to records obtained by KXAN. That’s equivalent to about 12% of its budget for fiscal year 2025.

Smith, the sheriff, told the Commissioners Court last November that although vehicles purchased with that money would be used for the 287(g) program, “that doesn’t mean, if we’re out here, we won’t run to another call or take another call that comes across the radio. We will do that. We try not to separate 287(g) from our other law enforcement duties. We do it all together.”

About 120 of 198 licensed officers in the Smith County Sheriff’s Office participated in the program. Together, they conducted 124 immigration enforcement actions between October 2025 and July. KXAN requested a list of 287(g) stops from the department, in addition to any associated charge. Smith County listed no associated criminal charge for more than 100 of these stops.

Jose Rodriguez and his 23-year-old son, Pablo Rodriguez, were among those affected.

One afternoon in late June, the pair cruised along Loop 323, a circular segment of highway in Tyler, a city of 113,000 people in East Texas. They’d spent hours working in the summer heat at a construction job and were headed to Chick-fil-A to pick up lunch for their family.

Then red and blue lights appeared behind them. The law enforcement agent said that he’d pulled their black extended-cab work truck over because of a missing license plate on the trailer attached to the pickup and a missing dual-wheel mud flap.

Body and vehicle camera footage showed the detective requesting that Jose Rodriguez get out of the truck. “Any English at all?” the detective later asked. Jose Rodriguez raised his right hand, holding his thumb and index finger close together.

“Un poquito?” the detective asked, followed by, “Are you a U.S. citizen?”

The man shook his head and answered. “No.”

Seconds later, the detective pulled Jose Rodriguez’s hands behind his back and put him in handcuffs.

He was eventually taken from the Smith County jail to an ICE detention facility, about two hours west of Tyler. His son, who is a U.S. citizen, said Jose Rodriguez was detained for about three months before being deported to Mexico.

KXAN could find no criminal convictions or arrests on his record when the Smith County detective took him into custody in June.

“Just like that, he’s gone,” Pablo Rodriguez later told KXAN. “My dad’s gone.”

Law enforcement officers, Pablo Rodriguez said, “portray us as criminals, rapists, violent people. We’re not that. We’re just regular people trying to find a better life. The only difference is our skin. That’s pretty much it.”

The future of the program in Texas

Elections earlier this month have left the 287(g) program’s future uncertain, at least in Texas.

While the Trump administration has reached agreements with local law enforcement to work with immigration officials, Congress has broader oversight authority. That includes decisions about funding. In January, Democrats will take over both chambers of Congress and many, including freshman Texas Sen. James Talarico, have criticized ICE tactics. It’s unclear, however, how much of their focus will be on immigration enforcement and specifically on the 287(g) program.

More locally, state Sen. Charles Schwertner, the Republican lawmaker who authored a measure in 2025 that required most Texas sheriff’s offices to participate in the program, wants to expand the mandate during the coming legislative session to include other law enforcement agencies, like police departments. So does the conservative think tank where Blair works.

But support for such legislation may be harder to get after November’s midterm election.

Schwertner retained his state Senate seat, and Republicans maintained their majority in that chamber, but Democrats took control of the governor’s mansion and the state House of Representatives for the first time in a generation. Any new bills would require legislative approval from both chambers and the governor’s signature, or enough legislative support to override a veto.

In a press release well before the election, Democrat Gina Hinojosa called on Gov. Greg Abbott to “demand accountability from the Trump administration and stop enabling ICE operations that are terrorizing communities and violating the law.” The release did not mention the 287(g) program by name. Hinojosa beat Abbott in this month’s election and will take over as governor in January. She did not respond to a request for comment for this story.

The state program could also be affected by this month’s election of Democrats Nathan Johnson, who won the race for state attorney general, and Sarah Eckhardt, who won her bid to become state comptroller.

Johnson, as a state senator, opposed the mandate that sheriffs’ offices participate in the program. He will inherit responsibility for enforcing the law, which requires most sheriffs to seek agreements with ICE by Dec. 1. Johnson said he will use his discretion in deciding whether to sue sheriffs who fail to comply if they have “legitimate law enforcement reasons for not having a 287(g) agreement.”

He also questioned the state attorney general’s continued participation in the program. Current Attorney General Ken Paxton signed a 287(g) task force model agreement in February 2025.

“The attorney general’s office has tremendous, vast responsibilities,” Johnson said. “Never included among them since the creation of this state was outsourcing your employees to a federal agency for a purpose in which we’re not trained or qualified and which distracts me from the mission of my office.”

Johnson didn’t entirely rule out working with ICE in some capacity if it allowed his office to investigate crimes committed by ICE agents in Texas.

Eckhardt, meanwhile, will take over oversight of a $20 million grant program that state lawmakers created two years ago to help sheriff’s offices cover any costs of participation in the 287(g) program not reimbursed by the federal government. By late September, the comptroller’s office had awarded more than $6.5 million to 78 sheriff’s offices, according to figures obtained by KXAN.

During her campaign, Eckhardt warned that expenses for the program could eventually fall on local taxpayers, calling it “unsustainable.” After winning her seat, she said she would “do a 287(g) audit to show how that expense is driving up property taxes.”

Even if state leaders don’t expand the participation requirement or remove the current mandate, departments can choose to keep collecting federal money to enforce immigration law.

In Fayette County southeast of Austin, Sheriff’s Lt. David Beyer told KXAN that the 287(g) funding his office had already received totaled about $800,000, which helps purchase equipment it can also use for ordinary police work.

“If they want to pay us extra to do that job,” Beyer said, “we’re more than happily going to accept those funds, because that saves our taxpayers money.”

This story is an adaptation of an investigation by KXAN. Read the original reporting.

text:
The majority of veterans support reopening the Afghan Special Immigrant Visa (SIV) program after the Trump administration stopped it earlier this year.

Roughly 70% of veterans want to reopen the scheme that offered permanent residency to Afghans who worked alongside U.S. forces during the Afghanistan war, while 19% do not, according to polling commissioned by the veterans' nonprofit No One Left Behind that was carried out by Hart Research and North Star Opinion Research.

Created by Congress in 2009, the SIV program offered interpreters, contractors and guides who worked alongside Americans permanent residency paths in the U.S. after the 20-year war that was launched in October 2001 following the 9/11 terrorist attacks. It concluded in 2021 when President Joe Biden controversially withdrew American troops.

The U.S. State Department issued 18,319 Afghan SIVs to principal applicants and their family members in Fiscal Year 2025.

But following the expiration of initial application deadlines at the end of 2025 and a January 2026 presidential proclamation blocking Afghan entry, visa issuances effectively ground to a halt.

"The Afghans who worked with my unit took the same risks we did, and they stayed behind when we rotated home,” said Andy Sullivan, executive director of No One Left Behind, who served as an Army infantry officer in Afghanistan and Iraq.

“Our government promised them a safe, legal way here. Republicans, Democrats, and veterans all want the SIV program reopened, and Congress and the Administration have the public support to act before the year ends.”

Pollsters interviewed 1,011 registered voters, including 489 veterans, between Sept. 16 and 23. The poll's margin of error is +/- 3.1 percentage points for voters and +/- 4.4 percentage points for veterans.

Poll Findings

While supporters of the freeze cite national security re-vetting and fraud concerns, veteran advocacy groups argue the closure abandons tens of thousands of vetted allies to Taliban reprisals and undermines future coalition trust.

“In Kabul, our troops and diplomats relied on Afghans who risked their lives to work with us. Every partner we will need in the next conflict is watching how we treat them,” said Ryan Crocker, a former U.S. ambassador to Afghanistan and Iraq, and a senior adviser to No One Left Behind.

The new poll found a bipartisan appetite to reopen the system. Democrats favor reopening it by a margin of 80% to 11%, independents 59% to 28%, and Republicans 59% to 28%.

It also found that 86% of veterans agree the U.S. should give Afghans who worked with the American military and government a safe, legal pathway to the U.S.

Another 62% of veterans would feel more favorably toward a member of Congress who voted to reopen the program, compared with 13% who would feel less favorably.
