text:
Sign up to receive the Early Edition in your inbox here.

A curated weekday guide to major news and developments over the last 24 hours. Here’s today’s news:

IRAN WAR

President Trump yesterday told Axios that he won’t make a decision about the next step in the Iran war until the new year. Trump said “I am not rushing into any decision. We will see what happens after the beginning of the year,” echoing statements he made on Wednesday. Barak Ravid reports.

IRAN WAR – OTHER DEVELOPMENTS

Iraqi security forces today deployed in Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold of Iran-aligned Kataib Hezbollah armed group, under a deal that seeks to limit the reach of the group. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi this week ordered security forces to move against the Iranian ally, which officials accused of running an oil-smuggling network siphoning state-owned oil. Kataib Hezbollah has rejected the smuggling accusations. Maher Nazeh, Muayad Hameed, and Eman Abouhassira report for Reuters.

A U.K. judge today said two men charged over September’s Royal Air Force Fairford security incident will stand trial in Nov. 2027. U.K. prosecutors said U.K. national Mohmed Abdulkarim arranged for five men to drive to RAF Fairford at the behest of a man called “Ali,” who is alleged to have been “acting in the interests of the Islamic Republic of Iran.” Nouman Essghir’s charge relates to alleged reconnaissance of the base on Aug. 22, 2026. U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Iran was likely involved and Iran’s ambassador to the United Kingdom has denied it. Sam Tobin reports for Reuters.

U.S. Senate Republicans yesterday blocked a measure directing Trump to end the Iran war or win congressional approval to continue it, in the first vote about the issue since the midterm elections. The resolution had passed the House in September by the largest bipartisan margin to date, but failed by a vote of 51 to 48 in the Senate. Robert Jimison reports for the New York Times.

Head of Israeli spy agency Mossad Roman Gofman last week pushed for renewed U.S.-Israeli strikes against Iran during a visit to the United States last week, sources told the Wall Street Journal. The sources said Gofman presented Trump administration officials with Israeli intelligence about Iran’s nuclear program, and advocated for a new multiday campaign of airstrikes against Iran. Anat Peled reports.

RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR

Ukrainian capital Kyiv’s Mayor Vitali Klitschko today said Russian overnight strikes targeted bridges in Kyiv and killed eight people. Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky said 28 people were injured across attacks on nine regions. Another strike on a railway station in the western city of Lviv killed two people, according to the city’s Mayor Andriy Sadovyi. Dan Woodland and Sarah Rainsford report for BBC News.

U.S. Special Envoy Jared Kushner during closed-door peace talks in recent months has discussed NATO membership for Ukraine if Ukraine cedes territory to Russia, sources told the Wall Street Journal. The sources said the idea has been raised in several conversations between European officials, Kushner, and fellow U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff, and most recently Kushner discussed the possibility with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Dublin last week. The other suggested solution has been to freeze the conflict along the front line, and give Ukraine security guarantees to protect it from a future Russian assault through an international treaty with the United States and potentially with European allies. Bojan Pancevski reports.

Trump yesterday called into a meeting Kushner and Witkoff were having with a group of European leaders and Zelenskyy, and told them “[Russian President Vladimir] Putin wants to end the war, he wants the deal done, he is getting tired of this,” sources in the room told Axios. A European official said Kushner and Witkoff told European leaders that Trump pressed Putin to move on the peace talks, and asked Chinese President Xi Jinping for his help in ending the war during Trump’s bilateral meeting with Xi. Barak Ravid reports.

OTHER GLOBAL DEVELOPMENTS

Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz today said Russia violated Poland’s airspace overnight with three objects, allegedly two missiles and one drone. The incursions were reported as Poland prepared to hold military exercises today involving the “Coalition of the Willing” that groups allies of Ukraine. Kosiniak-Kamysz denounced Russia’s provocation. Marek Strzelecki, Kuba Stężycki, and Kacper Pempel report for Reuters.

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova today accused Estonia of planning to erect a new “Iron Curtain,” and said Russia would respond after Estonia said it would close its border with Russia for at least six months. Estonia’s government made the announcement today, and said it would decide after six months whether to extend the suspension or not. Zakharova said “Should Tallinn proceed with these plans, our country will take the necessary political and ​diplomatic measures in response to safeguard its ​national interests.” Reuters reports.

Comm. of the U.K. Cyber & Specialist Operations Command Gen. Sir Rob Magowan told Sky News that the United Kingdom is conducting offensive cyber operations against Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea, in an interview published today. Magowan said the “cyber domain… is becoming increasingly important in warfare,” and that “as a military commander, I want a range of options against my adversary.” Deborah Haynes reports.

Up to 100,000 young people per year from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the United Kingdom, and vice versa, under a new youth mobility scheme set to be agreed today, sources told BBC News. U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said a “Channel action plan” on immigration could also be agreed. EU officials said today’s Brexit reset deal won’t take effect unless the United Kingdom agrees to cut university tuition fees for Europeans studying at U.K. universities, and they have given the United Kingdom six months to agree or negotiate an alternative. Kate Whannel and Nick Eardley report; BBC News reports.

U.K. Foreign Minister Ed Miliband yesterday announced that the government was ordering the expulsion of Myanmar’s Defense Attaché and was summoning Myanmar’s charge d’affaires, after Myanmar yesterday was found guilty of genocide by the U.N. International Court of Justice. A panel of international judges voted nine-to-six in ruling that Myanmar committed genocide and the President of the ICJ Yuji Iwasawa said Myanmar had the “intention to destroy” a substantial part of the Rohingya population. Myanmar’s government today dismissed the ruling, and spokeswoman for Myanmar’s President Min Aung Hlaing, Khine Khine Soe, noted that “not all 15 judges agreed with the decision.” Aleks Phillips, Anna Holligan, and Jonathan Head report for BBC News; AP News reports.

U.S. CLIMATE DEVELOPMENTS

The Marine Minerals Administration, a branch of the Interior Department, yesterday leased 31.5 million acres of the Pacific Ocean to private deep-sea mining company Wetstone U.S. Ventures for $6 million, in the first sale of its kind. The lease only allows the company to do mapping and other preliminary work on the seabed which sits off American Samoa. Environmentalists oppose deep-sea mining as underwater plumes of sediment could destroy deep-sea ecosystems, and more than 45 countries have called for a ban or pause on seabed mining. Eric Niiler reports for the New York Times.

The Senate yesterday passed a bipartisan bill that’s designed to cut permitting timelines for energy and infrastructure projects. The bill would make new limits on the duration of lawsuits, and the scope and length of reviews under the Clean Water Act and National Environmental Policy Act, which critics fear will weaken environmental protections and the rights of Native American tribes. Ben Geman reports for Axios.

U.S. FOREIGN AFFAIRS

Trump, Putin, and Xi yesterday agreed in a joint statement after their meeting that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.” The statement released after the trilateral meeting cited a commitment by the three countries to engage in a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks. Putin after the meeting acknowledged that the declaration did not set ambitious goals, and added that nobody would be forced to comply with its decisions. Lara Jakes reports for the New York Times; Jarrett Renshaw, Trevor Hunnicutt, and Steve Holland report for Reuters.

Former State Department policy chief Jeremy Lewin in September suggested to Guyanese Foreign Secretary Robert Persaud that Guyana should consider ceding some of its territory to neighboring Venezuela, a comment that shocked officials and forced the United States to reassure them that U.S. policy regarding the countries’ borders had not changed, sources told Reuters. Venezuela has long claimed the Essequibo region in Guyana that is rich in gold, diamonds, and bauxite. Lewin told Reuters he held “preliminary” talks with the Guyanese and Venezuelans regarding the territorial dispute. Sarah Kinosian, Gram Slattery, and Humeyra Pamuk report.

U.S. IMMIGRATION DEVELOPMENTS

The families of U.S. deportees to South Sudan told AP News that their relatives endured hunger, thirst, and other deprivations while being detained. The families said guards have solicited and received thousands of dollars from them, and were told the money would be used to improve conditions. Instead, the guards pocketed most of the money, while detainees went days without food or clean water. Joseph Falzetta reports.

U.S. DOMESTIC DEVELOPMENTS

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC) plans to block the confirmation of White House aide Eric Ueland to head the Government Accountability Office by opposing Ueland’s inclusion in a catchall nomination package Senate Republicans plan to approve next month. Tillis said “I’ve already issued a presumptive hold if it comes out of committee,” and that he “won’t allow him to go through en bloc.” Tillis and other Republicans have raised concerns that Ueland could not take on the comptroller general role as although he is “an honorable guy,” they don’t believe Ueland can objectively lead the independent oversight agency in his capacity as a close Trump ally. Jennifer Scholtes reports for POLITICO.

Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR) is urging Congress to secure lawmakers’ phone calls, emails, and video meetings from the executive branch following a report last week about the “threat of hacking and cyberattacks on senators and staff on their official and personal devices and accounts.” Wyden said the Trump administration’s “threats to investigate members of Congress who do our job and oversee the executive branch are a five-alarm warning that the Senate needs to ramp up the security of our communications as soon as possible.” Charlie Savage reports for the New York Times.

U.S. AI DEVELOPMENTS

A bipartisan coalition of over two dozen House lawmakers is forming a new “AI Safety and Innovation Caucus.” The group will be led by Reps. George Whitesides (D-CA), Don Beyer (D-VA), and Nathaniel Moran (R-TX), and aims to balance creating AI safeguards that mitigate the technology’s risk with “ensuring the United States remains a global leader in innovative AI technologies,” according to an announcement first shared with POLITICO. Whitesides said “we want to be a conduit through which effective, responsible legislation can be refined and brought to the floor of the House.” Owen Dahlkamp reports.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office yesterday announced that Bonta issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia as part of a probe of whether the company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China in contravention of U.S. export restrictions. Bonta said “the conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors.” Dan Mangan reports for CNBC.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ACTION

The White House yesterday named the Pentagon’s Chief Information Officer Kirsten A. Davies as its new national cyber director after Sean Cairncross’ departure. Sources told Axios that Cairncross’ departure was amicable, and that Davies’ introduction was sought by Trump’s new Chief of Staff Stephen Miller because Miller believed Cairncross “lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job.” Alex Isenstadt, Maria Curi, and Marc Caputo report.

Trump yesterday told NBC News he still considers SpaceX CEO Elon Musk an ally, despite Musk on Wednesday saying “I’m not MAGA.” Trump did warn that when people “veer” from Trump’s definition of MAGA, “they don’t do very well,” but still offered support to Musk, as “Elon’s got very good intentions… I mean, he was with me the whole – he traveled with me.” Gabe Gutierrez and Amanda Terkel report.

The Justice Department has assigned federal prosecutor Bill Essayli to work on the “grand conspiracy” criminal investigation into the 2022 raid on Mar-a-Lago, and special counsel Jack Smith’s inquiry into the classified documents found there, sources told POLITICO. The sources said Essayli will continue to oversee the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California as the first assistant U.S. attorney there. Daniel Lippman and Josh Gerstein report.

The DOJ yesterday abandoned its lawsuit to block Sen.-elect Mary Peltola (D-AK) from taking office. The DOJ asked a federal court to declare its lawsuit moot two days after the Alaska race was called for Peltola. Bayliss Wagner reports for the New York Times.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION LITIGATION

A federal judge yesterday ruled that religious messages sent by Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins to the agency’s 100,000 employees were unconstitutional. Rollins sent messages from her official email account on holidays such as Independence Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas, and Easter, but did not send messages commemorating holidays from other religions. The judge said Rollins’ emails violated the First Amendment’s establishment clause, pointing to her position of authority, her use of an official email account, and the messages suggesting that Christianity is the shared faith of USDA workers. Jonathan J. Cooper reports for AP News.

A federal judge yesterday allowed for Trump’s libel lawsuit against the New York Times, several of its reporters, and a major publishing house over reporting on his business and financial dealings, to proceed. Trump filed the lawsuit in Sep. 2025, and the judge allowed it to proceed as he ruled that some of the statements suggesting Trump had likely committed “complex” tax crimes appeared to have been based on insufficient input from those with expertise to make such assessments. text:
A group of asylum seekers has sued the Department of Homeland Security, Secretary Markwayne Mullin and other administration officials.

The plaintiffs are seeking to stop Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents from rearresting immigrants without a change in circumstances that would justify their detention.

In their lawsuit, the plaintiffs say the Trump administration implemented a new policy, directing ICE agents to re-arrest noncitizens even when there’s been no significant change in their circumstances. These plaintiffs want a federal judge to block the practice and require ICE to make individual assessments before re-detaining someone.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | A California nurse vanished into ICE custody. She's among thousands missing from a public ICE database

The noncitizens who’ve sued have been in the U.S., in some cases, for decades.

They allege that because the administration wants to increase immigration arrests, ICE agents are re-detaining immigrants even if there is no change in their circumstances. For example, they have no criminal charges, present no danger to the public, are not a flight risk and have attended all ICE check-ins.

“Defendants’ rescission of the Changed Circumstances Policy and adoption of the Re-Detention Policy is a predictable result of the Executive Branch’s directives to carry out the 'largest [m]ass [d]eportation [p]rogram in history,'” the lawsuit states.

"The Re-Detention Policy was implemented to further the Executive’s strategy of subjecting noncitizens—including those with pending applications for immigration relief—to prolonged and harsh detention conditions to coerce ‘self-deportation.’”

An ACLU attorney who’s representing the plaintiffs says these types of arrests are a departure from a longstanding practice.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Supreme Court to decide whether Trump can ban asylum applications at the border

“It’s sort of happening everywhere, and I think what’s so scary to people is, especially those who are showing up to these check-ins that they’re required to attend, and then just being apprehended with no notice, and that being so alarming, right? To be following the rules you're supposed to follow and being taken away from your family and community anyway,” said Raneem Ashrawi, a staff attorney with the ACLU of Georgia.

Ashrawi says re-arresting noncitizens when there is no significant change in their case is a violation of the Fourth Amendment, which prohibits repeated arrests when the facts are the same.

Scripps News has contacted the Department of Homeland Security for comment, but has not received a response.

The plaintiffs who sued administration officials say their re-arrest affected not only them but their families as well.

One plaintiff spoke about lost wages. As the primary provider, he said, while he was detained, his family had to rely on their church. Another plaintiff said that in his absence, his 3-year-old son with autism started to have behavioral issues.

The lawsuit is also seeking to certify a class, which could provide protections for more people, as opposed to just the main plaintiffs. According to the ACLU, many of these noncitizens are asylum seekers, and some have Social Security numbers and authorization to work in the U.S. The ACLU says thousands of noncitizens could fall into a category of being re-arrested, even if nothing has changed with their status since their last check-in.

(The Center Square) – Six Virginia residents and a nonprofit sued federal immigration officials Monday, saying officers made arrests without warrants before determining whether each person was in the country unlawfully or was likely to escape before officers could get a warrant.
The Centreville Immigration Forum and the six residents filed the lawsuit in federal court in Alexandria against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and agency officials. They are asking a judge to block the arrest practices described in the complaint.
Federal law sets two conditions for the type of arrest at issue. An immigration officer must have reason to believe the person is in the country unlawfully. The officer must also have reason to believe the person is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained.

One plaintiff, Alvaro Alvarez Flores, says he was driving to work in Newport News on July 13 when an unmarked SUV cut him off. He handed an officer his Virginia driver’s license. An officer asked where he was from, and he answered Mexico, according to the complaint.

text:
A NYCHA residents’ association is among the plaintiffs challenging the federal rule, which advocates say could force thousands of families to separate or lose their housing assistance.

A coalition of public housing residents and immigrant advocates filed a federal class action lawsuit Thursday challenging a Trump administration rule that could force thousands of families with mixed immigration status to choose between staying together and keeping their federally subsidized homes.

The lawsuit, filed Thursday in U.S. District Court in Massachusetts, seeks to block a new U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) rule scheduled to take effect Dec. 14. The plaintiffs argue that the regulation violates federal housing law and constitutional protections.

Plaintiffs include the Alfred E. Smith Houses Resident Association, representing tenants at a New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) development in Lower Manhattan. According to the complaint, 16 of the development’s 1,876 households have mixed immigration statuses and could face displacement under the rule.

The legal challenge follows HUD’s announcement of the final regulation on Nov. 10, which would require members of households that receive federal housing assistance through programs like Section 8 and Section 9 to verify their U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status.

Under existing law, mixed status households can receive reduced federal rental assistance based on the number of eligible family members. Those who do not qualify for subsidies can still live with eligible relatives, including children who are U.S. citizens.

The new rule would end the longstanding arrangement allowing mixed status families to receive prorated assistance indefinitely, potentially forcing households to separate or give up their rental aid. As City Limits previously reported, approximately 2,500 New York households could be affected by the changes.

Among those challenging the rule is a Honduran woman identified in the complaint as Jane Doe #2, who has lived in the United States since 2009. She resides in New York City with her husband, a lawful permanent resident, and their three U.S. born daughters.

The family has lived in a federally subsidized Section 8 apartment for nine years. Although the woman has been authorized to live and work in the country since receiving U nonimmigrant status in 2022, it does not qualify her for federal housing assistance under the law cited in the complaint.

According to the lawsuit, the family cannot afford market rate housing in New York City. The plaintiffs argue that the rule could force the woman to leave the apartment or cause the entire family to lose their home.

The lawsuit also challenges new documentation requirements that would apply to recipients of federal housing assistance, not just mixed status households. The plaintiffs argue that the requirements could disrupt benefits for eligible tenants, particularly elderly and disabled residents who may have difficulty obtaining the necessary records.

Nationwide, roughly 80,000 people, including approximately 36,000 eligible children, could face displacement under the regulation, according to estimates cited in the complaint.

In a statement provided to City Limits, HUD Secretary Scott Turner defended the change saying it fully implements the Housing and Community Development Act of 1980.

“This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD funded housing,” Turner said.

He added that the change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million in housing assistance to eligible Americans currently on waiting lists.

The plaintiffs dispute HUD’s interpretation of federal law, arguing that Congress explicitly authorized reduced subsidies for mixed status households. They are seeking a court order declaring the rule unlawful and preventing its implementation next month.

Housing lawyers who spoke to City Limits earlier this week urged households potentially impacted by the change to stay put.

“People need to know that until it goes into effect, nothing has changed,” said Lucy Newman, the supervising attorney of Legal Aid Society’s public housing unit. “They should not move, or evict out of fear.”

Here’s what else happened this week in housing—

ICYMI, from City Limits:

For the first time, NYCHA is using a federal program called Section 32 to repair 91 single-family to four-family houses—opening a path for public housing residents to buy their homes.

A career training program for the city’s public housing residents is getting $1 million from an unusual source: Kalshi, the prediction market company recently sued by New York State for allegedly operating as an illegal and unlicensed gambling platform.

All but one building in a portfolio of properties that recently went to foreclosure auction failed to receive any bids, raising alarm about the health of the city’s rent-stabilized housing. Tenants, and the mayor’s office, hope to steer the buildings to a buyer they say will work to preserve them.

ICYMI, from other local newsrooms:

The city is suing a landlord for evading fines and failing to make building repairs under a local fraud law, what City Hall described as a novel tactic to hold bad property owners accountable, according to Gothamist.

Astoria residents are opposing proposals for three new apartment buildings on Steinway Street, the Queens Eagle reports.

The city is billing 7,500 households under the new pied-à-terre tax on expensive second homes, what officials say will raise $500 million, according to The City Reporter.

The Mamdani administration shuttered its last remaining migrant shelter in the Bronx this week, potentially stymying a a subpoena from the Trump administration demanding the city disclose the names of undocumented immigrants with criminal records who lived there, the New York Times reports.

text:
Joins coalition of 20 AGs in recommending inquiries into accountability of immigration officers, detention practices, and DHS waste and corruption

RICHMOND, Va. — Virginia Attorney General Jones joined a coalition of 20 attorneys general in encouraging leaders of the incoming majorities in Congress to hold hearings on Trump Administration abuses in immigration enforcement. In a letter to congressional leadership — including the incoming chairs of House and Senate committees with responsibility over the judiciary, homeland security, and government oversight and accountability — Attorney General Jones and the coalition encourage Congress to hold hearings on the accountability of immigration officers, detention practices, and waste and corruption in the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

Attorney General Jones and the coalition also encourage the incoming chairs of these committees to feature testimony at the hearings from Americans directly harmed by immigration enforcement abuse, advocates for immigrant communities, and from state Attorneys General who have been using the tools at their disposal to fight against this abuse and for the rule of law. State officials and community leaders have important insights to share gathered through truth councils, accountability commissions, and other community engagement.

“Across the country communities are living in fear because of this administration’s lawless actions. It’s time to hold those who have terrorized and targeted our neighbors, with no respect for the law, accountable,” said Attorney General Jones. “Virginians are fighting to scrape by while DHS is pouring money into the pockets of Trump donors, violating the law and people’s rights, and tearing families apart.”

Donald Trump’s DHS and its agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and Customs and Border Protection (CBP), have operated as if they are exempt from accountability and the rule of law. In 2025, DHS began a months-long campaign of lawlessness across multiple American cities. Since the beginning of Trump’s second term, DHS agents have shot at least 25 people across the United States.

Use of force by immigration agents has also increased dramatically. In just the first three months of the current administration, there was a nearly fourfold increase in reported ICE use-of-force incidents. Independent researchers have subsequently documented more than 400 incidents of misuse of crowd-control weapons in 16 cities across the country in just 12 months, resulting in over 200 injuries to demonstrators, bystanders, and journalists attempting to cover the events.

Attorney General Jones and the coalition write to Congressional leaders: “In the face of immigration enforcement conduct that is both immoral and unlawful, the outgoing House and Senate majorities were content to look the other way. The incoming majorities need to confront this head-on. The American people voted for real, serious oversight — with teeth and consequences for any agency or individual who would ignore the rule of law.”

Immigration detention practices are in dire need of reform and oversight as well. By ICE’s own accounting, close to 60 people have died in ICE custody in the past two years, enough to make 2025 the deadliest year in immigration detention in over two decades.

DHS has also wasted significant sums of money in its rushed and ill-conceived efforts to rapidly expand immigration detention. DHS spent approximately $1 billion purchasing warehouses in a grossly inhumane effort to house people in them before shifting course. Now DHS has purchased four prisons from CoreCivic, a significant donor to President Trump’s inaugural committee and his PACs, for the extraordinary sum of $2.2 billion. DHS paid CoreCivic $495 million for a prison in Minnesota that CoreCivic offered to the State of Minnesota for just $75 million in 2025. Americans deserve to know whether DHS is inflating the purchase price of these facilities and diverting their tax dollars into the coffers of the President’s supporters.

Joining Attorney General Jones in the letter to Congressional leaders is Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, who led the coalition, and the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawai’i, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Nevada, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, and Washington.

text:
Five men arrived at a construction equipment company on the outskirts of Green Valley looking for work when a sheriff’s deputy offered the men a ride into town and brought them to a nearby restaurant — where Border Patrol was ready to detain them.

Unaware to the five men, an onsite security guard at the construction equipment company had called the Pima County Sheriff’s Department and U.S. Border Patrol, despite the men not causing any issues. That March 2023 incident report — obtained through a public records request by the ACLU of Arizona — offers a glimpse into how local law enforcement agencies regularly assist federal immigration authorities.

Public records, firsthand anonymous interviews with recently deported people, and information from migrant aid organizations indicate unclear boundaries between immigration enforcement and ordinary policing. As the Trump administration expands federal, state, and local authority to enforce immigration laws, key questions emerge: What does that look like in practice? And what are the harms to local communities?

“You could argue that there’s no inherent problem with collaboration between agencies,” said John Mitchell, an immigrants’ rights attorney with the ACLU of Arizona. “But the reality is more complicated when you see how state and local law enforcement are given some level of unchecked power, and how they translate that into their actual enforcement.”

During his second term, President Donald Trump rapidly expanded the 287(g) program, which allows local law enforcement agencies to enter into agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and assume limited federal immigration enforcement duties.

At the start of 2025, 133 state and local agencies participated in the program. By February 2026, ICE had signed an additional 1,079 agencies to 287(g) agreements, according to the ACLU report “Deputized for Disaster.” One of those newly signed agencies is the Utah County Sheriff’s Office with its Task Force Model, which gives local police the authority to investigate immigration status of anyone they come across, including witnesses and victims of criminal investigations. It could even happen during a traffic stop.

Andres, a father from Mexico, moved to Utah to reunite with his daughter. About a year later, in November 2025, a Utah County sheriff’s deputy pulled him over for a traffic infraction, he said. After Andres showed his Mexican identification, the deputy called immigration authorities. He was detained for about 24 days before being deported to Nogales, Sonora, a major border city in Mexico south of Arizona, where he shared his experience with the ACLU of Arizona.

The Task Force Model can lead to racial profiling, according to the ACLU report — which means police often use an individual’s perceived race, ethnicity, or national origin to determine whether to investigate the person for legal violations, including those related to immigration status. But racial profiling is not unique to 287(g) agreements. It is a longstanding and troubling practice documented among law enforcement agencies, including those that are not actively participating in the program. And this isn’t only happening in Arizona. As of October, more than 2,500 cities and states nationwide have signed 287(g) agreements.

In Arizona, the Pima and Santa Cruz County sheriff’s offices have no active 287(g) agreements. Still, incident reports obtained through public records requests show instances of assistance and coordination with federal immigration authorities.

In September 2025, a Santa Cruz County sheriff’s deputy pulled over a driver for a cracked windshield. When the deputy approached the driver’s window, he noticed three men in the backseat.

“I asked [the driver] to tell me what was going on. I added that I already knew what was occurring,” the deputy wrote in the incident report.The driver said he had picked up the men in Nogales, Arizona and was taking them to Phoenix. According to the incident report, the deputy detained the driver in their patrol unit and activated the child locks on the civilian vehicle to prevent the other three men from leaving. Border Patrol agents arrived shortly after and took over.

Mitchell cautioned that incident reports are one-sided accounts written from an officer’s perspective. And in this case, the deputy’s report lacked enough detail to establish suspicion of a crime within the sheriff’s jurisdiction.

“State and local law enforcement officers don’t have the same amount of training and specialized background to distinguish border crimes from immigration violations,” Mitchell said. “And building off of that, you see a lot of oversimplification and bias creep into the actual enforcement practices of state and local police.”

As he sat inside a migrant shelter in Nogales, Sonora, a border city in Mexico, last December, Carlos, a man from Mexico who lived in the United States for four years, recalled the moment of his arrest. He said a sheriff’s deputy in Twin Falls, Idaho pulled him over while on his way to work one morning, saying Carlos had resembled the description of a suspect in an open case. When Carlos handed his Mexican passport, the deputy called ICE and laughed as he handcuffed Carlos. Carlos said he believed that the deputy’s reaction had been primarily based on racial profiling — an example of how racial bias and xenophobia creeps into law enforcement practices and is often not addressed by training or other accountability measures.

Miguel, a father who was deported to Nogales, Sonora last winter, said an SUV cornered his car as he drove on a highway in Seattle and forced him to pull over. Three men, who didn’t identify themselves, began questioning Miguel about his immigration status. Miguel showed them his Washington driver license, then the men called ICE. Given their lack of uniforms and badges, Miguel questioned whether the men were immigration officers. But he complied out of fear of escalating the situation into a violent encounter.

Mitchell noted: “People have no obligation to follow their lawful commands until they have identified themselves as law enforcement agents. But in practice, that’s not how it works.”

“Law enforcement officers should not be escalating a situation, but that is not at all what we’re seeing now,” Mitchell said. “We are seeing agents using violence and excessive force and other unlawful tactics in order to fulfill the aims of the Trump administration.”

The migrant aid organization, Kino Border Initiative (KBI), shared the story of Jairo, a lawful permanent resident who lived in Arizona for 22 years. After dropping his son at a bus stop, several men approached his vehicle and identified themselves as ICE agents but showed no identification.

Through his window, Jairo repeatedly told them he was a permanent resident. But the men broke into his car, then assaulted and arrested him. When Jairo’s wife tried to intervene, the men beat her too. KBI said she had a miscarriage two days later. Jairo was deported to Mexico.

In another instance last May, ICE agents forcibly entered the Tucson home of Karla Toledo, a DACA recipient who has lived most of her life in the United States. When Toledo demanded a warrant, ICE agents forced their way into her home without showing one.

“Do you exercise your rights, or do you keep yourself insulated from the possibility of a law enforcement agent escalating the situation?” Mitchell said. “That should never be a choice that people have to make.”

title: Should an 8-year-old be alone in ICE detention? - Baptist News Global
description:
Barbara Nicole Hildago has a complicated relationship with her biological mother, who brought her to the United States from Venezuela.
Two weeks ago, while on her way to school, ICE agents broke her guardian’s car window and kidnapped her.
Nicole was detained in Dallas and transferred to Corpus Christi.
Data from 2025 show more than 1,800 children were detained in ICE holding rooms around the country, 40 of those right here in Dallas.
Related: Republican leaders worried ICE murders will damage their agenda These people would all be alive if it weren’t for ICE | Analysis by Mara Richards Bim
text:
Barbara Nicole Hildago has a complicated relationship with her biological mother, who brought her to the United States from Venezuela. But that’s not really the point. Nicole is 8. Two weeks ago, while on her way to school, ICE agents broke her guardian’s car window and kidnapped her.

No matter our feelings about current immigration policies, this act and others like them are sick and cruel. Nicole was detained in Dallas and transferred to Corpus Christi. Her loved ones didn’t know where she was for days. She is in a detention center. She is 8. Can you even imagine? A second grader.

See the video here.

We don’t have to think very hard about how traumatizing this entire experience will be for Nicole. There are plenty of reports of what conditions are like in these types of facilities. Lights are never turned off, food is moldy and drinking water unclean, medical care subpar and a child’s education inadequate. I can’t even let myself think about the risk to her physical safety. The family said she could be there for up to three to four months.

The sad reality is Nicole’s not the only one. Data from 2025 show more than 1,800 children were detained in ICE holding rooms around the country, 40 of those right here in Dallas. You can find the data here. You have questions, I’m sure. You want to know what each child did to deserve being detained. You wonder why they couldn’t just come legally. Why could they just not cooperate with agents.

But can we set those aside and remember these are children.

One of my favorite stories in Scripture is the story of Rizpah. She’s only mentioned twice, so I’m not surprised if you haven’t heard of her. She is introduced as a concubine of Saul and the mother of two men who were unfairly executed to settle some type of bloodguilt between King David and the Gibeonites. The bodies of her sons and five others were left exposed, denied burial and left to scavenging animals — a denial of dignity to the dead and to their families. So Rizpah acted.

The Scripture says she maintained vigil from the beginning of barley harvest until the autumn rains, driving off animals, chasing away birds, day after day in the scorching sun, night after night in isolation. Rizpah’s witness is entirely embodied; she doesn’t speak a single word that is recorded. Her vigil becomes a ministry of presence. She refuses to let the dead be forgotten. She refuses to allow the community to look away.

There are plenty of ways for us to act. Free Families, a national coalition to end family and child detainment offers many ways to participate in advocacy efforts. You can be trained as a court observer, you can show up to a vigil, you can be present at the field office respite tent. You can join ICE watching groups in your neighborhood. You can order know your rights cards and make whistle kits. You can contact yoru elected officials and demand they stop this cruelty.

Rizpah offers us a faithful biblical example of what we can do. Sometimes the most transformative act of faith is simply refusing to look away. So let’s not.

Heather Mustain serves as associate pastor at Wilshire Baptist Church in Dallas.

text:
The U.S. Department of Labor (DOL) has proposed a major rewrite of Program Electronic Review Management (PERM), the labor certification step that starts most employer-sponsored green card cases. Our Immigration Team explains what the proposal would change and what employers can do now to prepare.

The proposal would replace today’s menu of recruitment options with one uniform, tougher recruitment model

A new two-year layoff bar would block filings by employers that laid off U.S. workers in the same or a similar occupation and area

Comments are due on or about January 16, 2027; employers can review pending PERM cases and layoffs now

A proposed federal rule could make employer-sponsored green cards slower, more paperwork-heavy, and more exposed to enforcement.

The U.S. Department of Labor (DOL) has proposed a major rewrite of Program Electronic Review Management (PERM), the labor certification step that starts most employer-sponsored green card cases. If adopted, the changes would add time, documentation, and enforcement exposure for employers.

The proposed rule is scheduled for publication in the Federal Register on November 17, 2026. Written comments will be due 60 days after publication, on or about January 16, 2027. If finalized as proposed, the rule would take effect 60 days after the final rule is published and apply to applications filed on or after day 90, leaving employers a 90-day transition window.

How PERM Works Today

PERM is the first hurdle in most employer-sponsored green card cases in the employment-based second and third preference (EB-2 and EB-3) categories. Before an employer can ask U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to approve a green card petition, the DOL must certify two things: that there are not enough able, willing, qualified, and available U.S. workers for the job, and that hiring a foreign worker will not hurt the wages or working conditions of similar U.S. workers. Employers make their case in three steps: a DOL ruling on the prevailing wage for the job, a recruitment campaign, and a notice of the filing to U.S. workers.

What the Rule Would Change

The proposal would swap today’s menu of recruitment options for one tougher, uniform playbook and back it with stronger enforcement.

One recruitment model. Every employer would follow the same steps: a state workforce agency job order, its own website, outside job boards, social media where it normally recruits, and at least one job fair or campus event. Ads would run at least 90 days. Employers would also have to certify, under penalty of perjury, that PERM recruitment matches how they hire for non-PERM jobs, and recruiting through channels less accessible to U.S. workers would be presumed bad faith.

A new two-year layoff bar. Employers could not file if they laid off U.S. workers in the same or a similar occupation in the same area in the prior two years, up from 180 days today. Layoffs after filing would trigger notice and rehiring duties and could lead to the certification being revoked.

More paperwork up front, no shortcut for shortage jobs. The recruitment report, all resumes, and proof of advertising would be filed with the application, and incomplete filings would be returned without review rights. Schedule A, the shortcut for shortage-listed fields such as nursing and physical therapy, would be eliminated, so those employers would need full PERM recruitment. The DOL puts the effect at roughly 23,835 petitions a year.

Tougher enforcement. Expanded certifications would be backed by federal criminal statutes. Findings would be referred to the DOL Office of Inspector General (DOL-OIG), the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the Department of Justice (DOJ), and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC). Violators could be barred from the program for up to three years, including attorneys, agents, and successors in interest.

Why It Matters for Employers

This is not just a paperwork change. The proposal would treat routine PERM filings as potential evidence in discrimination and compliance cases, and it would bring multiple agencies into the same file. That fits the broader enforcement push employers are already seeing, and the DOL expressly ties the proposed rule to enforcement against staffing firms.

Longer timelines, uncertain savings. The minimum pre-filing period would grow to roughly four to five months: 90 days of recruitment, a 30-day wait, then filing within 30 days. The DOL projects millions in annual net savings, largely from dropping newspaper ads, but that assumes the new online and job-fair recruitment costs nothing.

Workforce decisions are immigration decisions. A layoff in one occupation could close PERM for that occupation for two years, so reductions in force need immigration counsel at the table. The DOL itself acknowledges this cost cannot be quantified.

Some employers are more exposed than others. Staffing and information technology (IT) consulting firms face the most exposure, given client layoff tracking and third-party worksite notice posting. Health care employers lose a shortcut: sponsoring nurses and physical therapists would require recruitment, adding time and the risk that qualified U.S. applicants respond.

Human resources (HR) systems become compliance systems, and discrimination risk rises. Applicant tracking settings, interview practices, and who screens applicants all matter, and every reviewer would be named in the report. The DOL says meeting PERM requirements does not show an employer is following federal anti-discrimination laws, including Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Failing to rehire a qualified laid-off worker could support an inference of discrimination.

What to Do Before the Rule Is Final

Employers do not have to wait for a final rule to prepare.

Take stock of PERM cases. Inventory pending and planned PERM cases and decide which can finish recruitment and file under current rules. If the rule is finalized as proposed, it would take effect 60 days after publication and apply to applications filed on or after day 90, leaving employers a 90-day transition window.

Map your layoffs. Track layoffs from the past two years by occupation and location and build a process to keep tracking them going forward.

Compare hiring practices. Compare standard hiring practices with PERM practices and close any gaps.

Consider submitting comments. Written comments are due on or about January 16, 2027. The DOL specifically asks about the two-year layoff period and how employers must post notice of a filing for remote jobs.

text:
Tensions over immigration enforcement are growing in the Salem and Roanoke area as protesters gather amid concerns about possible U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity and reported sightings of federal agents.

Protesters gathered in downtown Salem Thursday, voicing concerns about the impact of immigration enforcement on immigrant families.

"It's been pretty emotional, but I've got to be out here. I'm not locked up," one protester said.

Those demonstrating against ICE said they believe the agency's actions are creating fear in immigrant communities and called for more humane treatment.

"I really think the things these ICE people are doing to others are inhumane and immoral, and I would really like to see them better treated. There's a better way than this," another protester said.

Some said they have spoken with people who are afraid to leave their homes, including individuals who are legally in the United States.

"I've talked to several people who I know very well who say they're afraid to come out of their homes, and they're here legally," a protester said.

Community members also brought donations to support families who may be afraid to leave their homes.

SEE ALSO: LCS tackling low SOL scores and achievement gaps following results from VDOE report cards

The demonstration brought attention to a rumored ICE facility in Roanoke, which protesters said has raised concerns among residents.

"We decided to come to the ICE facility in Roanoke. It's kind of undercover," one person said.

Another protester said the facility's location is not new information.

"This is an ICE facility, and it's been released by the Department of Homeland Security for years. So it's nothing new," the protester said.

One demonstrator said recent activity near the facility has heightened concerns.

"In the last three days, the vehicle count has just tremendously escalated. Several unmarked cars from out of state," the protester said.

The demonstrator also expressed concern about the facility's proximity to a local church.

"And it's right next to one of our many beautiful Salem churches where we preach love of neighbor. And this is such a contradiction. We're just horrified," the protester said.

ABC13 reached out to ICE to confirm whether agents have been operating in the area and whether any arrests have been made. The agency had not responded as of publication.

Not everyone in the Salem neighborhood agrees with the protesters' concerns.

Across the street, another woman voiced her support for immigration enforcement, saying people should enter the country legally.

"This is America. You come here legally, or don't come at all," she said.

She also criticized Democrats over immigration policy, saying she believes their decisions are contributing to problems in the country.

"Democrats are causing a lot of problems for this country and letting the Islamic people in," she said.

The woman also raised concerns about religious persecution, arguing that some Americans do not understand the potential consequences of their political choices.

"One day they're gonna come to the conclusion, when they start getting their heads chopped off 'cause they're Christians, then they're gonna understand they shouldn't have voted for them," she said.

As concerns about immigration enforcement continue in the region, residents remain divided over ICE's presence and its role in the community.

text:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin put out a statement Wednesday expressing concerns over Texas’ cooperation with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

This comes after Democrats won every statewide seat in the midterm election, gaining control of the state House and the governor’s office for the first time in decades.

Mullin said he worries that Democratic politicians will try to turn Texas into a "sanctuary state" once Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa takes office in January.

"If Texas were to stop cooperating with ICE and become a sanctuary state, it would be one of the worst derelictions of duty we’ve seen in a very long time," Mullin said.

Related

Cities review their policies

The backstory:

Outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott previously issued executive orders and signed state laws requiring local agencies to assist ICE with federal immigration operations.

However, in the wake of the election, some municipalities have begun reexamining how their police officers interact with federal agents.

Houston Mayor John Whitmire issued a Nov. 6 executive order limiting when the city’s police officers can contact ICE about administrative immigration warrants.

Whitmire has said the intention is to reduce fear in Houston's immigrant communities and rebuild trust between residents and law enforcement.

Houston saw one of two shootings involving federal immigration agents in Texas this year. The other happened in Austin, where the mayor has also instructed police to look at revising their policies when it comes to immigration enforcement.

Related

Mullin points to previous Texas cases

What they're saying:

In his statement, Mullin argued that federal operations in the state have been successful and claimed that a lack of cooperation with ICE could have an effect on public safety.

He referred to a long list of cases where people without proper documentation were removed from Texas after being convicted of crimes such as murder, manufacturing and trafficking drugs, child sex trafficking, and, in one case, plotting a terror attack.

"We are calling on Governor-elect Hinojosa and other leaders throughout the state to continue cooperating with us," Mullin said. "If they do not, then crime and violence will plague the Lone Star State."

What Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has said about the issue

The other side:

Hinojosa has not responded to a request for comment on Mullin’s statement. However, she did discuss some of her views on immigration enforcement in a recent interview with The Texas Tribune.

The soon-to-be governor noted that she is committed to keeping the border secure by working with local law enforcement and the federal government, but said she feels some things need to change within the country.

Related

"What ICE is doing is making us less safe," she told The Texas Tribune. "I do not think we should be facilitating the chaos that ICE has wrought in Texas. That is something that we’ll make sure to do what we can to stop that."

Hinojosa did not specifically say whether she would rescind Abbott's order directing law enforcement to help ICE agents detain unauthorized migrants.

She did mention prioritizing "accountability measures" such as making sure federal agents are not masked and that they are equipped with body cams and dash cams. Hinojosa also discussed finding new ways to secure the border with technology rather than a wall, such as in places like the Big Bend region.

"I’ve talked to President Trump on border security, and he understands my commitment to keeping a secure border," she told The Texas Tribune. "And I hope to work with him to make sure that happens."

text:
Ruben Garcia has spent the last few years fighting the Texas attorney general’s office in court over allegations that his organization, Annunciation House, harbored undocumented immigrants and participated in human smuggling, among other things.

So when the office suddenly dropped its suit last week, without explanation, Garcia felt immense relief. Annunciation House runs shelters for migrants around El Paso, and he said the litigation had cost the organization a lot, from lawyer fees to lost donors. It’s now one of a handful of headline-grabbing cases that outgoing Attorney General Ken Paxton has backed out of in the last few weeks.

Paxton’s office dropped another lawsuit this month against Houston-area immigrant activist group FIEL. It has also dropped its support for a doctor who was reprimanded for prescribing ivermectin during the pandemic, and it gave up on another lawsuit against the NCAA for allowing transgender athletes to participate in events, as well as one against Muslim civil rights group CAIR.

Several lawyers and former attorney generals said the office’s efforts to cancel so many cases before a new administration takes over is unusual. Paxton will only lead the office until January, when Democrat Nathan Johnson is set to take over.

“It's not at all normal,” said Rob McKenna, former Republican attorney general for the state of Washington. “I can't think of another example of an AG doing that.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Paxton’s office did not respond to a request for comment about why the cases were dropped, and several of the groups impacted said they didn’t receive an explanation, either. The office isn’t required to explain its reasoning, but several critics interpreted the move as a kind of confession.

“For the state to dismiss a series of cases is humiliating,” said James Tierney, a former Democratic attorney general for Maine. “The lawsuits have no merit, and he knows it.”

Tierney said that usually, if the AG or lawyers under him believed in a case, they would attempt to sway a new administration to continue pursuing it. McKenna said it’s more common to see lawyers slow-walk their cases after an election, not close them, but there were a few reasons the office might be doing so besides admitting defeat.

“It may be that General Paxton has decided that if he can't control the case, he doesn't want the case to be pursued,” McKenna said. “Maybe he's concerned that his successor will settle the case on terms favorable to the target, and he doesn't want that target to be treated favorably in that way. The other possibility is that he thinks his successor will dismiss the case if he doesn't do it, and he doesn't want his successor to get the credit for doing that.”

Some of the cases dropped were done so “with prejudice,” which means the agency has forfeited the right to pursue the organization on similar charges in the future, like in the lawsuits against Annunciation House and FIEL. Others were dropped without prejudice, so a future conservative attorney general could revisit them.

Johnson is among those who see the office’s latest moves as an admission.

“My guess is they don’t want to grant me the privilege of terminating their bad work. They don’t want me taking credit,” he told Texas Monthly. “If a case had any merit to it, why would they drop it? If they’re dropping it now, why’d they file it in the first place?”

He elaborated in a statement to the Chronicle.

“Irrespective of the likely political motivation behind it, I applaud the termination of these lawsuits. It marks the first tangible and important result of the election,” he said.

Others felt that the office is attempting to avoid accountability for bringing baseless lawsuits.

“My concern is that the reason why they are doing this is to try to cover up what they have done,” said Justin Nelson, a lawyer who ran against Paxton in 2018. “I think they're hoping that what Paxton did to that office will be less of an issue if the cases go away beforehand.”

Nelson ran against Paxton partly because he felt the office was using its power for political purposes, and not for the benefit of Texans. Now that Paxton is out, along with many of the state’s Republican leadership, he’s hoping Johnson will investigate the past conduct.

Paxton’s office hasn’t ended all its controversial suits. It’s still pursuing cases against Tylenol and Blackrock that Johnson has expressed skepticism about. The agency also revived a suit this month against Houston over Mayor John Whitmire’s directive limiting city police involvement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. And it’s attempting to protect GOP efforts to string concertina wire at the border with a settlement announced Thursday.

U.S. Rep. Chip Roy, who previously served under Paxton, said the number of dropped cases is a small percentage of the agency’s overall caseload, and that it made sense that the office wouldn’t want to “perpetuate a case that the incoming attorney general is probably not going to carry forward.”

“They're political,” he said of the suits. “It doesn't mean they're without substance.”

But Cesar Espinosa, co-founder of FIEL, made it clear that while the attorney general’s office may be done with his group’s case, it wasn’t necessarily done with the office.

“This was a great expenditure for us,” he said. “It took us away from our mission to educate, empower, and protect our community. So, somebody should be held accountable for those damages.”

Groups who feel they were the subject of meritless or malicious lawsuits may seek to recoup losses from the state.

“They know they're wrong, and they are trying to now do damage control, seeing how badly they lost their election,” Espinosa said, referring to the GOP. “They're trying now to cover their tracks.”

text:
Eva Yi Xie, a Princeton doctoral student studying neuroscience, was detained by ICE on Thursday while traveling home from a conference in Washington, D.C., according to messages posted on Bluesky and X by her adviser, professor Carlos Brody.

“Eva is [a] brilliant computational and experimental systems neuroscientist. She is also a valued colleague, mentor, and friend, and we are privileged that she chose our labs for her thesis research. She went to a conference to present her work, and now she’s in a detention center,” Brody posted on Bluesky, urging people to contact elected officials on Xie’s behalf. “She should be home.”

Brody said in the social posts that Xie was detained at Reagan National Airport, sent her colleagues a call for help on Slack, and was taken to an ICE facility in Chantilly, Virginia. The Immigration and Customs Enforcement Online Detainee Locator System listed Xie in custody but did not provide her location.

“The University has arranged for legal counsel to represent the student,” Princeton spokesperson Michael Hotchkiss told PAW in an email.

A third-year Ph.D. student, Xie was in Washington to present her research at the Society for Neuroscience Research annual meeting. “It seems wildly unfair,” Brody told The Daily Princetonian in a written statement. “Eva is a brilliant law-abiding student and wonderful person who has many talents to contribute to the United States. Detaining her, with the intent of deporting her, makes no sense whatsoever. It is cruel, and it is our country shooting itself in the foot.”

Xie, a graduate of MIT and the Bronx High School of Science, emigrated to the U.S. from China in 2016, according to a profile in The Science Survey, Bronx Science’s student newspaper. She told the newspaper she was grateful for the chance to pursue research in the U.S. and give back to her community. “Here, if you are brave enough to step out of your comfort zone, you can definitely achieve something,” she said.

Xie majored in computer science and mathematics at MIT before joining Brody’s lab, where her research focuses on the neural basis of decision-making, as she wrote in an online bio. “With the very recent development of large-scale neurophysiological recordings and connectome datasets, we now have unprecedented opportunities to investigate: How do multiple brain regions interact to support decision-making?” Xie wrote.

Graduate School Dean Rodney Priestley sent an email to Princeton Neuroscience Institute graduate students Thursday night, assuring them that the University “will stay in close contact with the student’s family, her legal team, and her PNI colleagues as this situation is resolved.”

NEW YORK (PIX11) – Two more counties, Nassau and Chautauqua, will join a lawsuit against Gov. Kathy Hochul's law banning formal agreements between local law enforcement and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, court filings show.

The lawsuit, filed in August, challenges the governor's "Local Cops, Local Crimes Act" barring agencies from entering or maintaining 287(g) agreements with ICE, which can deputize local law enforcement to make immigration-related arrests. Initially, 15 New York sheriffs signed onto the suit.

Discover more local reporting on our homepage

On Thursday, a federal judge approved the group's request to update their complaint to add Chautauqua's sheriff, Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, and both Nassau County's sheriff and police commissioner. Blakeman, a Republican who challenged Hochul in the recent election, previously promised he would join the lawsuit.

It comes after an Albany judge denied the sheriffs' attempt to pause the law while the court case plays out.

Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James have defended the law as a way to protect public safety. The state also took legal action against Rensselaer County, the lead plaintiff in the suit, to force compliance with the new law.

"This lawsuit is nothing but a frivolous waste of taxpayer dollars. The courts have already declined to block this law once, and we are confident they will do so again. In the meantime, we expect all law enforcement agencies in New York to uphold state law," they said in a statement after the lawsuit was filed.

A lawyer for the suing counties did not immediately respond to PIX11 News' request for comment.

Emily Rahhal is a digital reporter who has covered New York City since 2023 after reporting in Los Angeles for years. She joined PIX11 in 2024. See more of her work here and follow her on Twitter here.

text:
The Senate rejected a war powers resolution on Thursday that would have directed President Trump to seek congressional approval before resuming attacks on Iran. The resolution failed on a vote of 51-48. Three Republicans voted in favor, while Pennsylvania Democratic Senator John Fetterman voted in opposition. The House approved the resolution in September. Both the House and Senate previously approved a war powers resolution back in June, but President Trump largely ignored it. Thursday’s failed vote in the Senate came after Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries suggested he would not block funding for attacks on Iran in the government funding package due by December 11. Meanwhile, a Pentagon official said Thursday the cost of the war on Iran has topped $48 billion. That figure does not include damage to U.S. bases, the cost of providing healthcare to hundreds of injured troops or the tens of billions of dollars in higher fuel costs triggered by the war.

The Senate has approved a permitting reform bill that would weaken environmental laws to speed approval of new housing, roads, energy projects and other infrastructure. While the bill would make it easier to build new transmission lines and wind and solar farms, it would also speed construction of fossil fuel power plants and new data centers, including on public lands. Meanwhile, Native leaders and advocacy groups strongly opposed the legislation, saying it would weaken tribal sovereignty and threaten cultural and sacred sites. This is Oregon Democratic Senator Jeff Merkley, who voted “no.”

Sen. Jeff Merkley: “First, it makes it a lot easier to build data centers. Did anybody notice data centers were a big issue in this most recent election? Here we come right in after the election, and we’re going to pass a bill that makes it easier to do data centers by striking down tools that states have when they decide they do not want to have a data center because it threatens key clean air or clean water issues.”

Despite those objections, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known as BAAJA, passed on a vote of 62-33 with 14 Democrats in favor, including Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer. In a statement, Food & Water Watch said, “Sen. Schumer’s alignment with Republicans over a majority of his own Democratic caucus in voting to advance this terrible pro-polluter, pro-data center permitting bill is all the reason needed to demand that Schumer step down as leader of the Senate Democrats.” The bill now goes to the House and is expected to be voted on the week after next.

Here at the COP31 U.N. climate summit, negotiators published a “slimmed-down” draft text on Thursday that stripped out any reference to fossil fuels, or ending their use. Instead, the document promotes carbon capture and storage, an unproven technology that critics say will never have a meaningful impact on the climate crisis. Activists at the COP are demanding more financing to help poorer countries adapt to a warming world. This is Iona Stewart of the climate action group Global Witness.

Emily Iona Stewart: “Mentions of human rights, especially human rights and environment defenders, which had previously been introduced by the Brazilians, are now being walked back in this cover decision. So that’s really worrying for us. Another thing: fossil fuels, still not in there. Where is the text on phasing out fossil fuels and having a concrete roadmap for all of the parties? We need that now. And then, finance. There’s not enough momentum on making sure that countries who have already signed up and pledged to give climate finance actually deliver on those pledges.”

In Ukraine, officials say eight people were killed and dozens injured overnight, as Russia launched a massive drone and missile attack. In Kyiv, Russian bombs struck three ⁠bridges over the Dnipro River. Meanwhile, in Kharkiv, a Russian drone damaged a hospital, wounding four people.

The Russian attacks came after Ukraine bombed the Kerch Bridge, the only link between mainland Russia and Russian-annexed Crimea. Engineers say it could take years for Russia to repair the damage.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky defended the bridge strike and warned of further action.

President Volodymyr Zelensky: “We have long been telling Russia: Enough of striking bridges, our cities and villages, Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, railways and grain ships. Enough of this war. But every time, Russia chooses a new escalation.”

Meanwhile, Poland’s military said it was investigating a suspected violation of its airspace by Russia near Poland’s border with Ukraine, after an unidentified object crash-landed this morning.

In Minnesota, a Somali American Uber driver is fighting for his life after he was allegedly run over multiple times with his own vehicle by a passenger who disliked his Muslim name. Mohamed Yusuf remained in critical condition Thursday with life-threatening injuries following Saturday’s attack. It follows last month’s raid on the D.C. home of Somali American Minnesota Congresswoman Ilhan Omar by federal agents. And it follows president Trump’s repeated racist attacks demonizing Somali American communities. Trump has called Somalis “garbage” and “low-IQ people” who “contribute nothing.” Just weeks ago, Trump wrote on social media, “Fight back Minnesota, fight back!”

A Colorado federal judge has held ICE officials and the Trump administration in contempt over a practice to instantly rearrest immigrants after a court has ordered their release from ICE jail. In her ruling, U.S. District Court Judge Charlotte Sweeney wrote that ICE “made ⁠a mockery of court orders.” The ACLU has described the practice as “sham releases.” At the center of the case is the detention of Mexican immigrant Ramón Quintero Álvarez, who has lived in the U.S. for more than 30 years. Álvarez was immediately rearrested late last month shortly after his release from an Aurora ICE jail.

In Huntsville, Texas, a man on death row repeatedly moaned out in pain during a botched execution that took over an hour. Reinaldo Dennes remained strapped to a gurney as prison officials struggled to locate a vein to administer a lethal dose of pentobarbital. After more than an hour Thursday evening, vein lines were ultimately found in his neck and one of his feet. Seventy-year-old Dennes reportedly exclaimed that his leg felt like it was on fire. This comes just over a month after the botched execution attempt of Christa Pike in Tennessee that drew widespread condemnation. Pike survived two lethal injections and was left hospitalized in critical condition and unconscious for nearly a week. She’s now back in prison.

The White House has picked Eric Ueland to run the Government Accountability Office, Congress’s independent watchdog, for a 15-year term. Ueland is a longtime Republican operative who served as a Big Pharma and fossil fuel lobbyist before joining the Trump administration in 2016. Senate Republicans are skipping the bipartisan process used for every GAO head since 1980, in which top lawmakers submit a short list of candidates. Twenty-one inspectors general are urging congressional leaders to reject Ueland’s confirmation, writing, “the credibility of any oversight institution depends on two pillars: strict adherence to statutory safeguards designed to protect its independence, and leadership defined by proven, nonpartisan fidelity to objective evidence. Mr. Ueland’s nomination fails on both counts.”
