title: DHS pushes through billions for deportations, border projects | CNN Politics
authors: Priscilla Alvarez, Audrey Ash, Annie Grayer
description:
At DHS, it’s been business as usual, and officials have continued to ink contracts at a pace similar to the one before the elections.
Democratic Rep. Henry Cuellar, the ranking member on the House Appropriations Homeland Security subcommittee, told CNN he’s exploring how to put curbs on how the funds are used.
That includes placing some restrictions on ICE and providing more funds to the Homeland Security inspector general for oversight.
Democratic lawmakers already have plans to scrutinize who DHS struck contracts with — and how they did it — in a series of oversight measures.
A $100 million contract in August went to supporting the 287(g) program in Texas, which deputizes local law enforcement to perform some immigration law enforcement actions.
text:
On a recent Tuesday afternoon, Deputy Homeland Security Secretary Troy Edgar stood before dozens of contractors and industry leaders and boasted of his department’s multibillion-dollar budget, claiming that it was bigger than that of American Airlines.

The message — described by two people who were in attendance — was clear to those in the room: DHS was eager as ever to spend money to advance President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign promise. The department needs more detention space, more airlines, more of everything to solve for what Edgar described as a supply chain issue, the people said.

It’s the latest example of how DHS is taking advantage of the billions of dollars in its coffers despite waning public support for the president’s immigration crackdown. And the effort comes as Democrats, flush from massive midterm victories, prepare to use their majorities to conduct tough oversight of the department’s spending and look for ways to rein it in.

In recent months, DHS has awarded a nearly $1.3 billion contract for Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportation flights, at least $1.5 billion for border infrastructure, a multimillion-dollar contract to transport ICE detainees, and nearly $13 million for a canine facility.

“They want to use their spending authority that they’ve got to do what they want to do before there is a new sheriff in town,” GOP Rep. Mark Amodei, who oversees the DHS budget in the House for the remaining weeks of the Republican majority, told CNN.

A Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement that the department is using the funds “to strengthen border security, hire more ICE officers, fully fund the 287(g) program, and expand detention space,” adding that thanks to legislation passed this year, “ICE and CBP are FULLY FUNDED through the rest of President Trump’s term — ensuring our mission to protect the homeland continues undeterred.”

Democrats hope to build ‘guardrails’

In the immediate days after the midterms, Trump appeared to briefly waver on his immigration policy, acknowledging that it was “too tough” in a “60 Minutes” interview. He later defended his policy and has elevated Stephen Miller — the administration’s staunchest advocate for mass deportations — to White House chief of staff. At DHS, it’s been business as usual, and officials have continued to ink contracts at a pace similar to the one before the elections.

Last year, Republicans passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, providing $75 billion for ICE to spend over the next four years, and $65 billion for Customs and Border Protection. In June, Congress approved a roughly $70 billion immigration enforcement package — the Secure America Act — meant to fund ICE and CBP through the end of the second Trump administration.

A CNN analysis of government records found that in fiscal year 2026, which ran from October 2025 through September 2026, ICE and CBP signed new contracts valuing at over $41.7 billion — with the potential to increase to $63.7 billion. That’s more than three times the amount from the year before: In the twelve months prior, which includes three months of the Biden administration, the two agencies only awarded $12.3 billion worth of contracts.

Democratic Rep. Henry Cuellar, the ranking member on the House Appropriations Homeland Security subcommittee, told CNN he’s exploring how to put curbs on how the funds are used.

“Once we have control, then there’s a lot more we can do on guardrails,” he said, referring to bringing the funds under his committee’s oversight. That includes placing some restrictions on ICE and providing more funds to the Homeland Security inspector general for oversight.

Democratic lawmakers already have plans to scrutinize who DHS struck contracts with — and how they did it — in a series of oversight measures. But pulling back the billions in funding is likely to be an uphill battle given that Democrats would need Trump to agree, or assemble an unlikely veto-proof majority.

“The only thing stopping (DHS) is the Congress or the public pressuring the president to put limitations on it,” said Claire Trickler-McNulty, a former senior ICE official.

Even before Democrats take over, Amodei, who is retiring, told CNN he is keeping track of how DHS is making spending decisions to monitor whether the agency is veering into politically unpopular territory.

“We’re keeping an eye on what they’re doing. But it appears to be a bit of a far cry on the earlier days of warehouses and airplanes and whatever the heck,” he said.

As of September, ICE has already set aside $22.2 billion using funds from the pair of bills passed by Republicans, with $91 billion left to spend, while CBP had obligated $45.2 billion from those same funds with $45 billion left to spend, according to data compiled by Senate Budget Committee Democratic staff.

Some of the department’s largest contractors, meanwhile, have been proceeding with their plans.

In a quarterly earnings call this month, CoreCivic — one of the largest private prison and immigration detention operators in the US — told investors that they don’t expect DHS to slow down post-election and anticipate detention population to continue to increase.

“There’s nothing that would cause us to think otherwise. They have the secure funding to do so, and that goes through 2029, and they can continue to enter contracts and utilize bed capacity through that funding up until then. We believe that they’ll continue to do so,” said CoreCivic President and CEO Lucibeth Mayberry.

Some Homeland Security officials told CNN the pace of spending has been steady since Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin scrapped his predecessor Kristi Noem’s policy of signing off on contracts that surpassed the $100,000 mark and now they simply have more money and contracts to distribute.

Other officials have shared with contractors that they’re accelerating contracting, particularly with companies that have historically worked with the department.

“They went into overdrive,” a source familiar with the contracting process told CNN. “It’s the fear of the unknown.”

Billions to buy detention facilities, planes

In Front Royal, Virginia, the agency’s canine division facility is getting a $12.8 million revamp; in Georgia, the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center is getting a new ammo storage facility valued at $2.2 million.

A $100 million contract in August went to supporting the 287(g) program in Texas, which deputizes local law enforcement to perform some immigration law enforcement actions. The contract pays for 24/7-armed support for the transportation of detainees from local law enforcement to ICE custody. While only $100 million has been obligated so far, the contract has the potential to increase to $382.3 million.

Several of the 2026 contracts are for construction at aging CBP facilities. Some of the highest CBP contracts, all valued at more than $100 million apiece, are for designing, building, or maintaining structures in Texas, California, Florida and New Mexico.

That’s in addition to border wall spending. CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott said in June that border wall construction is “ahead of schedule and below budget,” citing previous wall money appropriated by Congress and the president’s “big beautiful bill” which allocated $46.5 billion for construction.

The Supreme Court also recently allowed Trump to continue border wall construction in the Big Bend region of Texas – including Big Bend National Park – pausing a lower court ruling that temporarily blocked that work while it considers whether the administration had the authority to bypass environmental requirements.

This week, Rep. Veronica Escobar of Texas, alongside other Democratic lawmakers, urged the Homeland Security inspector general to investigate the contracting process behind an award of nearly $7.5 billion for border infrastructure projects in the Big Bend region.

One of the largest contracts in the last two years was signed this October with CSI Aviation, a flight charter company that’s held lucrative contracts with DHS in the past. Valued at $1.28 billion, the contract is for on-demand flight services for “enforcement and removal operations under the ICE Air program.” At least $885 million has been paid to CSI through that contract, indicating some services have already been provided.

DHS was already under intense scrutiny over the purchase of the planes CSI Aviation is contracted to fly. In 2025, DHS spent hundreds of millions of dollars on contracts and 10 planes to create a mini deportation airline for ICE. CNN previously reported the majority of those planes remained parked in a hangar in Louisiana, with no firm plan in place to fly them.

ICE has also been spending heavily on purchasing detention facilities from two of its largest contractors.

Private contractors own and operate 34 detention facilities nationwide, GEO Group CEO George Zoley told investors this month. Of those, GEO Group owns and operates 20, while CoreCivic is responsible for 12.

CoreCivic announced the sale of four facilities to DHS this year for a total of around $2.2 billion, according to company filings with the SEC. Mayberry told investors that company officials “continue to have discussions with ICE about the potential acquisition of additional CoreCivic detention facilities,” though she cautioned that talks are in preliminary stages. CoreCivic is charged with the care of more than 60,000 ICE detainees.

In a report released this week, the Government Accountability Office found that ICE’s current plans indicate that the agency expects to obligate remaining detention funds from the president’s “big beautiful bill” by the end of next year.

A federal judge said that the US Immigration and Customs ⁠Enforcement agency (ICE) “made a mockery of court orders” in Colorado and that the court found government officials in contempt ⁠for instantly re-arresting a ⁠man whom ​the judge had ordered released.

US district judge Charlotte Sweeney declined to take any further action because she ⁠said the officials had “cured the contempt by ceasing the practice at issue” as sworn by an official in court.

At least 18 people ‌in Colorado have been held in detention longer than they should have been or have been re-arrested within minutes of their judge-ordered release in the past six weeks, CPR News, the news division of Colorado Public Radio, reported.

The report said that immigration attorneys estimated the number may be ‌higher given that some immigrants represented themselves.

The phenomenon of immigration detainees being released and then quickly re-detained has been noticeable in recent months and legal advocates say the trend is on the rise.

Sometimes a person is re-arrested days later, sometimes without even leaving the detention center and, according to advocates, often in violation of a federal court order.

ICE, which is part of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), has been the face of ​Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown and deportation drive that rights groups say has violated free speech and due process rights.

Human rights groups also say the crackdown has created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised ⁠concerns about racial profiling.

The Trump administration has maintained that ​its actions aim to ​improve domestic security and are ​in compliance with the law. ICE and the DHS did not ​immediately respond to ‌a request ​for comment on what ​the judge said on Wednesday.

Democrats, who won majorities in the House and Senate in the midterm elections, now aim to hold the Trump administration accountable for its immigration policies.

description:

Now, some immigrants, including the teen, are chronicling a new challenge: restricted phone access, one of few ways for those in temporary holding cells along the border to reach the outside world.
Judge Gee earlier this year ordered additional oversight in some holding facilities, finding conditions were unsuitable for children.
Kahn said limited access to phone calls is happening as concerning conditions increase inside the facilities.
The woman’s youngest child had lost weight, developed a stutter and cried constantly, she wrote in a declaration on her 11th day in the holding cell.
text:
On his second day being held inside a border station holding cell in San Diego, a 15-year-old migrant described the conditions as “horrible.”

“It isn’t a place for children, or humans,” the teen wrote in a declaration filed in federal district court last week.

Under the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, legal advocates say children are spending longer — weeks or more than a month — in temporary holding cells along the border from California to Texas despite guidelines stating detentions should not exceed 72 hours.

In declarations filed over the past year, parents and children have recounted spending 23 hours a day in cement cells, having to use a partially exposed toilet and sleeping on thin mattresses in cold temperatures. They were in the custody of Customs and Border Protection or its subagency, the U.S. Border Patrol.

Now, some immigrants, including the teen, are chronicling a new challenge: restricted phone access, one of few ways for those in temporary holding cells along the border to reach the outside world.

“We don’t know what’s happening because we can’t call anyone,” the teen, detained with their mother and father, wrote in September. “We can’t even tell the ones we love where we are.”

A group of legal advocacy nonprofits representing migrant children is now asking U.S. District Chief Judge Dolly M. Gee in California to affirm that the federal immigration authorities must provide phone calls to children and families in its custody. Judge Gee earlier this year ordered additional oversight in some holding facilities, finding conditions were unsuitable for children.

The recent motion was filed as part of the Reno v. Flores case, which was filed in the 1980s and resulted in a legal settlement that for decades has set the standards and requirements for the care and release of children in federal immigration custody.

Lawyers for the government have not yet responded to the motion, but in previous filings they have argued that its care of children is “exceeding” requirements set by the court.

Spokespeople for the Department of Homeland Security and CBP did not respond to questions from inewsource about the latest legal filings.

The family detentions and limited phone access, described by 10 immigrants detained at the border between April and November, comes as the Department of Homeland Security under President Donald Trump touts overseeing a year and a half of “zero releases” at the border.

The president has previously criticized his predecessor for releasing migrants into the U.S. during a period of record unauthorized border crossings. But attorneys for children in the case say the Trump administration’s policy of not releasing any migrants found in the U.S. without status means that children spend longer in harmful detention conditions.

Three legal advocacy groups, the Center for Human Rights and Constitutional Law, the National Center for Youth Law and Children’s Rights, are representing the plaintiffs in the case.

Trump’s sweeping immigration crackdown is affecting children in myriad ways.

On Nov. 4, an 8-year-old Haitian boy was arrested by immigration officers after his court appointment in San Diego. The boy was reunited with his family this week after a public outcry and criticism from members of Congress.

Across the country, children as young as 1 and others who are elementary schoolers and teens have appeared in immigration court with no attorney to represent them after the Trump administration ended funding for legal services for unaccompanied migrant children.

Those children are also spending longer in government custody, after new rules have made it harder for family members to come forward to sponsor them.

Scott Peters, a Democratic U.S. House representative in San Diego, said there should be more oversight inside of facilities where children are being held.

“Whether these kids are coming in with families trying to relocate, to seek asylum or whether they’re already in our communities, the way we’re treating children is just reprehensible.”

Days with limited phone access

The temporary holding cells, located in ports of entry and border stations across the country, are intended for brief stays to process migrants who turned themselves into immigration authorities or are encountered after crossing the border.

In declarations to the court, families have described little or no time outside during dayslong detentions, poor food for children and lights being left on throughout the day and during sleeping hours.

Sarah Kahn, a senior staff attorney at the Center for Human Rights and Constitutional Law, has visited temporary holding cells in Chula Vista and in Laredo and Del Rio, Texas, as counsel for children in the Flores case.

Kahn said limited access to phone calls is happening as concerning conditions increase inside the facilities.

“We’ve seen medical issues,” she said, “kids with coughs that weren’t being treated, kids with rashes, allergic reactions, kids who were not eating, who were losing weight, anxiety, a kid who was stuttering who had never stuttered before, kids who are regressing behaviorally, a child with autism who stopped talking.”

Kahn said she and other attorneys representing children in the Flores case are some of the only individuals outside of CBP who have access to the holding cells.

The level of access described by immigrants varied. Some said they were allowed no calls, only one phone call or that they were given only a couple minutes for the call.

Some also said they were not being provided with information on free legal services to help them navigate their asylum claim. The Flores Settlement requires that children be provided with such a list, as well as be informed about their rights.

Dozens of children detained at the border

Dozens of children this year have spent more than three days in CBP holding cells in San Diego despite guidelines which generally limited detentions to three days, inewsource reported earlier this year.

In more recent filings, families have described troubling conditions for children.

One woman detained at a Border Patrol station in Chula Vista in September with her three children and husband said they left their cell for only one hour a day and were not allowed to call their lawyer or other family members.

The woman’s youngest child had lost weight, developed a stutter and cried constantly, she wrote in a declaration on her 11th day in the holding cell.

“My daughter is only four years old. I don’t know how long she can survive in a cell,” the woman wrote. “She is so afraid. She doesn’t understand why we are here.”

In November, a 16-year-old detained in a station in Laredo said they were put in a cell alone and slept on a thin mattress on a bedframe with two aluminum blankets but no pillow.

The teen said bright lights were on all night and they had nothing to do but read posters on the wall and watch agents move outside the window.

“There is nothing else,” the teen said.

Agents told the teen they could have one phone call but did not provide access to the teen’s cell phone so they could look up a family member’s number or provide them with information for contacting an attorney, according to the teen’s declaration.

“I had one chance to use the phone and no number to call,” the teen wrote.

A hearing for the motion is scheduled for Dec. 18 in Los Angeles.

title: We sued the government over your right to see court records – and won
description:
The picture, like the court record, was incomplete.
Federal prosecutors asked Brindisi to seal key portions of the record that might shed light on why.
The people also have a First Amendment right to see the court record, and Syracuse.com has a First Amendment right to report it.
Where they find legitimate reasons to hold back materials from the public, judges should redact sensitive portions instead of sealing the whole document.
It is often in the interest of the prosecution or the defense to seal court records that may embarrass them or expose them to public criticism.
text:
In a victory for the public’s right to know, Syracuse.com | The Post-Standard won its legal fight to reveal secret federal court filings in the abandoned prosecution of an immigrant accused of assaulting a federal officer in December 2025.

U.S. District Judge Anthony Brindisi ruled Oct. 8, 2026, that he would unseal court documents that help explain why the government dropped its case against dairy worker Marvin Aguilar-Garcia. His case was one of hundreds of shoddy federal immigration cases nationwide to fall apart once they got to court.

Aguilar’s story, reported by staff writer Michelle Breidenbach in May, painted a picture of the Trump administration’s aggressive campaign to arrest and deport undocumented immigrants, even those with pending asylum claims or other legal status. The government knew Aguilar, who came here illegally from Guatemala in 2012, was living and working in Lewis County. Agents went to great lengths to lure him out of his home, stop his car on a pretext, and then charge him with a felony on phantom evidence.

The picture, like the court record, was incomplete. The government did not explain its abrupt decision to drop the charges five days before Aguilar’s trial was supposed to begin in February. Federal prosecutors asked Brindisi to seal key portions of the record that might shed light on why. Absent that knowledge, the public could reasonably conclude that the government was trying to hide official misconduct or simply bury a bungled case.

We applaud Brindisi for not letting that happen. Trust in the judicial system rests on the public’s ability to observe it. The judge’s careful ruling reveals where the government’s prosecution went off the rails without compromising the secrecy of the grand jury proceedings or the privacy rights of the officers involved.

The grand jury’s ‘no true bill’

The unsealed documents, described in detail by Brindisi in his ruling, show that the government could not produce evidence to support the key charge of the indictment: that Aguilar threw a book at Border Patrol Agent Trevor Baize, injuring him. Prosecutors attempted to get the grand jury to issue a new indictment, replacing the word “book” with “object.” The grand jury refused, issuing a “no true bill,” court records say.

That should have doomed the case. Instead, prosecutors were willing to go to trial on the first (erroneous) indictment. According to Brindisi’s ruling, prosecutors dropped the charges days after revealing to the defense that Baize had a history of anti-immigrant posts on social media.

Brindisi rejected the government’s argument that Baize’s privacy interest outweighed the public interest in knowing the content of his social media posts. “Conduct or speech by law enforcement officers reflecting potential bias have obvious public ramifications where those officers exercise governmental authority and appear as witnesses in criminal prosecutions,” the judge wrote.

Such conduct also likely violated Customs and Border Protection’s professional standards. In most workplaces, that would get you a reprimand. Baize got a promotion just before the trial was to begin, according to the unsealed court documents.

The principles at stake

Keeping portions of the court record secret “directly impeded Syracuse.com from carrying out its important responsibility of reporting fully, accurately, and contemporaneously on a newsworthy prosecution of paramount public concern,” lawyers for Syracuse.com argued in a July motion. The news organization was represented by attorney Michael J. Grygiel, of the Foley Hoag law firm, and Heather Murray, associate director of the Cornell Law School First Amendment Clinic.

Why did Syracuse.com go to such lengths to report on a case so far away, when the accused was sure to be deported anyway?

The presumption that court proceedings are open to the public is a bedrock principle of English common law and 250 years of U.S. jurisprudence. By observing the courts in action, the people get a more complete understanding of the judicial system and the facts necessary to assess its fairness.

The people also have a First Amendment right to see the court record, and Syracuse.com has a First Amendment right to report it.

The norms of federal jurisprudence are also under siege by the Trump administration. The conduct of this case by the U.S. Department of Justice shows once again why the federal judiciary should keep federal prosecutors on a short leash. In case after case, government lawyers have shown they cannot be trusted to tell the truth. Judges are the last line of defense against unethical prosecutions and outright misconduct. More than ever, they need to show some backbone.

Setting a precedent

Brindisi’s ruling could provide a roadmap for other judges confronted with requests from litigants to seal broad portions of the record from public view. It is a shockingly common occurrence.

A forthcoming academic study of 2 million federal civil cases found that judges grant 90% of motions to seal. Motions to intervene on behalf of unsealing the record — like Syracuse.com’s intervention in this case — are vanishingly rare. Third parties argued for transparency just 0.3% of the time in federal civil cases, a different study found.

Federal judges must do better to protect the public’s right to know. They should look skeptically upon motions to seal broad portions of the record, not rubber stamp them. Where they find legitimate reasons to hold back materials from the public, judges should redact sensitive portions instead of sealing the whole document.

It is often in the interest of the prosecution or the defense to seal court records that may embarrass them or expose them to public criticism. It is rarely in the interest of the public to hide those facts. In the vast majority of cases where a news organization like ours does not intervene, judges must advocate for maximum transparency and accountability. Their own legitimacy depends on it.

text:
BOSTON – ICE Boston removed Jean Leonard Teganya, 54, to Rwanda Nov 8. Teganya was convicted of two counts of immigration fraud and three counts of perjury in 2019 after an international investigation led by Homeland Security Investigations found he concealed his past involvement with the political party that incited the Rwandan Genocide in 1994 and its youth militia, the Interahamwe, which carried out much of the genocide.

Teganya was removed to Kigali, Rwanda, and handed over to local law enforcement officials to face justice in his home country.

“After decades of evasion, Teganya has finally returned home to Rwanda to face justice for his crimes. Dozens of witnesses bravely testified to atrocities he tried to conceal during the worst genocide since the Holocaust, and he was found guilty of his lies,” said HSI New England acting Special Agent in Charge Jeffrey Grimming. “The United States will not be a safe haven for those running from justice and HSI will work every day to uphold the integrity of our immigration system.”

Teganya was enrolled as a medical student at the National University of Rwanda before the genocide and was a member of the MRND political party, the ruling Hutu-dominated party that incited the genocide. The evidence at his criminal trial demonstrated that Teganya directly participated in the gruesome murders of at least three people from the Tutsi ethnic group who were hiding at the hospital and four Tutsi students he hunted down in his dormitory. Teganya also raped at least two Tutsi women and led teams of soldiers and Interahamwe who raped other Tutsi women and students. He further led these teams of soldiers and Interahamwe throughout the hospital to find Tutsi men, women, and children who were then hacked to death behind the maternity ward. The evidence at his criminal trial demonstrated that Teganya directly participated in the gruesome murders of at least three people from the Tutsi ethnic group at the hospital and four Tutsi students he found in his dormitory. Teganya also raped at least two Tutsi women hiding at the hospital and led teams of soldiers and Interahamwe who raped other Tutsis. He further led these teams of soldiers and Interahamwe throughout the hospital to find Tutsis who were then murdered behind the maternity ward.

“Jean Leonard Teganya committed terrible human rights abuses and then fraudulently deceived our immigration system in a cowardly attempt to evade justice for his horrific crimes,” said acting ICE Boston Field Office Director Joseph Sher. “ICE Boston will continue working with our federal partners to identify, arrest, and remove illegal aliens responsible for atrocities abroad, ensuring that our communities do not become a refuge for these dangerous criminals.” At the end of the genocide in mid-July 1994, Teganya fled Rwanda, eventually arriving in Canada. Canadian authorities determined that Teganya was not entitled to remain in Canada. After 15 years, Teganya evaded Canadian authorities and fled across the border into the United States. On Aug. 3, 2014, Teganya was encountered walking on foot after he crossed from Canada into Houlton, Maine. Teganya was taken into custody.

On July 1, 2019, Teganya was sentenced to 97 months in federal prison. Following the completion of his criminal sentence, Teganya was placed in immigration proceedings and, on March 30, was issued a final order of removal.

One of Teganya’s medical school classmates, Eric Tabaro Nshimiye, was recently convicted of perjury for lying during his testimony in Teganya’s criminal trial.

ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations conducted the removal to Rwanda and HSI New England investigated the criminal matter with the assistance of HSI’s Human Rights Violators and War Crimes Center. Significant assistance was provided by the Department of State Diplomatic Security Service Kigali.

Established in 2009, the HRVWCC furthers the government’s efforts to identify, locate, and prosecute human rights abusers in the United States, including those who are known or suspected to have participated in persecution, war crimes, genocide, torture, extrajudicial killings, female genital mutilation, and the use or recruitment of child soldiers.

Currently, HSI has more than 227 active investigations into suspected human rights violators and is pursuing more than 1,773 leads and removals cases involving suspected human rights violators from 95 different countries. Since 2003, the HRVWCC has issued more than 80,500 individual lookouts and stopped over 423 human rights violators and war crimes suspects from entering the U.S.

text:
A Princeton University doctoral student was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after attending a neuroscience conference in Washington, D.C., according to the university and members of her research lab.

Eva Yi Xie, a third-year Ph.D. student at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute, was detained by ICE on Thursday at an airport near Washington, D.C. and is believed to be being held in Chantilly, Virginia, according to The Daily Princetonian, the university's student newspaper.

The Brody Lab, a neuroscience research group at Princeton University, said in a post on X that Xie was detained at Ronald Reagan National Airport while returning from the Society for Neuroscience conference, where she had presented a research poster.

Read More on News

Princeton has arranged legal representation for Xie, university spokesperson Michael Hotchkiss told The Daily Princetonian.

Trump’s push for mass deportations has transformed ICE into a central force in the administration’s immigration crackdown, dramatically expanding arrests and removals across the country. ICE deported 483,200 people and made more than 491,000 immigration arrests in fiscal year 2026, the highest annual totals in the agency’s history, according to DHS data.

Although the administration says its campaign is aimed at enforcing immigration law and removing dangerous offenders, federal data and independent analyses show that many of those arrested have no criminal convictions, while students and immigrants who entered through legal pathways have also been caught up in the crackdown.

Xie emigrated from Shanghai, China, to the United States in 2016 and attended the Bronx High School of Science in New York, according to a 2020 profile in The Science Survey, the school's student newspaper. The profile said Xie initially struggled with English, but went on to become a finalist in the Regeneron Science Talent Search for research focused on using genomics to improve treatments for heart disease.

Newsweek has contacted Princeton University, ICE, and the Department of Homeland Security for comment via email outside office hours. The offices of New Jersey Senators Cory Booker and Andy Kim, as well as the government of New Jersey, have also been contacted for comment. Kim’s office and Princeton University declined to comment further on the case.

The Brody Lab said Xie sent a message to her lab colleagues on Slack asking for help on November 19 before they lost contact with her. The lab said her lawyers were working to secure her release.

Carlos Brody, a Princeton neuroscience professor who advises Xie, criticized her detention in a statement to The Daily Princetonian, describing her as a “law-abiding student.”

"Detaining her, with the intent of deporting her, makes no sense whatsoever. It is cruel, and it is our country shooting itself in the foot," he said.

Xie graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2024, with degrees in computer science and mathematics and a concentration in economics, according to her portfolio.

Princeton Graduate School Dean Rodney Priestley told neuroscience graduate students that the university would remain in contact with Xie’s family, legal team and colleagues as the situation developed, according to an email obtained by The Daily Princetonian.

It remains unclear what immigration status Xie held at the time of her detention.

Federal Prosecutors Dispute Need for Broader Disclosure Federal prosecutors have opposed the defense request for extensive additional investigative materials.
text:
Religious congregations seek fuller disclosure of undercover federal operations conducted during Minnesota's immigration enforcement surge, raising questions about government surveillance, freedom of association, religious liberty, and the limits of investigative authority.

MINNEAPOLIS, MN (November 20, 2026).

Three Twin Cities churches have entered a federal court dispute over government surveillance conducted during and after a major immigration enforcement operation in Minnesota, seeking additional disclosure about undercover activities involving religious and civic organizations.

The churches argue that information already revealed through criminal proceedings raises serious questions about the extent of federal monitoring and its potential effects on constitutionally protected activities.

The congregations involved are First Universalist Church and Hennepin Avenue United Methodist Church in Minneapolis, and St. John the Evangelist Episcopal Church in St. Paul.

Their involvement follows revelations that federal undercover agents attended meetings, monitored activists, and collected information during operations associated with immigration enforcement and protests in the Twin Cities.

The dispute is connected to a federal criminal case involving 15 people accused of conspiring to impede or injure federal officers.

The defendants have not been convicted merely because they were indicted, and the churches' filing does not establish that every surveillance activity under examination was unlawful.

Churches Enter Existing Criminal Proceedings

Attorney Irina Vaynerman of Groundwork Legal filed a friend-of-the-court brief Wednesday, November 18, on behalf of the three congregations.

The brief supports a request by defense attorney Kevin Riach for additional disclosure of government investigative materials.

Riach represents Isaac Sant, identified in the proceedings as a lead defendant.

In June, a federal grand jury charged 15 people in connection with protests and blockades around the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building.

Prosecutors allege that the defendants conspired to interfere with federal officers.

The indictment is an allegation of criminal conduct, not proof of guilt.

According to MPR News, information gathered through undercover participation in activist meetings and encrypted messaging groups forms a significant part of the government's case.

Defense attorneys have challenged the completeness of the materials prosecutors provided through the discovery process.

Discovery is the legal procedure through which parties obtain information relevant to a case, including evidence that may be important to the defense.

The churches are asking the court to consider the broader implications of information withheld or not yet disclosed.

Undercover Operations Extend Into Community Spaces

Documents described in the proceedings identify federal investigative activities under the names Operation Puppet Master and Project Whipple Shield.

According to MPR News, Homeland Security Investigations obtained years of financial records involving labor unions and sent undercover personnel to meetings at churches, libraries, parks, and union facilities.

The records also describe surveillance involving organizations engaged in opposition to immigration enforcement operations.

The disclosed activities include an undercover agent attending a Sunrise Movement meeting at First Universalist Church in December 2025.

A report from that meeting did not identify a crime but indicated that additional attendance was considered necessary to determine whether legal violations had occurred.

Other records describe agents observing activities associated with Hennepin Avenue United Methodist Church and attending a meeting at St. John the Evangelist Episcopal Church.

In one instance, an undercover agent reportedly recorded license plate information associated with vehicles outside a meeting.

These disclosures have generated concern because the locations involved were not merely public protest sites. They included places used for religious gatherings, community organizing, and civic participation.

However, the fact that federal investigators monitored an activity does not by itself establish that the monitoring violated the law. That question depends on the legal authority, investigative justification, methods used, and applicable constitutional protections.

Religious Leaders Describe Effects on Congregations

First Universalist Senior Minister Jen Crow told MPR News that the surveillance revelations have affected how members of her congregation approach church activities.

According to Crow, some members have become more cautious about unfamiliar individuals, while others have stopped attending in person.

She also described an incident in January in which she said agents repeatedly circled the church during a memorial service.

That account is attributed to Crow and should be distinguished from findings independently established by a court.

Her concerns illustrate one potential consequence of government surveillance: people who believe their participation in religious or civic activities is being monitored may become reluctant to attend gatherings or express their views.

That potential effect is commonly described in constitutional litigation as a chilling effect.

The First Amendment protects religious exercise, speech, peaceful assembly, and association.

Those protections do not automatically prevent law enforcement from investigating suspected criminal conduct. They do, however, establish important limits on government action directed at protected expression or association.

The central legal issue is whether the surveillance was supported by legitimate investigative objectives and conducted within constitutional boundaries.

Federal Prosecutors Dispute Need for Broader Disclosure

Federal prosecutors have opposed the defense request for extensive additional investigative materials.

In a September 10 filing cited by MPR News, Assistant U.S. Attorney Tory Sailer argued that the request was excessively broad and unnecessary for preparing the defense.

The government also raised concerns that releasing additional information about undercover operations could jeopardize agents and confidential informants.

Those arguments present a competing interest that the court must consider.

Law enforcement agencies sometimes rely on confidential investigative methods to examine suspected criminal conduct. Courts may limit disclosure of sensitive information when legal standards permit.

At the same time, defendants are entitled to information required for a fair trial, including material that may support their defense.

The churches contend that the public interest in understanding the surveillance extends beyond the immediate criminal charges.

A court considering these arguments must distinguish between evidence legally required for the defense, information protected by investigative privileges, and broader public demands for transparency.

An Unusual Coalition Raises Civil Liberties Concerns

The churches are not the only outside organizations questioning the scope of the surveillance.

MPR News reported that the Cato Institute, the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, and the Society for the Rule of Law previously submitted a brief supporting additional disclosure.

Their involvement is notable because the organizations represent legal and policy perspectives that do not always align with the political positions of immigration enforcement protesters.

The shared concern is the potential effect of broad government surveillance on constitutionally protected activity.

That concern does not resolve the defendants' criminal case or determine the legality of specific investigative methods.

It does demonstrate that questions about surveillance, civil liberties, and disclosure can extend across ideological divisions.

What the Court Must Determine

The immediate issue is whether the government must provide additional investigative records.

The broader controversy concerns the extent to which federal authorities monitored religious and civic organizations and whether those activities were appropriately limited to legitimate law enforcement purposes.

The disclosed materials establish that undercover investigative activities occurred. They do not establish the full scope of those activities or that every person or organization monitored was suspected of criminal wrongdoing.

The court has not been shown in the reviewed reporting to have issued a final ruling resolving the churches' concerns.

For Minnesota congregations, the outcome could influence confidence in the privacy of religious gatherings and community meetings.

For federal authorities, it may clarify the extent of disclosure required when undercover investigations intersect with protected speech, religious practice, and political association.

The case also presents a fundamental question for democratic governance: how should public institutions maintain the ability to investigate genuine threats while ensuring that lawful participation in religious and civic life does not become a basis for unjustified government scrutiny?

The federal court's response will determine the next stage of that dispute.

text:
Journalists working for MPR News, Sahan Journal, and independently allege that officers used pepper balls, chemical irritants, and tear gas against them while they documented a federal immigration operation. The lawsuit raises questions about press freedom and police crowd-control practices.

ST. PAUL, MN (November 20, 2026).

Three Minnesota photojournalists have filed a lawsuit against St. Paul police officials, alleging that officers used excessive force against them while they were documenting a federal immigration enforcement operation and the protests that followed in November 2025.

The lawsuit, reported Thursday, November 19, by the Minnesota Reformer, concerns an incident on November 25, 2025, in St. Paul's Payne-Phalen neighborhood.

The plaintiffs are Aaron Nesheim of Sahan Journal, Kerem Yücel of MPR News, and freelance photojournalist Timothy Evans.

They allege that St. Paul police officers fired pepper balls, deployed tear gas, and used pepper spray against journalists who were visibly engaged in newsgathering.

The allegations have not been established as judicial findings. The lawsuit initiates a legal process in which the defendants will have an opportunity to respond and contest the claims.

Immigration Operation Draws Protesters and Journalists

The confrontation occurred during a federal immigration enforcement operation on Rose Avenue.

According to the Minnesota Reformer's account, federal immigration agents attempted to arrest a man who fled into a residence.

A crowd gathered outside as the operation continued.

Journalists arrived to document the federal activity, the public response, and the conduct of law enforcement officers.

The three plaintiffs say they were carrying professional cameras and wearing visible press identification.

Evans was also wearing protective equipment identifying him as a member of the press.

The complaint alleges that the journalists were positioned apart from the main group of protesters when St. Paul police officers deployed crowd-control weapons.

According to the lawsuit, the officers' actions affected both demonstrators and journalists as police were leaving the area.

The distinction between demonstrators and journalists is central to the case.

Members of the press have the right to document events in public places, subject to lawful and constitutionally permissible restrictions. Their presence at a protest does not automatically make them participants in that protest.

At the same time, press identification does not exempt journalists from all lawful police orders or guarantee immunity from incidental exposure to crowd-control measures.

The legal dispute will depend on what officers did, what circumstances they faced, and whether their actions were justified under the law.

Journalists Describe Injuries

The complaint alleges that Yücel was sprayed with a chemical irritant at close range while photographing the scene.

He also alleges that officers struck him with pepper balls in the upper body.

According to the lawsuit, he experienced significant breathing difficulties and required ambulance transportation.

The complaint states that all three journalists experienced irritation affecting their eyes and respiratory systems.

Evans reportedly suffered bruising that persisted for approximately a month.

The plaintiffs also describe psychological effects following the confrontation and say they sought mental health treatment.

These accounts are allegations contained in the lawsuit and reported by the Minnesota Reformer. Their accuracy, the extent of any injuries, and the legal responsibility of individual officers remain matters for the proceedings.

Constitutional Claims and Police Accountability

The lawsuit alleges violations of the First, Fourth, and Fourteenth Amendments to the United States Constitution.

The First Amendment protects freedom of speech and the press.

The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures, including certain uses of force by government officers.

The Fourteenth Amendment provides constitutional protections that can be relevant to claims involving state and local government conduct.

The plaintiffs also assert claims involving assault and battery.

Police use-of-force cases are highly dependent on specific circumstances, including the conduct of officers and civilians, the nature of any threat, and whether the force used was objectively reasonable.

The plaintiffs contend that they were engaged in lawful newsgathering and were not threatening officers.

Their complaint alleges that the journalists were standing apart from protesters and were identifiable as press members.

Those assertions, if supported by evidence, could become important in evaluating the reasonableness of the officers' actions.

Police Chief Named in Lawsuit

The complaint names St. Paul Police Chief Axel Henry and alleges failures involving officer training and supervision.

The plaintiffs argue that inadequate preparation and oversight contributed to the alleged violations.

Such claims require evidence establishing the applicable legal standards and the relationship between supervisory conduct, departmental practices, and the alleged injuries.

The filing of a lawsuit against a police chief does not establish that the chief personally ordered or approved the conduct being challenged.

The Minnesota Reformer reported that a St. Paul Police Department spokesperson declined to comment because the matter involves pending litigation.

That response should not be characterized as an admission of wrongdoing.

The department's Civilian Internal Affairs Review Commission is also investigating the incident, according to the reporting.

The outcome of that review may provide additional information about officer conduct, departmental procedures, and possible administrative findings.

Press Freedom During Public Demonstrations

The case has implications extending beyond the three plaintiffs.

Photojournalists frequently work in unpredictable environments where protests, police operations, and confrontations can develop rapidly.

Their work provides the public with visual documentation of government actions and events that might otherwise remain poorly understood.

When journalists face force while carrying out that work, questions arise about whether police practices adequately distinguish between lawful newsgathering and conduct that may justify intervention.

A finding that officers intentionally targeted identifiable journalists without lawful justification would raise serious constitutional concerns.

However, the court must evaluate the evidence rather than assume the plaintiffs' allegations have already been proved.

The case also highlights the importance of police training concerning interactions with journalists during crowd-control operations.

Departments may need clear procedures addressing press identification, access to public areas, use-of-force decisions, and the treatment of journalists who are documenting police activity.

Plaintiffs Seek Damages and Court Intervention

The three journalists are seeking financial damages and attorney's fees.

They are also requesting injunctive relief intended to prevent future unconstitutional conduct against them.

An injunction would require a court to determine that the applicable legal standards for such relief have been met.

The lawsuit therefore seeks more than compensation for alleged injuries. It also asks the judiciary to address the possibility of future violations.

The litigation will provide an opportunity to examine evidence about the November 2025 operation, including officer actions, the journalists' locations, and the circumstances surrounding the deployment of chemical weapons.

For St. Paul, the case presents another test of public confidence in law enforcement accountability.

For Minnesota's news organizations, it raises concerns about the ability of reporters and photographers to document public events without facing unjustified interference.

The ultimate findings will depend on the evidence and the court's application of constitutional and state law.

Until then, the allegations remain disputed claims, and no determination of liability should be inferred from the filing.

title: 'Traumatizing': hunger striker in ICE detention tells of force-feeding ordeal - The Guardian
description:
The Trump administration responded to requests for comment by denying it had force-fed Cora Pérez.
Cora Pérez began a hunger strike in August to protest against his prolonged detention by federal immigration officials while his case plays out.
On Wednesday night, after weeks of communications, Cora Pérez was suddenly transferred to another detention center in Texas.
The Guardian’s reporting is based on court records, interviews, dozens of messages exchanged and an interview conducted with Cora Pérez via a facility phone.
In Cora Pérez and the Uzbek man’s cases, like in others, they did not have any legal representation to challenge the force-feeding requests.
text:
The text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food. If I don’t eat it, they put the tube in me to feed me.”

A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez, 32, said in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.

The Trump administration responded to requests for comment by denying it had force-fed Cora Pérez. But the detainee sent more details – and his is far from an isolated case.

Cora Pérez was one of two men on hunger striker at a Texas facility for whom ICE sought and received a federal judge’s permission to force-feed in recent weeks, a Guardian investigation found.

Cora Pérez and the other man were locked up inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an ICE detention facility in south Texas, just a few miles from the US-Mexico border, on the coast near where Elon Musk’s SpaceX launches rockets. Cora Pérez began a hunger strike in August to protest against his prolonged detention by federal immigration officials while his case plays out. At first he only drank water, then after three weeks, he says he began to drink one Ensure nutritional shake per day.

On 30 October, court records show ICE received permission to forcibly feed and hydrate him, and to restrain him while doing so.

The next day he says six guards at the center held him down, while medical staffers inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach – a process he called “traumatizing, both physically and psychologically”.

On 3 November, ICE then received permission from a federal judge to force-feed another hunger striker at Port Isabel, from Uzbekistan, federal court records show. The DHS says the Uzbek man has not been subjected to the practice, however.

On Wednesday night, after weeks of communications, Cora Pérez was suddenly transferred to another detention center in Texas. His relative says neither of them were alerted to any plans to transfer him, or a reason for it.

The DHS did not specify why Cora Pérez was transferred, adding that ICE makes custody determinations on a “case-by-case” basis based on “various factors”.

The revelations come as ICE’s detention practices continue to come under fire amid allegations of mistreatment, and as an increasing number of sporadic hunger strikes have been breaking out in ICE facilities across the country.

The two men’s cases in Texas, revealed here for the first time, are some of the most recent instances of government lawyers seeking a federal judge’s permission, as required by ICE policy, and receiving the go-ahead to force-feed detained hunger strikers. The Guardian’s reporting is based on court records, interviews, dozens of messages exchanged and an interview conducted with Cora Pérez via a facility phone. It further reveals how the Trump administration is increasingly obtaining such court orders to force-feed detained immigrants, a secretive practice widely condemned as torture by human rights organizations and medical ethics groups.

Detainees driven to hunger strike are typically using it as a last resort to protest against poor conditions and the Trump administration’s preference for arrest and prolonged detention while their civil immigration cases proceed through the system.

Cora Pérez said detention center staff inserted the feeding tube and left it in his body, a not uncommon practice, according to experts, and introduced nutrition – first a “clear liquid”, followed by a “milky liquid”, he recalled – through the tube twice more that day, before he cracked and said he broke his hunger strike, citing what he called “horrific torture”. He began voluntarily drinking nutritional shakes the following day, he said.

“ICE does not hold back on anything, and they do anything they want, like we have seen, even killing their own US citizens,” he wrote to the Guardian, referring to the fatal shootings of Renee Good by an ICE officer and Alex Pretti by a border patrol officer in January of this year during Trump’s pivotal immigration crackdown on Minneapolis.

Detained hunger strikers subjected to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding, have rarely spoken out about their cases or revealed their identities, much less while still detained. Cora Pérez’s messages offer a rare glimpse at conditions inside a detention center’s restricted medical unit where hunger strikers and suicidal detainees are held.

“They just took [the Uzbek man] in an ambulance after [him] fainting in front of the medical lobby where they take our vitals, our weight and our temperature,” Cora Pérez said in an alarmed message last Monday morning.

The Uzbek man was returned the following day to the facility, Cora Pérez said.

“I see him every day because I see him in the room in front of me, but they don’t let us talk to each other,” he added.

The Guardian independently confirmed the Uzbek’s man identity but is not publicly naming him, because efforts to contact him have been unsuccessful. The man arrived at the Mexico-US border in April 2022 and was released into the country while navigating his immigration case. He was arrested by border patrol officials in April of this year and placed in detention. The man does not appear to have any criminal record and the DHS did not point to any criminal history.

In a statement, DHS said that after they received the court’s permission to force-feed the Uzbek man, he “has voluntarily taken in fluids and there has been NO force-feeding or forced hydration”.

Security operations at the sprawling Port Isabel facility in Los Fresnos, Texas, are run by a private prison company, Akima Global Services, while healthcare is primarily handled by government workers.

“ICE respects detainees’ rights to exercise self-expression and medical autonomy by refusing nourishment and medical care,” the DHS said in a statement. “ICE Health Services Corps may provide involuntary medical treatment only to prevent imminent life-threatening harm or death. Medical staff may provide treatment only to medically stabilize the patient, bringing the detainee outside the imminent harm, incapacitation, or death.”

The US attorney’s office in the southern district of Texas, which represented ICE in its force-feeding request, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Virginia-headquartered Akima Global Services, and its parent company Nana Regional Corporation, based in Alaska, did not respond to a request for comment.

Force-feeding cases are shrouded in secrecy. After a detainee launches a hunger strike, ICE often sequesters them in medical isolation cells for monitoring, according to ICE’s detention standards. The DHS said that ICE continues to offer hunger strikers three meals per day.

After a certain period of not eating, which varies per case, ICE will request a federal judge’s permission to force-feed the hunger striker. Many court records, and sometimes entire court dockets, are sealed and hidden from public view. In Cora Pérez and the Uzbek man’s cases, like in others, they did not have any legal representation to challenge the force-feeding requests.

The Guardian found at least five instances in which ICE requested permission to force-feed hunger strikers in Port Isabel since January 2025. The federal judge who ruled on Cora Perez and the Uzbek man, Rolando Olvera, has similarly ordered in at least three other cases, records show. Olvera’s judicial assistant said the court had no comment for this article.

ICE is known to have requested permission to force-feed at least 21 detainees across the US since January 2025, the Guardian found, but the number is probably higher since an unknown number of records and dockets remain sealed, unsearchable and not feasible to locate. Most of the cases coinciding with the second Trump administration and tracked by the Guardian are in Texas and Florida, with others in Georgia, Arizona and Washington state. Under the Biden administration, ICE force-feeding requests were also made in Louisiana and California.

Amy Zeidan, an emergency medicine physician based in Atlanta and an expert on healthcare in immigration detention, said force-feeding hunger strikers can amount to “torture”, and lead to significant psychological distress. She also said it was a violation of medical ethics.

“Essentially it’s like inserting a straw into your nose,” Zeidan said. “You have a gag reflex, so most times people will gag, and that’s really uncomfortable. And people will even vomit repeatedly if it continues to irritate their gag reflex.”

Zeidan added that the forceful insertion of a feeding tube can lead to the swelling of the nostrils and the throat, and even tear them, leading to bleeding.

“It is like torture – somebody is doing a painful procedure to you that you don’t consent to,” Zeidan added. “Autonomy is a fundamental principle of medical ethics. We can’t do something to patients if they don’t want to, even if we think it’s good for them.”

There are numerous cells and rooms inside the Port Isabel medical unit, including isolation cells and shared rooms for ill detainees, according to Cora Pérez. In recent weeks, there were five people in the Port Isabel medical isolation cells used for hunger striking or suicidal detainees, he added. He described the cells as “practically freezing”, constantly surveilled with a security camera, and with just a bed, toilet and sink. As well as himself, he says he observed the Uzbek man, a Middle Eastern man, a “tall” eastern European man and a Black man of unknown nationality in the isolation cells. Unit detainees are escorted by facility staff to showers and sometimes receive yard and television access, he said.

Cora Pérez worries for the other detainees. The Black man, whose identity or nationality he does not know, seems to have “serious mental health problems”, Cora Pérez observed.

“He harms himself and spends the night yelling and hitting the door, and does not let anyone sleep,” he said.

The Guardian has independently confirmed the eastern European and Middle Eastern men’s identities, but is not publicly naming them because efforts to contact them have been unsuccessful. The DHS did not comment on the other men inside the medical isolation unit, saying they could not comment without the Guardian providing their identities.

Cora Pérez had left his son and parents in Cuba and requested asylum at the Mexico-US border in 2023, according to a relative who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity due to fear of retaliation by immigration authorities. Cora Pérez went to live with the relative in Florida, where he worked in maintenance at a hotel and as a food delivery worker, he said.

In March 2025, Cora Pérez was arrested by local police and later convicted of two misdemeanors, including “breach of peace” and “obstructing an officer without violence”, according to local records. He was sentenced to two months in jail, his relative said. But ICE placed a hold on him and as he was being released in June 2025, immigration officials took him into custody – a common system – and soon transferred him to the Adelanto detention center, a privately-run facility in California.

Days in Adelanto turned to weeks, then months, then a over year, according to a federal court order denying one of his petitions requesting his release. His multiple requests to immigration and ordinary federal courts for release from detention, while he fights his asylum case, have been unsuccessful.

“All his claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and he will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law,” DHS said. “Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the US.”

In August, he stopped eating to protest against his protracted detention.

“I have spent two birthdays behind ICE’s bars,” he wrote. “The reasons I did the hunger strike in Adelanto are for my political asylum, for the time I have spent detained, [and] because I have a 14-year-old son who is starving to death in Cuba because he does not have my help.

“Also due to the mistreatment by the officials,” he added.

Cora Pérez did not tell his family about the hunger strike, so as not to further worry them. It was not until he was transferred to Port Isabel in late September that he confessed to his relative he had been on a prolonged hunger strike.

“He doesn’t share details so that I won’t get upset or worry,” the relative said in a phone interview.

Cora Pérez’s mother, who is in Cuba, “does not know anything, because she is sick, and with his detention she has gotten worse”, the relative added, between tears. “I don’t want her nor his grandmother to know anything about it,” the relative added.

On 30 October, the federal prosecutors requested permission for ICE to forcibly feed and hydrate Cora Pérez. Hours later, a federal judge approved the procedures without hearing from Cora Pérez. Cora Pérez told the Guardian in various instances he felt it was unfair he was not given the opportunity to present his case to the judge before the judge approved his force-feeding.

“It’s very disturbing because the judge is basically making a decision on information that is only provided by one side,” said Linus Chan, a professor of clinical law and the director of the detainee rights clinic at the University of Minnesota law school. “That just seems ridiculous.”

Cora Pérez was force-fed the following day, he said in his messages and in a phone call, adding that he did not physically resist because he “had seen a lot of mistreatment of others detained”.

“[ICE does] what they want with us, whatever they want, because a federal judge gave them permission,” he added. “I have suffered on the island [of Cuba] and now at the hands of ICE.”

After asking Cora Pérez about the DHS’s denials that he was force-fed, he repeated that he was. “Brother, ICE says and does whatever they want. They deny, punish, retaliate and do everything at their own will. They have even sent Cubans to Africa,” he said.

The number of people detained by ICE has soared under the Trump administration. And due to policy and legal changes, tens of thousands of people are forced to stay in detention for long periods while they fight their immigration cases.

Chan, from the University of Minnesota, says prolonged detention and delays in their cases lead to logical conclusion. “That’s exactly when people protest,” he said.

“And the only form of protest, for many of these people, is a hunger strike,” he said.

As Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown continues and people are detained as a first resort while their cases play out, Chan said: “Hunger strikes will become more common.”

ROANOKE, Va. (WDBJ) - A father and grandfather who says he has lived in the United States for decades is afraid to leave for work after seeing friends and coworkers detained.

The man spoke with WDBJ7 in Spanish outside his home. He did not share his name, country of origin or immigration status.

During the interview, a car pulled up to drop off food. Before he knew why it was there, he appeared visibly shaken and knocked on the wall of his home to alert people inside.

Despite his fears, he wanted to speak about what he and others in his community are experiencing.

The man said he came to the United States seeking a better life after leaving a country affected by crime. Now, he said, he is troubled by how he sees people being treated here.

He said he no longer wants to go to work after seeing videos on his phone of people being detained, including friends and coworkers. He said he is worried about expenses but would rather lose his job than be detained.

He said people should be treated as human beings, not animals.

He also said a neighbor he had known for about 20 years was detained for three months. He described the neighbor as a good person and said the detention brought sadness to the neighborhood.

The man has three children and seven grandchildren, and young children were inside the home during the interview. He expressed concern about how witnessing detentions could affect children.

Addressing those he believes are responsible for the treatment he described, he said they would one day have to answer to God.

WDBJ7 again reached out to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for comment and to ask how many people have been detained in Roanoke this week. WDBJ7 also reached out to Congressman Ben Cline and has not received a response.

text:
iPost wins FOIL lawsuit against Orchard Park

Investigative Post sued Orchard Park over its refusal to release police reports involving calls to immigration agencies. Supreme Court Judge Dennis Ward this week ruled in our favor.

Share on

Orchard Park town hall. Image via WKBW.

In September 2025, Orchard Park police conducted a traffic stop of a vehicle that contained migrants. The encounter led to a call to a federal immigration agency, and criminal charges filed against the driver.

In January, Investigative Post filed a Freedom of Information request with the Orchard Park Police Department for any arrest or incident reports where officers responded to a scene and then called a federal immigration agency, be it ICE, Border Patrol or Customs and Border Protection. Arrest and incident reports are generally considered public records.

But Orchard Park denied the request — and a subsequent appeal — arguing that releasing the documents would “interfere with present or future judicial proceedings.” Investigative Post then sued.

On Tuesday, a Supreme Court judge ruled that Orchard Park can no longer keep details about that incident secret.

Investigative Post reported in December that local law enforcement in the Buffalo suburbs and Niagara County regularly contacts federal immigration agencies. Such contacts have resulted in multiple local ICE detentions, Investigative Post found, effectively turning local police into an arm of the Trump administration’s crackdown on migrants.

We followed up on that reporting by requesting records from Orchard Park.

During an October hearing, an attorney representing the town — Michael Perley of the firm Hurwitz Fine — argued that releasing and publishing the incident report would alert the driver and the other passengers that police and prosecutors know who they are. That might encourage them not to show up at future court hearings, or not to cooperate in the case with police, Perley argued.

Supreme Court Judge Dennis Ward, after reviewing the incident report in question, didn’t buy it.

“Those witnesses already know that the prosecution has their names,” he wrote in his Tuesday ruling. “The claim that the publication of their names would increase the likelihood of their lack of cooperation with the prosecution or the court is speculative, at best.”

Ward wrote that if he ruled in Orchard Park’s favor, the public hypothetically could be denied access to every police report that names someone who isn’t a criminal defendant.

“To provide a blanket shield on the disclosure of such documents would eliminate the availability to the public of such information in every case where the name of any witness was included,” Ward wrote. “That would defeat the intent of the FOIL statute. At that point, the exception would swallow the rule.”

Ward ordered Orchard Park to release the records by this coming Sunday.

Investigative Post was represented in the case by Kyle Clauss and Heather Murray of the Cornell Law School First Amendment Clinic. In a statement, Clauss called the ruling “a win for government transparency.”

“Rather than promptly disclosing the record as FOIL required, the Town of Orchard Park fought for months to keep it hidden without any valid basis for doing so,” Clauss said.

“The Erie County Supreme Court recognized that agencies must provide a specific justification for withholding records from public scrutiny, and the Town of Orchard Park failed to meet this burden.”

Perley did not respond to a request for comment.

Ward ordered Orchard Park to release the report by the end of the week. He denied a request to award attorney’s fees to the Cornell Law School. Clauss said he’s considering appealing that part of the ruling.

Although court officials are not supposed to interfere with ICE activity under the PROTECT Act, Ramachandran said court officials can enforce the same court rules they have for everyone else, but they do not.

text:
Despite the passing of the recent PROTECT Act, immigration enforcement officers are still going into courthouses and taking people into custody, the head of a Framingham-based non-profit agency that advocates on behalf of immigrants and for human rights.

The actions of ICE officers continuing to go into court is scaring people from going to court because they're afraid they'll be taken into custody and deported, said CASA MetroWest Worker Center co-Director Leela Ramachandran said.

"Folks are doing their best to follow through and go to court and get whatever method of justice they can," she said.

Gov. Maura Healey in August signed the PROTECT Act, which, in part is designed to prevent ICE agents from arresting people in "sensitive" locations, such as hospitals and schools with just a civil warrant. That includes courts. ICE can still arrest those who have federal criminal warrants.

ICE arrests continue at Massachusetts courthouses

Ramachandran said there have been several documented incidents of violations in courthouses throughout the state, including in Framingham and Marlborough. She said there have been at least five incidents locally.

Just on Wednesday, an unidentified person was taken into custody in Marlborough District Court. Ramachandran did not have any details on the person who was taken into custody.

A spokesperson for ICE did not return a call and email seeking comment. Marlborough District Court Clerk Magistrate Jennifer Lennon also could not be reached for comment.

More: Framingham MA volunteers track ICE activity. What they say is happening

ICE concerns are changing how people approach court

Ramachandran said there was a recent example of a man who was living out of state who had a warrant in Framingham. He rented a vehicle, drove here, found out ICE was in the courthouse and did not go in. He waited all day before driving back home because he was afraid to go to court.

He returned the following day on a bus and again found out ICE was in the courthouse and left again with an outstanding warrant for his arrest.

"He was weighing what could happen and left," she said. "He was trying to do the right thing."

Although court officials are not supposed to interfere with ICE activity under the PROTECT Act, Ramachandran said court officials can enforce the same court rules they have for everyone else, but they do not. She said ICE agents are constantly seen in courtrooms using their phones and texting people, which is not allowed in court.

Ramachandran said those in court to observe ICE are not allowed to text, just like others in the courthouse. She also alleged that court security officers show security footage to ICE agents. Court officers are not supposed to assist ICE agents under the provisions of the PROTECT Act.

More: Anxiety ramps up among Framingham immigrant community over reports of ICE raids

Framingham District Court Clerk Magistrate Robert Jubinville could not be reached for comment on Thursday, Nov. 19.

Ramachandran was among a large group of people who protested outside of the State House on Wednesday, Nov. 18 seeking to have Healey order stricter enforcement of the PROTECT Act.

A spokesperson for Healey could not be reached for comment on Thursday.

The fear of ICE in courts are making some people skip court, Ramachandran said. This is more than those who have criminal cases, she said. They include people obtaining restraining orders or witnesses for cases.

"Now, all of these folks are having concerns if they go to court, they'll be taken," she said. "They're choosing to stay home."
