text:
New York Attorney General Letitia James sued Holiday Inn parent IHG Hotels & Resorts, a Rochester hotel owner and a renovation contractor, on November 19, 2026, alleging that dozens of immigrant workers were forced to work without pay and threatened with deportation while renovating the property.

Workers allegedly endured schedules totaling as many as 112 hours a week and lived with their families in abandoned hotel rooms without heat, electricity, or running water. The state accuses IHG of continuing to benefit from the renovations after its managers learned about the conditions during a June 2024 inspection.

The dispute stems from renovations that began in spring 2023 at a downtown Rochester hotel owned by Nayan Patel and his company, Horizon Edge Hospitality. The property operated under a Holiday Inn franchise agreement that required improvements overseen by IHG.

Attorney Advertising

On June 14, 2024, IHG managers inspected the hotel's seventh floor, photographed the rooms and spoke with workers who said they had gone at least eight months without wages and faced threats of deportation, according to the complaint.

The managers relayed their findings to an IHG regional vice president. Four days later, the executive emailed Patel describing the workers as "squatters" who posed security and reputational risks to the Holiday Inn brand and instructed the owner to remove them.

IHG subsequently offered to restore the hotel's access to its reservation system, extended a deadline for Patel to pay more than $96,000 in overdue fees, and waived over $13,000 in interest. Company officials allegedly failed to investigate the workers' accounts or report them through IHG's internal reporting system.

Under the federal Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act, businesses can face civil liability for knowingly benefiting from ventures they knew or should have known involved forced labor. James is invoking that provision against IHG over its alleged knowledge of the Rochester workers' treatment.

Attorney Advertising

IHG disputes the accusations. In a statement reported by Reuters, the company condemned human trafficking and said the hotel owner and contractor should be held responsible for any violations of the law. It also emphatically denied having knowledge of the serious misconduct alleged in the lawsuit.

Contractor Roman Petrik and his company, Exterior Hotel Improvement, recruited workers from several states and countries, promising hourly wages and housing at the property. Payments allegedly stopped after the first two weeks, although employees continued working long hours to meet renovation deadlines.

One worker who was promised $18 an hour spent approximately 29 weeks working an average of 68 hours per week. State investigators calculated that he should have received about $30,506 but was paid only $2,200.

When workers demanded their wages or stopped working, Petrik allegedly threatened to have them deported. Patel is accused of making similar threats, claiming connections to immigration authorities and warning that workers could be removed from the country without receiving their earnings.

Living conditions deteriorated after workers and their children were moved to the hotel's abandoned seventh floor in September 2023 to accommodate paying guests. Rooms lacked functioning toilets, showers, heating, and electricity, while pests and vermin infested much of the floor. Some workers became ill, and at least three were allegedly evicted after demanding payment.

State investigators also accuse Petrik of repeatedly sexually assaulting a female worker after threatening to withhold her wages unless she complied with his demands. The woman eventually fled the hotel without receiving her pay and became homeless, according to the filing.

Additional claims against Patel, Petrik and their companies involve alleged violations of New York labor and human rights laws, including wage violations, retaliation and sexual harassment.

The Rochester property was rebranded as a Wyndham in January 2025. City officials closed the hotel in June 2026 following fire code and other violations.

text:
Sen. Elissa Slotkin is firing back at the Justice Department for threatening to prosecute her for recent comments she made about the need for congressional oversight.

In a letter to Slotkin publicly shared last week, U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz of Texas wrote that Slotkin’s recent “deterrence message” urging young people to think twice about working for the Trump administration may be “unlawful.” Reitz also told her she could be subject to sanctions and other “significant legal consequences” if she does not preserve all communications relevant to her “intent to weaponize congressional investigations.”

Slotkin, who serves on the Senate’s Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, is among the lawmakers who have made clear their plans to hold the Trump administration accountable for possible misconduct once the party takes control of Congress next year.

She hit back in a letter of her own to Reitz on Wednesday, noting that “in addition to my First Amendment rights, as a United States Senator, oversight is an important constitutional responsibility,” and telling Reitz, “Your threat of investigation is baseless, and you should withdraw your letter immediately.”

More articles

Slotkin is also one of the six Democratic lawmakers who cited military law in a 90-second video last year, reminding those in the defense and intelligence sectors to “refuse illegal orders” amid President Donald Trump’s deployment of troops to major U.S. cities for crime and immigration enforcement operations.

In the face of continued threats from the Trump administration, the lawmakers doubled down on their message in a press conference Thursday.

“It was important for us to come together a year later to say: number one, we stand behind the video we made. Number two, we won’t be intimidated out of calling out threats to our democracy,” Slotkin said Thursday. “We stand behind our men and women in uniform for the amazing work that they do, and I think we feel strongly that if this is the thing we need to do to stand up for the country we love, we have no problem doing that.”

In response to the video, Trump nicknamed the lawmakers — including Slotkin, Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona, Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado, Rep. Chris Deluzio and Rep. Chrissy Houlahan of Pennsylvania, and Rep. Maggie Goodlander of New Hampshire — the “Seditious Six” and in social media posts called for their executions.

The fallout from the video was immediate.

Slotkin said she received threatening messages and that her father’s house was swatted shortly before his death. Other lawmakers also spoke about their family’s fear for their safety.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth attempted to censure Kelly, demote his military rank and decrease his pension as punishment for his involvement in the video, which Hegseth argued was “conduct unbecoming an officer and a gentleman.” A federal judge in February blocked the Pentagon’s punishment of Kelly, which Hegseth has appealed.

Trump continues to rail against the lawmakers and the video. As recently as last week, the president again called for their prosecution in a social media post.

text:
TALLAHASSEE, Fla. (WCTV/Gray Florida Capital Bureau) - Florida’s capital city is threatening to end its cooperation with ICE. But state officials have a warning: Becoming a sanctuary city is illegal here.

Florida’s attorney general said a city does not have to sign a 287(g) agreement with ICE, but if one is already signed, like the city of Tallahassee has, backing out could come with consequences.

In the shadow of the state capitol, Tallahassee’s city commission voted 5-0 on Wednesday to consider ending their agreement with ICE, signed by the police chief without the input of the commission.

In response, Florida Governor-elect Byron Donalds said he won’t allow Tallahassee to become a sanctuary city.

Attorney General James Uthmeier echoed that sentiment.

“I’ve heard rumblings that there’s some localities that are looking at their 287 obligations here in Florida. I don’t write the law, I enforce it,” Uthmeier said. “We are always going to be a rule of law state.”

Florida politics:

Uthmeier sent a letter to the City of Doral, saying that if a city tears up an agreement with ICE without “extenuating circumstances,” they “likely” violate the law against becoming a sanctuary city.

“Local governments around the state do have Florida law statutory obligations to engage in best efforts to support the federal government in its mission,” he said.

Florida CFO Blaise Ingoglia said state law enforcement agencies might step in to conduct immigration enforcement in the capital city, like they did during a major raid in 2025.

The chair of Florida’s Republican party posted on social media that Tallahassee’s Democratic commissioners went “too far” and that the reconsideration might “end poorly.”

“And now, they have placed Amendment 3 on us to reduce our budgets, even further straining our budget to have an unfunded mandate to provide federal civil immigration services. I don’t think it’s tenable,” Tallahassee Mayor Jeremy Matlow said.

On November 7th, ICE agents in Los Angeles took a man in their custody to Adventist Health White Memorial Medical Center in Boyle Heights, a neighborhood which is more than 90 percent Hispanic and Latino.

ICE, the hospital, and local activists dispute much of what happened that day. On social media, some activists alleged that ICE, when not given free rein of the hospital, purposefully retaliated against the community. Regardless of which combination of actions happened and with what intent, three things occurred which no one really disputes.

First, ICE agents blocked access to the Adventist Health White’s Emergency Room for approximately two hours. According to the hospital:

Federal agents brought a person in their custody to our emergency department, and we cared for that patient with dignity and privacy, as we do for every patient. When agents formed a line across our ambulance entrance, which we did not request nor authorize, we diverted ambulances to nearby hospitals for about two hours to ensure every patient received timely care.

“White Memorial,” the hospital spokesperson insisted, “does not participate in immigration enforcement. We know last night frightened our neighbors. No matter what happens outside our doors, everyone who comes inside is our patient, and our focus will only be on that patient, and it will not change.”

Second, around the same time, local residents got word that ICE was at the hospital. As has happened across Southern California, Minneapolis, and around the nation in recent years, rapid response community defense measures kicked in. As Boyle Heights Beat reported, activists on the scene included Abraham Zavala of the group Union del Barrio. Zavala, who was born at Adventist Health White (as were his children), described it as “sacred ground.” At least two protesters, both of whom are U.S. citizens, were then detained by ICE, according to the Boyle Heights Immigration Rights Network.

And third, the intended damage was done: ICE wanted people to be frightened and they are, understandably, frightened. We will never know if any (or how many) people died during those two hours when the ER was not available at Adventist Health White. We will never know if someone’s life will be shortened by months or years because they couldn’t access emergency care that Saturday night. And we certainly won’t ever know who didn’t seek care at all that night because they saw on TikTok or on the local news that ICE had blocked access to their neighborhood hospital.

It may make Latinos think twice about getting medical care, or possibly forgo it entirely—especially if their immigration status makes them vulnerable.

ICE blocking that ER is a very tangible example of how medical racism manifests: armed agents of the state not only threatened to arrest anyone seeking care in the hospital, but they physically blocked access to all medical care in a Latino neighborhood. Such nasty work is rarely done so brazenly, and ICE’s harm that night is just a beginning.

How that harm will manifest is unpredictable. It may make Latinos think twice about getting medical care, or possibly forgo it entirely—especially if their immigration status makes them vulnerable. It may make undocumented family members less likely to accompany their ill relatives to the hospital, resulting in potentially substandard care. If racism is, as Ruth Wilson Gilmore writes, “the state-sanctioned or extralegal production and exploitation of group-differentiated vulnerability to premature death,” the seed planted that one night will likely result in medical health disparities and in needlessly premature deaths.

Narratives entwining health and racism are powerful. I grew up not too far from Boyle Heights, in the city of Oxnard, another majority-Mexican American community. The threat of raids and the occupation of a hospital ER will, no doubt, make worse an ongoing problem. Too many children in my hometown are not going to school because their parents fear some member of their family will be abducted en route. When I talk to Latinx medical providers—from a dentist in Oxnard to an eye doctor in Queens, New York—they tell me how empty their once-full calendars have become. Many of their Latinx patients are simply forgoing teeth cleanings or eye exams (or pap smears or mammograms) because the narrative is working: ICE can grab you anywhere, so you better stay put as much as possible. (Similarly, a recently deported gay immigrant told me that when he was cooped up for months avoiding ICE, he stopped taking the HIV-prevention medication PrEP, and then became HIV-positive.) In just one night, ICE amplified the narrative that seeking medical care can cost you the ultimate health penalty: arrest, possible deportation, and separation from your loved ones.

This is not a new situation in America, and it reminds me of a narrative born from the too-short life and tragic death of Dr. Charles Drew. Despite only living about 46 years. Dr. Drew was one of the most accomplished African American physicians in history. The narrative of his death also bloomed in predictable ways.

Like many Black children of my age, I learned about the mythology of Dr. Drew as a child, and was wowed and chilled by the irony of his death.

Prior to enrolling in medical school at McGill in the late 1920s, young Drew had already worked teaching biology and chemistry at the university level. Upon completing his MD, he joined the faculty of Howard Medical School and became a surgeon at Freedman’s Hospital in D.C., where he dedicated himself to the health of Black people. He then pursued a Doctor of Science at Columbia, where he wrote his dissertation, Banked Blood: A Study on Blood Preservation. While blood banks existed, they were not very effective. Medical science and the lay public had long imagined different races of people to have different types of blood. Even though the four major blood types (A,B, AB and O) had been discovered at the turn of the 20th century, many scientists and scientific organizations nonsensically segregated blood by race. Primitive blood banks had been used in World War I, but not knowing what blood type the wounded possessed (“dog tags” didn’t start listing blood type until the 1940s), combined with the crude storage techniques, made shock and infection common, which rendered transfusions of limited use.

Yet, despite his enormous achievements, racism haunted Drew throughout his career and—through the power of narrative—long after his death.

In the 1930s, Dr. Drew made a major breakthrough which broadly benefited all of humanity: he discovered how to separate blood plasma from the red and white cells of blood, and how to store it safely in such a way that it could be used for up to two months. Because anyone could be given plasma in an emergency, regardless of their blood type, his findings exponentially increased the life-saving capacity of blood transfusions. He also invented the “bloodmobile,” expanding how donations could be collected. Thus, Dr. Drew became the “father of the modern blood bank,” and the Allied Powers used his techniques to save countless lives in WWII.

Yet, despite his enormous achievements, racism haunted Drew throughout his career and—through the power of narrative—long after his death.

Drew was appointed the first director of the American Red Cross’s blood bank program in 1941. However, when the powers that be insisted that blood from “Negro donors” be rejected unless it was stored separately, he resigned in 1942.

Every year for more than a decade, Dr. Drew would travel to a free clinic in Tuskegee, Alabama, providing free surgery for poor Black people. In 1950, he and three other Black doctors drove more than 700 miles from D.C. to perform this service. On the last night of the clinic, he worked overnight in the operating theater. Then, he got into his car, drove home, and fell asleep at the wheel. After flipping several times, the car crashed in a field.

The other three doctors in the car with him that night suffered minor injuries, but Dr. Drew was in a bad way. And here, many Black children my age likely heard some version of the following myth:

Dr. Drew was taken to the nearest hospital, and was denied a blood transfusion…even though he had invented the process for using plasma in this way.

Or, Dr. Drew was taken to the nearest hospital, and they had his blood type…but the hospital wouldn’t give it to him, because it was “white blood” and they didn’t have any “Negro blood.”

Or, Dr. Drew was taken to the nearest hospital, which was segregated…and they were out of “Negro beds,” and while being transported to a Negro hospital, he died in the ambulance.

In truth, according to the three other doctors who were with him that night, Dr. Drew received immediate and competent care at the nearest hospital. Dr. John Ford, his friend who survived the crash, said Drew’s injuries were so severe that nothing could have saved him.

But the myths were born because they revealed much that was true (in the manner that “myths” are not false stories, but stories which reveal broad truths about history and society). Dr. Drew had been pushed out of the American Red Cross because of the segregation of “Negro blood” (a policy the organization continued until after his death). Black people routinely did die in the Jim Crow south because there weren’t “Negro beds” available, because the best resourced hospitals were segregated, and because of longer ambulance ride times. And Dr. Drew himself was a victim of the “state-sanctioned or extralegal production and exploitation of group-differentiated vulnerability to premature death” at least in part because of racism. Consider that he traveled to Tuskegee (a city synonymous with another horrific instance of medical racism) because there was not sufficient healthcare there for Black Americans, that he had to work all night because of this paucity of care, and that he was forced to drive home exhausted because there were few or no motels for Black people on his segregated driving route.

Narratives play a huge role in revealing fundamental truths, regardless of the exact incident which may incite them. Whether or not individual ICE agents meant to intimidate Latinos on November 7th is irrelevant; care was suppressed and people were made to feel intimidated in ways that will resonate in lethal ways for years to come. Similarly, how exactly Dr. Drew died did not stop African Americans, hearing of the death of the most prominent Black doctor of his time, from understanding that racism played a role in it. When racism and access to medical care collide, it is not only the actual subpar care that kills people, it is also the narratives that then affect people’s behavior. This manifests as the person who doesn’t call 911 because they’re worried the first responder might arrest their undocumented mother. Or the Black person afraid they have a sexually-transmitted infection who doesn’t trust going to a clinic. Or a would-be patient too frightened to approach a hospital because they have good reason to believe they may be made to feel unwelcome (or turned away entirely) if they are transgender, immigrant, or Black.

Narratives are powerful. One I have been suspicious of is the story that the Democratic Party is the anti-ICE party. Many mid-term voters cast their ballots for Democrats seemingly under the belief that ICE was the creation of Republicans while Democrats are the anti-ICE party. (Seeing people place “I Voted” stickers on the death sites of Rene Goode and Alex Pretti seemed especially egregious considering that for decades, Democrats have repeatedly funded the kinds of immigration agents who killed them.)

Then, on election night, I saw the Democratic U.S. Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan promise to “rip ICE apart.”

Godspeed to her and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed. Maybe as Senators they can help write a new narrative—one where racism and access to medical care are no longer intertwined, but ripped apart.

title: AG Letitia James sues former Rochester Holiday Inn, alleging forced labor and trafficking
description:
New York Attorney General Letitia James is suing Nayan Patel, the former downtown Rochester Holiday Inn owner and operator; its renovation contractor Roman Petrik; and Holiday Inn's parent company, IHG Hotels & Resorts.
The allegations overlap the timeline when the former Holiday Inn on State Street downtown began taking in asylum seekers from New York City.
Lawsuit accuses IHG of knowing about workers' conditions The lawsuit accuses IHG of knowingly benefiting from the alleged exploitation despite being informed of the workers' situations.

Workers were also denied legally required sick leave, the lawsuit alleges.
text:
State authorities claim one of the nation's largest hospitality companies overlooked human trafficking during renovations of a downtown Rochester hotel, allegedly labeling the unpaid workers "squatters" and pledging incentives if the hotel owner evicted them from the property.

New York Attorney General Letitia James is suing Nayan Patel, the former downtown Rochester Holiday Inn owner and operator; its renovation contractor Roman Petrik; and Holiday Inn's parent company, IHG Hotels & Resorts. The lawsuit accuses them of knowingly benefiting from what the Attorney General's Office argues was a forced labor scheme involving dozens of immigrant workers.

The lawsuit, filed in state Supreme Court, alleges workers were recruited with promises of hourly wages and housing at the hotel, but went months without pay, worked as many as 112 hours a week, and faced threats of deportation, eviction from the floor they were living on and arrest when they demanded their wages.

The allegations overlap the timeline when the former Holiday Inn on State Street downtown began taking in asylum seekers from New York City. That program brought aid workers into the hotel who learned of the problems and alerted authorities.

Rochester Mayor Malik Evans said in a statement that he is appalled by the allegations.

"The City of Rochester engaged these same owners in an attempt to bring that facility up to City Code and ensure the safety of hotel guests and employees – and ultimately forced its closure due to continued concerns," Evans wrote. "We will support Attorney General James as she proceeds with this lawsuit and remain committed to working with the foreclosing mortgage holder to get this important Downtown hotel property in the hands of a new owner."

The city ordered the hotel closed in June, citing multiple fire and building code violations. The building has been tied up in foreclosure proceedings since September.

In an email to WXXI News, a spokesperson from IHG said it condemns trafficking in any form and that the company denies that they had any knowledge of serious misconduct by Patel or Petrik.

WXXI News reached out to Patel and Petrik for comment but did not immediately hear back.

Lawsuit accuses IHG of knowing about workers' conditions

The lawsuit accuses IHG of knowingly benefiting from the alleged exploitation despite being informed of the workers' situations.

IHG required the renovations as a condition of the hotel’s Holiday Inn license. It dictated the scope of the work and conducted periodic inspections, according to the complaint.

During a June 14, 2024, visit, IHG officials inspected the seventh floor where the workers were living, photographed the rooms, and spoke directly with workers who allegedly told them they had not been paid for at least eight months, were living in uninhabitable conditions, and had been threatened with deportation, according to the lawsuit.

Four days later, IHG Regional Vice President George Hall allegedly emailed Patel that the people living on the seventh floor, who are described in the email as squatters, posed security and reputational risks to the Holiday Inn brand and that Patel was responsible for removing them, the lawsuit complaint said.

James alleges that IHG made no effort to find out whether the workers had been paid, and that none of the IHG employees involved reported the situation to the company’s own reporting hotline.

The following month, IHG told Patel that it was glad the issue involving "squatters" had been resolved and told him he would need to complete the company’s anti-human trafficking training, according to court filings.

The complaint states that IHG thought it was important for Patel to complete the anti-trafficking training because they were concerned that the workers at the hotel had been subjected to human trafficking.

"IHG did not hire the renovation contractor or its workers, and we did not know they were subject to forced labor as alleged by the Office of the Attorney General," a company spokesperson wrote in an email to WXXI News. "We did not own or operate the hotel and did not manage the construction project."

The spokesperson said the former Holiday Inn was removed from IHG's system in 2024 due to concerns about safety issues, the property's conditions, among other things.

"We never allowed the hotel to reopen to guests, and we terminated its license to operate as a Holiday Inn in January 2025," the email said.

Denied wages, and alleged threats of deportation

The lawsuit complaint alleges workers regularly worked 10- to 13-hour days, six days a week, totaling approximately 60 to 80 hours per week. At times, particularly ahead of IHG inspections and renovation deadlines, workers were required to put in as many as 98 to 112 hours a week.

One worker, promised $18 an hour, worked about 68 hours per week for 29 weeks. He should have received approximately $30,506; but Petrik allegedly paid him just $2,200 over the entire period, according to the Attorney General's Office.

When workers demanded their wages and staged work stoppages between October 2023 and February 2024, Petrik allegedly laughed at them, told them immigration officials were regularly at the hotel and said he could have them deported at any time, according to court filings.

Some workers were unable to purchase food for themselves or their families because they were receiving little to no pay. The lawsuit complaint alleges at least three workers were illegally evicted after seeking their wages.

Workers and families allegedly living in uninhabitable conditions

The lawsuit also alleges that workers and their families, including children, were forced to live in dangerous conditions on the hotel's abandoned seventh floor in September 2023 to make room for paying guests.

The floor, which had been decommissioned since at least 2016; lacked electricity, running water, functioning toilets or showers, and working heating and cooling systems. The rooms had no door locks, and most were infested with pests and vermin, the lawsuit alleges.

Workers and their children spent the winter without heat. Some workers became ill from the living conditions and because of the exposure to construction dust, paint, and extreme cold. Workers were also denied legally required sick leave, the lawsuit alleges.

Irene Sanchez, executive director of Enlace Services Inc., said the organization's outreach team alerted the attorney general's office after workers shared their experiences.

"Our advocates have helped families put food on the table, get medical care, and find other support in the community," Sanchez said. "Workers need to know they can count on that support long after they first speak up. That’s why we urge local agencies to keep their services separate from ICE enforcement. Every worker should feel safe reporting abuse or asking for help without fear of deportation.”

Lawsuit seeks damages, unpaid wages

Petrik, Patel, and their companies are also accused of violating the federal Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act by trafficking workers and obtaining their labor through threats of deportation, eviction, and financial harm.

A worker also claims to have been sexually assaulted, but it is unclear if authorities will pursue criminal charges.

James is seeking unpaid wages, restitution, damages, and penalties for the workers, as well as repayments for each defendant that was made from their work.

The Trump administration moved Thursday, November 19, 2026, to end its lawsuit challenging Democrat Mary Peltola's victory in Alaska's U.S. Senate race while asking a federal appeals court to VacaturVacatur is a court order setting aside or nullifying an earlier judgment or ruling. An appellate court may consider vacatur when a case becomes moot before appellate review is completed, although vacatur is an equitable remedy and is not automatically granted.Read more → an earlier ruling against the Justice Department.

Federal prosecutors told the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit that the completed election had made their case Mootness DoctrineThe mootness doctrine generally requires courts to stop deciding a case when later events eliminate the live dispute between the parties. If a court can no longer provide meaningful relief, the case may be dismissed as moot.Read more →. The department had sought to delay certification of the results while investigators examined whether voters confused Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan with an independent candidate sharing his name.

Peltola secured more than 50% of first-choice votes in the November 3 election, winning the race without additional rounds of ranked-choice counting. Her victory was confirmed November 17, leaving the Justice Department's proposed investigation unable to affect the outcome.

Attorney Advertising

Prosecutors acknowledged that ballots cast for independent candidate Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. had already been mixed with other votes, preventing investigators from determining whether some voters intended to support the Republican senator.

The department is asking the Ninth Circuit to vacate U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason's November 1 dismissal and return the lawsuit to the district court for dismissal as moot. Gleason had ruled that prosecutors lacked standing because their proposed investigation offered no workable remedy for alleged voter confusion.

The Justice Department sued Alaska on October 22, seeking to block certification if the Republican incumbent lost by a margin smaller than the number of votes cast for Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher from Petersburg. Prosecutors alleged that his candidacy was intended to confuse voters and divert Republican support toward Peltola.

Gleason dismissed the case two days before the election, finding that federal officials had failed to establish how a court could provide the requested relief while protecting Ballot SecrecyBallot secrecy is the principle that a voter's choices on a completed ballot should remain private and should not be traceable back to that individual. Election systems use procedures designed to separate a voter's identity from the voter's selections while still maintaining records showing whether the person participated in the election.Read more →. Alaska officials also opposed the federal challenge, arguing that the Justice Department lacked authority to interfere with the state's certification process.

The League of Women Voters of Alaska and Common Cause, which intervened in the lawsuit, have asked the Ninth Circuit to affirm the dismissal and consider SanctionsSanctions are penalties or other corrective measures a court may impose for violating court rules, disobeying court orders, filing improper claims or papers, abusing the litigation process, or engaging in other prohibited conduct.Read more → against federal attorneys involved in the case. The organizations argue that the government's legal claims lacked a valid basis and that its pursuit of the appeal warrants judicial scrutiny.

President Donald Trump and Sen. Sullivan have accused Democrats of orchestrating the retired teacher's candidacy to split Republican support. Peltola has denied involvement in recruiting Sullivan Jr., who maintains that his campaign was legitimate.

Federal and state investigators continue examining allegations surrounding Sullivan Jr.'s entry into the race, including reported efforts to recruit candidates with names resembling Republican incumbents. The FBI and Alaska Bureau of Investigation are conducting inquiries separate from the civil litigation.

text:
Will Venezuelan TPS Be Restored on November 20?

No automatic reinstatement is scheduled for November 20, 2026.

On November 18, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit extended a temporary stay preventing enforcement of a lower court’s decision that would restore Venezuelan TPS protections.

That stay will remain in place until seven days after the appeals court publishes its judgment, unless another court order changes the situation.

On November 19, the federal government withdrew its latest emergency application to the U.S. Supreme Court following the appeals court’s decision.

Importantly, this withdrawal does not mean TPS has been restored or that the underlying legal dispute has been resolved.

The litigation primarily concerns the termination of Venezuela’s 2023 TPS designation. Venezuela’s separate 2021 designation was also terminated, effective November 7, 2025.

Is Your TPS Work Permit Still Valid?

This was one of the most important questions Carolina raised during our interview.

Some Venezuelans have employment authorization documents displaying expiration dates that differ from the dates on which their TPS protections ended.

However, the expiration date printed on a work permit does not always establish whether that authorization remains valid.

Its validity depends on several factors, including the TPS designation, the employment authorization category, applicable court orders, and official government notices.

Someone who has lost TPS-based employment authorization may still have a valid work permit obtained through another immigration category.

A pending asylum application, however, does not automatically authorize employment. Eligible asylum applicants must obtain employment authorization under the applicable rules.

What If You Have a Pending Asylum Application?

Borja raised a question that affects many families: What happens if you lose TPS but still have an asylum application pending?

A pending asylum application may have important legal consequences, but it is essential to understand what it does—and does not—provide.

Under federal immigration law, a person with a bona fide pending asylum application generally does not accumulate unlawful presence for purposes of the three- and ten-year inadmissibility bars during the qualifying period, provided the statutory conditions are met.

One important exception involves unauthorized employment while the asylum application is pending.

This protection also does not erase unlawful presence that may have accumulated before the asylum application was filed.

A pending asylum application does not automatically grant lawful immigration status.

It also does not guarantee that a person cannot be detained or placed in removal proceedings. The applicable procedures and protections depend on the individual’s circumstances and the status of the asylum case.

What Should Venezuelans Who Lost TPS Do?

My recommendation is to review your immigration situation individually rather than assume that losing TPS eliminates every possible option.

Your prior immigration status, pending applications, employment authorization, and immigration court history may all affect your legal position.

As the litigation continues, it is especially important to follow official court decisions and USCIS announcements instead of relying on rumors or outdated information.

I thank Borja Voces and Carolina Sarassa for inviting me to Noticiero Univision Edición Digital and for giving our community an opportunity to better understand these developments.

By: Jagan Tamirisa | November 19, 2026 On November 17, 2026, the Department of Justice (DOJ) published a final rule (Department of Justice, Appellate Procedures for the Board of Immigration Appeals, 91 Fed.
73876 (Nov. 17, 2026)) introducing significant changes to appeals before the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA), which reviews certain decisions made by Immigration Judges and immigration authorities.

Appeal Deadline Reduced from 30 Days to 10 Days Previously, individuals generally had 30 days to appeal an Immigration Judge's decision.
text:
By: Jagan Tamirisa | November 19, 2026

On November 17, 2026, the Department of Justice (DOJ) published a final rule (Department of Justice, Appellate Procedures for the Board of Immigration Appeals, 91 Fed. Reg. 73876 (Nov. 17, 2026)) introducing significant changes to appeals before the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA), which reviews certain decisions made by Immigration Judges and immigration authorities.

Effective December 17, 2026, the rule generally reduces the deadline for filing many immigration appeals from 30 days to just 10 calendar days. It also introduces procedures allowing the BIA to dismiss many appeals without issuing a detailed written decision. The changes are intended to reduce the BIA's growing backlog and speed up immigration appeal decisions.

Importantly, the new procedures generally apply to decisions issued on or after December 17, 2026, and do not apply retroactively to appeals involving earlier decisions.

Which Immigration Cases Are Affected?

The new rules primarily affect appeals before the BIA, including Immigration Judge decisions involving removal proceedings, adjustment of status (Form I-485), cancellation of removal, certain immigration waivers, and other immigration relief. The rules do not generally apply to USCIS decisions on H-1B, L-1, O-1, or other nonimmigrant visa petitions, which follow separate administrative appeal procedures. However, individuals holding these visa classifications may be affected if they are placed in removal proceedings and appeal an Immigration Judge's decision to the BIA. Certain asylum appeals and other specified cases are subject to different procedural requirements.

Appeal Deadline Reduced from 30 Days to 10 Days

Previously, individuals generally had 30 days to appeal an Immigration Judge's decision. Under the new rule, many appeals must be filed within just 10 calendar days.

For example, if an Immigration Judge denies a Form I-485 application for adjustment of status (green card) in removal proceedings, the individual generally will have only 10 calendar days to appeal that decision to the BIA, rather than the previous 30 days.

Certain asylum appeals will continue to have a 30-day deadline. However, the shorter deadline applies to some asylum-related decisions, including cases involving certain statutory bars to applying for asylum. The applicable deadline depends on the type of case and the reasons for the Immigration Judge's decision.

BIA May Dismiss Appeals Within 15 Days

Another significant change concerns how the BIA reviews appeals. Under the new rule, the BIA generally will not conduct a full review of every appeal. For most covered cases, further review will occur only if a majority of permanent BIA members votes to consider the appeal. Otherwise, the appeal may be dismissed without a separate, detailed written opinion. These summary dismissals generally must be issued within 15 days after the appeal is filed.

This means an individual may receive a final administrative decision without the opportunity to submit additional written arguments. Certain categories of appeals, including specified custody and detention matters, are excluded from these procedures.

All Appeal Issues Must Be Identified in the Notice of Appeal

Individuals filing an appeal must identify the specific legal or factual issues they are challenging in the Notice of Appeal (Form EOIR-26). For example, if an individual believes that the Immigration Judge incorrectly evaluated evidence, applied the wrong legal standard, or improperly denied immigration relief, those issues must be identified when filing the appeal. Issues not identified in the Notice of Appeal will generally be considered waived, meaning the individual may lose the opportunity to raise them later in the appeal.

Although identifying appeal issues has long been required, the new rule expressly reinforces this requirement. With the shorter filing deadline and expanded dismissal procedures, preparing a complete and accurate Notice of Appeal becomes particularly important.

Changes to Written Arguments and Briefing

When the BIA accepts an appeal for further review, both sides generally have 20 days to submit their written arguments, rather than receiving separate briefing deadlines. Extensions will be limited to exceptional circumstances, and reply briefs generally will not be permitted unless the BIA authorizes additional briefing. Some of these procedural changes were already implemented under the earlier February 2026 interim rule and are retained in the final rule.

Why Is This Rule Being Finalized Now?

DOJ initially introduced these changes through an interim final rule published in February 2026. However, in March 2026, a federal district court set aside several provisions, including the shorter appeal deadline, expanded summary dismissal procedures, and the express waiver requirement for issues omitted from the Notice of Appeal.

Following a public comment period, DOJ issued the November 17 final rule adopting these provisions with certain modifications. DOJ maintains that the final rule addresses the procedural concerns raised in the earlier litigation. However, further court proceedings may affect its implementation.

What Should Individuals Facing Immigration Proceedings Know?

Individuals facing removal proceedings should carefully review the applicable appeal deadlines and seek appropriate legal guidance before an Immigration Judge issues a decision. The shorter filing period may leave very little time to identify legal errors, prepare the Notice of Appeal, and arrange representation.

An unfavorable BIA decision may also make a removal order administratively final. Although federal court review may be available in certain cases, filing a petition for review generally does not automatically prevent removal.

“We started spotting them in the service elevators and started engaging with them and inviting them to attend some of our activities and events,” Sanchez said. “And slowly gained their trust. That’s how we identified them and started working with them.”

Sanchez said Enlace alerted the Attorney General’s Office and the Worker Justice Center of New York to the workers' concerns in 2024.

The Attorney General’s Office says workers were promised hourly wages and housing at the hotel, but most stopped receiving pay after their first two weeks. The lawsuit alleges they routinely worked 10- to 13-hour days, six days a week, sometimes logging 98 to 112 hours in a single week ahead of inspections and renovation deadlines.

One worker, promised $18 an hour, worked approximately 68 hours a week for 29 weeks, according to the complaint. The state alleges the worker earned about $30,506 but received just $2,200.

Sanchez said the workers’ families, including children, were also affected. The lawsuit alleges they were housed on the hotel's abandoned seventh floor, which lacked heat, electricity, running water and functioning bathrooms. The floor had been out of service since at least 2016, according to the state.

“It was a large group of workers that was impacted,” Sanchez said. “Workers were talking about families and children also being involved, living in inhumane conditions where nobody should have been living.”

The lawsuit alleges Petrik and hotel owner Nayan Patel threatened workers with immigration enforcement when they demanded wages. At least three workers were also allegedly evicted after seeking payment.

“It was a very scary time for them,” Sanchez said. “They were working so often without pay and in those conditions because they literally had no money to go nowhere else.”

The state further alleges IHG knew workers were being exploited but continued to benefit from the renovation. According to the Attorney General’s Office, IHG managers spoke with workers during a June 2024 visit and were told they had not been paid for at least eight months, were living in poor conditions and had been threatened with deportation. **The company allegedly failed to investigate the wage complaints.

Sanchez said Enlace and partner agencies helped relocate workers to safer housing. Many have since found jobs and are receiving health care and mental health support.

“They are being treated with respect and with dignity,” Sanchez said. “Some of them got married, some have children, some are really learning English now. They are being part of the community now.”

The Attorney General’s Office is seeking unpaid wages, restitution, damages and penalties, along with profits the defendants allegedly earned from the workers' labor. The lawsuit also asks the court to bar Petrik and his company from the renovation business, and Patel and his company from the hotel business in New York.

13WHAM could not reach Petrik or Patel for comment.

Rochester Mayor Malik Evans condemned the alleged treatment of workers and said the city previously sought to address code violations at the property.

The City of Rochester is appalled by the allegations announced today against former operators of the hotel at 70 State St. The lawsuit brought by New York State Attorney General Letitia James brings attention to the scourge of human trafficking, and we applaud the OAG for investigating these serious allegations and bringing justice to victims.

The City of Rochester engaged these same owners in an attempt to bring that facility up to City Code and ensure the safety of hotel guests and employees – and ultimately forced its closure due to continued concerns. We will support Attorney General James as she proceeds with this lawsuit, and remain committed to working with the foreclosing mortgage holder to get this important Downtown hotel property in the hands of a new owner.

Sanchez said Enlace continues to provide free, confidential case management and support services. Workers or members of the public who believe someone may be facing similar circumstances can contact Enlace at 585-566-2559.

description:

text:
The Reach of Immigration-Related Retaliation Expands: California Amends Labor Code Section 1019

Immigration compliance is increasingly becoming a state-law issue as well as a federal one. Employers operating across jurisdictions face an increasingly complex patchwork of requirements affecting immigration enforcement, employment verification, worker protections, and employer communications involving immigration status.

California continues to expand its rules in this area, including through recent legislation addressing workplace immigration enforcement and employee notice requirements. Effective January 1, 2027, Assembly Bill 2495 (AB 2495) significantly broadens Labor Code Section 1019, expanding the rights protected, individuals covered, and immigration-related conduct that may give rise to liability.

This state legislative activity also comes against a backdrop of increased federal scrutiny of immigration-related recruiting and hiring practices. Recent Department of Justice and Department of Labor activity involving the PERM labor certification program reflects heightened attention to whether recruitment processes provide U.S. workers a genuine opportunity to apply and receive consideration. Although the federal and California legal frameworks address different conduct and protect different interests, together they reinforce the importance of carefully designed and consistently administered recruiting, sponsorship, and employment-verification practices.

The California changes are particularly significant as employers take a closer look at sponsorship requests, foreign-national hiring, work authorization, and workforce planning. Decisions and communications that employers may view primarily as immigration or business matters may increasingly be examined through a retaliation lens under California law.

Expanding the Range of Protected Conduct

Historically, Section 1019 focused largely on rights under the Labor Code or applicable local ordinances. Beginning January 1, 2027, it will cover the exercise or attempted exercise of rights under virtually any federal, state, or local law applicable to employees. Immigration-related conduct connected to wage-and-hour complaints, discrimination concerns, safety complaints, leave requests, accommodations, whistleblower activity, or other statutory rights may therefore give rise to claims.

In addition to those who formally assert rights, the legislation protects individuals who:

Make good-faith workplace complaints;

Seek information regarding legal compliance;

Inform others regarding workplace rights;

Encourage others to exercise workplace rights; or

Assist another individual in asserting workplace protections.

Protection does not require a formal complaint: asking about workplace rights, assisting a coworker, or seeking compliance information may suffice.

A New Focus on Conduct That May “Dissuade” Employees

A significant change is the statute’s focus on conduct that may discourage individuals from exercising workplace rights before any complaint is made. The amended law prohibits conduct related to actual or perceived immigration status that would reasonably tend to dissuade a person from exercising a legal right or induce an action the person has a legal right to decline.

The focus thus extends beyond whether retaliation occurred to whether comments or conduct could reasonably discourage protected activity, creating litigation risk from interactions not previously viewed as actionable.

Although each situation is fact-specific, employers should be mindful of communications such as:1

Referencing an employee’s immigration or visa status during a workplace dispute;

Suggesting that raising concerns could affect future sponsorship opportunities;

Asking unnecessary immigration-status questions unrelated to a legitimate business need;

Making statements that could be interpreted as discouraging employees from reporting workplace concerns; or

Linking work authorization to complaints about wages, leave, discrimination, safety, or other protected rights.

Claims may arise even if an employee never files a complaint or exercises the underlying right.

Coverage Now Extends Beyond Current Employees

AB 2495 also expands the definition of “employee” to include:

Applicants;

Current employees; and

Former employees.

Coverage of applicants may affect recruiting and hiring. Liability turns not on actual immigration status but on whether conduct related to actual or perceived status could be viewed as retaliatory or as discouraging the exercise of workplace rights. The law does not prohibit lawful questions about work authorization or future sponsorship needs. Employers generally remain free to decide whether to sponsor employment-based visas and to ask whether applicants are authorized to work in the United States and need sponsorship now or in the future. Those questions, and decisions based on the responses, should be grounded in legitimate business considerations and administered consistently. Employers should also evaluate how sponsorship-related screening interacts with their broader recruiting practices and applicable federal anti-discrimination requirements.

Questions about work authorization and sponsorship, including follow-up questions, should serve a legitimate business purpose, be asked consistently, and avoid statements that could discourage the exercise of workplace rights. Coverage of former employees also extends potential exposure beyond active employment.

Where Employers May Face Increased Exposure

Compliant employment-verification practices remain essential. Employers should continue to follow federal Form I-9 and E-Verify requirements while ensuring that employment-verification practices are applied consistently and are not used, or perceived as being used, in response to protected workplace activity. Requests for additional documentation, unnecessary immigration-status inquiries, or changes in verification practices involving an employee who has raised workplace concerns may receive particular scrutiny.

The potential exposure, however, extends beyond the employment-verification process. Even employers that do not intend to retaliate may face liability arising from routine decisions and conversations about sponsorship, work authorization, immigration status, or compliance.

Areas to review include:

Recruiting channels, application processes, and applicant screening practices;

Layoffs, reductions in force, and workforce restructuring affecting sponsored positions or related occupations;

Questions regarding current work authorization and future sponsorship needs;

Communications regarding sponsorship decisions;

Form I-9 and E-Verify practices;

Internal complaint and investigation procedures;

Manager and supervisor training;

Responses to employee concerns regarding wages, leave, discrimination, safety, or other workplace rights; and

Communications involving immigration status, visa sponsorship, or future employment authorization.

As employers reassess sponsorship strategies, recruiting practices, layoffs, hiring priorities, and long-term workforce planning against a changing federal immigration landscape, immigration-related decisions and communications may receive increased scrutiny from multiple directions. Employers generally retain discretion over sponsorship, but discussions should remain tied to legitimate business considerations and separate from workplace complaints or other protected activity.

Compliant employment-verification practices remain essential. Routine employment-eligibility verification, document review, and immigration-status communications may give rise to claims. Actions that appear to single out employees based on actual or perceived immigration status may receive heightened scrutiny, particularly when connected to workplace complaints or disputes.

Section 1019 does not diminish employers’ federal immigration obligations or ability to make lawful hiring and sponsorship decisions. Employers must continue to verify employment authorization, evaluate sponsorship needs, and plan their workforces consistent with business objectives and legal requirements. Those actions should be supported by documented business and compliance considerations and should not appear to discourage employees or applicants from exercising workplace rights.

Significant Penalties Remain Available

The amendments are more than technical. Individuals subjected to an unfair immigration-related practice may already sue under Section 1019 for equitable relief, damages, and available penalties. Existing law authorizes civil penalties of up to $10,000 per employee or person per immigration-related violation. Employers may also face injunctive relief, attorneys’ fees in certain circumstances, and other remedies under California law.

Looking Ahead

Before January 1, 2027, employers should review recruiting practices, sponsorship communications, complaint procedures, manager training, and employment-verification processes to confirm they are applied consistently and serve legitimate business and compliance objectives. Managers, recruiters, talent acquisition teams, and human resources professionals should understand how to discuss immigration-related issues lawfully and recognize that comments about immigration status, sponsorship, or work authorization may receive heightened scrutiny when connected to workplace rights.

Proactive compliance may reduce litigation risk. Given the law’s focus on conduct that may “dissuade” workers from exercising legal rights, employers should review not only formal decisions but also everyday communications during hiring, onboarding, investigations, and employee-relations matters. Because these issues intersect with immigration, employment, and anti-discrimination laws, employers should consider consulting experienced counsel on complex or high-risk situations.

Democrats who will soon be at the head of congressional committees are indicating to members of the administration that they will soon be answering questions about their actions during the past two years. On November 18, Representative Robert Garcia (D-CA), who is expected to chair the House Committee on Oversight and Governmental Reform, sent letters today to a number of Trump administration figures demanding they preserve all records, communications, and information pertaining to future investigations.

Those letters went to Donald Trump Jr. concerning alleged conflicts of interest, his stake in the World Liberty Financial cryptocurrency venture, and the fact a Russian oligarch close to Russia’s president Vladimir Putin paid for his wedding party; to Eric Trump concerning alleged conflicts of interest and World Liberty Financial; and to Jared Kushner over alleged conflicts of interest, his control of the private equity firm Affinity Partners—which received a $2 billion investment from Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund and is a major stockholder in an Israeli company that has hundreds of millions of dollars invested in Israeli defense contractors—and allegations that he has used his role in the government to enrich himself and his companies.

The letter to Kushner arrived on the same day Ariel Sabar of The Atlantic reported that Affinity Partners updated a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on November 5, two days after the midterm elections, revealing that it also owns a $32 million stake in a U.S. defense contractor that makes crucial components for the U.S. systems deployed in the theaters in which Kushner has been acting as Trump’s negotiator. That information appears to have been so late it violated legal requirements.

Letters went to Kimberly Guilfoyle about pay-to-play schemes during her tenure as U.S. ambassador to Greece and to Trust for the National Mall chief executive officer Catherine Townsend on the $600 million in both taxpayer money and private donations from those with business before the government that are supposed to be funding Trump’s ballroom.

Letters went to White House chief of staff Stephen Miller about abuses by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement under his direction, to former DHS secretary Kristi Noem about abuse of funds and corruption, and to Noem’s advisor Corey Lewandowski regarding corruption and self-dealing, steering of lucrative contracts to allies, and his role in DHS and ICE abuses.

Letters went to Vice President J.D. Vance and former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles about the cover-up of the Epstein files; to Attorney General Todd Blanche about the cover-up of the Epstein files, the failure of the Department of Justice (DOJ) to comply with the Epstein Files Transparency Act, the DOJ’s botched release and review of documents, and the decision to transfer Jeffrey Epstein’s associate Ghislaine Maxwell to a minimum-security prison camp; and to Federal Bureau of Prisons Director William K. Marshall III and Federal Prison Camp Bryan Prison Warden Tanisha Hall about Maxwell’s transfer just days after she offered favorable testimony about Trump, as well as the privileges she has enjoyed since the transfer.

Garcia’s list is just a starting point. More news will continue to drop. Just today, Avi Asher-Schapiro, Andy Kroll, and Alex Mierjeski of ProPublica reported that Trump officials appear to have figured a way around the prohibition on the slush fund Trump wanted to create over the leaking of tax information by an IRS contractor during his first term. While the law allows a $1,000 payment to victims of such a leak, Trump appointees at the Department of Justice signed paperwork that settled with five individuals and companies connected to Trump for $2.5 million, with more plaintiffs on the way.

Administration figures are sending their own messages to the Democrats, either to bully them into backing down or to draw favorable attention from Trump and his allies. White House counsel William Scharf and U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas Aaron Reitz have sent public letters to Democrats warning that their promises to conduct oversight may be unconstitutional and illegal.

On Monday, Scharf sent an extraordinary memo to the general counsels of executive departments and agencies telling them that no personnel may agree to appear before any congressional committee without approval from the White House Office of Legislative Affairs and the Office of the White House Counsel: that is, himself.

A White House official told Liz Landers of PBS: “The Trump Administration will not be extorted, intimidated, or threatened into submission by politically motivated baseless investigations. We are ready to engage with Congress, this process ensures reasonable requests are respected, but baseless political attempts to undermine our mission will not be accepted as the status quo by Democrats’ [sic] who want to slow the administration down from its historic work.”

Legal commentator Liz Dye wrote in Public Notice that “this is a radical departure from prior policy, contrary to both law and precedent.” On November 11, Dye noted that Attorney General Todd Blanche, Trump’s former criminal defense lawyer, has been “desperately assuring” those who stick with the administration that “he’s got their backs.”

On the Fox News Channel he said: “If you work in this administration, you have a lawyer. It’s me.” Dye also noted that in fact, Blanche is likely going to protect Trump and himself rather than the little guys and that in any case, the lawyers leaving the DOJ since the election are well aware that “while a presidential pardon might keep them out of jail, it won’t save their law licenses.”

Reitz has targeted Garcia, as well as Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Elissa Slotkin (D-MI), Adam Schiff (D-CA), and Elizabeth Warren (D-MA). They are having no part of it. Slotkin noted that his public threats against members of Congress who have explicit constitutional protection for their speech “is evidence that your threat of investigation is more about publicity and your political ambitions than any sort of legitimate inquiry.”

Today Kyle Cheney of Politico reported that six experts in congressional power and constitutional law say Reitz’s threats are “farcical.” One said the administration’s attack on Congress is “even more laughable than usual.”

As Judd Legum reported in Popular Information on Tuesday, November 17, Reitz has repeatedly vowed to use the law to hurt “libs” and enemies of “our Christian values,” saying “it’s either kill or be killed.” In 2025, when he was running for the office of Texas attorney general, he told a group of supporters that those on “the left” “are deadly threatened by what’s coming. They know that I’m going to destroy them. If I can’t sue you, I’m going to investigate you. If I can’t investigate you, I’m going to drag you into so much trouble, you might as well just declare bankruptcy now.”

Reitz makes it clear that key administration figures remain tied to Trump. Senator Blumenthal has taken to asking Trump’s judicial nominees if they are willing to say that voters elected Joe Biden president in 2020 or if the U.S. Capitol was attacked on January 6, 2021. They still are not. As Blumenthal notes, Trump’s appointees’ refusal to acknowledge the fact that Biden won in 2020 indicates that they lack the objectivity and independence the justiciary requires.

Indeed, rather than moderating their positions after the historic midterm election made it clear how unpopular they are, Trump loyalists appear to have decided to hammer through their policies, despite their rejection by the American people on November 3. New White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, a white nationalist who describes immigration as an “invasion,” has said he intended to expand the administration’s deportation program despite its unpopularity.

And yet, in Strength in Numbers on November 17, pollster G. Elliott Morris explained that while much ink has been spilled about voters turning against Trump over rising costs in 2026, voters turned against Trump over immigration and deportations in 2025. That shift was especially clear in the Hispanic voters who helped to put Trump in office in 2024. Angry at sweeping deportations rather than the removal of violent criminals they thought Trump promised, they moved 28 points toward Democrats, helping to turn Texas, as well as other states, blue.

MAGA members of Congress are also doubling down on their ideology, especially after more moderate Republicans were swept out of office in November. In the House, Republicans have chosen MAGA bombthrower Jim Jordan, who is simply a messaging agent and who in almost twenty years in Congress has never sponsored a bill that became a law, to be their leader.

In the Senate, Republicans today declined, once again, to stop Trump’s war on Iran. While Senate majority leader John Thune (R-SD) blamed Trump for his party’s losses in the midterms, Senator Ron Johnson (R-WI), who in January 2021 tried to get a false slate of Trump electors into then–Vice President Mike Pence’s hand just before Congress began the counting of electoral votes, seemed to dismiss voters’ demand for affordability. Yesterday, on Fox Business, he called Social Security “grotesque” and a “Ponzi scheme.” He added: “You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”

Trump administration officials are trying to rig government programs in their own favor by replacing the acting comptroller general of the Government Accountability Office (GAO), the nonpartisan independent office that audits federal programs, with MAGA Republican Eric Ueland. Ueland is an ally of Office of Management and Budget director Russell Vought, who has been withholding funds for programs he doesn’t like despite congressional appropriations. Norman Ornstein of The Contrarian says the Republicans’ attempt to force Ueland into the GAO is “a middle finger to the law and to Congress.”

At the state level, as Kate Riga of Talking Points Memo reported today, Republican MAGA officials are rushing to restrict voting before 2028.

The doubling down of MAGA political figures on their ideology stands in marked contrast to the right-wing figures trying to distance themselves from Trump and MAGA in the wake of the election.

Alex Karp, the chief executive officer of tech giant Palantir, who shifted rightward to ingratiate himself with the Trump administration, used the word “progressive” eight times when he talked to Politico’s Playbook after the election. “I’ve been a Democrat my whole life,” he said, adding “I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet.” He said the Democrats have “absolutely” corrected enough in 2026 that he could support them in 2028.

Billionaire Elon Musk put close to $300 million into the 2024 elections on behalf of Republicans, slashed government jobs when he headed Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), and pumped close to a half a billion dollars—that we know of—into the 2026 midterm elections to make sure Republicans continued to control the Senate and Texas, where Musk has located his businesses. And yet, in an interview at the New York Times 2026 DealBook Summit, Musk distanced himself from Trump and the Republicans, insisting he is “not MAGA.”

It turns out that some of those who cooperated with Trump and his allies now appear eager to work with incoming Democratic investigators. Michael S. Schmidt of the New York Times reported today that Kirkland & Ellis, one of the elite law firms that, under threats from the administration over its “diversity, equity and inclusion (D.E.I.) related employment practices,” agreed to do $125 million in pro bono work for charitable causes Trump supports, actually has done close to $12 million in free work for the Trump administration. This arrangement seems to have enabled the administration to circumvent Congress.

According to Schmidt, in its seven-page letter to Congress, the law firm noted that it hired a lobbying firm close to the White House to cut the deal with a deputy to Stephen Miller and that, apart from a social media post by Trump, the agreement had never been written down.

text:
A lawsuit filed by Attorney General Letitia James alleges dozens of immigrant workers were exploited during the renovation of a now closed downtown Rochester hotel.

The suit, filed against the owners and operators of the former Holiday Inn, the renovation contractor and Holiday Inn's parent company, IHG Hotels & Resorts, claims workers were forced to work up to 112 hours a week, often without being paid. It also alleges they were left to live in dangerous and uninhabitable conditions with no heat, electricity or running water.

James says the contractor allegedly recruited workers from multiple states and countries for the project. According to the suit, workers were promised hourly wages and housing at the hotel, but after their first two weeks, the pay largely stopped. James alleges the contractor routinely delayed and withheld wages.

According to the AG's office, workers who demanded their wages were threatened with deportation, eviction or arrest. One worker was even allegedly sexually assaulted repeatedly by the contractor and he threatened to refuse to pay her if she didn't comply, James' office says.

The suit also alleges IHG Hotels & Resorts knew about the exploitation but continued to benefit financially from the renovation project. James' office says its investigation revealed that IHG Hotels & Resorts visited the site in June 2024, inspected living conditions and spoke with workers who told IHG managers that they had not been paid for at least eight months, were living in intolerable conditions and had been threatened with deportation when they asked for their wages.

After that, Attorney General James says IHG did not follow up to find out whether the workers had been paid, and she alleges none of the IHG employees involved reported the situation to the company’s own reporting hotline.

text:
Dozens of protesters gathered outside Ocean Knoll Elementary School Thursday morning where less than 24 hours earlier a mother was taken by immigration enforcement agents after dropping off her kindergartener at school, according to a city official.

Encinitas City Council Member-elect Brad Lefkowits (Dist. 4) said in a Facebook reel multiple immigration enforcement vehicles were parked outside the elementary school where the mother, who has not been named, had just dropped off her child and participated in the school's food drive.

"When that mom left the campus, they followed her, pulled her over, broke her window and arrested her," Lefkowits said in the video. "It's hard to put into words the chaos and fear this puts into our community when this happens."

Lefkowits said inside the abandoned vehicle were photographs of the Ocean Knoll kindergartener as well as the food and target gift card from the drive.

The Encinitas Union School District confirmed the arrest near its elementary school and said in a statement district personnel were working with the family to provide support.

"The presence of immigration enforcement officers near our schools creates fear and uncertainty for many of our families. It is unacceptable that they are being confronted with the fear of immigration enforcement while simply trying to get their children to school," A statement from EUSD said, in part.

Local

NBC San Diego has reached out to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security regarding the incident and has not yet heard back.

Incidents near schools over the last few months have urged local political and school leaders to demand change from federal authorities.

The San Diego Unified School District this week penned a letter to DHS after a Fay Elementary third grader was detained by ICE at an immigration appointment. The letter demanded an end to family separations, enforcement near schools, and several other policy changes to "prevent this trauma from ever happening again."

The boy was held for weeks and ultimately taken to a facility in Texas. He has since been released to family in San Diego.

The OUSD meanwhile said its had to expand its immigration support services because at least 20 families have been impacted by immigration enforcement efforts.

"Our families are telling us that there is a lot of fear right now in our communities," OUSD board member Nancy Lincona said. "We serve families as they come forward and so we're constantly identifying new families that need support as they reach out for help."
