text:
Leads coalition of 20 AGs in recommending inquiries into accountability of immigration officers, detention practices, and DHS waste and corruption

Encourages Congress to include the voices and experiences of community members, advocates, and AGs who are fighting for the rule of law

November 19, 2026 (SAINT PAUL) — Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison today led a coalition of 20 attorneys general in encouraging leaders of the incoming majorities in Congress to hold hearings on Trump Administration abuses in immigration enforcement. In a letter to congressional leadership — including the incoming chairs of House and Senate committees with responsibility over the judiciary, homeland security, and government oversight and accountability — Attorney General Ellison and the coalition encourage Congress to hold hearings on the accountability of immigration officers, detention practices, and waste and corruption in the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

Attorney General Ellison and the coalition also encourage the incoming chairs of these committees to feature testimony at the hearings from Americans directly harmed by immigration enforcement abuse, advocates for immigrant communities, and from state Attorneys General who have been using the tools at their disposal to fight against this abuse and for the rule of law. State officials and community leaders have important insights to share gathered through truth councils, accountability commissions, and other community engagement.

“I led this coalition of attorneys general in encouraging incoming Congressional leaders to hold hearings on abuses in immigration enforcement because we are supposed to be a nation of laws — but DHS has acted like an agency that answers to no one, and it must be held accountable,” Attorney General Ellison said. “It is critically important to take a clear, hard look at the facts now and establish a complete public record so that we have a clear picture of the problems we need to solve. This record must include the experiences and voices of people who have been directly harmed and those, including state attorneys general, who have advocated for them and fought for the rule of law. As the chief legal officers of our states, we attorneys general have sworn oaths to uphold the Constitution — and we recognize no exception to the Constitution for immigration agents. We look forward to working with the new majorities in Congress to make sure the Constitution applies to all Americans and protects all Americans from the abuses of the lawless Trump Administration.“

Trump abuses in immigration enforcement, corruption

Donald Trump’s DHS and its agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and Customs and Border Protection (CBP), have operated as if they are exempt from accountability and the rule of law. In 2025, DHS began a months-long campaign of terror across multiple American cities. Since the beginning of Trump’s second term, DHS agents have shot at least 25 people across the United States. In Minnesota, they include Renee Good and Alex Pretti, whom DHS agents killed, and Julio Sosa-Celis, whom they injured when they shot him through the door of a house where children were present.

Use of force by immigration agents has also increased dramatically. In just the first three months of the current administration, there was a nearly fourfold increase in reported ICE use-of-force incidents. Independent researchers have subsequently documented more than 400 incidents of misuse of crowd-control weapons in sixteen cities across the country in just 12 months, resulting in over 200 injuries to demonstrators, bystanders, and journalists attempting to cover the events.

Attorney General Ellison and the coalition write to Congressional leaders, “In the face of immigration enforcement conduct that is both immoral and unlawful, the outgoing House and Senate majorities were content to look the other way. The incoming majorities need to confront this head-on. The American people voted for real, serious oversight — with teeth and consequences for any agency or individual who would ignore the rule of law.”

Immigration detention practices are in dire need of reform and oversight as well. By ICE’s own accounting, close to 60 people have died in ICE custody in the past two years, enough to make 2025 the deadliest year in immigration detention in over two decades.

DHS has already wasted significant sums in its rushed and ill-conceived efforts to rapidly expand immigration detention. DHS spent approximately $1 billion purchasing warehouses in a grossly inhumane effort to house people in them before shifting course. Now DHS has purchased four prisons from CoreCivic, a significant donor to President Trump’s inaugural committee and his PACs, for the extraordinary sum of $2.2 billion. DHS paid CoreCivic $495 million for a prison in Minnesota that CoreCivic offered to the State of Minnesota for just $75 million in 2025. Americans deserve to know whether DHS is inflating the purchase price of these facilities and diverting their tax dollars into the coffers of the President’s supporters.

Attorney General Ellison has used the power of his office to halt abuses in immigration enforcement and draw attention to waste and corruption by, among other things, suing to have Operation Metro Surge declared illegal and unconstitutional, which is still ongoing; suing the Trump Administration for access to the evidence in the shootings of Renee Good, Julio Sosa-Celis, and Alex Pretti, which is also still ongoing; suing outgoing Texas Governor Greg Abbott to compel the return of the ICE officer criminally charged in Minnesota in the shooting of Alex Pretti to face the charges laid against him; and calling for a congressional investigation into DHS’s purchase of the Appleton prison from CoreCivic at a wildly inflated price. The Minnesota Truth Council, in which Attorney General Ellison’s Office actively participated, also recently released its preliminary report and will issue its final report and recommendations on December 1.

text:
The leaders of Russia, China and the United States — Presidents Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump — have wrapped up an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China, with what Chinese media is calling a landmark “peace declaration.” The four-point plan calls for the three nations to reduce nuclear risks, increase oil refining, promote reforms to the United Nations and limit the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court. This is President Trump.

President Donald Trump: “In another area of potential cooperation between us, I’ll be suggesting ways to protect our nation’s sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction.”

President Putin faces an ICC warrant seeking his arrest for war crimes committed in Ukraine, including the unlawful transfer of children from Russian-occupied areas. Neither the U.S., nor China, nor Russia is a party to the Rome Statute that established the International Criminal Court.

During the summit, President Trump lavished praise on President Xi and referred to President Putin as “my friend.” That prompted Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk to write on social media, “God, protect us from such friends.”

On Capitol Hill, House Democrats voted 251-11 on Wednesday to nominate New York Congressmember Hakeem Jeffries to be the next speaker of the House. Jeffries is poised to make history as the first African American to fill the role. The vote came during a closed-door caucus meeting. Afterward, seven incoming Democratic congressmembers issued a joint statement explaining their opposition to Jeffries. They wrote, “Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues.”

In Gaza, thousands of Palestinians have been forced to flee again after Israeli tanks and bulldozers pushed past the ceasefire’s “Yellow Line” on Wednesday and into Palestinian-held territory. Israeli troops operating east of the “Yellow Line” have gradually pushed the boundary westward and now occupy about two-thirds of Gaza’s territory, with 2 million Palestinians trapped in an increasingly narrow strip of land, most of them forced to live in tents. This is Salam Aql, a Palestinian woman who says she was displaced for the 15th time on Wednesday.

Salam Aql: “They ordered an evacuation, but we wanted to stay because we are exhausted from being displaced so many times. We are tired. I swear to God, we are tired. But as we were sitting there, gunfire started coming in. The boy was sitting in front of the tent and was hit in the leg. Once he was wounded, we could not stay any longer. We are scared.”

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said the military is ready to take more land and turn the newly seized areas into permanent parts of Israel’s security zones. The Palestinian Health Ministry says Israeli forces have killed over 1,600 Palestinians in Gaza since last October’s so-called ceasefire.

An Israeli court has once again extended the detention of Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya, the director of Kamal Adwan Hospital in Gaza, by six months. Dr. Abu Safiya was seized by the Israeli military along with several of the hospital’s staff and patients during a raid on Kamal Adwan in December 2024. He’s been held without charge ever since. Dr. Abu Safiya’s legal team condemned the latest extension of his imprisonment as “neither a fair nor a transparent process.” The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights has said that it has received information that Dr. Safiya “has been subjected to torture and other ill-treatment, including prolonged solitary confinement, repeated severe assaults resulting in grave injuries, and denial of medical care.”

Judges at the International Court of Justice have found that Burmese security forces committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims during military operations nearly a decade ago. It’s the first time the court has held a nation accountable for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention. The ruling follows the 2017 military crackdown by government forces and ethnic Rakhine mobs that killed about 10,000 people and drove more than 730,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh. Ahead of today’s verdict, survivors hoped the ICJ would deliver justice and pave the way for them to return to their homeland. Hasina Khatun is a Rohingya refugee who was forced to flee her home when a mob burned her village to the ground.

Hasina Khatun: “To save our lives, we fled into the jungle, where we spent five days. Our children suffered from the cold, as we had no warm clothes, blankets or tarps. We endured immense hardship. Later, as the Myanmar military continued its attacks, we left the jungle and returned to the village before moving to the riverbank for shelter. But even there, we were not safe. We witnessed Myanmar soldiers taking away my husband and other men from the area right before our eyes.”

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made a surprise visit to Caracas on Wednesday, where he announced the U.S. and Venezuela have signed an agreement to restore military ties. Under the deal, the two countries will work together on areas such as joint training, intelligence sharing and border security. It’s Hegseth’s first visit to Venezuela since U.S. forces violently abducted former President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, National Assembly deputy Cilia Flores, back in January. The deal comes after months in which Washington has effectively controlled Venezuela’s oil sales. This is Defense Secretary Hegseth.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth: “In the last year, the country that previously sent its oil wealth to Cuba or to China from rigs built by Americans and Venezuelans has now signed a historic oil deal with the United States through the Department of War that is bringing energy dominance for the benefit of Americans and for Venezuelans for decades to come. In fact, this makes the Strait of Hormuz a nonfactor for the Western Hemisphere.”

Hegseth also traveled to Colombia Wednesday, where Colombia’s Trump-backed right-wing president, Abelardo de la Espriella, turned down a U.S. plan for joint operations against drug cartels.

Anthropic has become the first major AI lab to become a publicly traded corporation, after completing what’s become the largest initial public offering in history. On Wednesday, Anthropic said it had raised a record $107.3 billion, giving it a valuation of more than $1.5 trillion. This comes after Anthropic warned in its IPO filings that, without proper safeguards, its technology poses “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

New research has shown that advanced AI models repeatedly flagged civilians and civilian infrastructure as military targets in simulated scenarios. Anthropic’s models performed worst overall, according to the study by the independent evaluation company Vals AI. In tests using real satellite imagery of southern Iran, Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 misidentified the school in Minab — which was hit by a U.S.-Israeli attack in February, killing more than 120 children — as a military target in most hypothetical runs. The Pentagon has touted its heavy reliance on AI models in its war with Iran.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency is urging users of the computer language Java to immediately patch a serious security flaw, which could allow hackers to take over a server without needing a password or login. The bug was discovered by the cybersecurity startup Calif on Tuesday, using advanced AI tools. Java has been described as the “backbone of the internet”; it runs on billions of devices across government agencies and is used by the majority of Fortune 500 companies.

title: Attorney General James Sues Over Forced Labor and Trafficking at Rochester Holiday Inn
description:
“A company that calls itself a leader in the fight against human trafficking cannot look away when workers inside its own hotel ask for help,” said Attorney General James.
Attorney General James alleges that Petrik routinely delayed and withheld wages, leaving some workers with little or no compensation for months of work.
Attorney General James additionally alleges that Patel and Petrik subjected workers and their families, including children, to dangerous living conditions inside the hotel.
Attorney General James is seeking unpaid wages, restitution, damages, and penalties for the workers, as well as disgorgement of the profits each defendant made from their labor.
The Labor Bureau is part of the Division for Social Justice, which is overseen by Chief Deputy Attorney General Meghan Faux.
text:
NEW YORK – New York Attorney General Letitia James today filed a lawsuit against the owners and operators of a former Holiday Inn in downtown Rochester, its renovation contractor, and Holiday Inn’s parent company, IHG Hotels & Resorts (IHG), for allegedly exploiting dozens of immigrant workers through forced labor, wage theft, and threats of deportation. An Office of the Attorney General (OAG) investigation found that workers were forced to work up to 112 hours a week, often without pay, and left to live in dangerous and uninhabitable conditions with no heat, electricity, or running water. When workers demanded their wages, they were met with threats of deportation, eviction, or arrest. One worker was allegedly even sexually assaulted repeatedly by the contractor, Roman Petrik, with threats of non-payment if she did not comply. The OAG found that IHG knew workers were being exploited but continued to benefit financially from the renovation, prioritizing its financial interests over the workers’ safety and rights.

“A company that calls itself a leader in the fight against human trafficking cannot look away when workers inside its own hotel ask for help,” said Attorney General James. “These workers came to New York to do an honest job. Instead, they were cheated out of their pay, left without heat through a brutal Rochester winter, and threatened with deportation for speaking up. My office will hold each of these defendants accountable and fight to get these workers every dollar they earned.”

The OAG launched an investigation into Petrik and his contracting company after receiving reports of potential exploitation from the Worker Justice Center of New York and Enlace. The OAG determined that Petrik had recruited workers from multiple states and countries to renovate the Rochester Holiday Inn, owned by Nayan Patel and his company. Workers were promised hourly wages and housing at the hotel as part of their employment, but after their first two weeks on the job, the pay largely stopped. Attorney General James alleges that Petrik routinely delayed and withheld wages, leaving some workers with little or no compensation for months of work.

The investigation revealed that workers regularly worked 10- to 13-hour days, six days a week, totaling approximately 60 to 80 hours per week. At times, particularly ahead of IHG inspections and renovation deadlines, workers were required to work as many as 98 to 112 hours in a single week. One worker, promised $18 an hour, worked about 68 hours per week for 29 weeks. Although the worker should have received approximately $30,506, Petrik allegedly paid him just $2,200 over the entire period.

Attorney General James alleges that when workers demanded their wages and staged work stoppages, Petrik laughed at them, told them immigration officials were regularly at the hotel, and said he could have them deported at any time. The owner, Patel, allegedly told workers he had close ties to the “head of immigration” and that they would be deported without ever being paid. Both men allegedly threatened to evict workers who stopped working. Some workers could not afford food for their families, and at least three workers were illegally evicted after seeking their wages.

The OAG also learned that Petrik used his control over wages to sexually harass and assault a female worker. Shortly after she arrived in August 2023, she was told she would need to go to Petrik’s hotel room if she wanted to be paid. When she left, the lawsuit alleges, Petrik followed her to her own room, punched her in the stomach, and sexually assaulted her. He told her she would never be paid and would be fired unless she gave in to his sexual demands, and he assaulted her repeatedly through December 2023. Soon thereafter, the woman fled the hotel, despite never receiving payment for her work, and became homeless. The OAG found that Petrik continued to harass her through at least March 2026.

Attorney General James additionally alleges that Patel and Petrik subjected workers and their families, including children, to dangerous living conditions inside the hotel. Initially housed on the fifth floor, workers were moved to the hotel’s abandoned seventh floor in September 2023 to make room for paying guests. The seventh floor had been decommissioned since at least 2016 and was unfit for human habitation, with no electricity, running water, functioning toilets or showers, or working heating and cooling systems. No doors had locks, and most rooms were infested with pests and vermin. Workers and their children spent the winter there without heat. Patel even blocked workers’ attempts to make their rooms more habitable, including efforts to install makeshift toilets and improve ventilation. These conditions made workers ill, and some were unable to work because of exposure to construction dust, paint, and extreme cold. Workers were also denied legally required paid sick leave.

The OAG investigation determined that despite publicly presenting itself as a leader in combating human trafficking, IHG knew and benefited from the forced labor used to renovate the hotel. IHG required the renovation as a condition of the hotel’s Holiday Inn license, dictated its scope, and inspected the work throughout. During one visit on June 14, 2024, IHG inspected the seventh floor, photographed the rooms, and spoke directly with workers. The workers told them they had not been paid for at least eight months, were living in intolerable conditions, and had been threatened with deportation when they asked for their wages.

The IHG managers reported what they learned to an IHG regional vice president. Four days later, that same executive emailed Patel that “squatters” on the seventh floor posed “security and reputational risks” to the Holiday Inn brand and that it was his responsibility to remove them. IHG then offered to restore the hotel to its reservation system, extended Patel’s deadline to pay $96,350.50 in overdue fees, and waived more than $13,000 in interest. Attorney General James alleges that IHG made no effort to find out whether the workers had been paid, and that none of the IHG employees involved reported the situation to the company’s own reporting hotline. The following month, IHG wrote to Patel that it was glad the issue with the “squatters” had been resolved, and told him he would need to complete the company’s anti-human trafficking training.

Today’s lawsuit, filed in New York State Supreme Court in Monroe County, alleges that Petrik, Patel, and their companies violated the federal Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act by trafficking workers and obtaining their labor through threats of deportation, eviction, and financial harm. It alleges that IHG violated the same law by knowingly benefiting from a venture it knew or should have known relied on forced labor. Attorney General James also asserts that the contractor, Petrik, violated New York State Human Rights Law by subjecting a worker to sexual harassment and a hostile work environment, and violated New York Labor Law by failing to pay minimum, promised, and overtime wages, taking illegal deductions, and denying paid sick leave. The lawsuit alleges both Patel and Petrik illegally retaliated against workers, another violation of the Labor Law.

Attorney General James is seeking unpaid wages, restitution, damages, and penalties for the workers, as well as disgorgement of the profits each defendant made from their labor. The lawsuit also asks the court to bar Petrik and his company from the renovation business and Patel and his company from the hotel business in New York.

“Our outreach advocates took the time to listen and earn the workers’ trust. As that trust grew, workers felt safe telling us what was happening inside the hotel. Some told us they had gone months without pay and that when they asked for their wages, their employer threatened to call ICE. Enlace brought their concerns to Attorney General James’ office and the Worker Justice Center of New York,” said Irene Sanchez, Executive Director of Enlace Services, Inc. “Throughout the investigation, we’ve provided comprehensive case management and immigration services. Our advocates have helped families put food on the table, get medical care, and find other support in the community. Workers need to know they can count on that support long after they first speak up. That’s why we urge local agencies to keep their services separate from ICE enforcement. Every worker should feel safe reporting abuse or asking for help without fear of deportation.”

“These workers and their small children were trapped in dangerous, uninhabitable conditions, with no pay and nowhere else to go,” said Olivia Post Rich, Senior Attorney at the Worker Justice Center of New York. “They showed immense courage standing up for their rights despite the threats and abuse they experienced. We hope this lawsuit sends a clear message that New York does not tolerate exploitation of our most marginalized community members.”

This matter is being handled by Assistant Attorneys General Abigail Ramos and Laura Revercomb, Social Justice Coordinator Francisca Montana, Auditor Investigator Erica Ciccarelli, and Investigator Yuliya White, under the supervision of Civil Enforcement Section Chief Fiona Kaye, Deputy Bureau Chief Young Lee, and Labor Bureau Chief Karen Cacace. The Labor Bureau is part of the Division for Social Justice, which is overseen by Chief Deputy Attorney General Meghan Faux.

Money is hard enough but without Medicaid, Amir wonders how he can afford follow-up care for his kidney cancer.
In Afghanistan, Amir was important, respected, well-off, potent.
He said he would love to serve the U.S., a country which, despite his struggles here, he says he loves.
text:
By Rose Hoban

Sahar Amir’s wife, daughter and son spoke little after they loaded bags into a van and set off into the night. Inside the vehicle headed from Kabul, Afghanistan, to the Pakistan border, the atmosphere was grim.

Amir — not his real name — was an attorney in Afghanistan. From 2009 to 2011, he worked with the U.S. military processing supply procurement for Bagram Air Force Base. For almost a decade after that, he was a prosecutor with the Office of the Afghanistan Attorney General, in the Department for the Elimination of Violence Against Women. While in that office, he led multiple high-profile cases against government officials, religious figures, even Taliban members accused of raping girls and young women. His victories at trial put perpetrators behind bars for years at a time.

“He was known for his courage, confidence and determination,” recalled a former colleague who now lives in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. “Cases involving members of the Taliban, terrorists or violent extremists accused of violence against women were often assigned to him.”

When Kabul and the country fell to the Taliban in August 2021, foreign friends told Amir to wait at home and avoid wading into the chaos at the Kabul airport. They promised to help him get out of the country. But the help never arrived. By January 2022, he needed to flee. The only person Amir could confide in was his father, a man in his 80s.

“My dad said, ‘Do not talk with anyone. Just leave the country,’” Amir said.

That night at multiple Taliban checkpoints, money changed hands, and the van continued into the darkness, arriving at the border around 6 a.m. The guards there began to argue with Amir, accusing him of working for the government.

“I said, ‘Brother, I was a taxi driver.’” Amir recalled. “He said, ‘No, no, no, you are not taxi driver. Tell us the truth.’ I said, ‘What I am saying is this: I am not (with the government).’”

Amir said he and the Taliban border guard went on like this for almost 45 minutes when his daughter began to cry.

“He said, ‘Okay, leave him, leave him. His daughter is crying. Leave him,’” Amir said. With another bribe, the guard waved the van through the border. The family entered Pakistan.

Amir, it turns out, was predicting his own future. After three years of applying for visas to Germany, Canada, Australia, in January 2025 the U.S. granted him entry on a Special Immigration Visa. Now he’s a Lyft driver around Raleigh, hustling to support his family while his children go to school and his wife, who speaks little English, keeps their small apartment in order.

He was making do until summer 2026 when he was diagnosed with cancer and required surgery to remove his kidney. The family got support from North Carolina Medicaid to cover health care. Their assistance from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program had already ended in February.

On Oct. 1, though, all the medical support ended. A new federal rule, created by the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act, stripped medical care from Amir, his family and another 10,500 refugees and others in North Carolina who were admitted to the U.S. on humanitarian grounds. According to the state Department of Health and Human Services, a total of 12,500 lost food aid earlier in the year.

Now Amir wonders how he’ll manage any further cancer treatment.

Sitting in limbo

Before the administration of President Donald Trump, refugees who arrived in the U.S. would be connected to local resettlement agencies. The newcomers would have a year or so to apply for green cards and begin their path to citizenship.

In 1996, Congress restricted which new arrivals to the U.S. qualified for Medicaid, establishing so-called public charge rules. Most immigrants who’ve arrived here, even through traditional lawful channels, have had to wait for five years before they can get Medicaid and other benefits. However, Congress created an exception for refugees, along with asylum seekers, people who had been victims of human trafficking or domestic violence, and others admitted to the U.S. on humanitarian grounds. Those immigrants also were eligible for subsidies on the Affordable Care Act marketplace to purchase health insurance.

Families like Amir’s, with Special Immigrant Visas, were exempt from public charge rules. They received streamlined entrance from a country that was grateful for their help during the Afghanistan conflict.

In October, that all changed. With very limited exceptions, all those people lost access to any assistance — even the ability to receive an income-based subsidy on an ACA plan. Now, the only way for people in the Special Immigrant Visa pool to get benefits is to receive a green card.

“But since probably about mid-2025, the Trump administration has paused many green card applications, so people are no longer receiving those,” said Jennifer Taylor from Refugee Hope Partners, a Raleigh-based nonprofit that has helped refugees from more than 80 countries. “They’re just kind of in limbo, waiting.”

Taylor explained that since that time, almost no refugees have been admitted to the U.S., except for white Afrikaners from South Africa. Around the world, everyone else continues to wait.

Amir’s family arrived on Jan. 2, 2025. Had his family’s flight been delayed just a few weeks, until after Trump’s inauguration, they would have been refused entry. On his first day in office, Trump signed an executive order essentially shutting down all refugee entries to the U.S.

Even though Amir and his family submitted their green card paperwork while still in Pakistan, they’ve waited, along with thousands of other Afghan refugees who helped the U.S. military during Operation Enduring Freedom, the 20-year Afghan conflict.

“As Afghans who stood alongside the United States, supported it and worked closely with it, I expected America to provide us with full support in return,” said Amir’s former prosecutor colleague, who’s now a housewife in Louisiana. “We came to the United States legally, after going through a long waiting process. Unfortunately, instead of receiving the support we expected, I feel that the U.S. government is treating us as if we were criminals.”

In the past, Taylor said, families like Amir’s and his former colleague’s would have gotten green cards within six months to a year of arriving in the United States, and it was a “pretty normal process.

“It went smoothly. Now what’s happening is they’re just not receiving it,” she said.

“Even when they talk to their lawyers or different things like that, the whole process is stalled.”

At times, Amir’s frustration with the lack of progress for his green card bubbles over.

“Please see in the system, I am active. I am already in,” he said, shuffling through several inches of forms and other paperwork. “Please just issue my green card.”

Without that green card, Amir can no longer get Medicaid or SNAP benefits. The bank balance he showed on his phone was $475. He had an unpaid credit card balance, and the rent was due in less than a week.

Money is hard enough but without Medicaid, Amir wonders how he can afford follow-up care for his kidney cancer.

Frightening diagnosis

In early 2026, Amir began to feel pain in his lower back.

“I had seen him for back pain earlier in the year, and he had a history of kidney stones,” said Matt Oettinger, a family physician who works at NeighborHealth, a community clinic based in Raleigh.

NeighborHealth has a good reputation among local immigrants and refugees, and resettlement agencies frequently send people there. About 40 percent of the clinic’s patients speak languages other than English, including the Dari and Pashto languages widely spoken in Afghanistan.

At first Oettinger treated Amir for kidney stones, but the pain persisted and worsened. One of Oettinger’s colleagues ordered an image and found a mass.

“We got him in to a specialist pretty quickly,” Oettinger said.

That July, Amir had surgery at WakeMed to remove his cancerous left kidney.

“They think that they got it all. Right now, the prognosis is good, but they need to continue watching,” Oettinger said. “He has other chronic medical problems, too, that he needs care for.”

Including post-traumatic stress.

Oettinger said that about 500 NeighborHealth patients — 5 percent of its total customers — lost their Medicaid coverage in October.

Federal rules prohibit the clinic from providing free care, but patients can pay on a sliding scale. Despite those low-cost services, Amir said that without Medicaid it will be hard to afford the follow-up treatment. At the same time, he wants to pay his share.

So, Amir’s done what many other Americans have: He set up a GoFundMe campaign.

Twin fears: the Taliban & ICE

NC Health News agreed to identify Amir with a pseudonym and not show his face in photos because he said his family in Afghanistan — father, siblings and their families — could be at risk.

Now, though, Amir worries about a risk closer to home as he drives people around Raleigh: Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

“They are arresting people,” he said about ICE. “They arrest the people, and they take to jail, and then they will send you to Louisiana” where the U.S. is holding detainees before deportation.

Refugee Hope Partners’ Taylor said many Afghan refugees share Amir’s hesitation about revealing his identity. While technically Amir and his family are in the country legally, she said she wasn’t certain that would keep ICE from picking up any of them.

“Fear is one of the biggest things that we see,” Taylor said. “Just fear of the unknown, fear of what’s next, fear of ‘what happens to my family if we end up getting deported or detention’ or things like that.

“They left home for a reason. They left their country for a reason, and they cannot go back.”

Amir describes his biggest worry about ICE: “They will deport me directly to Pakistan, and Pakistan will deport directly to Afghanistan.”

That’s already happening. Pakistan is in the process of pushing refugees back into Afghanistan. According to The New York Times, Pakistan’s government has forced the return of more than 2.7 million Afghan citizens to their home country since 2023.

Amir cannot return there, despite his desire to see family members again. The Taliban has released most of the people he helped put in prison, and they’d be out to get him.

Even before the Taliban’s return, Amir faced the wrath of the people he prosecuted. He showed NC Health News photographs of his house in Kabul pockmarked with bullet holes after masked men shot at it at the conclusion of one of his high-profile cases. The head of the office for Elimination of Violence Against Women gave him firearms and weapons training. Two bodyguards became his constant companions.

Leslie Schneider, a Virginia prosecutor, was an international legal adviser in Afghanistan with a gender justice assistance project before 2020. She told NC Health News that it was very hard to prosecute the types of cases Amir worked on.

“There was such a resistance for getting justice for women who were victims of crimes that the top people who worked with [the former head of the office], they all had some degree of security presence,” she said.

Amir’s former colleague told NC Health News: “His work was important not only for enforcing the law, but also for protecting women’s rights and helping victims seek justice — regardless of the power or influence of the accused.” We did not name her at her request.

She recalled that in Afghanistan, handling such cases involved “serious personal risks.”

And now, under the Taliban, no one is doing that work.

‘Simple taxi driver’

Schneider remembered Amir, if not his specific cases. She said that she and other Americans who worked in Afghanistan are haunted by the memories of many of their former comrades left behind and frustrated about their circumstances in this country.

She said she hears from Afghan refugees in situations similar to Amir’s almost every month.

They have so much to mourn. Amir remembers the killing of his 21-year-old cousin who was a CIA interpreter in Kandahar province. Amir was just a few meters away when he witnessed a suicide bomber blow himself up. And, in August 2021, when the Taliban returned to Kabul, he saw his life’s work shattered.

In Afghanistan, Amir was important, respected, well-off, potent. On his phone he keeps photos of himself standing with former president Hamid Karzai, with the vice president, with provincial leaders, presenting at international conferences.

Now, he describes himself as a “simple taxi driver,” making $150 on a good day and struggling to pay the rent. Before his surgery, he could work 12 hours a day. Now he can only manage eight or nine hours before the pain overwhelms him.

But he remembers what he was like in court in his home country, speaking forcefully, delivering justice for women who had been wronged. He would love to keep arguing cases. He said he would love to serve the U.S., a country which, despite his struggles here, he says he loves.

First, though, he has to stay alive. And without consistent health care, without Medicaid, that may not be possible.

text:
The Trump administration’s plans to build a “smart border wall” through a 500-mile stretch of Texas that includes the Big Bend national park recently got the green light from the supreme court. But those efforts are likely to slam into a big, blue wall.

Last week’s decision – the result of a continuing challenge to the administration’s decision to waive dozens of federal laws to speed wall construction in the Big Bend region – dealt a major blow to environmentalists and park enthusiasts, as well as locals who value the region’s remoteness, landowners who could see their properties devalued and businesses that rely on outdoor tourism.

But the ruling also came less than a week after Republicans suffered staggering losses in the midterms – including the once-in-a-generation flipping of Texas from red to blue. The state elected a Democratic governor after more than 30 years, and its first Democratic senator since the 1980s. The blue tsunami that handed both chambers of the US Congress to the Democrats with sizable majorities also flipped the Texas state house and weakened Republican control over the state senate.

That could all throw a wrench in the Trump administration’s plans.

The border wall is a federal project, so the White House will still have a great deal of power to push it forward. But for the first time, US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), the agency overseeing construction, will now face open hostility from the Lone Star state’s government as it contemplates resuming building efforts.

“Texas sovereignty and land should be protected,” Gina Hinojosa, the governor-elect, said in response to the ruling. “By letting the federal government bulldoze our land, the supreme court is continuing to put corporate profits before the people of Texas.”

The unthinkable is now possible

The Big Bend conflict stretches back to last year when the Republican-dominated Congress poured a whopping $46.5bn into border wall expansion in Trump’s “big, beautiful” spending bill. Early this year, CBP started indicating plans to use much of that money in the Big Bend region in Texas.

Texas Republicans, including Greg Abbott, the outgoing governor, largely stayed quiet as party colleagues orchestrated an unpopular wall expansion that threatened to carve up private property, destroy ancient rock art and mar beloved parks – all in a region whose cliffs, brush and isolation already make it the section of the border with the fewest unauthorized crossings by far.

The administration’s shifting plans to build border security infrastructure through Big Bend have sparked major protests in Texas. Bulldozers started plowing up ground near the park’s beloved Santa Elena Canyon in August, drawing a national backlash as activists circulated videos of the destruction.

Rodney Scott, the CBP commissioner, paused construction days after it started and traveled to the region to meet with stakeholders. Shortly after, US district judge Kathleen Cardone issued a temporary injunction blocking CBP from continuing the project, while the case challenging the Trump administration’s waivers of federal environmental and historic preservation laws continued.

With the supreme court’s ruling this month, CBP is now free to continue construction. But without a willing partner in Texas, those plans will face new hurdles.

The proposed border wall runs through several Texas public land holdings, including Big Bend Ranch state park, Black Gap wildlife management area, Seminole Canyon state park and several small tracts owned by the Texas general land office, which manages some state lands and holds extensive mineral rights.

Incoming Democrats are already looking to block construction on those lands. A bill filed jointly by César Blanco, a state senator, and Eddie Morales, a state representative, both Democrats, would ban border security construction on state parks. With Democrats holding a majority in the state house of representatives for the first time in two decades and the governor’s office for the first time since 1994, the Trump administration faces the real – and once unthinkable – possibility that bills such as this could pass.

“Incredibly disappointed by the supreme court’s decision,” Blanco tweeted after the decision was published. “Just last week, Texans made it clear they want leaders focused on what matters to their families and communities. Destroying our natural landscapes is not the direction we should be going.”

Benjamin Flores, the incoming Texas land commissioner, who will run the general land office, wrote in a statement that he “will protect every acre of state land, honor every lease, and ensure no one breaks ground on state property without written permission from the land office”.

“Our transition team is working to get a full picture of any agreements the land office has already made affecting state land in the Big Bend,” Flores wrote. “Once I’m sworn in, I’ll review every one of them with our legal team and act within the law to protect the land and the Texans who depend on it.”

Neither Texas parks and wildlife nor the general land office disclosed to the Guardian whether they had yet signed agreements allowing CBP to build on state land.

The people are watching

Texas Republicans’ strategy of playing dead while the Trump administration’s wildly unpopular border wall expansion through Big Bend sparked outrage from conservatives and liberals alike almost certainly cost the GOP at the polls. Both Brewster and Val Verde counties, Big Bend’s two largest, flipped by double digits compared with the 2024 election that sent Trump back to the White House.

The Trump administration is also likely to face more scrutiny over its Big Bend border wall expansion when the new Congress convenes, with solid Democratic majorities in both chambers.

A group of 23 Democrats led by Veronica Escobar, a US representative of El Paso, Texas, asked the office of inspector general on Monday to investigate whether the political donations or ties influenced the doling out of $7.5bn worth of border wall contracts the Trump administration signed for the Big Bend region.

“The processes CBP used to award these contracts lacked any transparency, and there has been no opportunity for public oversight of the contracts, or even for the public to understand the scope of the contracts,” the letter reads.

Advocates will also be looking to Congress to either undo the waivers of federal environmental and historic preservation laws that homeland security issued earlier this year to speed smart wall construction, or to pass a standalone measure to at least exempt Big Bend national park – whose natural beauty has inspired the loudest public outcry.

“Are they going to resume bulldozing where they left off? Just because they’ve been given the green light doesn’t make it acceptable,” Bob Krumenaker, a former Big Bend superintendent, who now chairs the non-partisan group Keep Big Bend Wild, wrote in an email. “Will they ever listen to the will of the American people?

“Clearly, the only way to stop the destruction is through legislating the next Congress,” he added. “That’s our laser focus right now.”

Scott, however, said the agency will continue to push ahead with construction in the region, citing the supreme court ruling as evidence that his agency “has the legal authority and responsibility to secure America’s borders”.

Scott said that plans for the park would change, but did not say how.

“Specific to Big Bend national park, CBP has re-evaluated the terrain, listened to local stakeholders and made meaningful adjustments that will secure this critical stretch of border while preserving the unique landscape and public access for generations to come,” Scott wrote in a statement. “I look forward to sharing details about the updated plans soon.”

Whatever comes next, the park’s advocates will be watching, said Laiken Jordahl, a public lands advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity, one of the plaintiffs in the lawsuit challenging homeland security’s authority to waive federal laws to expedite border construction at Big Bend.

“The second a bulldozer enters that national park, we will have eyes on every piece of vegetation that is destroyed, every speck of dirt that moves,” Jordahl said. “It’s so clear that people across Texas oppose this – their newly elected leadership opposes this.”

text:
A federal judge found immigration authorities in contempt after they released a migrant as ordered and then immediately arrested him again, saying the practice “made a mockery” of court orders requiring detainees’ release.

U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney ruled in Colorado on Tuesday that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials violated her order to release Ramon Quintero Alvarez by October 28, unless the government showed cause to keep him detained. The Mexico-born father-of-two, who has lived in the U.S. since entering in the early 1990s, had been detained since February.

ICE official Nichole Black testified on November 4 that she was ordered to re-detain released detainees with “some type of criminality.”

Read More on News

Quintero Alvarez had previously been arrested on criminal charges, but charges stemming from his most recent arrest were dropped on April 24, the papers said without specifying the charges.

Sweeney said Black told the court Quintero Alvarez was released and "then 'walked out to the lobby,' exited the detention facility 'into a public area' where 'officers met him outside and rearrested him.'"

"Ms. Black said in her own words that she believed it was permissible to simply escort someone to a public area and immediately re-detain them despite a court order to the contrary," the Biden-appointed judge wrote in a 15-page order.

“This should—and, in the Court’s opinion, must—shock any reader."

Black said she knew of about 10 such cases, a figure the court said was later increased to 18.

Sweeney noted that it had an agreement with federal prosecutors requiring the government to carry out the release of detainees in accordance with judges’ orders.

"And yet despite—or perhaps in spite—of this memorandum and court orders that have ordered petitioners’ immediate release, the Court observed that Respondents and ICE’s new “policy” of immediately re-detaining petitioners following release made a mockery of court orders mandating petitioners’ immediate release," Sweeney wrote.

In response to the judge's findings, the Department of Homeland Security told Newsweek a court order "does not immunize the alien from immigration enforcement for all time."

“ICE complies with all lawful court orders. When an illegal alien is ordered released by a judge, that does not immunize the alien from immigration enforcement for all time," a spokesperson said. "Instead, if ICE does not appeal the ruling, it may seek to rearrest the alien in a way that complies with the judicial decision. To suggest that ICE cannot do this is nothing short of sabotage."

Newsweek contacted ICE for comment via email outside of regular office hours on Thursday.

Black said she had been acting on a “direct order” from deputy field office director George Valdez, who had received an order from acting field office director Nathan Rasper.

Rasper testified that he told officials to consult ICE lawyers before re-arresting someone to determine whether another arrest was lawful. He said ICE colleagues in Minnesota had told him people could be re-arrested after being released.

Rasper said Black had misunderstood his instructions, which he acknowledged “were not clear.” He said he ordered the office to stop the practice following Black's November 4 testimony and release those who had been re-arrested under it.

‘Any Reader May Be Lost for Words’

Sweeney found Black and the Trump administration in contempt for knowingly disobeying the court’s release order but declined further action.

“To recap: civil contempt is appropriate where clear and convincing evidence shows that a valid court order existed—check—Respondents had knowledge of that order—check—and Respondents disobeyed it—check,” Sweeney wrote.

“Sometimes, behavior stuns and renders a listener speechless,” Sweeney wrote. “To the extent any reader may be lost for words as to what ICE and Respondents did in this case and others in this judicial district like it—and the ridiculous nature of the justification for their behavior."

Federal judges have repeatedly squared off with Trump administration lawyers over the president’s immigration crackdown, including disputes over detention practices and compliance with court orders.

In a separate case this month, U.S. District Judge S. Kato Crews ordered the administration to release Edgardo Garcia Vargas after ICE arrested him minutes after his court-ordered release. Crews called the re-arrest an “ongoing due process violation” and warned that another arrest without a hearing could lead to contempt proceedings.

The Trump administration has sought to increase immigration arrests and deportations under it's hardline mass deportation campaign. In Colorado, ICE arrests nearly doubled from 259 in March to 499 in July 2026, according to federal data obtained through the Freedom of Information Act by the Deportation Data Project. There were 549 arrests in July 2025.

Update 11/19/26, 8:19 a.m. ET: The DHS's response was added.

text:
A federal appeals court in Pasadena is scheduled to hear arguments Thursday, Nov. 19, in the Trump administration’s challenge to a ruling against an Immigration and Customs Enforcement policy governing warrantless home arrests.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit has scheduled a 9:30 a.m. session in Courtroom 1 of the Richard H. Chambers Courthouse at 125 S. Grand Ave. The proceedings will be livestreamed through the court’s website.

The appeal, Kidd v. Mullin, concerns ICE’s use of a practice known as “knock-and-talk,” in which officers approach residences to contact occupants. The legal dispute centers on whether immigration officers may enter areas of residential property without a judicial warrant when their purpose is to carry out an arrest.

The lawsuit was filed in 2020 on behalf of Osny Sorto-Vasquez Kidd, a Hacienda Heights resident, the Inland Coalition for Immigrant Justice and the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights.

According to the ACLU Foundation of Southern California, which represents the plaintiffs alongside other attorneys, ICE officers have used deceptive practices, including identifying themselves as police, to gain access to residential property.

The plaintiffs contend that ICE’s arrest practices violate Fourth Amendment protections against unreasonable searches and seizures.

A federal district court ruled against the challenged policy. The government argues on appeal that the lower court improperly restricted lawful immigration enforcement practices. The plaintiffs are asking the Ninth Circuit to uphold the ruling.

The case has implications for residents across Southern California, including Pasadena, because the litigation involves classes of people in Los Angeles County and six other counties who have been subjected to, or face a risk of, the challenged practices.

The appellate judges are not required to issue a decision immediately after oral arguments.

text:
Back in January, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) announced two deaths at Camp East Montana, the nation’s biggest immigrant detention center. At the time, the facility at Fort Bliss in El Paso, Texas, was operated by a tiny contractor most people had never heard of.

The agency reported that Geraldo Lunas Campos, a 55-year-old from Cuba, had been found “in distress” and died after “lifesaving measures.” Victor Manuel Diaz, a 36-year-old from Nicaragua, had been found with “a ligature around his neck”—likely suicide.

ICE, it turns out, didn’t share the full story. By the end of January, a medical examiner had determined that Lunas Campos actually died by homicide—guards asphyxiated him while restraining him to stop him from self-harm. Now, records obtained in a Freedom of Information Act request show that ICE privately blamed its contractor for failing to stop Diaz’s death—so much so, that the agency cited it as one of multiple reasons for ending the company’s roughly $1.3 billion contract.

The records are communications between ICE and the contractor, Acquisition Logistics, a small Virginia-based company that went from relative obscurity to the subject of national headlines after the Trump administration asked it to build and manage Camp East Montana in 2025. At the time, it had no prior experience in incarceration and was so small it operated out of a single-family home. Archived screenshots of its website—whose header simply said “Site maintenance in progress”—showed it had once specialized in supply chain management.

When ICE ended its contract in March, a year and a half early, the agency didn’t elaborate publicly on the reason, simply saying a bigger company would possess the “size, maturity and pedigree” to implement “higher standards of medical care, more thorough case processing and intake procedures, and delivery of performance requirements according to well-defined accountability measures.” The records Mother Jones obtained include “Contract Discrepancy Reports” and other documents that outline, in more detail, exactly what standards were not met—and the deadly consequences.

Acquisition Logistics’ relationship with ICE soured quickly, the records show. In the beginning, its main point of contact for Camp East Montana was not the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), but the Pentagon: Even though the camp would detain immigrants, the Navy had awarded the contract. “It’s weird,” Charles Tiefer, a professor emeritus of government contracting at the University of Baltimore law school, told me at the time.

“It seems messy,” added Claire Trickler-McNulty, who served as an ICE official in the Obama, Biden, and first Trump administrations.

As I reported then, DHS had tried to award the contract before the Navy did, to a firm called Deployed Resources, but canceled the deal days later “for convenience,” according to a government website that cited an executive order about “wasteful spending.”

This was an extremely unusual move, and some current and former ICE officials speculated that ­Deployed lost the job for political reasons. The Washington Free Beacon reported in 2023 that Deployed had snagged no-bid contracts for immigrant detention under President Joe Biden, and that a member of its board was married to the former chief of staff for Kamala Harris’ husband, Doug Emhoff. (The DC Enquirer called it “Kamala’s cronyism.”) A DHS spokesperson dismissed this as speculation, saying the contract was canceled due to an “inability to meet the specialized needs of the facility.”

Not long after ditching Deployed, ICE put the Fort Bliss contract out for bids again, and then quickly pulled it a second time, without explanation. The job went to Acquisition Logistics in the summer of 2025 under a Navy special contracting program in which only small businesses could apply. “If you want a detention center run by people who know what they’re doing, you hold serious competition, but that takes time,” Tiefer, the contracting expert, told me. “This is the third time they’re trying to make a procurement, and they’re under the gun—gotta get those detention centers up and running, gotta meet the quota. They were just betting [Acquisition Logistics] would have the minimum competence to hold the thing together, join in picking the subcontractors, and supervise them.”

It was “an absolute rush,” says Congresswoman Veronica Escobar, an El Paso Democrat whose district includes the camp. “Donald Trump and Stephen Miller wanted to do it the easiest, quickest way possible.”

Things went about as smoothly as one might expect. Although Camp East Montana was up and running in impressive time—ground broke in July 2025 and new detainees were arriving by August—a worker died during construction and, by September, journalists were documenting horrific conditions inside. ICE’s own inspectors found 60 violations of federal detention standards in 50 days, the Washington Post reported. “That was somewhat shocking,” recalls Michelle Brané, who led the Biden administration’s Office of the Immigration Detention Ombudsman, the main oversight body for ICE detention.

It’s not unusual for a new detention facility to have problems, so the best practice is to open it slowly—but that didn’t happen here, says former ICE official Trickler-McNulty, who has worked on contracts and detention standards. “None of it sounds like good governance,” she told me.

In October 2025, after Camp East Montana was operational, the administration transferred oversight of Acquisition Logistics’ contract from the Pentagon to ICE, according to emails I obtained. Later that month, an ICE contracting officer wrote CEO Ken Wagner to say that the funding wasn’t officially locked in yet, but that the company should proceed anyway because the work was “mission-essential.”

Wagner agreed, but by November 2025, emails show that his firm was desperate for cash. (Many federal contractors have struggled to be reimbursed promptly on Trump’s watch, according to Brané.) “As a small business, ALC and subs cannot continue to perform at such a high risk. Payrolls have to be met, vendors have to be paid, and it really is a crisis situation,” a company rep wrote to ICE.

Some funding came through soon after, but the relationship remained strained. On December 11, Wagner explained in a letter that ICE’s communications with his team had been “ineffective and, at times, perceived as threatening.”

“This has created an environment of uncertainty, hindered productive dialogue, and is creating significant concerns between ALC and our subcontractors,” he wrote. With discussions “eroding,” Wagner added, he was seeking “assistance in resetting our relationship to move forward in a more productive fashion.”

He provided excerpts from the allegedly threatening communications—all redacted in the documents I received. But other records show that ICE had expressed concerns over Acquisition Logistics’ lapse of liability insurance, a detainee’s escape, and problems with medical care. The agency had even sent a “Show Cause Notice” to the company in early October, days after taking control of the contract. “[Y]ou are hereby provided the opportunity to present any facts or explanations that demonstrate why the contract should not be terminated,” an ICE officer had written.

It had been complicated, Wagner said in his letter, for his company to transition from Pentagon to DHS control and navigate the agencies’ different expectations. He remained worried about a “lack of payment 75 days into the Option Period,” which posed “unnecessary and significant risks” to his business.

“Despite our repeated efforts to seek clarification and guidance, ALC has not received a government response to our concerns, leading to resource inefficiencies in our operations,” Wagner wrote. He requested a meeting with ICE officials to discuss solutions and figure out how to stop “de-railing productive hours” to messy back-and-forth.

Little seemed to improve. In February, an ICE contracting officer sent Acquisition Logistics another “Show Cause Notice” threatening to end the partnership. The CEO likely understood what this meant, Tiefer told me: “He can hear they’re clicking the rifle bolts on the firing squad. He’s writing his will at this point.”

The camp’s security protocols were not up to standard either, ICE said. In January, an officer’s firearm had gone missing, along with the spare key to the locker where it was stored. Transportation delays resulted “in significant operational disruptions” and janitorial services were inadequate. Housing units were supposed to be cleaned daily by staff, but an inspection found they were cleaned only once a week—and that guards had, on occasion, convinced detainees to clean for them by offering cookies.

Some of these allegations appeared in a Government Accountability Office report over the summer and received media coverage, but the records I obtained from ICE went into greater detail.

For one, in February, subcontractor Amentum Services “unilaterally” decided to cut detainees’ food intake below the contractual minimum of 3,000 calories a day. This deprivation resulted in “active hunger strikes” and “threats of riots,” ICE wrote. (Neither Amentum nor Acquisition Logistics and ICE responded to requests for comment for this story.)

Another subcontractor, Akima, let its guards track daily operations at the facility in a damaged logbook with missing pages—which became a problem, ICE wrote, after Geraldo Lunas Campos died. A witness told the Associated Press that Lunas Campos was handcuffed, tackled by guards, and put in a chokehold until he went unconscious. ICE’s report offered new details: Lunas Campos was restrained on the ground by four officers after he’d tried to hang himself, it said. One officer placed an arm around the man’s neck and another around his armpits with clasped hands, and all four officers were on top of him. When they eventually turned Lunas Campos on his side, he was unresponsive, with vomit on the floor.

“Lack of timely and complete information regarding the destruction of the logbook impeded the [Detainee Death Review] panel’s ability to establish an accurate timeline and conduct a thorough review,” ICE wrote, and also to assess officers’ compliance with use-of-force standards.

Lunas Campos’ family is suing Acquisition Logistics, Akima, and the guards for wrongful death, according to an attorney representing them, Will Horowitz, who told me it’s unclear whether the incident was adequately investigated by the government. “There’s so little that has been said in public about this.”

Another serious allegation involved the case of Victor Manuel Diaz, who was shipped to Camp East Montana after ICE arrested him on January 6 in Minnesota.

Eight days later, ICE wrote in its notice to Acquisition Logistics, custody officers moved Diaz from his dormitory to a medical holding room after he said he’d experienced harassment and “possible sexual abuse”—a detail that hadn’t been publicly reported, according to Rep. Escobar. (ICE has only cited the alleged harassment.) Diaz was scheduled for a Prison Rape Elimination Act interview. A behavioral health provider wrote that he had a “disheveled appearance, depressed mood, flat affect, and low, quiet speech,” though he’d denied that he was contemplating suicide.

ICE’s detention standards require placing at-risk detainees in suicide-resistant cells with “constant or close monitoring”—specifically, at irregular intervals no more than 15 minutes apart. But Diaz was put in a holding room with less frequent monitoring “despite risk indicators,” the agency wrote. He was observed awake at 2 p.m. and asleep at 2:30 p.m. and 3 p.m., the log indicated. Half an hour later staff found him hanging from a sheet he’d removed from his bed.

Staffers took Diaz’s body down and placed it on the bed. Failing to find a pulse, camp medical personnel began CPR and other emergency measures. He was officially pronounced dead at 4:09. Although the “medical response was initiated promptly after discovery,” ICE noted, “the timeline indicates a possible delay in recognizing the emergency and notifying ICE”—and CPR should not have been performed on a soft surface like the bed. “The incident suggests a lack of staff vigilance and possible gaps in suicide prevention training, as staff failed to identify and respond to risk factors and did not maintain required observation protocols.”

ICE wrote that it had reviewed several cases of suicidal detainees at Camp East Montana in which officers hadn’t checked in at staggered 15-minute intervals as required—this problem has plagued ICE detention under past administrations as well, Brané told me. “Detainees on suicide watch are being placed in cells that contain objects and elements that can be used for self-harm,” ICE officials wrote, citing metal benches in holding cells, pony walls around toilets, and instruments affixed to the walls of medical bays.

Camp East Montana, the officials noted, also lacked policies to safely remove a person from suicide watch—one detainee, name redacted, was taken off watch despite suicidal ideation and a plan to act on it. And though detainees are supposed to receive mental health screening within 12 hours of admission, at least one wasn’t screened for about a month, despite indications of mental illness, the agency wrote.

Months before Diaz’s death, ICE also had raised concerns with Acquisition Logistics because the facility’s medical holding rooms lacked “vision panel doors” that would allow officials to monitor the people inside; the company had promised to install the panels but hadn’t. The “failure to promptly address a previously identified and documented security deficiency,” its notice said, “represents a significant lapse in corrective action and facility safety management, and is a material contributing factor in the inability to prevent or timely intervene in the suicide of Mr. Diaz.”

“This incident resulted in the loss of life and exposes the facility, staff, and detainees to increased risk,” ICE added.

“This was a known screw-up,” Tiefer says of the vision panel doors. It seems “the suicide was the straw that broke the camel’s back and led ICE to dump Acquisition Logistics.”

Diaz had entered the United States in 2024 and was working to send money home to his family in Nicaragua, to help them save for a house. “Victor was law-abiding. He had never been in trouble in Nicaragua and, as we understand, was detained by ICE for missing an immigration court date—not for any crime,” his family said in a statement after his death.

In late February, 24 members of Congress wrote to DHS, citing safety concerns and calling for Camp East Montana to be “shut down.” On March 3, ICE sent another notice of “non-conforming performance” that again highlighted Diaz’s death and the infrequent cleaning of housing units, along with a detainee’s escape in October. Ten days later, it announced publicly that the contract would be terminated and that Amentum, the subcontractor that had cut meals to less than 3,000 calories, would take over. Amentum was a much bigger firm, with a long history of federal contracting. But conditions at the facility remained dire afterward, according to a lawsuit against ICE that cites, among other problems, medical neglect, staff violence, and inadequate food.

ICE apparently wasn’t “seeking a huge change if they just signed a contract with a vendor that was already running parts of the facility they were ostensibly unhappy with,” says Trickler-McNulty, the former ICE official, when I asked about the inadequate meals. But the administration “wants this facility; they likely didn’t want disruption in detention services, so they signed the agreement.”

Brané views the contract swap as a sign of just how bad conditions had become under Acquisition Logistics: worse than even ICE could tolerate. But “it’s probably gotten just as bad at a lot of facilities,” she says, noting that DHS shut down the independent oversight office she used to lead. “We are hearing more and more of these kinds of things, and there is no place to file a complaint and have it addressed, and so conditions have deteriorated across the board.”

Rep. Escobar told me she is glad Acquisition Logistics was fired and that she wants the company to be investigated. But she says it’s not the only entity that should be held accountable. For months, detainees had told her about poor conditions, but the career ICE personnel working at the facility brushed her off. They were “saying, ‘It’s all a lie,’ and it wasn’t,” she says. “They know better. There should have been alarm bells screaming up and down the chain.”

The administration should have forced Acquisition Logistics to address deficiencies immediately—or fired the company quicker, she says. Normally, Trickler-McNulty adds, ICE would use financial sanctions to hold a company accountable for problems early on, but the records we obtained show no signs of that. “There’s blame to be laid not just at the contractor’s feet,” Escobar says. “We have an obligation in Congress to look at the enablers.”
